sections.title: Four Moves, In Order

sections.say: Find the joints, then take one move at a time.

cards.fr: la deuxième à droite
cards.body: Short, unstressed, and sitting between two content words. Prenez carries a verb and droite carries a direction, and the thing that decides which street you take is the two syllables between them.
cards.head: Why this word and not another
cards.label: the most-missed word

cards.fr: la première à gauche
cards.body: La première rue à gauche is the full form and it is not what is said in a hurry. With rue dropped, the ordinal is carrying the whole meaning on its own.
cards.head: The noun is not there
cards.label: rue is dropped

cards.fr: C'est la deuxième rue, après le feu.
cards.sub: [seh lah deu-ZYEM RÜ ah-PREH luh FEU]
cards.body: The counting starts at the lights, not where you are standing. Nothing in the sentence says so and a French speaker would not think to.
cards.head: Counted from where
cards.label: not from where you stand

cards.fr: Comptez deux rues, puis tournez à droite.
cards.sub: [kohⁿ-TAY deu RÜ pwee toor-NAY ah DRWAHT]
cards.body: Count two and turn at the next one, which is the third. An ordinal and a cardinal doing the same job land you one street apart, and both are said.
cards.head: Two streets is the third
cards.label: the off-by-one is real

cards.fr: C'est la deuxième ou la troisième ?
cards.body: You held the route and lost one word of it. Asking about that word gets you four words back. Asking lesson 24's rung 2 gets you all fourteen again at the same speed.
cards.head: When you only lost this
cards.label: ask about the word, not the sentence

sections.title: The Word You Will Lose

sections.say: Four, one per screen. Three of them send you to the wrong place and the fourth loses you a move you did hear.
sections.title: What Goes Wrong

errors.why: Both end on the same sound and one of them is a turn. English keeps them a whole word apart. Under speed, inside a chain, the difference is one syllable at the front.
errors.right: à droite is right, tout droit is straight on.
errors.wrong: Hearing à droite and tout droit as the same thing.

errors.why: It is get off a train, a bus or a tram, and it is also go down. The corpus publishes both senses. On a metro nobody is talking about stairs.
errors.right: Descendez ici means get off here.
errors.wrong: Taking descendre to mean go down.

errors.why: A hurried speaker drops the verb from every move after the first. Counting verbs gives you one move out of four, and the other three go past unrecorded.
errors.right: deuxième à gauche is a whole move with no verb in it.
errors.wrong: Waiting for a verb before you count a move.

errors.why: Puis and ensuite are audible and the commas between moves are not. Three moves can arrive with no spoken joint at all, which is the case the fourth rung ends on.
errors.right: A comma is a joint too.
errors.wrong: Counting only the words you can hear.

sections.say: Four pairs that differ by one syllable and by several hundred metres. You can see the French here, so this is the contrast rather than the test.

rule.body: Every pair below shares most of its sounds. Inside a chain, unstressed, with the next move already starting, the part that differs is the part you have least time for.
rule.title: The difference is at the front, or in the middle

cards.fr: deuxième, not douzième
cards.ipa: /dø.zjɛm/ · /du.zjɛm/
cards.tip: One vowel apart, and both are ordinals that fit the sentence perfectly. This is the pair that actually costs a learner a street, and it is the best trap in this unit.
cards.promptSound: Prenez la deuxième à droite.

cards.fr: à droite, not tout droit
cards.ipa: /a dʁwat/ · /tu dʁwa/
cards.tip: One is a turn and one is not a move at all. They end on the same sound and English keeps them a whole word apart, which is why the ear never learned to separate them.
cards.promptSound: Tournez à droite au feu.

cards.fr: Tournez, not Retournez
cards.ipa: /tuʁ.ne/ · /ʁə.tuʁ.ne/
cards.tip: Retournez sends you back the way you came. The whole difference is an unstressed syllable at the front, which is the first thing lost when a chain is moving.
cards.promptSound: Tournez à gauche au feu.

cards.fr: Continuez, not Contournez
cards.ipa: /kɔ̃.ti.nɥe/ · /kɔ̃.tuʁ.ne/
cards.tip: Both open on the same two syllables and one of them means go around the thing rather than through it. At a roundabout that is a different exit.
cards.promptSound: Continuez jusqu'au rond-point.

drill.promptSay: Prenez la deuxième à droite.
Prenez la douzième à droite.
Tournez à droite au feu.
Allez tout droit au feu.
Retournez à la gare.
Contournez le rond-point.

steps.label: The four
steps.title: Pairs That Cost You A Street

sections.title: One Syllable, A Different Street

sections.say: Read these rather than decode them. An announcement is a shape, and once you know the shape you only have to catch the number inside it.

lines.en: The train for Lyon will depart from platform twelve.
lines.fr: Le train à destination de Lyon partira voie douze.

lines.en: The train from Marseille is arriving.
lines.fr: Le train en provenance de Marseille entre en gare.

lines.en: The train will be about twenty minutes late.
lines.fr: Le train aura un retard d'environ vingt minutes.

lines.en: This train does not stop at Massy station.
lines.fr: Ce train ne dessert pas la gare de Massy.

lines.en: Next stop, Châtelet. Change here for line four.
lines.fr: Prochain arrêt, Châtelet. Correspondance ligne quatre.

sections.title: How A Station Talks

questions.q: Which two words separate a train that is leaving from one that is arriving?
questions.why: Four syllables apart and opposite platforms. Partira and entre are the ordinary verbs; the two long phrases are the announcement register and they arrive first.
opts: à destination de and en provenance de

questions.q: Where does the destination sit in one of these sentences?
questions.why: The destination is fronted, which is what makes an announcement recognisable before you have understood any of it. Ordinary French would put it after the verb.
opts: In the middle, after the verb
Near the front, before the verb

questions.q: Why is « aura un retard » harder than « est en retard » ?
questions.why: The nominalised form is what makes it sound official, and it pushes the figure further from the start of the sentence. The number is the only part you actually need.
opts: The delay is a noun, so it arrives later in the sentence

questions.q: A negative announcement is the expensive one. Why?
questions.why: Ce train ne dessert pas la gare de Massy is the same shape as every other line here. The ne and the pas are the only difference and they are the two quietest words in it.
opts: It tells you a stop is NOT happening, and missing the ne costs you a journey
It is always about a strike

sections.say: Lesson 24 in A2 authored six ways to ask again, once, for the whole band, and this lesson adds none of them. What it adds is the case where you only lost one word.

cards.fr: Pardon ?
cards.body: One word, and it gives away nothing about why you missed it. Lesson 24 in A2 put it first because it costs you nothing at all and because it is what a French speaker says without thinking.
cards.head: Rung 1
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 1

cards.fr: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.body: Asks for the whole thing again. In the street the whole thing is fourteen words, so this is a much bigger ask here than it was at a restaurant table.
cards.head: Rung 2
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 2

cards.fr: Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: The first rung that names the fault. Reach for it when she has already repeated the route at exactly the same speed, which is what happens if you used rung 1.
cards.head: Rung 3
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 3

cards.fr: C'est la deuxième ou la troisième ?
cards.body: You held the route. You lost one word of it. A targeted question gets you four words back; a generic one gets you the whole route again at the speed that defeated you the first time.
cards.head: The state lesson 24 in A2 does not cover
cards.label: name what you missed

cards.fr: À gauche ou à droite, pardon ?
cards.body: Après le pont ou avant ? and C'est quelle rue, pardon ? do the same job for the joint and for the name. Each one names the missing piece and asks for that piece only.
cards.head: Three more of the same shape
cards.label: the joint, or the name

cards.fr: Pardon ?
cards.body: The A1 capstone has been assessing the repair move in an exam round since it shipped, and no lesson taught it until lesson 24 in A2 did. Reach for the lowest rung that will actually fix the problem.
cards.head: Where you are already tested on this
cards.label: The A1 capstone assesses it

sections.title: Ask For The Piece You Lost

sections.say: Six instructions, and the joint is inside four of them. You have heard every one of these at least three times by now.
sections.title: Write The Instruction

sections.say: Eleven turns. He starts asking questions before you have finished your sentence, and one of the things he says goes past you.
sections.title: The Ticket Window

turns.ai: Bonjour, monsieur.
turns.en: Good evening.

alts.en: Hello. A return to Nantes.
alts.fr: Bonjour, madame. Un aller-retour pour Nantes.

alts.en: Hello. I would like a return to Nantes.
alts.fr: Bonjour. Je voudrais un aller-retour pour Nantes.

turns.user: Bonjour. Un aller-retour pour Nantes, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: Hello. A return to Nantes, please.

turns.ai: Vous partez quand ?
turns.en: When are you travelling?

alts.en: Tomorrow, if possible.
alts.fr: Demain, si possible.

alts.en: This evening, if you have anything.
alts.fr: Ce soir, si vous avez.

turns.user: Demain matin, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: Tomorrow morning, please.

turns.ai: Il y a un train à sept heures dix et un à neuf heures.
turns.en: There is a train at ten past seven and one at nine.

alts.en: The nine o'clock train.
alts.fr: Le train de neuf heures.

alts.en: Is there anything later?
alts.fr: Est-ce qu'il y a quelque chose plus tard ?

turns.user: Celui de neuf heures, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: The nine o'clock one, please.

turns.ai: Vous voyagez seul ?
turns.en: Are you travelling alone?

alts.en: No, two of us.
alts.fr: Non, à deux.

alts.en: Yes, one seat.
alts.fr: Oui, une seule place.

turns.user: Oui, seul.
turns.userEn: Yes, alone.

turns.ai: Vous avez une carte de réduction ?
turns.en: Do you have a discount card?

alts.en: No, sorry.
alts.fr: Non, désolé.

alts.en: Yes, here it is.
alts.fr: Oui, la voici.

turns.user: Non, je n'en ai pas.
turns.userEn: No, I do not have one.

turns.ai: Aller simple ou aller-retour ?
turns.en: One way or return?

alts.en: A return.
alts.fr: Un aller-retour.

alts.en: One way, actually.
alts.fr: Aller simple, finalement.

turns.user: Aller-retour, s'il vous plaît.
turns.userEn: Return, please.

turns.ai: C'est complet à neuf heures. Il reste des places à onze heures.
turns.en: Nine is full. There are seats at eleven.

alts.en: Eleven, fine.
alts.fr: Onze heures, très bien.

alts.en: Is there really nothing before that?
alts.fr: Il n'y a vraiment rien avant ?

turns.user: D'accord, onze heures.
turns.userEn: All right, eleven then.

turns.ai: Alors, départ onze heures quatre, voie douze, correspondance à Massy voie trois.
turns.en: So, departure eleven oh four, platform twelve, change at Massy, platform three.

alts.en: The connection, which platform is it?
alts.fr: La correspondance, c'est quel quai ?

alts.en: Can you repeat the platform, please?
alts.fr: Vous pouvez répéter la voie, s'il vous plaît ?

turns.user: Pardon, c'est quelle voie à Massy ?
turns.userEn: Sorry, which platform at Massy?

turns.ai: Voie trois. C'est écrit sur le billet.
turns.en: Platform three. It is written on the ticket.

alts.en: Fine, thank you.
alts.fr: Très bien, merci.

alts.en: Platform three, right.
alts.fr: Voie trois, d'accord.

turns.user: Merci beaucoup.
turns.userEn: Thank you very much.

turns.ai: Et le guichet est de ce côté, la sortie est en face.
turns.en: And the ticket office is on this side, the exit is opposite.

alts.en: Left or right, sorry?
alts.fr: À gauche ou à droite, pardon ?

alts.en: The exit, which way is it?
alts.fr: La sortie, c'est par où ?

turns.user: Pardon, la sortie est de quel côté ?
turns.userEn: Sorry, which side is the exit?

turns.ai: Tout droit, puis à gauche après les escaliers.
turns.en: Straight on, then left after the stairs.

alts.en: Thank you, goodbye.
alts.fr: Merci, au revoir.

alts.en: After the stairs, right. Thanks.
alts.fr: Après les escaliers, d'accord. Merci.

turns.user: Tout droit, puis à gauche. Merci, bonne soirée.
turns.userEn: Straight on, then left. Thanks, have a good evening.

sections.setting: The ticket windows at Lyon Part-Dieu, a Thursday evening, four people in the queue behind you.

sections.say: Your half of this exchange is the short half. Two openings, four questions, and the four ways to ask for the piece you missed.
sections.title: Say Your Half

sections.say: Her half and yours, one last time.

cards.say: Continuez tout droit, puis tournez à gauche.
cards.back: A sequence of moves. GO, TURN, PASS, ARRIVE, and the joints between them.
cards.front: A direction is not a sentence. What is it?

cards.say: Allez au bout de la rue, puis tournez à gauche.
cards.back: puis, ensuite, après, jusqu'à, au bout de. And a comma, which has no sound.

cards.say: Prenez la deuxième à droite.
cards.back: Prenez, but only when a street or an ordinal follows it. Prenez le boulevard is not a turn.
cards.front: Four verbs mean go. Which of them is a turn?

cards.say: C'est juste après la pharmacie.
cards.back: ARRIVE. C'est, vous verrez, ça sera. Easy to hear as an afterthought.
cards.front: The move type with no verb of motion in it

cards.say: la deuxième à droite
cards.back: The ordinal. Short, unstressed, between two content words.
cards.front: The most-missed word in a direction

cards.say: Comptez deux rues, puis tournez à droite.
cards.back: The third. An ordinal and a cardinal land you one street apart.
cards.front: Count two streets and turn. Which street is that?

cards.say: Pardon, madame. Je cherche la gare, s'il vous plaît.
cards.back: Apology first, then the goal. Pardon, madame. Je cherche la gare.
cards.front: You stop a stranger in the street

cards.say: Bonjour. Un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.
cards.back: Greeting first, then the transaction, and no verb of demand.
cards.front: You are at a ticket window

cards.say: Le train en provenance de Marseille entre en gare.
cards.back: en provenance de. À destination de is the one that leaves.
cards.front: A train that is arriving, not leaving

cards.say: Le train aura un retard d'environ vingt minutes.
cards.back: Aura un retard d'environ vingt minutes. The delay is a noun.
cards.front: How a station says a train is late

cards.say: C'est la deuxième ou la troisième ?
cards.back: Ask about that word. C'est la deuxième ou la troisième ?
cards.front: You held the route and lost one word

sections.title: Everything She Said

sections.say: Twenty-one missions. Here is what changed.
sections.body: You came in able to ask where the station is and unable to use the answer. A direction is now four kinds of move joined by five small words, and you have heard the same four moves arrive with no joint at all. The exam that follows is weighted the way the situation is: two thirds of it is listening, because in this one situation your own turn is the easy half.

stats.k: Announcements in the corpus before this lesson

stats.v: 6, and they are lesson 24 in A2's

sections.title: Where You Are

sections.say: Five rounds of six. Ten of the thirty you cannot read, which is the highest proportion in this app and the lowest in the real thing.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Six you have to hear. Nothing is written down. You can replay each one; the real exam plays it once.
rounds.label: Follow it

questions.q: Listen. Where do you end up?
questions.say: Passez devant la banque, traversez le pont, tournez à gauche au feu, c'est après la pharmacie.
questions.why: Three landmarks are named and only one of them is where you stop. The bank and the bridge are PASS moves and the lights are a TURN.

questions.q: Listen. What do you do first?
questions.say: Prenez la deuxième à droite, longez le parc, traversez la place, c'est au coin.
questions.why: The first move is the turn. Everything after it is a landmark you pass, and the corner is where the route ends rather than where it starts.

questions.q: Listen. Which turning?
questions.say: Allez jusqu'au carrefour, prenez la première à gauche, c'est en face de la poste.
questions.why: Première is said and gauche is said. The first right is the trap that gets the ordinal right and the side wrong, which is the commonest way to lose a street.

questions.q: Listen. When do you turn right?
questions.say: Traversez le pont, longez le quai, puis tournez à droite avant la gare.
questions.why: Avant, not après. Both would fit the sentence and only one was said, and the two are one syllable apart inside a chain that is already moving.

questions.q: Listen. Which turning do you take?
questions.say: Sortez de la gare, tout droit, deuxième à gauche, c'est au coin.
questions.why: Deuxième and gauche, and neither première nor droite was said at all. Three moves out of four here have no verb in them, which is what makes the ordinal do the work.

questions.q: Listen. Which exit at the roundabout?
questions.say: Continuez jusqu'au rond-point, prenez la troisième sortie, longez le canal, c'est là.
questions.why: Troisième. At a roundabout the ordinal counts exits rather than streets, and getting it wrong there puts you on a whole different road.

rounds.say: Six on sequence. The moves are the same in every option and only their order differs.
rounds.label: Hold the order

questions.q: Listen. The two turnings, in order?
questions.say: Prenez la deuxième à droite, puis la première à gauche, c'est en face.
questions.why: Every option contains the same four words and only the order differs. This is the whole of the Owns in one item: knowing the vocabulary gets you nothing here.

questions.q: Listen. What is the SECOND move?
questions.say: Traversez la place, remontez la rue, prenez la première à droite, continuez.
questions.why: Four moves, no spoken joint at all. Only the commas separate them, and a comma is the joint you cannot hear.

questions.q: Listen. Which side is it on when you arrive?
questions.say: Tournez à gauche, allez jusqu'au pont, traversez, c'est sur votre droite.
questions.why: Gauche is said first and droite is said last. Sur votre droite is a side of you rather than a direction to turn, and holding which came last is the whole task.

questions.q: Listen. Which street do you take?
questions.say: La première est un sens unique, prenez la deuxième.
questions.why: The first is named only to be ruled out. A learner listening for an ordinal hears première first and stops listening, which is exactly what the sentence is built to punish.

questions.q: In « Prenez la deuxième à droite », which word do learners lose?
questions.why: It is short, unstressed, and it sits between a verb and a direction. Both of the words around it carry meaning you already know, so the ear skips to them.

questions.q: You hold three moves but in the wrong order. What happens?
questions.why: A route's order is hard, not soft. Cross then turn and turn then cross put you on opposite sides of the same bridge, which is why the drill scores orderings.
opts: You end up somewhere else entirely
Nothing, order does not matter in French
You have to go back to the station

rounds.say: Six on announcements and on getting there. These you can read.
rounds.label: The station voice

questions.q: « Le train en provenance de Marseille » means the train is
questions.why: En provenance de is arriving and à destination de is leaving. Four syllables apart, opposite platforms, and both are fronted before you have understood anything else.

questions.q: « Le train à destination de Lyon partira voie douze. » Which platform?
questions.why: Douze. Lesson 3 in A1 owns the numbers and this is what they sound like read as a block at the end of a long official sentence, which is the only place they get hard.

questions.q: « Ce train ne dessert pas la gare de Massy. » What does it tell you?
questions.why: The negative announcement is the expensive one and it has the same shape as every other line. Ne and pas are the two quietest words in it.
opts: The train does not stop at Massy
Massy is the end of the line

questions.q: Which of these is NOT how a station announces a delay?
questions.why: The first three nominalise the delay or give a reason, which is what makes them sound official. The fourth is what a person says, and a station never apologises in the first person.
opts: Le train aura un retard d'environ vingt minutes.
Le train est annoncé avec dix minutes de retard.
En raison d'un incident, le trafic est interrompu.
Le train est un peu en retard, désolé.

questions.q: A closed vehicle. Fix this.
questions.why: You are inside a bus, so en. The corpus states the rule at fr.a1.deplacements.014 and this lesson quotes it rather than restating it. À bus and en bus do not fold together, so the preposition is genuinely being tested.
accept: Je vais au travail en bus.
je vais au travail en bus
en bus
questions.answer: Je vais au travail en bus.
questions.prompt: Je vais au travail à bus.

questions.q: You are on it, not in it. Fix this.
questions.why: À pied, because you are on your feet rather than inside anything. En pied and à pied fold to different strings, so this item discriminates; if they folded together it would have had to be an mcq.
accept: Il va à la gare à pied.
il va a la gare a pied
à pied
questions.answer: Il va à la gare à pied.
questions.prompt: Il va à la gare en pied.

rounds.say: Six on the short half. Which opening, and how to ask.
rounds.label: Your half

questions.q: At a ticket window. Ask for a return to Lyon, starting with the greeting.
questions.why: Greeting first, then the transaction, no verb of demand. Aller-retour and aller simple are the real test here; the hyphen is not, because it folds away and un aller retour is the same answer.
accept: Bonjour. Un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.
bonjour un aller retour pour lyon sil vous plait
Un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.
un aller retour pour lyon
questions.answer: Bonjour. Un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.

questions.q: You stop somebody in the street. Say you are looking for the station.
questions.why: Apology first, then the goal. Je cherche and un aller-retour do not fold together, so what is being tested is which shape you reached for and not how you spelled it.
accept: Pardon, madame. Je cherche la gare, s'il vous plaît.
pardon madame je cherche la gare sil vous plait
Pardon, je cherche la gare.
je cherche la gare
questions.answer: Pardon, madame. Je cherche la gare, s'il vous plaît.

questions.q: He told you the platform and you missed it. Ask which one. « C'est quel ... ? »
questions.why: Quel is lesson 23 in A1's question word and the useful part is that this is what you ask AFTER he has already told you. It names one thing, so you get one thing back.
accept: C'est quel quai, s'il vous plaît ?
cest quel quai sil vous plait
C'est quel quai ?
quel quai
questions.answer: C'est quel quai, s'il vous plaît ?

questions.q: Ask what time the next train is. Six words: « Le prochain train ... ? »
questions.why: Rising intonation on a full sentence. TCF caps a candidate who produces only one question form, which is why the scenario shows three ways to ask the same thing.
accept: Le prochain train est à quelle heure ?
le prochain train est a quelle heure
à quelle heure
a quelle heure
questions.answer: Le prochain train est à quelle heure ?

questions.q: Ask for a single to Nantes.
questions.why: Simple, not retour. The two fold to different strings, which is what makes this item worth setting: it tests the word you chose rather than the punctuation you used.
accept: Un aller simple pour Nantes, s'il vous plaît.
un aller simple pour nantes sil vous plait
Un aller simple pour Nantes.
un aller simple
questions.answer: Un aller simple pour Nantes, s'il vous plaît.

questions.q: You stop a stranger in the street. Which opening?
questions.why: The first and third are counter forms and a passer-by does not sell tickets. The fourth is the agent's line, not yours. The failure is not rudeness, it is using the wrong shape.
opts: Un aller-retour pour Lyon, s'il vous plaît.
Pardon, madame. Je cherche la gare, s'il vous plaît.

rounds.say: Six on asking again. The six rungs are lesson 24 in A2's; the last two are what this unit adds.
rounds.label: When it goes wrong

questions.q: You asked again and it came back at the same speed. Which rung now?
questions.why: Rungs 1 and 2 both just ask for a repeat, and she cannot fix a fault you have not named. Rung 3 is the first that says it was the speed, and lesson 24 in A2 owns the repair ladder.
opts: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

questions.q: The cheapest thing you can say when you caught nothing at all. One word.
questions.why: Lesson 24 in A2 put it at rung 1 because it gives away nothing about why you missed it and because it is what a French speaker says without thinking about it.
accept: Pardon
Pardon ?
pardon
questions.answer: Pardon ?

questions.q: You held the route and lost only the number of the street. Ask about it. « C'est la ... ou la ... ? »
questions.why: This is the state lesson 24 in A2 does not cover, because in a restaurant you either caught it or you did not. Here you routinely catch three moves of four, and naming the missing one gets you four words back instead of fourteen.
accept: C'est la deuxième ou la troisième ?
cest la deuxieme ou la troisieme
la deuxième ou la troisième
deuxieme ou troisieme
questions.answer: C'est la deuxième ou la troisième ?

questions.q: You caught everything except which side. This asks for all fourteen words again. Ask for the one you lost.
questions.why: Rung 2 is not wrong, it is over-wide for this state. Lesson 24 in A2 taught you to reach for the lowest rung that will actually fix the problem, and a targeted question is lower than any of the six.
accept: À gauche ou à droite, pardon ?
a gauche ou a droite pardon
à gauche ou à droite
a gauche ou a droite
questions.answer: À gauche ou à droite, pardon ?
questions.prompt: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

questions.q: You held both moves and lost the joint between them. Ask about the joint.
questions.why: Saying you understood nothing is false and expensive: it gets the whole route back at the same speed. You understood almost all of it, and the joint is the one word worth asking for.
accept: Après le pont ou avant ?
apres le pont ou avant
après le pont ou avant
questions.answer: Après le pont ou avant ?
questions.prompt: Je n'ai pas bien compris.

questions.q: Say it back. Two moves and the joint between them.
questions.why: Repeating a short chain back is what a French speaker does to confirm they have it, and it is scored generously here because the point is holding the order rather than the accent.
questions.target: Tournez à gauche, puis tout droit.

sections.say: Three things, and the first one is the whole lesson.
sections.body: Find the joints, then take one move at a time. A spoken direction is not a sentence, it is a sequence, and every French direction is built from the same four kinds of move joined by the same five small words. Four of the verbs mean go, so the verb is not what tells you which move you just heard. The word that decides which street you take is usually the shortest one in the sentence. And when the route goes past you, you have almost never lost all of it: name the piece you lost, and you get that piece back rather than the whole thing again at the speed that beat you.
sections.title: What You Take With You
points: Find the joints, then take one move at a time.
GO, TURN, PASS, ARRIVE. Four kinds of move, and ARRIVE is the one with no verb of motion in it.
puis, ensuite, après, jusqu'à, au bout de. And a comma, which does the same job and has no sound.
The ordinal is the most-missed word in a direction: short, unstressed, and between two words you already know.
Ask for the piece you lost, not for the sentence. Lesson 24 in A2 owns the six ways to ask again.

errorTriggers.description: Translates the first move word by word and loses everything after it, because the second move started while the first was still being decoded.
Hears the verb and the side and loses the ordinal between them, so the right kind of turn is made on the wrong street.
Holds all the moves and loses their sequence, which lands the learner somewhere else entirely rather than merely late.
Cannot tell an arriving train from a departing one, because both announcements are fronted and the two phrases that separate them come before any verb.
Uses à with a closed vehicle or en with an open one, because English has one word for both and neither preposition is stressed.
Uses the counter form on a stranger or the street form at a counter, which reads as nonsense one way and as lost the other.
Nods and walks rather than asking again. The exchange completes, nobody corrects it, and the habit survives because it never visibly fails.
Asks for the whole route again when only one word was lost, and gets fourteen words back at the speed that defeated them the first time.

grammarIntroduced: That a spoken direction is a sequence of moves rather than a sentence, and that every French direction is built from four kinds of move: go along, change heading, pass a landmark, arrive
The five joints that separate one move from the next, puis, ensuite, après, jusqu'à and au bout de, and the fact that a comma does the same job with no sound at all
Multi-step direction chains received at speed, climbing from one move to four, as reception rather than production
Ordinals used inside a direction, la première, la deuxième and la troisième à droite, which no published row in the corpus carried before this lesson
The public transport announcement as a genre: destination fronted, number read as a block, delay nominalised, and delivered faster than conversational speech
The two openings of an information request, the street form and the counter form, as two shapes rather than as a politeness gradient, which belongs to a2.29
en against à with transport modes, as APPLICATION of the preposition system a2.04, a1.21 and a1.22 already taught, with the rule quoted from a published corpus row rather than restated
The targeted repair, C'est la deuxième ou la troisième ?, for the state where three moves of four were held, which a2.07's six general rungs do not cover
That the direction verbs are used here as whole forms and the mood they are in is named by nobody in this band, which a2.32 also does and neither unit cites the other for

lessons.intro: You can already say what hurts. This lesson is about the question that comes back at you, and about what to say when the word will not come.

rung.body: Lesson 24 in A2 authored six, ordered by what they cost you. Rung 1 gives away nothing; rung 6 asks for it in writing. Reach for the lowest one that will actually fix the problem.
rung.title: One of lesson 24 in A2's six ways to ask again

examples.note: Rung 3, the first that names the fault.

slot.body: What, where, since when, how bad. A doctor asks for them in almost any order, and knowing which slot a question wants is most of understanding the question.
slot.title: What a symptom report is made of

examples.note: This one wants how bad, and it is the one that stops people.

dosage.body: Three separate facts said in one breath, and the frequency is the one that matters most. Trois fois par jour and toutes les trois heures sound similar in English and are not the same instruction.
dosage.title: How much, how often, and for how long

examples.note: Every three hours, which is eight times.

ordonnance.body: What the doctor writes and the pharmacist reads. Sur ordonnance means the pharmacist cannot hand it over without one, and it is four words long, so it goes past easily.
ordonnance.title: The prescription, as a piece of paper

examples.note: The refusal, and it is short.

construction.body: French has three and English has one. Avoir mal à a body part, avoir plus a symptom noun, or a bare verb. Nothing in the English predicts which one French will take, and you choose before the word arrives.
construction.title: Which shape the symptom takes

examples.note: avoir mal à, and lesson 27 in A1 owns this one.
A bare verb, where English uses a noun.

describeAround.body: A symptom is inside you and you cannot point at it, so when the word is missing you say what it is like instead. C'est comme une brûlure gets you further than stopping does, and a doctor will wait for it.
describeAround.title: Saying it without the word

examples.note: Like something you already have a word for.
When neither of the doctor's two options fits.

drills.coach: Say which of the four slots each question wants. The French answer is the second thing, not the first.
pairs: Ça vous lance ou ça vous brûle ?
Vous êtes allergique à quelque chose ?

drills.coach: Say the French, then say how many times a day it means. The second answer is the one that matters.
pairs: Three times a day, before meals
Trois fois par jour, avant les repas.
Toutes les trois heures, pas plus.

lessons.reframe: English gives you one shape for a symptom. French picks one of three, and the choice is made before the word arrives.

overview.introFr: Trois constructions, quatre cases, et le mot qui manque.

sections.say: You can already say what hurts. This lesson is about what he asks next.

beats.text: A walk-in clinic in Nantes, a Tuesday afternoon. You have had the sentence ready since the waiting room.

beats.en: Hello. What brings you in?
beats.fr: Bonjour. Qu'est-ce qui vous amène ?
beats.speaker: The doctor

beats.en: (I have had stomach pain for three days.)
beats.fr: J'ai mal au ventre depuis trois jours.
beats.stage: Clean, correct, and exactly what you practised. Lesson 27 in A1 gave you this sentence.

beats.en: Right. Is it a shooting pain or a burning one?
beats.fr: D'accord. Ça vous lance ou ça vous brûle ?
beats.stage: Two words you have never met, in a question you have to answer now.
beats.speaker: The doctor

beats.prompt: You do not know either verb. What do you do?

options.en: hope he moves on
options.fr: Say nothing and wait.

options.en: say what it is like instead
options.fr: Je ne connais pas le mot. C'est comme une brûlure.

followUp.works: He nods and writes. You did not have the word and you answered the question anyway, which is the whole of what he needed.
followUp.breaks: He waits, then asks something simpler. You have lost the one piece of information only you had, and he is now guessing.

beats.body: Your sentence was right. What stopped you is that a symptom lives inside you and cannot be pointed at, so when the word is missing there is nothing to gesture at. Describing around it is not a failure. It is the move.
beats.coach: You cannot point at a pain. So say what it is like, using a word you already have.

right.en: like something you can already name
right.fr: C'est comme une brûlure.

wrong.en: which ends the turn and tells him nothing
wrong.fr: Euh... je ne sais pas.

beats.heading: The word was never the problem

beats.text: He asked for how bad. You gave him how bad. Neither of you used the word he started with.

sections.title: The Word You Did Not Have

closing.text: You cannot point at a pain. Say what it is like instead.

setting.place: A walk-in clinic, third floor, the room smells of hand gel

sections.say: Four goals. Two of them are about listening, because this is the one situation where misunderstanding costs more than not being understood.

goals.s: French has three and English has one. The choice happens before the word arrives.
goals.t: Pick the right shape for a symptom

goals.s: A doctor asks about where, since when and how bad, in any order, using words the lesson never taught.
goals.t: Answer the questions you did not prepare for

goals.s: Three times a day and every three hours are not the same instruction, and nobody writes it down for you.
goals.t: Get a dosage right by ear

goals.s: Describe around it. Lesson 24 in A2 gave you six ways to ask again; this adds what to say when asking again will not help.
goals.t: Keep going when the word is missing

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do

sections.say: English gives you one shape for a symptom. French picks one of three, and the choice is made before the word arrives.

cards.fr: J'ai mal à la tête.
cards.body: You already have this one. Lesson 27 in A1 built five sections on it and you are not going to walk them again. It is here because the other two only make sense against it.
cards.head: Shape 1 · a body part
cards.label: Lesson 27 in A1 owns this

cards.fr: J'ai de la fièvre.
cards.body: A noun you HAVE. La fièvre, la grippe, un rhume, la nausée, des frissons. English also uses a noun here, which is why this one feels safe and is not always right.
cards.head: Shape 2 · a symptom noun
cards.label: avoir plus a noun

cards.fr: Je tousse.
cards.body: A verb, on its own, where English hands you a noun. Je tousse, je saigne, j'éternue, je vomis. This is the shape anglophones almost never reach for and it is the commonest one in a clinic.
cards.head: Shape 3 · a bare verb
cards.label: the verb, alone

cards.fr: J'ai mal à la tête · J'ai de la fièvre · Je tousse
cards.sub: my head hurts · I have a fever · I have a cough
cards.body: English uses a verb for the first, a noun for the second and a noun for the third. French uses three different shapes and none of them lines up. That is why the choice has to be made before the word arrives.
cards.head: The choice is not translatable
cards.label: nothing predicts it

sections.title: Three Shapes, One English

sections.say: A doctor wants four facts and will ask for them in any order. Knowing which one a question wants is most of understanding the question.

rows.say: Qu'est-ce qui vous amène ?

detail.say: Qu'est-ce qui vous amène ?
detail.body: Amener is bring, so the question is what brings you in. A learner who parses the verb loses the turn. It is stored whole and it is always the first thing said.
detail.title: The opener, and it is not about travel

rows.say: Où avez-vous mal exactement ?

detail.say: Où avez-vous mal exactement ?
detail.body: Lesson 27 in A1 built this answer for you. What is new is only that somebody asked, and that ici plus a finger is a complete answer when the body part will not come.
detail.title: The slot you are ready for

rows.say: Ça a commencé il y a trois jours.
cells: Ça a commencé il y a trois jours.

detail.say: Ça a commencé il y a trois jours.
detail.body: Lesson 14 in A2 owns depuis and everything about the tense it wants. You can also answer with il y a and sidestep it entirely, which is what the second answer here does.
detail.title: Two ways to fill it

rows.say: Ça vous lance ou ça vous brûle ?
cells: Ça vous lance ou ça vous brûle ?

detail.say: C'est plutôt une douleur sourde.
detail.body: Two verbs nobody taught you, in a question that expects one of them back. You do not need either: c'est comme plus a word you already have answers it completely.
detail.title: The slot that stops people

sections.title: What A Report Is Made Of

sections.say: English gives you one shape for a symptom. French picks one of three, and the choice is made before the word arrives.
sections.title: Which Shape Does It Take

check.q: Why does « J'ai mal partout » still count as shape 1?
check.why: Avoir mal is what makes it shape 1. Lesson 27 in A1 taught what comes after it; here the point is only that the shape survives when the body part does not.
opts: Because partout is a body part
Because avoir mal is the shape, and what follows it can be a place instead
Because it has mal in it
It does not, it is shape 2

check.why: A noun you have. English says I am dizzy, which is an adjective, and none of the three French shapes is an adjective. This word was not in any deck: the rule had to do the work.

check.why: A bare verb where English hands you a noun. La toux exists as a word and is almost never how a person reports it. This is the shape anglophones reach for last and clinicians hear most.

sections.say: English gives you one shape for a symptom. French picks one of three, and the choice is made before the word arrives.

rule.body: My head hurts is a verb in English and shape 1 in French. I have a cough is a noun and becomes shape 3. The English predicts nothing, which is why the choice has to be a reflex.
rule.title: English is not a clue

cards.fr: verb, not noun
cards.ipa: /ʒə tus/
cards.tip: English gives you a noun and French gives you a verb. J'ai une toux is understood and marks you out immediately.
cards.promptSound: Je tousse.

cards.fr: noun, with de la
cards.ipa: /ʒe də la fjɛvʁ/
cards.tip: Here the noun IS right. De la is the article that means an amount, and lesson 8 in A1 owns it; nothing new is claimed about it here.
cards.promptSound: J'ai de la fièvre.

cards.fr: shape 1
cards.ipa: /ʒe mal a la tɛt/
cards.tip: English uses a verb, French uses avoir mal. Lesson 27 in A1 owns this shape and everything that follows it.
cards.promptSound: J'ai mal à la tête.

cards.fr: noun, plural
cards.ipa: /ʒe de vɛʁ.tiʒ/
cards.tip: English uses an adjective. None of the three French shapes is an adjective, so je suis vertige is not a near miss, it is a different language.
cards.promptSound: J'ai des vertiges.

cards.fr: noun
cards.ipa: /ʒe la no.ze/
cards.tip: Another English adjective that becomes a French noun. Je suis nauséeux exists and is not what a person says at a counter.
cards.promptSound: J'ai la nausée.

cards.fr: verb
cards.ipa: /ʒə sɛɲ/
cards.tip: English uses a verb too, so this one is free. It is here to prove the rule is not simply the opposite of English.
cards.promptSound: Je saigne.

sections.title: Pick The Shape, Fast

sections.say: The words are hidden until you have answered. Do not try to catch every word: catch which of the four slots he wants.

lines.en: What brings you in?
lines.fr: Qu'est-ce qui vous amène ?

lines.en: Where exactly does it hurt?
lines.fr: Où avez-vous mal exactement ?

lines.en: Is it a shooting pain or a burning one?
lines.fr: Ça vous lance ou ça vous brûle ?

lines.en: Are you allergic to anything?
lines.fr: Vous êtes allergique à quelque chose ?

lines.en: Are you taking any other medication?
lines.fr: Vous prenez d'autres médicaments ?

sections.title: Five Questions, Unseen

questions.q: Line 1. Which slot does he want?
questions.why: It is the opener and it always is. Amener is bring, so he is asking what brings you in, and a learner who stops to parse the verb has already lost the turn.

questions.q: Line 2. Which slot does he want?
questions.why: Where. You can answer it with ici and a finger, which is a complete answer and needs no body part at all.

questions.q: Line 3. How many options is he offering you?
questions.why: Two verbs joined by ou. You do not need either of them: c'est comme plus a word you already have answers the question completely.

questions.q: Line 4. What is he checking?
questions.why: Allergies, and it is asked at every consultation and every pharmacy counter. It is the one answer in this lesson that matters medically rather than conversationally.
opts: Whether anything causes you a reaction

questions.q: Line 5. How many of these five wanted a yes or a no?
questions.why: Lines 3, 4 and 5. Three of the five can be answered in one word, which is worth knowing when you are unwell and building sentences is expensive.

sections.say: You do not have to understand a question to answer it. You have to know which of the four it is.
sections.title: His Question, Your Slot

check.q: Which of these three needs no French from you at all?
check.why: Montrez-moi is an instruction, not a question. You point. It is the only turn in the consultation where the answer is not language.

items.en: Where exactly does it hurt?

items.fr: Montrez-moi où ça fait mal.

items.en: Does it hurt when I press?
items.fr: Ça fait mal quand j'appuie ?

check.q: He offers you lance or brûle and neither is right. What do you say?
check.why: Plutôt is the hedge that makes an approximate answer acceptable. Picking the wrong one on purpose gives him information that is not true, which is worse than hedging.

items.en: Shooting or burning?

check.q: Which of these three would you answer with a shape rather than a yes?
check.why: All three take oui or non, and only the fever one invites you to say more using shape 2. Knowing a yes will do is what keeps a consultation moving when you are unwell.

sections.say: Lesson 24 in A2 authored six ways to ask again, once, for the whole band, and this lesson adds none of them. What it adds is the case where asking again gets you nothing.

cards.fr: Pardon ?
cards.body: One word, and it gives away nothing about why you missed it. Lesson 24 in A2 put it first because it costs you nothing at all.
cards.head: Rung 1
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 1

cards.fr: Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: The first rung that names the fault. A doctor will slow down without a flicker; it is a thing patients ask for several times a day.
cards.head: Rung 3
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 3

cards.fr: Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?
cards.body: Narrows the failure to one word rather than the whole turn. In a clinic this is often the right rung, because usually only one word was missing.
cards.head: Rung 5
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 5

cards.fr: Je ne connais pas le mot. C'est comme une brûlure.
cards.body: The six rungs all ask the other person for something. Here the missing word is YOURS, not his, and no amount of repeating supplies it. Say what it is like instead, using a word you already have.
cards.head: When none of the six helps
cards.label: the word is yours, not his

cards.fr: C'est difficile à expliquer.
cards.body: Five words that stop the silence from ending the turn. A doctor who hears it waits. A doctor who hears nothing moves on and starts guessing.
cards.head: Buy yourself a second try
cards.label: keeps the turn open

sections.title: Asking Again Will Not Help

sections.say: Eleven turns, start to finish. Twice he uses a word this lesson never taught you, and both times you can answer anyway.

sections.setting: A walk-in clinic in Nantes, Tuesday afternoon. You have been waiting forty minutes and you are not at your best.

sections.say: The pharmacy is three moves: say what you need, hand over the paper, understand the answer. The third one is the only hard part.

cards.fr: Je voudrais quelque chose contre la toux.
cards.sub: [zhuh voo-DREH kel-kuh shohz kohⁿtr lah TOO]
cards.body: Contre plus the symptom. It works for anything you can name, and lesson 7 in A2 shipped je voudrais as a fixed form you use whole.
cards.head: You open
cards.label: contre plus a symptom

cards.fr: Voici mon ordonnance.
cards.body: Two words and a piece of paper. From here the pharmacist leads and you are listening rather than producing.
cards.head: You hand it over
cards.label: the paper does the talking

cards.fr: Vous avez une ordonnance ?
cards.body: The counter usually opens with this rather than with a greeting question. Oui or non answers it completely.
cards.head: He asks first
cards.label: his opener

cards.fr: C'est sur ordonnance.
cards.body: Four words meaning he cannot sell it to you without a prescription. A learner waiting for a longer explanation misses the whole answer.
cards.head: The refusal, and it is short
cards.label: four words, and it is a no

cards.fr: Vous préférez le générique ?
cards.body: Asked at every French counter. It is the same medicine at a lower price and oui is a complete answer.
cards.head: The one you can say yes to
cards.label: oui is enough

sections.title: At The Counter

sections.say: Four instructions, heard once each, the way they are said across a counter. Catch the number and catch the word after it.

lines.en: One tablet morning and evening.
lines.fr: Un comprimé matin et soir.

lines.en: Three times a day, before meals.
lines.fr: Trois fois par jour, avant les repas.

lines.en: Every three hours, no more than that.
lines.fr: Toutes les trois heures, pas plus.

lines.en: On an empty stomach, half an hour before eating.
lines.fr: À jeun, une demi-heure avant de manger.

sections.title: How Many, And When

questions.q: Line 1. How many times a day?
questions.why: Matin et soir is twice, and neither the word two nor the word fois appears in it. A learner listening for a number hears none.

questions.q: Line 2. When, relative to eating?
questions.why: Avant les repas. Avant and après are one syllable apart and they are the whole instruction, which is why they are the trap in the next mission.

questions.q: Line 3. How many times in twenty-four hours?
questions.why: Every three hours is eight, not three. Trois fois par jour and toutes les trois heures share a word and are nearly three times apart, and that is the harm bar this section exists for.

questions.q: Line 4. Can you take it with breakfast?
questions.why: À jeun means on an empty stomach. It is two syllables and it changes the whole instruction, and it appears in only two published rows anywhere, both above this level.

sections.say: Four pairs that share a word and mean different amounts. This is the one place in the app where getting it wrong matters outside the app.

rule.body: Trois fois par jour and toutes les trois heures both contain trois. One is three times and the other is eight. The number you hear is not the number of doses, and the word around it is what tells you which.
rule.title: The shared word is not the instruction

cards.fr: 3 a day, not 8
cards.ipa: /tʁwa fwa paʁ ʒuʁ/
cards.tip: Both contain trois. Fois par jour counts doses; toutes les trois heures counts the gap between them, and over a day that is nearly three times as much.
cards.promptLabel: three times against every three hours
cards.promptSound: Trois fois par jour, avant les repas.

cards.fr: 8 a day, not 3
cards.ipa: /tut le tʁwa.zœʁ/
cards.tip: Toutes les is every. Pas plus on the end is the ceiling and it is the quietest part of the sentence.
cards.promptSound: Toutes les trois heures, pas plus.

cards.fr: avant, not après
cards.ipa: /a.vɑ̃ le ʁə.pa/
cards.tip: One syllable apart and it is the whole instruction. Some things do nothing on a full stomach and some are hard on an empty one.
cards.promptSound: Trois fois par jour, avant les repas.

cards.fr: nothing beforehand
cards.ipa: /a ʒœ̃/
cards.tip: À jeun is two syllables and it is a condition on everything else in the sentence. Two published rows in the whole corpus carry it and both are above this level.
cards.promptSound: À jeun, une demi-heure avant de manger.

drill.promptSay: Trois fois par jour, avant les repas.
Toutes les trois heures, pas plus.

opts: Before eating, on an empty stomach
drill.promptSay: À jeun, une demi-heure avant de manger.
Un comprimé matin et soir.
Pas plus de six par jour.
C'est un traitement de sept jours.

sections.title: Three Times, Or Eight

sections.say: One card, and then back to the French.

cards.fr: C'est combien de fois par jour ?
cards.body: This lesson teaches you the French for a dose, which is what lets you follow one. Deciding what dose to take is the pharmacist's job or the doctor's, and asking them is normal and expected. You have just proved you can hear the difference between three times a day and every three hours; that skill is what makes the question above worth asking, and asking it is what a French speaker does too.
cards.head: Two different jobs
cards.label: ask it at the counter

sections.title: Understanding, Not Deciding

sections.say: Six, one per screen. Every one of them is understood and every one of them marks you out as translating.
sections.title: What Anglophones Say

errors.why: English hands you a noun and French wants the verb. La toux exists and is what you call the symptom in the abstract, not what you say when you have it.
errors.right: Je tousse.
errors.wrong: J'ai une toux.

errors.why: Je suis chaud does not mean you have a temperature, and what it does mean is not something to say to a doctor. Fever is a noun you HAVE.
errors.right: J'ai de la fièvre.
errors.wrong: Je suis chaud.

errors.why: A word-for-word translation of my head hurts. French puts the person first and the part second. Lesson 27 in A1 built five sections on this shape and this is the only place it is worth naming the error.
errors.right: J'ai mal à la tête.
errors.wrong: Ma tête fait mal.

errors.why: Être malade is being ill in general. Avoir mal is a specific pain in a specific place, and the two are not interchangeable even though English blurs them.
errors.right: J'ai mal au ventre.
errors.wrong: Je suis malade au ventre.

errors.why: Pour is how long something WILL last. For a thing that started and is still going, French wants depuis, and lesson 14 in A2 owns that word and everything about it. You can also sidestep it: ça a commencé il y a trois jours.
errors.right: depuis trois jours
errors.wrong: Pour trois jours.

errors.why: Je me sens malade is heard as being about to be sick. Je ne me sens pas bien is the general one, and it is what you say in a waiting room.
errors.right: Je ne me sens pas bien.
errors.wrong: Je me sens malade.

sections.say: What the pharmacist sticks on the box, and the note underneath it. Read it once, then answer.
sections.text: Prendre le traitement : un comprimé matin et soir, à jeun, une demi-heure avant le repas, pendant sept jours. Ne pas dépasser deux comprimés par jour. Note du pharmacien : si les symptômes persistent après une semaine, reprenez rendez-vous. Ne pas prendre avec un autre traitement sans en parler à votre pharmacien.
sections.title: The Label On The Box

glossary.note: What the doctor prescribes, as a whole. Not a single dose and never a drug name.
Two syllables, and a condition on the whole instruction. Only two published rows in the corpus carry it, both above this level.
Ne pas dépasser is how a ceiling is written on a box. It is never said as a bare number.
Si les symptômes persistent is a fixed opening on any label, and what follows it is what to do when the treatment has not worked.
Reprendre is to take again. The label carries the instruction for its own failure.
Published at fr.a2.symptomes.108. The person the last line sends you back to.

questions.a: Almost. One tablet morning and evening is two a day, and the ceiling is two a day, so here they meet exactly. They do not always, and the ceiling is the one that stops you doubling up when a dose is missed.
questions.q: The label gives a dose and a ceiling. Are they the same number?

questions.a: À jeun, meaning nothing in the stomach, and une demi-heure avant le repas, meaning a specific gap before eating. Either one on its own is not the instruction, and the second is the one people drop.
questions.q: Two separate facts decide WHEN you take it. What are they?

questions.a: Reprendre rendez-vous, after a week. The label carries the instruction for its own failure, which is the part people stop reading before they reach.
questions.q: The note tells you what to do if it has not worked. What, and after how long?

questions.a: Whether you are taking anything else. It is asked by the doctor, printed on the box, and asked again at the counter, because it is the one answer in this encounter that matters medically rather than conversationally.
questions.q: The last line repeats something the doctor already asked at the consultation. What, and why twice?

sections.say: One card. Nothing here is ever the answer to a question in this lesson.

cards.fr: la RAMQ · la carte soleil · le CLSC · Info-Santé
cards.sub: the health board, the card, the local clinic, the phone line
cards.body: The French in this lesson is the same on both sides of the Atlantic. What changes is the paperwork around it: the carte soleil is the health card, the CLSC is the neighbourhood clinic, and Info-Santé is the number you call before deciding whether to go anywhere. Recognition only; every drill in this lesson stays France-standard.

questions.q: Which turn can you answer by handing something over?
questions.why: Voici mon ordonnance, and the paper does the rest. It is the one turn in the exchange where you need almost no French.

questions.q: Which turn asks the same thing the doctor already asked?
questions.why: The allergy question. It is asked twice on purpose, by two different people, because it is the one answer that matters medically.

questions.q: Which turn is the dosage?
questions.why: Matin et soir is twice a day and à jeun is a condition on both. Two facts in six words, said once, at counter speed.

questions.q: What does the last turn tell you to do?

sections.say: His half and yours, one last time.

cards.say: J'ai mal à la tête.
cards.back: J'ai mal à la tête. Shape 1, and lesson 27 in A1 owns it.

cards.say: J'ai de la fièvre.
cards.back: J'ai de la fièvre. Shape 2: a noun you have.
cards.front: English says I have a fever

cards.say: Je tousse.
cards.back: Je tousse. Shape 3: a bare verb where English used a noun.
cards.front: English says I have a cough

cards.say: J'ai des vertiges.
cards.back: J'ai des vertiges. An English adjective becomes a French noun.

cards.say: Qu'est-ce qui vous amène ?
cards.back: Qu'est-ce qui vous amène ? It is not about travel.
cards.front: The first thing he says, always

cards.say: Ça vous lance ou ça vous brûle ?
cards.back: Ça vous lance ou ça vous brûle ? Two verbs nobody taught you.

cards.say: C'est comme une brûlure.
cards.back: C'est comme une brûlure. Say what it is like, using a word you have.
cards.front: You do not have the word

cards.say: C'est plutôt une douleur sourde.
cards.back: C'est plutôt une douleur sourde. Plutôt is the hedge.
cards.front: Neither of his two options fits

cards.say: Vous êtes allergique à quelque chose ?
cards.back: Vous êtes allergique à quelque chose ? Asked twice, by two people.
cards.front: The one answer that matters medically

cards.say: Toutes les trois heures, pas plus.
cards.back: Trois fois par jour is three. Toutes les trois heures is eight.

sections.title: Three Shapes, One Way Out

sections.say: Twenty-two missions. Here is what changed.
sections.body: You came in able to say what hurts and unable to answer what came back. A symptom now takes one of three shapes and you pick before the word arrives. When the word will not come, you describe around it rather than stopping, which is the move that actually completes the encounter. And a dose is now two facts rather than a blur: how many, and when.
