the e keeps the g soft before o, and the cedilla keeps the c soft before o.
The ending goes silent, so the stem becomes the last sound and its vowel opens.
the nous cell, and nowhere else. je, tu, il, vous and ils leave it alone.
cards.front: Which cell does a -ger or -cer verb change in?

cards.back: the four cells where the ending is silent: je, tu, il and ils. nous and vous never.
cards.front: Which cells does a stem vowel change in?

cards.say: Nous mangeons ici.
Nous commençons.
Nous voyageons en train.
Je préfère le thé.
Nous préférons le thé.
Tu appelles Marie.
Nous appelons Marie.

cards.front: The verbs that take the accent

cards.back: protéger. Je protège mes photos. Nous protégeons nos photos.
cards.front: The one verb that needs both reasons

cards.back: The vowel one. mange and mangeons are the same sound, and that is why the e is written at all.
cards.front: Which of these changes can you hear?

sections.title: The Whole Lesson, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have taken four spellings apart and found two reasons under them. You know which cell a -ger or -cer verb touches and which four cells a stem vowel answers to, and you know that one small list has to be remembered because nothing predicts it. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Five rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Every question here is about why, not which.
rounds.label: The reason underneath

questions.q: Why does nous mangeons carry an e that manger does not?
questions.why: g is soft in front of e and i and hard in front of a, o and u. -ons starts with an o, so without the e you would be writing a word said with the g of gare.
opts: Because nous always adds a letter
So the g stays soft in front of the o

questions.q: Nous ___ ici. (manger)
questions.why: Stem mang-, nous ending -ons, and an e between them because of the o. The ending itself is untouched.
accept: mangeons
nous mangeons
questions.answer: mangeons

questions.q: Which one of these would be said with a hard k?
questions.why: A plain c in front of an o is hard. That spelling is not a smaller mistake than the others, it is a different word, and it is the reason the cedilla exists.

questions.q: Nous ___ la cuisine. (ranger)
questions.why: A verb the lesson barely showed you, and the reason works on it anyway. Any -ger verb takes the same e in the same cell.
accept: rangeons
nous rangeons
questions.answer: rangeons

questions.q: A verb you have never met: plonger, to dive. What is the nous form?
questions.why: You were not taught this verb and you did not need to be. The reason is about a g meeting an o, not about the word it happens to be in.

questions.q: Fix this. A note on a whiteboard: « Nous mangons ensemble. »
questions.why: Without the e the g goes hard in front of the o, and the reader gets a word that is not the verb you meant. Nothing about saying it aloud would have caught this.
accept: Nous mangeons ensemble
mangeons
questions.answer: Nous mangeons ensemble.

rounds.say: One cell in six, and five that are left alone.
rounds.label: Which cell moves

questions.q: Vous ___ en train. (voyager)
questions.why: No e. The vous ending starts with an e of its own, so the g was never in front of a back vowel and nothing had to be protected.
accept: voyagez
vous voyagez
questions.answer: voyagez

questions.q: Which form of commencer takes the cedilla?
questions.why: Only nous, because -ons is the only one of the six endings that starts with an o. Every other ending here begins with e.

questions.q: Nous ___ une pizza. (partager)
questions.why: The same e as mangeons and rangeons. Three verbs, one reason, and it is the letters that decide rather than the meaning.
accept: partageons
nous partageons
questions.answer: partageons

questions.q: « On commence à sept heures. » Why is there no cedilla here?
questions.why: on means we and takes third-person-singular agreement, so it never reaches the nous cell. That is why speech almost never puts this change in front of you.
opts: Because on takes the il form, and that ending starts with e
Because commencer only changes in the past

questions.q: Ils ___ le projet lundi. (lancer)
questions.why: Plain c. The -ent ending starts with an e, so the c is already soft and there is nothing to fix.
accept: lancent
ils lancent
questions.answer: lancent

questions.q: Fix this. A message to a swimming group: « Nous nagons le samedi. »
questions.why: nager is a -ger verb like the others, and the nous cell is where it needs the e. Nothing about nager makes it a special case.
accept: Nous nageons le samedi
nageons
questions.answer: Nous nageons le samedi.

rounds.say: Read the ending first. It decides what happens in front of it.
rounds.label: When the ending goes quiet

questions.q: Between je préfère and nous préférons, which one has the ending you can hear?
questions.why: -ons is a syllable of its own and -e is silent. That is the whole of what decides the vowel in front: with an audible ending the stem is not the last sound and stays closed.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is this?
questions.say: Je préfère le thé.
questions.why: This is the one change in the lesson your ear can settle. The vowel before the ending really does open, so préfère and préférons are audibly different words.
opts: Both are said the same way

questions.q: Elle ___ du pain. (acheter)
questions.why: The ending is silent, so the stem is the last sound and its e opens to è. This one is a choice rather than something to type, because a typed answer here cannot tell an accent from a bare letter.

questions.q: Nous ___ du pain. (acheter)
questions.why: No accent. The ending is a syllable of its own, so the stem is not the last thing heard and there is nothing to open.
accept: achetons
nous achetons
questions.answer: achetons

questions.q: Which of these four leaves its stem exactly as the naming form had it?
questions.why: The nous form, every time. Four of the six cells take a silent ending and change; nous and vous take an audible one and do not.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do not say in « répètent ».
questions.why: The whole ending, exactly as lesson 1 in A2 taught it. That silence is the condition: because nothing is said after the stem, the stem is the last sound and its vowel opens.

rounds.say: Five verbs, and this is the round where knowing the reason will not save you.
rounds.label: Double it or accent it

questions.q: Tu ___ Marie. (appeler)
questions.why: Two l. appeler writes the open sound by doubling the consonant, and the silent -es on the end tells you the stem is where the sound stops.
accept: appelles
tu appelles
questions.answer: appelles

questions.q: Nous ___ Marie. (appeler)
questions.why: One l. nous is one of the two cells where nothing moves, so the stem is spelled the way the naming form had it.
accept: appelons
nous appelons
questions.answer: appelons

questions.q: acheter takes an accent. Which of these ends the same way and doubles instead?
questions.why: jeter and acheter both end in -eter and behave differently, and nothing in either word predicts it. This is the memorised part of the lesson and it is five verbs long.

questions.q: Fix this. A message about a doctor: « Nous appellons le médecin. »
questions.why: The doubling belongs to the four cells with a silent ending. nous has an audible one, so the second l has nothing to do there.
accept: Nous appelons le médecin
appelons
questions.answer: Nous appelons le médecin.

questions.q: Je ___ le ticket. (jeter)
questions.why: Two t. jeter is on the short list that doubles, and the silent -e is what puts it in a cell where the stem has to carry the sound.
accept: jette
je jette
questions.answer: jette

questions.q: Nothing in an -eler or -eter infinitive says which spelling it takes. So what do you do?
questions.why: A short list you know you have to learn is worth more than a rule that pretends to cover it. Everything else in this lesson is worked out; these five are not.
opts: Guess from how common the verb is
Always double, and accept some mistakes
Use the accent, since it is easier to type
Learn these five by name, and derive everything else

rounds.say: Written, which is the only place any of this shows up.
rounds.label: On the page

questions.q: You are writing the note for the morning shift. Which line goes on the board?
questions.why: The cedilla keeps the c soft in front of the o. This is a choice rather than something to type, because a typed answer cannot tell a cedilla from a plain c.

questions.q: Nous ___ tout. (jeter)
questions.why: One t. Whatever a verb does in the silent cells, nous and vous always get the plain stem back.
accept: jetons
nous jetons
questions.answer: jetons

questions.q: Say the line you would have written on the board.
questions.why: Out loud there is nothing to get wrong here, and that is the point of the lesson: the cedilla exists so that this sentence sounds exactly like the one you already knew how to say.

questions.q: Fix this. A note about the tickets: « Je jete le ticket. »
questions.why: jeter doubles its t in the four silent cells, and je is one of them. The single t would be the nous and vous spelling.
accept: Je jette le ticket
jette
questions.answer: Je jette le ticket.

questions.q: Nous ___ nos photos. (protéger)
questions.why: Both reasons in one word: the e goes in because a g meets an o, and the é stays closed because the ending is audible. A learner holding four lists has nowhere to put this verb.

questions.q: Nous ___ en train. (voyager)
questions.why: Compare it with the vous form from round two. Same verb, and only one of the six cells ever needs the extra letter.
accept: voyageons
nous voyageons
questions.answer: voyageons

sections.say: Four things, and then the lesson that picks this up.
sections.body: You can write the nous form of any -ger or -cer verb, including verbs nobody has shown you, because the reason is about a letter meeting a vowel rather than about the word. You can move a stem vowel in the four cells where the ending is silent and leave it alone in the two where it is not. And you know which small part of this has to be memorised, which is five verbs, and why nothing else does. The next two units swap these endings for two other short sets and leave the method exactly as it is.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: The spelling changes so the sound does not.
Four patterns, two reasons. the e keeps the g soft before o, and the same for -cer. The other two answer to the ending going silent.
The -ger and -cer change is the nous cell and nothing else. the four cells where the ending is silent for the other two.
Only five verbs have to be learnt by name: appeler, rappeler, jeter double, and acheter and geler take the accent.

errorTriggers.description: Holds the four patterns as four lists and cannot say why any of them exists, so a verb outside the lists is a guess.
Puts the -ger or -cer letter on the wrong person, or misses that nous is the only cell that takes it: nous voyageons and vous voyageons.
Leaves the stem vowel closed where the ending is silent, or opens it where the ending sounds: je prefere, nous préfèrons.
Merges -eler and -eter into one rule: appèles for appelles, achettes for achètes, appellons for appelons.
Writes a plain c or a bare g in front of an o, which is not a smaller mistake than the others: commencons, mangons.

grammarAssumed: The six subject pronouns and the nine they cover, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
The present tense of regular -er verbs as a stem plus six endings, introduced in a2.01
That -e, -es and -ent are silent and -ons and -ez are not, introduced in a2.01
nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one, stated in a2.01
grammarIntroduced: The -ger and -cer spelling change, as a consonant protected in front of a back vowel
That the change occupies the nous cell alone, and is therefore met mostly in writing
The -eler, -eter and é_er stem-vowel change, as a response to the ending going silent
That the doubled consonant and the accent are two spellings of one open vowel
That which of the two an -eler or -eter verb takes is learnt per verb and not derived

acts.title: Le projet flou

opener.line: Tu annonces une date à une agence, et elle écrit un point d'interrogation : ta phrase disait moins que toi. EN: You give an agency a date and it writes a question mark: your sentence said less than you meant.

acts.milestone: Tu vois maintenant la différence entre annoncer une intention et poser une date. EN: You can now see the difference between announcing an intention and putting down a date.

acts.title: Un r, puis avoir

opener.line: Une seule lettre sépare ce que tu faisais de ce que tu feras : ici tu apprends à la poser. EN: One letter separates what you used to do from what you will do, and here you learn to put it there.

acts.milestone: Tu construis le futur de n'importe quel verbe en -er ou en -ir, aux six personnes. EN: You can build the future of any -er or -ir verb, at all six persons.

acts.title: Les trois groupes

opener.line: Prendre, attendre, vendre : ces verbes perdent une lettre au futur, et une seule. EN: Prendre, attendre and vendre lose one letter in the future, and only one.

acts.milestone: Tu mets au futur n'importe quel verbe régulier des trois groupes, sans hésiter sur le e. EN: You can put any regular verb from the three groups into the future.

acts.title: Proche ou simple

opener.line: Un train qui part dans dix minutes prend le futur lointain : ici tu comprends pourquoi. EN: A train leaving in ten minutes takes the far-off future, and here you find out why.

acts.milestone: Tu choisis entre les deux futurs par ce que ta phrase fait, et non par la distance. EN: You choose between the two futures by what your sentence does, not by how far away it is.

acts.title: L'infinitif gardé entier

opener.line: Tu dis étudirai et tu écris étudierai : ici tu apprends une lettre que ton oreille ne te donnera jamais. EN: You say étudirai and write étudierai: here you learn a letter your ear will never give you.

acts.milestone: Tu écris sans hésiter les verbes en -ier, -uer et -éer, même quand le e ne s'entend pas. EN: You can write the -ier, -uer and -éer verbs without hesitating, even when the e is silent.

acts.title: Les radicaux qui changent

opener.line: Quelques verbes en -er écrivent leur radical autrement au futur, et cette fois ils le font partout. EN: A few -er verbs spell their stem differently in the future, and this time they do it everywhere.

acts.milestone: Tu écris achèterai, appellerai, jettera et paieront sans te demander à quelle personne tu es. EN: You can write achèterai, appellerai, jettera and paieront without wondering which person you are at.

acts.title: La phrase au futur

opener.line: Refuser, demander, placer un pronom : au futur, rien de tout ça ne change, et tu vas le vérifier. EN: Refusing, asking, placing a pronoun: none of it changes in the future, and here you check that.

acts.milestone: Tu écris au futur une phrase négative, une phrase avec deux pronoms et une question. EN: You can write a negative sentence, a two-pronoun sentence and a question in the future.

acts.title: Les mots du futur

opener.line: Demain ne t'oblige à rien : ici tu apprends ce que ces mots font vraiment, et ce qu'ils ne font pas. EN: Demain forces nothing on you, and here you learn what these words really do.

acts.milestone: Tu places correctement demain, prochain, dans et d'ici là, et tu ne les laisses plus choisir ton temps. EN: You place these time words correctly and no longer let them pick your tense.

acts.title: Annoter un projet

opener.line: Deux personnes partent vivre à Québec, et tout leur projet tient en cent soixante mots : tu vas les marquer un par un. EN: Two people are moving to Québec City and their whole plan fits in a hundred and sixty words, which you will mark one by one.

acts.milestone: Tu lis un texte de projet et tu sais, pour chaque verbe, pourquoi il est à cette forme. EN: You can read a plan and say, for every verb, why it takes that form.

acts.title: Écrire ses projets

opener.line: À toi d'écrire : où tu en es, tes étapes dans l'ordre, et une fin qui dit pourquoi. EN: Your turn to write: where you are now, your steps in order, and an ending that says why.

acts.milestone: Tu as écrit ton propre projet et passé l'examen : quatre-vingts questions, dix rounds. EN: You wrote your own plan and sat the exam: eighty questions, ten rounds.

recorded.desc: The letting agency's written reply (act 1), one female France-French voice, one take, read at dictation pace, formal but not cold. Every future verb keeps its r clearly audible before the ending; do not swallow « examinerons » into three syllables.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in authored order, at conversational speed. Line 1 is the only imparfait and must NOT be marked by pace or emphasis: the whole mission is whether the learner hears the r on its own.
The two rule decks. Read each form once, plainly, with the voice falling on the r plus the ending. On the endings card, read the six endings as a list with an even beat, never as a chant.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Read the six identically in pace; the wrong versions in promptSound are never spoken.

The platform conversation (act 3), two voices, Belgian French welcome, one take. The -re futures (partira, attendrons, prendrai, descendra, dirai, lirez, vendrons) must each keep the consonant before the r audible: attendrons is a-tan-drons, never a-tan-ons.
The three-group deck. Read the infinitive, a beat, then the future form, so the learner hears what was kept and what was dropped. On the third card, prendre and prendrai must be clearly separable.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in authored order, conversational pace. No emphasis on any verb: the mission is whether the learner can place the group from a normal sentence.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence, six of them. Same pace throughout; the invented forms in promptSound are never spoken.

The minutes conversation (act 4), two voices, one male one female. Karim speaks quickly and casually; Léa reads her written sentence slowly, as someone reading back what they typed. That contrast IS the teaching point, so it must survive the edit.
The two contrast decks. Read the futur proche cards lightly and quickly, as speech; the futur simple cards evenly, as an announcement. Never exaggerate: both must sound like ordinary French.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational speed. Lines 1 and 2 are the same verb in the two forms and must be read at the same pace, or the learner counts performances instead of words.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order. Read at ordinary speed and do NOT sound the silent e of étudierai, jouerons or créeront. The mission is that the ear gives no help here, so an over-careful reading destroys it.
The silent-e deck. Read the infinitive, a beat, then the future form, at normal speed. The written e is not pronounced in either.

The managing agent's notice (act 6), one voice, France French, formal and neutral, one take at dictation pace. The open è of appellerons, jettera and se lèvera must be clearly audible, and nettoieront must not be read as nettoyeront.
The stem-change deck. On cards one and two, the contrast between the infinitive (closed e) and the future (open è) is the whole teaching point and must be audible without being exaggerated.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational speed. No emphasis on the changed syllable: the learner has to catch the open è on their own.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence, six of them. Card six's correct sentence is about essayer, not about envoyer: read what is written in `fr`, never the promptSound.

The customer-service call (act 7), two voices: a tired but polite agent and a firm customer, Belgian French welcome. The ne is often dropped in real speech; here it must be pronounced, because the mission is about where it sits.
The sentence-frame deck. Read each line at natural speed with no pause between ne and the verb, so the learner hears one block rather than a grammar exercise.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational speed. Lines 1, 2 and 3 all start with a time marker and end in a different tense; read the markers identically, with no extra weight, or the mission answers itself.
The marker deck. The first three cards are the same situation in three tenses, so they must be read at the same pace and pitch; only the verb differs.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Read après-demain as one word, and la semaine prochaine with no pause before prochaine.

The plan narrative (act 9), one voice, one take, natural reading pace, Belgian or France French. Even throughout: the futur simple verbs must not be stressed more than the present ones, because the mission is to tell them apart by form.

The model plan (act 10), one voice, one take, warm and unhurried, as somebody reading back a message they have just written. The four connectors (D’abord, Ensuite, Au mois de septembre, Dans deux ans, Finalement) each take a small pause before them: they are the shape the learner will copy.

lessons.intro: You already say what you are going to do with aller plus an infinitive. This lesson gives you the other future, the one that fits in a single word. Its stem is the infinitive itself, kept as far as its r, and its endings are the present tense of avoir. Once you can build it, the lesson is about when a French speaker reaches for it rather than for je vais.

yeni.body: Les verbes en -ayer, -oyer et -uyer changent leur y en i devant un e muet, et le futur compte comme tel. Le changement vaut à toutes les personnes. EN: Verbs in -ayer, -oyer and -uyer turn their y into i, at every person.
yeni.title: payer donne paierai

emuet.body: Dans étudierai, jouerons ou créeront, le e de l'infinitif ne s'entend presque pas. Il s'écrit quand même, parce que le radical du futur est l'infinitif complet. EN: In these verbs the written e is barely audible, and it is written all the same.
emuet.title: Un e qu'on écrit sans l'entendre

proche.body: Le futur proche est en deux mots : aller au présent, puis l'infinitif. Il garde un fil avec maintenant : c'est décidé, c'est lancé, ou tu le vois arriver. EN: The futur proche is two words and keeps a thread back to now.
proche.title: aller plus infinitif

simple.body: Le futur simple tient en un mot : radical plus terminaison. Il annonce, il écrit, il engage. C'est le futur des horaires, des courriels et des promesses. EN: The futur simple is one word, and it is the tense of timetables, emails and promises.
simple.title: Un seul mot, une seule forme

radical.body: Le radical, c'est le morceau qui porte la terminaison. Au futur, ce morceau est l'infinitif lui-même, gardé jusqu'à son r. Rien à enlever, rien à chercher ailleurs. EN: The stem is the part that carries the ending, and for the future it is the infinitive itself, kept as far as its r.
radical.title: Le radical, c'est l'infinitif

examples.note: prendre perd son e, garde son r
la marque commune de tous les radicaux

marqueur.body: Demain, la semaine prochaine, dans deux ans : ces mots disent quand, pas quel temps. Après demain, tu peux mettre le présent, le futur proche ou le futur simple. EN: Time words say when, not which tense.
marqueur.title: Un marqueur situe, il ne commande pas

negation.body: Le futur simple est en un seul mot, donc ne et pas se placent autour de lui, exactement comme au présent. Les pronoms restent devant le verbe. EN: One word means ne and pas simply wrap around it, as in the present.
negation.title: Un verbe en un mot, facile à entourer

promesse.body: Quand tu écris au futur simple, tu prends un engagement : la date, le paiement, la réponse. Ton lecteur peut te le rappeler plus tard. EN: The futur simple commits you, and the person reading can hold you to it.
promesse.title: Ce que le futur simple engage

infinitif.body: Pour les autres temps, tu coupes l'infinitif avant d'ajouter quelque chose. Au futur, tu ne coupes presque rien : tu écris le verbe comme dans le dictionnaire, puis la terminaison. EN: Other tenses cut the infinitive first; the future barely cuts it at all.
infinitif.title: L'infinitif fait tout le travail

examples.note: la seule coupure du futur régulier

lessons.title: Le futur simple : la formation

drills.coach: Deux piles. Demande-toi : est-ce que ton lecteur pourra te le rappeler ? EN: sort by whether the reader can hold you to it.
drills.title: Annonce ou intention

drills.q: Demain, je ... à la maison. (travailler)
drills.why: Le r porte le futur. EN: the r carries the future.
drills.coach: Cherche le r. Sans r, c'est l'imparfait. EN: look for the r.
drills.title: Le r avant la terminaison

drills.q: Nous ... devant la gare. (attendre)
drills.why: attendre donne attendr-, puis -ons. EN: attendre gives attendr-, then -ons.
drills.coach: Pour un verbe en -re, enlève le e et arrête-toi là. EN: for an -re verb, drop the e and stop.
drills.title: Un e part, rien ne s’ajoute

drills.coach: Deux piles. Est-ce que la phrase part de maintenant, ou est-ce qu’elle annonce ? EN: does it start from now, or does it announce?
drills.title: Le fil avec maintenant

drills.coach: Lis chaque phrase à voix haute, puis écris-la de mémoire. Le e est toujours là. EN: read each one aloud, then write it from memory.
drills.title: Le e qu’on n’entend pas

drills.q: Nous ... un taxi à la sortie. (appeler)
drills.why: appeler double son l partout. EN: appeler doubles its l everywhere.
drills.coach: Au futur, le radical change aux six personnes, sans exception. EN: in the future the stem changes at all six persons.
drills.title: Accent, consonne ou i

drills.q: Je ... la maison. (ne ... pas, vendre)
drills.why: ne avant, pas après. EN: ne before, pas after.
drills.coach: Le verbe tient en un mot. ne passe devant, le deuxième mot suit. EN: the verb is one word; ne goes in front and the second word follows.
drills.title: Autour du verbe

drills.coach: Deux piles. Le marqueur donne-t-il une date, ou seulement une direction ? EN: does the marker give a date or only a direction?
drills.title: Situe, ne commande pas

drills.coach: Trois piles dans ta tête, deux ici : ce qui est déjà vrai, et ce qui est annoncé. EN: what is already true, and what is announced.
drills.title: Verbe par verbe

drills.q: Ton projet se termine par « Dans deux ans, je passerai un examen ». Que manque-t-il ?
drills.why: Une dernière phrase ferme le texte. EN: a last sentence closes the text.
opts: une fin qui donne ta raison
drills.coach: Un présent pour partir, des étapes dans l’ordre, une fin qui donne ta raison. EN: a present to start from, steps in order, an ending that gives your reason.
drills.title: Un projet complet

sections.body: Le futur, c'est l'infinitif jusqu'au r, puis avoir. Le radical est l'infinitif, gardé jusqu'à son r : parler donne parler-, finir donne finir-, prendre donne prendr-. Les terminaisons -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont sont celles d'avoir au présent, sauf pour nous et vous, qui gardent seulement la fin. EN: The future is the infinitive as far as the r, then avoir. The stem is the infinitive as far as its r, and the endings are avoir's present, except at nous and vous where only the ending is kept.
sections.title: La règle en trois lignes

sections.body: Les verbes en -er et en -ir gardent leur infinitif entier : parler donne parler-, finir donne finir-. Les verbes en -re perdent leur e final et gardent tout le reste : prendre donne prendr-, écrire donne écrir-, vivre donne vivr-. C'est la seule lettre qui tombe dans tout le futur régulier, et les trois radicaux finissent par un r. EN: -er and -ir verbs keep the whole infinitive; -re verbs drop only the final e, and all three stems end in an r.
sections.title: Une seule coupure dans tout le système

sections.body: Le futur proche (aller au présent plus l'infinitif) garde un fil avec le moment où tu parles : la décision vient d'être prise, la chose est déjà lancée, ou tu la vois arriver. Le futur simple coupe ce fil et pose un fait à venir. Ce n'est pas une question de distance : un train qui part dans dix minutes prend le futur simple, parce qu'un horaire s'annonce, et « un jour, je vais arrêter de fumer » prend le futur proche, parce que la décision est déjà prise. EN: the futur proche keeps a thread back to now; the futur simple states a coming fact. Distance decides nothing.

sections.body: Première famille : les verbes en -ier, -uer, -éer et -ouer gardent leur infinitif entier, et le e qui s'y trouve ne se prononce presque pas. Tu dis étudirai et tu écris étudierai. Deuxième famille : quelques verbes en -er écrivent leur radical autrement, avec un accent grave (achèter-, lèver-), une consonne doublée (appeller-, jetter-) ou un i à la place du y (paier-, emploier-). La différence avec le présent est le seul vrai piège : au présent, nous et vous gardent la forme simple ; au futur, le radical change aux six personnes. EN: one family keeps a silent written e, the other respells the stem, and unlike the present the change covers all six persons.

sections.body: envoyer ressemble à employer et ne se comporte pas comme lui : son radical de futur est enverr-, et il appartient à la liste des radicaux irréguliers, avec être, avoir, aller, faire, venir, voir, pouvoir, devoir, savoir, vouloir et falloir. La leçon suivante les donne tous. EN: envoyer looks like employer and behaves differently; its stem is enverr-, and the next lesson gives the whole irregular list.

sections.body: demain, la semaine prochaine, dans deux ans, un jour, bientôt, d'ici là : ces mots disent QUAND, et rien de plus. Après n'importe lequel d'entre eux, le présent, le futur proche et le futur simple sont tous possibles, et c'est ce que fait ta phrase qui décide. Ce qui est fixe, ce sont leurs propres règles : prochain se met après le nom, dans compte vers l'avenir quand il y a compte vers le passé, et après-demain prend un trait d'union. EN: these words say when and nothing more; what is fixed is their own placement, not the tense that follows.

overview.introFr: Tu sais déjà dire ce que tu vas faire avec aller plus l'infinitif. Cette leçon te donne l'autre futur, celui qui tient en un seul mot. Son radical, c'est l'infinitif gardé jusqu'à son r, et ses terminaisons sont celles d'avoir au présent. Une fois la forme construite, tout le travail est de savoir quand un francophone choisit l'une plutôt que l'autre.

sections.text: Madame, Monsieur, nous avons bien reçu votre dossier. Nous examinerons votre demande cette semaine et nous confirmerons la date par écrit. L'agence ferme à dix-huit heures ; si personne ne répond, une réponse arrivera par courriel. Vous trouverez les clés dans la boîte aux lettres le jour de l'état des lieux. Le chauffage marchera dès le premier octobre, et le magasin du rez-de-chaussée ouvrira à neuf heures tous les matins. Nous vous demandons de signer le bail avant le premier septembre. La réunion des locataires commencera à quatorze heures le samedi suivant. Nous restons à votre disposition.

sections.text: Chers voisins, voici ce qui changera dans l'immeuble au mois de mars. Nous appellerons une entreprise lundi pour le chauffage du deuxième étage. Les techniciens nettoieront les conduits mardi et mercredi, entre huit heures et midi. Vous ne paierez rien de plus ce mois-ci : la copropriété emploiera son budget de réserve. Chacun jettera ses cartons dans le local du fond, et non dans la cour. Le gardien se lèvera plus tôt pendant les travaux et il ouvrira la porte dès sept heures. Nous achèterons aussi deux vélos pour les livraisons du rez-de-chaussée. En cas de bruit, appelez-moi directement. Nous essaierons de finir avant les vacances de printemps.

sections.say: Le futur, c'est l'infinitif jusqu'au r, puis avoir.
sections.text: L'année prochaine, Sofia et Malick quitteront Bruxelles. Ils déménageront à Québec au mois d'août, avec leur fille de six ans. Sofia travaille déjà pour une entreprise canadienne, et elle continuera le même travail depuis son nouveau bureau. Malick cherchera un poste dans une école ; il envoie des candidatures depuis janvier. Ils vont visiter trois quartiers avant de choisir, parce qu'ils veulent une école tout près. D'ici là, ils vendront la moitié de leurs meubles et ils garderont seulement les livres et la vaisselle. Le déménagement coûtera assez cher : ils paieront une partie en juin et le reste en juillet. Leur fille commencera l'école en septembre et elle apprendra vite, disent ses parents. Le premier hiver leur demandera du courage, mais ils ne regretteront rien. Pour l'instant, ils remplissent des formulaires et ils comptent les semaines. Tout commencera vraiment le jour de l'arrivée.

sections.say: Le futur, c'est l'infinitif jusqu'au r, puis avoir.
sections.text: Voici mon projet pour l'année prochaine. D'abord, je terminerai ma formation en juin. Ensuite, je chercherai un travail à Montréal, parce que ma cousine y habite déjà. Je préparerai mon dossier pendant tout le mois de juillet : le CV, les lettres, les diplômes traduits. Au mois de septembre, je déménagerai. Je louerai un petit appartement près du métro, pas trop grand, parce que je voyagerai souvent. Je continuerai mes cours de français le soir, deux fois par semaine. Dans deux ans, je passerai un examen officiel. Je ne changerai pas d'avis : j'y pense depuis trop longtemps. Finalement, j'inviterai ma famille à venir me voir, et on visitera la ville ensemble. Ce projet me demandera du travail, mais il en vaut la peine.

sections.say: Le futur, c'est l'infinitif jusqu'au r, puis avoir.
steps: 1. Commence au présent : dis où tu en es aujourd’hui. EN: start in the present and say where you are now.
2. Annonce la première étape avec un marqueur : en juin, la semaine prochaine. EN: announce the first step with a time marker.
3. Enchaîne trois étapes au futur simple, avec d’abord, ensuite, finalement. EN: chain three steps in the futur simple.
4. Ajoute une phrase négative : ce que tu ne feras pas. EN: add a negative sentence, something you will not do.
5. Termine par une raison, pas par une étape. EN: finish with a reason, not with another step.
sections.title: Cinq étapes pour écrire ton projet

sections.setting: Un centre de formation à Namur. La conseillère prépare ton dossier et veut des dates, pas des intentions.

sections.brief: Ton ancien professeur de français t'écrit et te demande ce que tu feras dans les deux prochaines années. Réponds-lui par un message. Dis d'abord où tu en es aujourd'hui, puis raconte tes étapes dans l'ordre, jusqu'à la fin.
sections.title: Écris ton projet

criteria.label: Des futurs bien construits
descriptors: 4 : Six verbes au futur simple au moins, tous corrects : le radical garde son r, les terminaisons suivent le sujet, et les verbes en -ier, -uer ou à radical changeant sont bien écrits.
3 : Presque tous les futurs sont corrects. Une ou deux fautes de terminaison ou un e muet oublié.
2 : Plusieurs radicaux sont coupés ou rallongés, ou les terminaisons ne suivent pas le sujet. Le lecteur comprend, mais il bute.
1 : Moins de six futurs, ou des formes inventées à presque chaque verbe.

criteria.label: Le bon futur au bon endroit
descriptors: 3 : Le futur simple porte les étapes annoncées, le présent dit où tu en es aujourd'hui, et un futur proche, s'il y en a un, parle bien d'une décision déjà prise.
2 : Le partage tient dans l’ensemble, mais une ou deux phrases prennent la mauvaise forme.
1 : Tout est au même temps, ou le futur proche et le futur simple sont mis l'un pour l'autre sans raison.

criteria.label: Des phrases complètes
descriptors: 3 : Au moins une phrase négative correcte, les pronoms devant le verbe, et trois marqueurs de temps bien placés.
2 : La négation ou la place d’un marqueur hésite une fois, sans gêner la lecture.
1 : ne ou pas est mal placé plusieurs fois, ou les marqueurs manquent et le lecteur ne sait plus quand.

criteria.label: La mission complète
descriptors: 2 : Un projet sur deux ans, entre 90 et 130 mots, dans l’ordre, avec une fin qui donne ta raison.
1 : Il manque un élément : pas d'ordre, pas de fin, ou moins de 90 mots.

sections.briefEn: Your old French teacher writes and asks what you will be doing over the next two years. Answer with a message: say where you are now, then give your steps in order, through to the end.
sections.produce: Écris un projet de 90 à 130 mots, avec au moins six verbes au futur simple, au moins un verbe au présent pour dire où tu en es, une phrase négative, trois marqueurs de temps et une fin qui donne ta raison.

watchFor.pattern: The r of the stem missing, so the future reads as an imparfait (je terminais ma formation en juin, je cherchais un travail).
watchFor.feedback: Il manque le r du futur : je terminerai, je chercherai. Sans lui, ta phrase parle du passé.

watchFor.pattern: The infinitive cut before the ending (je parlai, je terminai, nous choisirerons, je vendai).
watchFor.feedback: Écris l'infinitif en entier, puis la terminaison : terminer plus ai donne terminerai.

watchFor.pattern: An -re verb mishandled: the e kept (je prendreai), an -er added (nous attenderons), or the r dropped (ils vendont).
watchFor.feedback: Pour un verbe en -re, enlève seulement le e final : prendre donne prendr-, attendre donne attendr-.

watchFor.pattern: The silent e dropped from an -ier, -uer or -éer verb (j’étudirai, je continurai, je jourai, je lourai).
watchFor.feedback: Ces verbes gardent tout leur infinitif : étudierai, continuerai, jouerai, louerai. Le e s'écrit même si tu ne l'entends pas.

watchFor.pattern: A stem-changing -er verb left unchanged, or changed only at je (j'acheterai, nous achetrons, nous appelerons, elle jetera, je payerai written as payrai).
watchFor.feedback: Au futur, ces radicaux changent aux six personnes : j'achèterai et nous achèterons, j'appellerai et nous appellerons.

watchFor.pattern: An ending that does not follow the subject (les cours commencera, nous terminerai, ils partira).
watchFor.feedback: La terminaison suit le sujet, comme à tous les temps : ils partiront, nous terminerons.

watchFor.pattern: An irregular stem attempted: serai, aurai, irai, ferai, viendrai, pourrai, verrai, enverrai, or an invented regular version of one (je alerai, je faisera, j’envoierai).
watchFor.feedback: Ces verbes ont un radical à eux, et la leçon 6 du B1 te les donne. Ici, choisis des verbes réguliers.

watchFor.pattern: The whole message in the futur simple, with no present tense saying where the writer stands today.
watchFor.feedback: Commence par une phrase au présent : pour l'instant, je travaille, je suis des cours. Sans elle, on ne sait pas d'où tu pars.

watchFor.pattern: Aller plus the infinitive used for every announced step, so a plan reads as a list of intentions (je vais terminer, je vais chercher, je vais déménager).
watchFor.feedback: Dans un message qui annonce un projet, le futur simple engage : je terminerai, je chercherai, je déménagerai.

watchFor.pattern: The two futures stacked in one verb (je vais terminerai, je vais déménagerai).
watchFor.feedback: Une machine à la fois : soit je vais terminer, soit je terminerai.

watchFor.pattern: Negation in English order or doubled (je changerai ne pas, je ne changerai pas rien), or object pronouns behind the verb (je préparerai le en juillet).
watchFor.feedback: ne passe devant le verbe et pas le suit. rien prend la place de pas, et les pronoms restent devant.

watchFor.pattern: Time markers missing or misplaced (la prochaine semaine, le prochain mois, il y a deux ans for a future date, après demain without its hyphen).
watchFor.feedback: prochain se met après le nom, et dans compte vers l’avenir : la semaine prochaine, dans deux ans.

watchFor.pattern: Under 90 words, no ending, or a text that stops at the last step with no reason given.
watchFor.feedback: Relis la mission : un projet sur deux ans, de 90 à 130 mots, avec une dernière phrase qui donne ta raison.

graderNotes: Count the futur simple verbs by FORM, not by meaning: a stem ending in r plus one of the six endings. An auxiliary plus infinitive (je vais partir) is a futur proche and counts for criterion « choix », never for the six.
Word count EXCLUDES the greeting and the sign-off. Count the body only, with 10% tolerance (81-143) before criterion « tache » loses its point.

Do NOT mark an irregular stem wrong if it is correctly formed: serai, aurai, irai, fera, pourra and the rest are right French and simply belong to the next lesson. Mark them only when the learner has invented a regular version of one.

Both paierai and payerai are correct. Accept either without comment. Accept both essaierai and essayerai, and both nettoierai and nettoyerai only where the -ayer pattern applies; -oyer and -uyer verbs must change.

A present tense with future meaning is correct French for a settled near plan (« en juin je termine ma formation »). Count it under « choix » only if the whole text does it and nothing is ever announced.
Narrator gender is unknown: judge agreement for internal consistency only, and do not require it, since nothing in this task needs a past participle.
Accept any destination and any professional plan, including regional vocabulary (le cégep in Québec, la haute école in Belgium, une formation en alternance in France).
Feedback language: simple French (B1), addressed as « tu », with one short English gloss allowed per comment.
sections.modelAnswer: Bonjour Madame, merci de votre message. Pour l'instant, je travaille dans un magasin et je suis des cours du soir. D'abord, je terminerai ma formation en juin. Ensuite, je chercherai un travail à Montréal, parce que ma cousine y habite déjà. Je préparerai mon dossier pendant tout le mois de juillet : le CV, les lettres, les diplômes traduits. Au mois de septembre, je déménagerai et je louerai un petit appartement près du métro. Je continuerai mes cours de français le soir, deux fois par semaine. Dans deux ans, je passerai un examen officiel. Je ne changerai pas d'avis : ce projet me demandera du travail, mais il en vaut la peine.
sections.modelAnswerEn: Hello Madam, thank you for your message. For now I work in a shop and I take evening classes. First, I will finish my training in June. Then I will look for work in Montréal, because my cousin already lives there. I will get my file ready all through July: the CV, the letters, the translated diplomas. In September I will move and rent a small flat near the metro. I will carry on with my French classes in the evening, twice a week. In two years I will sit an official exam. I will not change my mind: this plan will take work, but it is worth it.

sections.title: Toute la leçon sur un écran

sections.say: Le futur, c'est l'infinitif jusqu'au r, puis avoir.
sections.body: Tu construis le futur de n'importe quel verbe régulier, tu écris les e muets et les radicaux qui changent, tu poses une négation et une question, et tu choisis entre les deux futurs par ce que ta phrase fait. Le piège qui reste, c'est le marqueur pris pour un ordre : demain ne t'oblige à rien. Avant l'examen, relis ta mission écrite, entoure chaque verbe et écris à côté : radical, puis terminaison. Si les deux morceaux se voient à chaque fois, la leçon a marché. EN: Circle every verb in your task and write stem, then ending, beside it; if both parts show every time, the lesson landed.

sections.say: Le futur, c'est l'infinitif jusqu'au r, puis avoir.
sections.body: Le futur, c'est l'infinitif jusqu'au r, puis avoir. Tu fabriques la forme sans y penser, tu écris les e muets et les radicaux qui changent, et tu choisis entre les deux futurs par ce que ta phrase fait. La prochaine leçon garde la même machine et change le premier morceau : une douzaine de verbes très courants ont un radical à eux, comme être, avoir, aller et faire. EN: Next lesson: the dozen very common verbs whose stem is their own.
sections.title: Le futur, en résumé
points: Le radical : l'infinitif, gardé jusqu'à son r.
Les terminaisons : avoir au présent, sauf nous et vous.
Le e muet de étudier et jouer s’écrit toujours.
Le futur proche garde un fil avec maintenant ; le futur simple annonce.

errorTriggers.description: Writes every plan with aller plus the infinitive, so a dated commitment reads as an intention the reader cannot rely on.
Drops the r of the stem, or cuts the infinitive before adding the ending, so the future comes out as an imparfait or as a word that does not exist.
Mishandles an -re verb: keeps the e, adds an -er, doubles the r or shortens the stem, so the third group comes out as an invented form.
Picks between the two futures by how far away the event is, so a timetable ten minutes from now gets aller and a decision taken today gets the futur simple.
Writes these verbs the way they sound, dropping the silent e of the infinitive (étudirai, jourons, créront), so the stem is cut where nothing is heard.
Leaves the stem of acheter, appeler, jeter or payer unchanged, or changes it only at je, carrying the present tense pattern into the future.
Keeps English word order round the future verb: puts ne after it, stacks pas with rien, leaves the object pronouns behind the verb, or combines est-ce que with inversion.
Treats a time word as an instruction: forces the futur simple after demain, or refuses the present for a settled near plan, and misplaces prochain or dans.
Writes a whole plan in the futur simple, including the present-tense sentences that say where the writer is starting from, so the reader cannot tell the situation from the project.
Produces a plan with no starting point, no order and no ending: a pile of correct future sentences that never becomes a text somebody can act on.

grammarIntroduced: The futur simple of regular verbs: the infinitive as the stem, kept as far as its r, plus the endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont
The endings as the present tense of avoir, with nous and vous keeping only the ending rather than the whole form
All three regular groups, including -re verbs dropping the final e while keeping the r (prendre gives prendr-)

lessons.intro: A form asks for your last qualification and the only name you have for it is not one it recognises. This lesson is the four lines you give instead: what level it was, what you studied, how it went, and what that comes out at here.

sit.body: French keeps these apart with two different verbs and English uses one word for both. Sitting it is the day you turn up. Getting it is the letter that comes afterwards. Saying the first when you mean the second is a real sentence and nobody will correct you.
sit.title: Doing the exam, which is not the same as getting it

rung.body: Five of them, from maternelle to université. A rung is named by where it sits, not by what it is called, so the useful question is never what does this word mean but how old are you when you leave it.

examples.note: Not a college. Eleven to fifteen.

span.body: Pendant trois ans is the stretch you were in it. En trois ans is how long the whole thing took to finish. Both go with the past, because both are over, and between them they answer the second half of every question in this lesson.

hedge.body: Four short chunks, learned whole. You are not translating the name, because the name has nothing behind it here. You are giving the level and the length, which is what the other person is actually trying to write down.

examples.note: The plainest one, and it works for anything.

dossier.body: What level it was, what you studied, how it went, and what it comes out at here. Every act of this lesson adds one line. By the end you can say all four out loud without stopping, which is the whole thing a registrar is waiting for.
dossier.title: The four lines somebody writes down about you

examples.note: Line one, and it is the first thing they ask.

mention.body: Three of them, and they sit on the paper itself rather than in anybody memory: assez bien, bien, très bien. A French speaker hears the word and knows the range of marks behind it without being told the number.
mention.title: The word on the diploma above a plain pass

strength.body: Fort en is good at, moyen en is somewhere in the middle, and nul en is hopeless at. All three take en and none of them takes a preposition English would recognise. The middle one is the one people actually say about themselves.
strength.title: The three-point scale for a subject

examples.note: The top of the scale, already in the corpus.
The bottom, and it is not an insult.

registrar.body: Not an employer and not a teacher. They are recording what you did, not judging whether to take you on, and they will use vous from the first word to the last. Their questions are short and they come in an order you cannot predict.
registrar.title: The person filling in the form about you

examples.note: Short, and it wants one word back.

outOfTwenty.body: Ten is the line. Twelve is solid, fourteen is good and anything at sixteen is rare enough that people remember it. Nobody scores twenty. If you report a percentage instead, the number lands with no meaning attached.

rule.body: Passer un examen is the day you turn up and do it. Réussir un examen is the letter that comes afterwards. English uses one word for both, so what you produce says you were in the room, and nobody has reason to doubt it.

sections.text: Quand j'étais petite, j'ai voulu devenir médecin. J'ai fait mes trois ans de lycée à Nantes et j'ai eu mon bac à dix-sept ans. Après le bac, j'ai fait deux ans de médecine et j'ai raté le concours de deuxième année. J'ai arrêté, et j'ai recommencé en biologie. J'ai obtenu ma licence en trois ans, avec une mention assez bien. Je suis nulle en chimie et j'ai redoublé une seule matière. Aujourd'hui, quand on me demande mon niveau, je réponds que ça correspond à une licence, et que ça m'a pris cinq ans en tout. Personne ne connaît le nom de mon diplôme. Tout le monde comprend cinq ans.

sections.setting: A university admissions office in Lille. She has a form on screen and four boxes left to fill.

sections.body: Say the four lines out loud, once, about your own education. Nothing here is listening, so this one is on you: the point is to find out whether you can get from the level to the equivalence without stopping. If you dry up it will be on line four, and the fix is to have the number of years ready before you start talking.

You name what you studied, with faire de or the plain article
You report the result, out of twenty, without inverting it

questions.why: Le collège runs from eleven to fifteen. Le lycée starts at fifteen.

questions.q: Somebody says they went to college. In French that means they were
questions.why: Un collège takes eleven- to fifteen-year-olds. It is the word that costs people most.

questions.why: Primary school ends with nothing on paper. Le collège ends in le brevet and le lycée in the bac.

sections.say: They will not know the name of your diploma. Say what it was and how long it took.
sections.body: They will not know the name of your diploma. Say what it was and how long it took. You came in able to name school subjects, because the corpus had them and this lesson only put them in your hands. You leave able to give a stranger four lines they can write down: the level, the content, the result and what it comes out at here. Nobody learned the name of your qualification, and nobody needed to.
sections.title: What you can do now
points: the ladder: five rungs, and everything above the lycée is counted in years after the bac
the content: faire de for a school subject, the plain article for a field
the outcome: out of twenty, ten is the pass, and passer is not passed
the translation: four hedges, and the years always map even when the name does not
And if you lose what they asked, lesson 24 in A2 gave you six ways to ask again

recorded.desc: THE FIVE PHRASES, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, IN THE ORDER THE GRID PRINTS THEM AND WITH NO GAP BETWEEN THEM: « depuis une heure », « pendant une heure », « il y a une heure », « dans une heure », « en une heure ». FOUR OF THESE FIVE ARE ALREADY PUBLISHED CARDS and the fifth was written for this lesson, and the whole claim of the grid is that they are five answers about ONE hour. Five separate recordings are five performances: a reader who records them apart will give each its own shape and the learner will hear five different phrases rather than one phrase with five fronts. THE LAST TWO WORDS OF ALL FIVE MUST BE IDENTICAL. « une heure » is the constant. THE LIAISONS ARE NOT OPTIONAL AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME: depuis and dans pull a z across, pendant pulls a t, en pulls an n, and il y a pulls nothing at all. That difference is the only thing separating four of them by ear and a reader who softens it is removing the lesson. KEEP EVERY NASAL CLOSED: pendant is /pɑ̃dɑ̃/ with no n sound behind either vowel and dans is /dɑ̃/ with none behind its one.

THE AUDIO STEP OF THE TENSE TRAP, AND IT IS A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. « J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans. » then « J'habite ici depuis trois ans. », one take, in that order. READ THE WRONG ONE PLAINLY AND AT ORDINARY PACE rather than comically or hesitantly. It is perfectly pronounceable, it is what a fluent English speaker produces on their first attempt, and a reading that signals the error teaches that the error is audible. It is not audible; it is simply wrong about when. The two are FOUR SYLLABLES APART AND NO MORE, and the learner has to hear which four. Do not lean on them and do not swallow them. THEN THE SAME PAIR AGAIN WITH THE WEATHER: « Il a plu depuis ce matin. » then « Il pleut depuis ce matin. » Four lines, one take, wrong and right alternating, and the whole point is that neither wrong one sounds wrong.
clipIds: J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans.
Il a plu depuis ce matin.

recorded.desc: THE AUDIO STEP OF THE IL Y A TRAP, FOUR LINES, ONE TAKE: « Il y a un problème. », « Il y a deux jours. », « il y a une heure », « Il y a une heure de retard. » THE FIRST THREE WORDS OF ALL FOUR ARE IDENTICAL AND MUST SOUND IDENTICAL. That is the entire point of the take: the phrase carries no signal at all about which job it is doing, and everything is decided by what comes after. A reader who puts more weight on « il y a » in the ago lines, or pauses after it in the existence lines, is inventing a distinction French does not make and teaching the learner to listen for something that is not there. THE THIRD AND FOURTH LINES SHARE FOUR WORDS and differ only in what follows. Read them at the same pace and let the difference be the words themselves.
clipIds: Il y a une heure de retard.

recorded.desc: THE TABLE IN LYON. Four people, most of the way through a meal, and her question is ordinary curiosity rather than an interview. It is the commonest thing anybody says to a foreigner and she has asked it a hundred times. THE LEARNER'S OWN LINE IS THE TAKE THAT HAS TO BE RIGHT: « Euh... j'ai été ici... non... je suis... six mois. » is somebody reaching for the tense their own language handed them, hearing it not fit, starting again, and running out of sentence. The « non » is a self-correction and must sound like one: quick, quiet, and to themselves rather than to the table. HER RECOVERY LINE IS THE EXPENSIVE ONE. « Ah, tu es ici depuis six mois. Et avant ? » is her saying the sentence back correctly without noticing she has done it, and moving straight on. Any hint of correction, emphasis on « es », or kindness-about-a-mistake turns the scene into a telling-off and loses the whole point, which is that nothing visibly went wrong.
clipIds: Euh... j'ai été ici... non... je suis... six mois.
Je suis ici depuis six mois.
Ah, tu es ici depuis six mois. Et avant ?

recorded.desc: THE SIX DEPUIS SENTENCES, ONE TAKE, EVEN PACE, READ AS ORDINARY SPEECH AND NOT AS A LIST OF EXAMPLES. Every one of them is in the present tense and the learner is being asked to notice that nothing in the verb marks the three years, the six months or the morning. NOTHING MAY BE STRESSED. A lift on « depuis » would teach that the word is doing something dramatic; it is doing all the work quietly, which is the observation the whole act rests on. THE LIAISON IN « trois ans » IS OBLIGATORY: /tʁwa.zɑ̃/, one word, with the nasal closed. DEPUIS IS /dəpɥi/ WITH THE GLIDE, not /dəpwi/ and not /dəpy.i/. The app writes it duh-PWEE, which is the headword's own spelling and the one five published rows use.
clipIds: Elle habite ici depuis six mois.
Je suis ici depuis six mois.

recorded.desc: DEPUIS AGAINST PENDANT, ADJACENT, ONE TAKE, AND THEY MUST SOUND EQUALLY ORDINARY. « depuis une heure », « pendant une heure », « depuis deux heures », « pendant deux heures ». Both words are everyday and neither is more careful or more formal than the other, so any difference in weight between them teaches a distinction the language does not make: the difference is entirely in what is true about the world, and none of it is in the sound. PENDANT IS TWO CLOSED NASALS, /pɑ̃dɑ̃/, and the app respells it pahⁿ-DAHⁿ after repairing a headword row that had it as pahn-DAHN. A reader who lets an n out of either syllable is saying something else. THE LIAISON DIFFERS BETWEEN THEM: depuis pulls a z into « une », pendant pulls a t. Both are obligatory.

THE DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to every other take in this lesson: here the learner is spelling rather than comparing, and any pair-reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. FIVE OF THE SEVEN ARE A SMALL WORD PLUS A LENGTH AND NOTHING ELSE, and those five matter most: the learner has to hear where one word ends and the next begins across a liaison, so do not run « depuis trois » into a single syllable and do not put a gap in it either. Say it the way somebody would say it. THE LAST TWO ARE THE TRAP PAIR and they are the only two sentences in the lesson short enough to spell letter by letter. Their first three words are identical and must sound identical.

THE CONVERSATION, HER LINES ONLY, ONE TAKE, AS ONE CONTINUOUS EXCHANGE RATHER THAN AS SIX SEPARATE PROMPTS. She is the same neighbour a month later, she has more time, and she is enjoying it. « Tu es ici depuis longtemps ? » and « Tu travailles ici depuis quand ? » both use the word the learner has just spent half an hour on, and NEITHER MAY BE STRESSED: she is not testing anybody, and a lift on « depuis » would turn a conversation into an exercise. « Depuis quand » AT THE END OF THE SENTENCE is the spoken order and it should sound completely natural there, because it is: the written order at the front is the one that sounds careful. Read « On mange dans une heure ? » with the rising intonation of a suggestion rather than a question about a timetable, because it is one.

lessons.intro: Somebody is going to ask you how long you have been here, and the answer is three words long. What makes it hard is not the words: it is that English hands you a past tense for a thing that is still true, and French will not take it. Five small words share this job between them, each one wanting a different shape of time behind it, and once you know what the time is doing the word chooses itself.

pointAhead.body: A single point, measured forwards from now. The present tense again, and for the opposite reason: French uses it for something about to happen, so « je pars dans dix minutes » is a present about a future. So « le film commence dans une heure » is a present tense about something that has not happened, and no French speaker hears it as odd. There is another way to say it, with a verb in front, and that is lesson 15 in A2, which is the very next lesson. Lesson 13 in A2 owns dans in front of a place, which you did yesterday, and this is the other job.
pointAhead.title: Dans, and a present tense doing future work

examples.note: One hour from now, and the film has not started.
The verb is present and the event is not.

theTwoFors.body: Both of these come out as "for" in English and they are not interchangeable in French. Pendant closes the stretch. Depuis leaves it open. The English word is no help, because English uses one word for both and lets the tense carry the difference. French does the opposite: the preposition carries it and the tense follows. So « depuis deux heures » is two hours you are still inside, and « pendant deux heures » is two hours you came out the other side of.
theTwoFors.title: Pendant closes it, depuis leaves it open

examples.note: Out the other side of it.

aTenseComing.body: Ago points at a moment behind you, so the sentence around it has to be in a past tense, and you do not have one. That is not an oversight: the past tense is lesson 16 in A2, two lessons from here. You will meet il y a in this lesson, recognise it when you hear it, and pick it up to use on the day the tense arrives. Everything else here you can say today.
aTenseComing.title: Il y a is waiting for something

examples.note: Shown once, asked for nowhere. Read it and move on.

stillRunning.body: Every one of these five words wants a different shape of time behind it, and the fastest way to the right one is to ask what the thing is doing right now. Still running, and you want depuis. Finished, and you want pendant. Behind you, il y a. Ahead of you, dans. And if the question is not when but how long it took, en. You are not translating; you are checking a fact about the world, and the fact picks the word.
stillRunning.title: The question you ask before you pick

examples.note: Started three years ago and has not stopped.

howLongItTook.body: Dans says when it starts. En says how long it took. One of them is a point and the other is a length, and English uses "in" for both. Four of these five words tell you WHEN. En tells you how wide the whole job was, from the moment it started to the moment it finished. « Je pars dans dix minutes » is a departure time. « Je finis en dix minutes » is a stopwatch. And this is the one card the app's published French never made: the other four exist, side by side, and this one had to be written.
howLongItTook.title: En answers a different question

The same two hours as depuis and pendant, answering a third question.

whatComesNext.body: Lesson 5 in A2 gave this pattern its name on venir de: one form, two jobs, and the word after it settles which. Here it is three words instead of two. « Il y a » with a thing behind it says that thing exists. « Il y a » with a measurement behind it, and nothing after the measurement, says how far back. Nothing about the three words changes and nothing ever will, so there is no spelling to learn and no sound to catch. There is only the next word.
whatComesNext.title: You have had this shape before

examples.note: A measurement, and then a full stop. So it is a distance back.

presentNotPerfect.body: English says I have lived here. French says I live here, and adds depuis to say since when. The verb never moves. That is the whole of it, and it is the single place at this level where translating word for word produces something a French listener cannot decode. « J'ai habité ici depuis trois ans » does not sound like a mistake to them; it sounds like you moved out three years ago, which is the opposite of what you meant. Across every published French sentence in this app, 560 hold depuis and 31 of those sit beside a past tense. 447 hold pendant and 97 do.
presentNotPerfect.title: The verb does not move

measurementThenStop.body: A measurement and then a full stop means ago. A time word still being described is a thing. That last clause is not a decoration. « Il y a une heure » is an hour ago and « il y a une heure de retard » is an hour of delay, and the first four words are identical. In this app's published French, 33 sentences use it for ago and 130 use it for there is, and only two put anything at all after the measurement.

sections.say: A single point, measured forwards from now. The present tense again, and for the opposite reason: French uses it for something about to happen, so « je pars dans dix minutes » is a present about a future. French says « je pars dans dix minutes » with a present tense, and that is correct as it stands. The other way of saying it is lesson 15 in A2, which is next.

sections.say: Dans says when it starts. En says how long it took. One of them is a point and the other is a length, and English uses "in" for both. En also means how long something takes and dans also means how far ahead something is, and both of those are lesson 14 in A2, which is the very next lesson.

sections.text: Je suis à Lyon depuis six mois. J’habite dans le quartier de la Guillotière, et je travaille dans une école depuis le mois de mars. Le matin, je prends le tram : il passe toutes les six minutes, alors je ne pars jamais plus de dix minutes avant le cours. Le soir, je lis pendant une heure, toujours à la même table du même café. Il y a un homme qui vient tous les jours à la même heure, et il ne parle à personne. Ma voisine me demande souvent depuis quand je suis ici. Je réponds « depuis six mois », et elle dit toujours la même chose : « Déjà ? »
sections.title: Six Months In Lyon

glossary.note: A part of a city. Nothing about it is this lesson.

Joins a fact to what follows from it.

questions.a: Being in Lyon since six months ago, and working at a school since March. Both are still true, so French keeps the verb in the present. English would use "have been" for both and move the verb; French does not.
questions.q: Every verb in this passage is in the present tense, and two of the sentences are about things that started in the past. Which two, and what makes the present tense correct in both?

questions.a: The hour of reading has both ends on it. It starts, it finishes, and it happens again the next evening. Everything the passage uses depuis for is still going.
questions.q: The passage uses depuis three times and pendant once. What is different about the sentence with pendant in it?

questions.a: It exists. The word after it is un, which is an article and not a measurement, and that settles it before you get to the noun.
questions.q: « Il y a un homme qui vient tous les jours. » Which of the two jobs is il y a doing here, and how can you tell without reading the rest?

questions.a: That she expects the thing to still be true. Depuis quand can only be asked about something that is still running, so the answer will be in the present tense whatever it turns out to be.
questions.q: The neighbour asks « depuis quand ». What does that question tell you about the answer she is expecting?

sections.body: Before you pick the word, ask whether the thing is still running, finished, ahead of you or behind you. The word follows from the answer and never from the English. The clock and the calendar gave you when on a dial and when on a page. These five give you when measured from right now, forwards and backwards, and how wide a stretch was.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: depuis, pendant, il y a, dans, en. Five words, and every one of them wants a different shape of time behind it. Pick the shape first and the word picks itself.
If it is still happening, French keeps it in the present. English says I have lived here. French says I live here, and adds depuis to say since when. The verb never moves.
Both of these come out as "for" in English and they are not interchangeable in French. Pendant closes the stretch. Depuis leaves it open.

You have had this shape before. Lesson 5 in A2 called it what comes next decides, on venir de, and it is the same job here. A measurement and then a full stop means ago. A time word still being described is a thing.
Dans says when it starts. En says how long it took. One of them is a point and the other is a length, and English uses "in" for both.

Il y a for "ago" wants a past tense, and you do not have one yet. It arrives in lesson 16 in A2, and this is the phrase it will arrive holding. French says « je pars dans dix minutes » with a present tense, and that is correct as it stands. The other way of saying it is lesson 15 in A2, which is next.

Lesson 15 in A1 gave you the clock and lesson 13 in A1 gave you the calendar. Lesson 13 in A2 gave you en and dans in front of a place yesterday, and its own line was: À folds the article in. En throws it out. Chez leaves it alone.

errorTriggers.description: Picks the wrong one of the five, usually by translating the English preposition rather than by looking at what the time is doing. "For" gives depuis or pendant, "in" gives dans or en, and English does not distinguish either pair.
Puts the verb in a past tense after depuis, which is the English perfect being translated word for word. The single biggest interference point at this level and the reason this lesson exists.
Swaps the two words that both come out as "for". Pendant closes the stretch and depuis leaves it open, and a learner working from the English has nothing to decide on.

Reads il y a as "there is" where it means ago, or the other way round. The two jobs share all three words and only the next one settles it, which is doctrine §B.7's shape and the second of its four instances.
Merges the two that both come out as "in". Dans is when it starts and en is how long it takes, and learners produce the wrong one about half the time.

grammarAssumed: The full present of être, introduced in a1.06
The full present of avoir, introduced in a1.07
The nine subject pronouns, and that on takes the il form, introduced in a1.05
The numbers from one to a hundred, introduced in a1.02 and a1.27
The twelve month names and en in front of a bare month, introduced in a1.09
Telling the time, and à in front of a clock time, introduced in a1.12
The present of the regular -ER, -IR and -RE verbs, introduced in a2.01, a2.10 and a2.11
en and dans in front of a place, introduced in a2.04
grammarIntroduced: depuis with a present-tense verb to express a situation begun in the past and still obtaining, against the English present perfect which the learner will otherwise calque
depuis taking either a point of origin or a span, with no change to the verb in either case
The opposition between depuis and pendant as open and closed duration, and that English neutralises it under a single preposition
pendant as a bounded span compatible with any tense
il y a plus a completed measurement of time as a deictic point in the past, against il y a plus a nominal as an existential, and that the following constituent is the sole disambiguator
That the existential reading survives a temporal noun where that noun is itself modified, which bounds the rule
dans plus a span as a future point, expressed with a present-tense verb at this trail position
en plus a span as the time taken to complete an action, against dans as the time until it begins
The temporal senses of en and dans as distinct from the locative senses introduced in a2.04

lessons.intro: A screen tells you to do something and there is nobody to ask. Then you have to explain what it said to a person who cannot see it. This lesson is both halves, and the one thing that runs through them: every tech word in French has more than one name, and which one you use says who you think is listening.

menu.body: A list of options read out by a machine, each one ending in a number to press. It plays once at its own speed and there is nobody to ask. Listen for the number and for the one word that tells you which option is yours, not for the whole sentence.
menu.title: The recorded menu

examples.note: The word is connexion. The number is 1.
The word is technicien. The number is 3.

wifi.body: French took the word and not the pronunciation. It is two clean syllables, wee then fee, with the stress on the second. Say it the English way to a French technician and the sentence stops there, which is a strange way to lose a conversation about a router.
wifi.title: Said weefee, not why-fye

examples.note: The respelling is the whole lesson.

voice.body: One object, more than one name, and the name you pick says who you think you are speaking to. A screen, a support agent and a friend do not use the same word for the same thing. Nothing here is more polite than anything else; two of the three are simply wrong for the person in front of you.
voice.title: Who the word is talking to

examples.note: What an agent says, and what Canada writes.
What a friend in France says.

screen.body: An interface tells you to do things. It does not ask, it does not explain, and it will not say it again differently if you did not follow. These are fixed strings: learn each one whole, with what it means you should do next, the way you learned bonjour.
screen.title: What a screen says to you

examples.note: It wants the code, now, in that box.

borrowed.body: French borrows an English tech word, official French translates it, and Quebec resists hardest. Some words go one way only. Some have both a borrowed and a translated form, and then which one you use is a regional signal rather than a matter of being right.
borrowed.title: Taken, translated, or both

examples.note: Translated, and the English word is not used.

invisible.body: In a shop you can point. On a support line the other person has nothing but what you say, so you have to give four things nobody asks you for: what happened, when it started, what you already tried, and what the message said. That is the whole call.
invisible.title: They cannot see your screen

sections.text: AVIS AUX USAGERS. En raison d'une maintenance, le service de demande en ligne est indisponible du vendredi 18 h au lundi 8 h. Pendant cette période, il n'est pas possible de créer un compte ni de déposer un dossier. Les dossiers déjà déposés sont conservés et seront traités normalement. Si vous avez reçu un code de vérification avant le vendredi 18 h, ce code reste valable pendant sept jours. Pour toute question urgente, veuillez appeler le 3939 du lundi au vendredi. Nous vous remercions de votre compréhension.

glossary.note: The word a French service uses instead of down. It says nothing about why.
Borrowed straight from English, and pronounced the French way: [mehⁿ-tuh-NAHⁿSS].
Literally to put down. It is the verb every French administration uses for handing in a file.
The whole bundle of papers about you. Not a folder on a computer, in this sentence.
Nothing you already sent has been lost. This is the sentence people miss.
Still good, still usable. A ticket, a code and a passport are all valable.
What a public service calls the people who use it. A shop would say clients.
The closing formula. It means the notice is over, not that anything will be explained.

questions.a: Yes. Les dossiers déjà déposés sont conservés, and they will be processed as normal.
questions.q: You started an application on Thursday. Is it still there?

questions.a: No. The outage runs from Friday 18h to Monday 8h, and creating an account is named as one of the two things you cannot do.
questions.q: It is Saturday afternoon. Can you create an account?

questions.a: No. A code received before Friday 18h stays valid for seven days.
questions.q: Your verification code arrived on Thursday evening. Is it dead?

questions.a: The 3939 number, but only Monday to Friday. So on a Saturday the notice offers nothing at all, which it does not say out loud.
questions.q: It is genuinely urgent and it is Saturday. What does the notice offer?

errors.why: Reasonable, because email is what half the internet says and nobody in France would blink. In Quebec courriel is the ordinary word and the borrowed one reads as careless.
errors.right: Je vous envoie mon courriel.
errors.wrong: Je vous envoie mon email. (to an agent in Montreal)

errors.why: Reasonable, because courriel is the official term and being correct is usually safe. Here it is not: it is the word their bank uses and it lands as a joke.
errors.right: Envoie-moi un mail.
errors.wrong: Envoie-moi un courriel. (to a friend in Paris)

errors.why: Reasonable, because French really did take cliquer, scanner and zoomer the same way. This one it did not: télécharger arrived first and holds the ground completely.
errors.right: Je vais télécharger le fichier.
errors.wrong: Je vais downloader le fichier.

errors.why: Reasonable, because so many device words came straight across. Ordinateur is the one French built itself, and it is the borrowing that never happened.
errors.right: Mon ordinateur ne marche pas.
errors.wrong: Mon computer ne marche pas.

errors.why: Reasonable, because everybody drops the ne out loud and you will hear it dropped all day. On the phone to somebody official it is the one place the missing word is heard.
errors.right: Ça ne marche pas.
errors.wrong: Ça marche pas. (to a support agent)

errors.why: Reasonable, because mél is printed on French forms next to Tél. It is an abbreviation for writing, not a word for saying, and said aloud it is the same sound as mail anyway.
errors.right: Mon mail ne marche pas.
errors.wrong: Mon mél ne marche pas. (to anybody, out loud)
