sections.hint: Swipe. Six cards, and the big word is not a word.

cards.body: An -RE verb, so the machine says -u and out comes a word that does not exist. It is the commonest wrong past form an English speaker produces, and it comes from following a rule correctly.
cards.head: prendu
cards.label: prendre

cards.body: The same machine on the same kind of verb, and the same non-word out of the other end. Mettre and prendre are in one group and the group is -is.
cards.head: mettu
cards.label: mettre

cards.body: Faire ends in -re, so the machine reaches for -u again. Nothing about fait can be got from faire and it is the commonest verb in the whole set.
cards.head: faisu
cards.label: faire

cards.body: An -IR verb, so the machine says -i, and this time the real form ends in a t. Four verbs do this and they are the whole -ert group.
cards.head: ouvri
cards.label: ouvrir

cards.body: Another -IR verb, and the machine says -i again. This one lands in the -u group instead, which is the group that takes members from everywhere.
cards.head: couri
cards.label: courir

cards.body: There is no rule at all for an -OIR verb in lesson 16 in A2, so the machine has nothing to run and the learner guesses. Every -OIR verb in this lesson is in the -u group.

rule.body: Do not build these. Reach for the group it is in. An -RE verb can land in -is, an -IR verb in -u or in -ert. The end of the naming form tells you what the machine would do, not what the language has.
rule.title: The ending of the verb decides nothing

sections.title: Two Letters, One Sound

questions.q: J'ai eu peur. What comes out for those two letters?
questions.why: The e is not said and the u is the French u. Two letters, one sound, and it is not the sound either letter suggests.

questions.q: J'ai bu un café against J'ai eu peur. What is the difference?
questions.why: The vowel is identical. Bu is that vowel with a b in front of it and eu is the same vowel with nothing in front, which is what makes eu the hardest of the three to catch.

questions.q: Non, je n'ai pas eu le temps. Where is it in this one?
questions.why: In the gap, where lesson 16 in A2 put it, and it is very short. This is where it will actually arrive when somebody says it to you.

questions.q: Why is this the one form in the lesson you cannot learn from the page?
questions.why: You cannot read this one and get it right. Read it before you have heard it and you will put an o or an uh in it every time, which is the opposite of everything else in this lesson.
opts: Because the spelling gives you no clue at all about the sound
Because it changes for the person

sections.say: Four cards and then six to prove it. Nothing you hear will help on any of them: dû and du are one sound and the difference is entirely on paper.

rule.body: The little roof is the only thing keeping the past form of devoir apart from du, which means "some". It is the one accent in this set that changes what a word means.

questions.q: faire. Which group is its past form in?
questions.why: None. fait ends in a t and it is not in the -it group: the -it group is verbs whose naming form ends in -ire or -uire. faire is one of the five with no group, and it is the commonest verb of the thirty-three.

sections.body: Say the first word, and while it is out of your mouth ask which of the five groups the verb is in rather than what its ending should be. Four of the groups have an ending and the fifth is five words you have to have. Lesson 16 in A2 gave you the whole shape one lesson ago: a form of avoir, then the second word, and the small ones in the gap. Nothing about that changes here and none of it is taught again. What changes is the second word, for thirty-three verbs, and twenty-eight of the thirty-three fall into four groups by their ending.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Do not build these. Reach for the group it is in. They are not thirty-three separate facts. Twenty-eight of them fall into four groups by their ending, and five are in no group at all.
-is, -it, -u and -ert, and the -u group is 13 of the thirty-three on its own.
Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. That is lesson 9's line and it is exactly as true of the past form as it was of the present.
Five of them belong to nothing. Two come from a verb you cannot see in them, one is shorter than its verb, and one is a different word.
You cannot read this one and get it right. Read it before you have heard it and you will put an o or an uh in it every time, which is the opposite of everything else in this lesson.

Nothing in this app can test it. A typed answer, a spot-the-error and the dictée all strip accents before comparing, so all three would accept du and say it was right. The two words are one sound, so no listening question can ask either.
Five of them are already words you may have met, and none was labelled a past form when you did. A form used often enough stops being a form and becomes a word.

Three of these put a different word in front instead of avoir, and the form is all this lesson teaches you about them. Which verbs do it, and what happens to the form afterwards, is lesson 18 in A2. You will need all of this again at lesson 30 in A2, where the whole conversation is about what you studied and how it went.

errorTriggers.description: Runs lesson 16 in A2's regular rule on an irregular verb and produces a word that does not exist: « j'ai prendu », « j'ai ouvri ». THE ERROR THIS LESSON EXISTS TO PREVENT, and it is produced by applying a rule correctly rather than by carelessness, which is why it survives correction.

Puts a form in the group its naming form points at: courir into -i because it ends in -ir, prendre into -u because it ends in -re. It comes from treating the ending of the naming form as evidence, which is exactly what lesson 16 in A2 taught and exactly what does not hold here.

Learns a compound verb as a separate item instead of covering its front: treats « repris » as a thirty-fourth thing to memorise. It costs nothing today and it is the reason the list feels infinite, because every compound of every member looks like a new fact.

Reads « eu » and says something with an o or an uh in it. THE ONE ERROR IN THIS LESSON THAT IS ABOUT A SOUND: the two letters spell a single French u and nothing about them suggests it, so a learner who meets the form on paper before hearing it says it wrongly every time.

Writes « du » for the past form of devoir. The only accent in the set that changes what a word means, and the one error in the lesson that no typed surface, no spot-the-error and no listening question in this app can catch, because all three strip it or cannot hear it.

Leaves the naming form behind avoir: « j'ai prendre le bus ». It is lesson 16 in A2's error arriving by a new route, in which the learner looks for the past form, does not find one, and ships the verb as it stands rather than producing a non-word.

grammarAssumed: The passé composé with avoir, in six persons, introduced in a2.05
The regular past participle: -er to -é, -ir to -i, -re to -u, introduced in a2.05
That ne … pas encloses the auxiliary and not the participle, introduced in a2.05
That the participle is invariable after avoir, introduced in a2.05
The placement of a short adverb between auxiliary and participle, introduced in a2.05
The present of prendre, mettre and their compounds, and the compound-verb principle, introduced in a2.15
The present of aller, venir and tenir, introduced in a2.02
The present of faire, dire and lire, introduced in a2.12
The present of vouloir, pouvoir and devoir, introduced in a2.13
The present of savoir and connaître, introduced in a2.14
grammarIntroduced: The irregular past participles, thirty-three forms, presented as four morphological classes by termination (-is, -it, -u, -ert) plus a residue of five suppletive or unclassifiable forms
That the conjugation class of the infinitive does not predict the participle class, so an -RE verb may give -is, an -IR verb -u or -ert, and an -OIR verb -u
That a prefixed verb takes the participle of its base verb, extending a2.15's compound principle from the present to the past participle
The participle of avoir as eu, /y/, an orthography with no phonetic correspondence to its letters
The circumflex on dû as the sole orthographic distinction from the partitive du, and its loss in the feminine due
That five participles in the set are lexicalised as independent adjectives or nouns in the published corpus
être as auxiliary is named for venu, né and mort and reserved for a2.21; participle agreement is neither taught nor exemplified here

recorded.desc: Four cards, the same person said twice on each. ONE TAKE PER CARD. The stressed form carries the phrase stress because it ends the phrase; do not add more than that.
Four sentences, read as ordinary speech. In Moi, je suis prêt the moi is set off by a short pause and je is quick and unstressed.
ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, the four lines adjacent and in order. elle and elles MUST be read identically: no audible s, no lengthening. The first question depends on it.
Je lui parle has lui unstressed; Je parle avec lui has lui carrying the stress. sans elle is sahⁿ ZEHL, the z moved across, never a pause before elle.

c'est elle and c'est eux carry the liaison t onto the pronoun: seh TEHL, seh TUH. Ce sont eux is suh sohⁿ TUH. Read the written and said pair at the same pace; the difference is which one people choose, not how it sounds.
The wrong version is in promptSound and must be read at the same pace and intonation as the right one. Only the correct fr is played in the audio step.
Four chunks the learner has already met, read as ordinary speech. Excusez-moi as one word with the stress on moi.

lessons.intro: English says I before a verb and me everywhere else, and you pick between them without thinking. French does the same with je and moi, and with three more pairs. You already say Et toi ? and chez moi. This lesson is the rule behind them.

known.body: Et toi ? since lesson 1 in A1. Chez moi since lesson 13 in A2. Moi non plus since lesson 21 in A1. Every one of them is this set, and every one follows the same rule: no verb right after it.
known.title: You have been saying these for months

cestEux.body: Ce sont eux is what you write. C'est eux is what you will hear, and it is correct French too. With moi, toi, lui, elle, nous and vous there is only c'est.
cestEux.title: What you write, what you say

himOnly.body: In front of a verb, lui is him or her, and lesson 22 in A2 made a point of it. After a little word it is him and nothing else. For her, say elle: avec elle, sans elle, pour elle.
himOnly.title: The lui that keeps its gender

examples.note: in front of the verb, him or her

euxElles.body: eux is them for men, and for any group with a man in it. elles is them only when every person is a woman. It works the way ils and elles already do.
euxElles.title: One man in the group is enough

onItsOwn.body: je, tu, il and ils need a verb straight after them (only ne or a small word like le or lui can squeeze in between). When the person is on its own, after a little word, after c'est, as a one-word answer or out in front, French uses the other set. Lesson 9 in A1 gave you the first set and saved this one for later.
onItsOwn.title: No verb right after it

examples.note: a verb right after it, so je

sameFour.body: elle, nous, vous and elles are the same word in both jobs. Only je, tu, il and ils change: moi, toi, lui, eux. So the choice only ever matters for four people, and those four are the ones people say most.
sameFour.title: Half of them you already have

sections.body: The left column is the set lesson 9 in A1 gave you, and it only ever goes right in front of a verb. The middle column is everything else: after a little word like avec, sans, pour or chez; after c'est; alone as an answer; out in front for weight, with the left-hand word coming back for the verb; after que in a comparison; and joined with et. Four rows change and four do not. After a little word, lui is him only and her is elle, and eux covers any group with a man in it.

sections.text: Ce soir, Marc et Julie font une fête chez eux. Moi, je viens avec ma sœur Léa. Elle ne connaît pas les autres invités, alors elle reste à côté de moi. grammarIntroduced: The stressed (disjunctive) pronouns moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles as a set, completing the deferral on a1.05 sheet-stressed

Distribution: after a preposition, after c'est, as a verbless answer, left-dislocated for emphasis with the clitic subject resumed, after que in a comparison, and in coordinated subjects resumed by nous or vous
That four forms differ from the subject clitics (moi, toi, lui, eux) and four are homographic with them (elle, nous, vous, elles)
That stressed lui is masculine only, against the gender-neutral indirect-object lui of a2.24
eux for masculine or mixed plural reference, elles for all-feminine
The register pair ce sont eux (written) and c'est eux (spoken)
Recognition only of the stressed pronoun after an affirmative imperative (Excusez-moi, Montrez-moi); the imperative itself is not taught

recorded.desc: IL PARLE, IL FINIT AND IL VEND, ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE, ONE VOICE, IN THAT ORDER, AND THE THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE IN LENGTH AND IN WEIGHT. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson. The three endings are one letter, two letters and none, and not one of them is a sound: eel parl ee-SEE, eel fee-nee ee-SEE, eel vahⁿ ee-SEE. The third one must not be clipped, hurried or allowed to trail off because it is shorter on the page, and the first two must not have their endings leaned on because they have one. If a listener can tell from the audio alone which of the three has the shortest spelling, the recording has taught the opposite of what the screen teaches. Read them at conversational pace, one after another, with no teaching pause between them. RECORDED APART, IN THREE SESSIONS, the learner compares three performances instead of three cells and the whole screen is lost.

THE D PAIRS, EACH PAIR IN ONE TAKE BACK TO BACK, SINGULAR THEN PLURAL: Il vend ici / Ils vendent ici, Elle rend le livre / Elles rendent le livre, Il descend ici / Ils descendent ici. Here the difference MUST be audible, which is the opposite instruction from the cells clip and is why the two are separate recordings. The plural ends on a d and the singular does not: vahⁿ, then vahⁿd. It is a released consonant at the very end of the word, not a syllable, so do not put a vowel after it and do not lengthen it. In every pair the PRONOUN must sound identical on both sides, because it is: il and ils are one sound and so are elle and elles. Any difference in the pronoun, in pace or in emphasis destroys the pair, because the learner will use it instead of the d. The scene break card and the trap drill both play from this clip and both need the wrong-then-right ordering preserved.

THE SINGULAR TRIPLE, IN ONE TAKE, AND THE THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. je vends, tu vends, il vend, then je réponds, tu réponds, il répond. Do not help. Do not differentiate them, do not touch the final letter, do not let the s of vends or the d of vend surface in any of the three. Two of the three carry letters the third does not and none of those letters is a sound, which is the entire claim of the mission this plays under. If a listener can tell any of these three apart from the audio alone, the recording has taught the opposite of what the lesson teaches. Read them at conversational pace, one after another, with no pause for teaching.

All six forms as one continuous take, in the usual pronoun order (je, tu, il, nous, vous, ils), by one voice at one speed, then the eleven dictée sentences in the same take. The first three must be INDISTINGUISHABLE from each other, because they are: three spellings and one sound. The fourth and fifth add a whole syllable each and the d in front of it is said. The sixth adds only the d. Do not stress the verb anywhere; the weight belongs at the end of the phrase. The dictée sentences are the ones a learner will replay four times while typing, so they need to be even in pace and completely flat in emphasis: any lean on an ending is a hint the screen is not supposed to give.

The seven naming forms, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice. Every one of them ends in the same DR sound and that sameness is the teaching: the learner should come away hearing -dre as one ending rather than seven word-endings. The nasal vowel before the d is a vowel and not an N: vahⁿdr, not van-dr. Do not vary the intonation to keep the list interesting. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. One woman in her fifties at an ordinary market pace, in a hurry in the way somebody with a list is in a hurry, and entirely unbothered. The last line (« D'accord, merci. Je vais voir l'autre rangée. ») must be brisk and pleasant rather than pointed: the whole scene turns on nobody minding and nobody checking, so any hint of doubt or of correction in her voice would destroy it. She has already decided and she is being polite about it.
clipIds: Bonjour. Je cherche les fromages de la ferme.

lessons.intro: The last of the three regular patterns, and the one where the il form is finished before you expect it to be. Six endings, five of which you already have, and one of which is not there at all.

stem.body: vendre gives vend-. attendre gives attend-. perdre gives perd-. Take the last two letters off the naming form and what is left does not move, whoever is speaking. That is the same two letters you took off parler and off finir, and the same machine lesson 1 in A2 gave you. Nothing new has happened to the method. What is new is one of the six things you put on the end of it.
stem.title: What is left when -re comes off

examples.note: vend- with the je ending on it.
The same vend-, with the nous ending, which you can hear.

theD.body: Every one of these verbs has a d at the end of its stem, and a French consonant at the end of a word is not said while the same consonant in the middle of one is. il vend is vahⁿ and ils vendent is vahⁿd, because the -ent puts letters after the d even though the -ent itself is silent. So the three singular forms lose the d and the three plural forms keep it. That is the one thing your ear can do for you here, and it does nothing at all for the three that matter most.
theD.title: Silent at the end, said in the middle

examples.note: The same verb with letters after the d, so the d arrives.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, which on a -re verb means on vend and never on vendons: the spoken we takes the bare form, so the commonest way of saying we in French lands on the one cell of the six where nothing is written after the stem at all.
nousOn.title: The we that writes nothing

examples.note: The written one, with an ending you can hear.
The spoken one, taking the il form and writing nothing.

nothing.body: The il form of a regular -re verb is the stem and then the page stops. Not a silent letter you cannot hear, the way -e and -es and -ent are silent: there is no letter. il vend, elle attend, on répond. It looks short because it is short, and the reason it feels wrong is that the two lessons before this one both put something there. Nothing is missing and nothing has been taken away.
nothing.title: il vend, and there is no more of it

examples.note: The stem, and then the full stop.
The same thing on a second verb, so it is a rule and not a fact about vendre.

threeGroups.body: One frame, three verbs, three groups. il parle takes an -e, il finit takes an -it, il vend takes nothing at all. All three endings are inaudible, so this is a page distinction from beginning to end and no recording will ever help you with it. Those three cells are the whole of what the three regular patterns disagree about on the il form, and once you have them there is no fourth group waiting.
threeGroups.title: il parle, il finit, il vend

examples.note: One letter, from the group you met first.

notThisFamily.body: prendre, mettre and battre end in -re and are built another way, and so are apprendre, comprendre, permettre, promettre and combattre. prendre is one of the most common verbs in the language, so you will meet it long before anybody teaches it to you. Run this pattern on it and you produce a form no French speaker says. Knowing that a verb is not in this family is worth as much as building the ones that are, and lesson 9 in A2 is where the other family is taught.
notThisFamily.term: the ones that only look like it
notThisFamily.title: Ending in -re is not enough

examples.note: This one is in the family, and the il form is the bare stem.
And so is this one, whatever the length of the naming form suggests.

theSingularThree.body: Three spellings and one sound. -s, -s and nothing all arrive as nothing, exactly the way -e, -es and -ent did on an -er verb in lesson 1 in A2 and -is, -is and -it did on an -ir verb in lesson 3 in A2. So in the singular the pronoun is still carrying the person on its own, and the only place these three differ is the page. This is why the dictée in this lesson is longer than the listening.
theSingularThree.title: je vends, tu vends, il vend

examples.note: Ends in nothing, and is said exactly the same way.

sections.body: Three groups, three endings on the il form, and one of them is nothing. The two earlier units each shipped a sheet of their own: lesson 1 in A2 holds the -er endings in full and lesson 3 in A2 holds the -ir endings in full, and both are still the place to go for one pattern on its own. Neither of them could hold the table above, because neither of them knew the other two patterns existed yet. This one does, and it is the last one that will be needed, because there is no fourth regular group. Read the third row of it and nothing else if you are in a hurry: parle, finit, vend. One letter, two letters, none, and not one of the three reaches the ear. That is the whole of what the three regular patterns disagree about on the il form, and it is why this lesson spends its weight on writing rather than on listening. The rest of the table is the part you could have worked out: the plural endings are the same three you have had since lesson 1 in A2, and the -s on je and tu is the same silent -s you have been writing since lesson 10 in A1.
sections.title: Why this sheet holds three patterns and not one

sections.body: The method has not changed across three units and it will not change again: find the stem, add the person. What each unit gave you was a different short set of endings to add, and with this one the set is complete. Everything after it in this level is a verb that has to be memorised outright, starting with the three that end in -re and are built another way. prendre, mettre, battre and their compounds apprendre, comprendre, permettre, promettre, combattre are all at lesson 9 in A2, and one of them is among the most common verbs in the language, so you will meet it long before you are taught it. The habit worth carrying out of this lesson is a writing habit rather than a listening one. You have now met a form that is complete while looking unfinished, and the thing to do about it is to stop. The one thing your ear will give you here is the d: silent at the end of a word, said whenever letters follow it, which means the three plural forms have it and the three singular forms do not.
sections.title: What carries forward

sections.title: The Whole System, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have taken a third naming form apart and found the same two letters coming off it. You have put six endings on the stem, one of which is not there, and you have written the form for a verb this lesson never showed you. You know which three cells are one sound and which three wake the d up, and you know the three verbs that end the same way and are built another. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

on vend

rounds.say: One frame, three verbs. Only one of them writes nothing.
rounds.label: Three groups, three endings

questions.q: il parle, il finit, il vend. How many letters do the three endings have between them?
questions.why: One for -e, two for -it, and none at all for the third. All three are silent, which is why the page is the only place they exist.

questions.q: Il ___ ici. (parler)
questions.why: An -er verb takes -e on il. It is silent, and it is still a letter you have to write.
accept: parle
il parle
questions.answer: parle

questions.q: Il ___ ici. (finir)
questions.why: An -ir verb takes -it on il. Also silent, also two letters you have to write.
accept: finit
il finit
questions.answer: finit

questions.q: Fix this. One man, at the market: « Il vende le pain. »
questions.why: The -e belongs to the -er verbs. Carrying it across to a -re verb is the commonest way this goes wrong, because the -er pattern was learned first.
accept: Il vend le pain
vend
questions.answer: Il vend le pain.

questions.q: Which group writes nothing on the il form?
questions.why: Only this one. -er takes -e and -ir takes -it, and both of those are letters even though neither is a sound.

questions.q: Elles ___ le livre. (rendre)
questions.why: A plural subject takes -ent, and the d in front of it is said. elle and elles are one sound, so the d is the only audible sign of the number.
accept: rendent
elles rendent
questions.answer: rendent

rounds.say: The one thing your ear can do here, and the three things it cannot.
rounds.label: What the d tells you

questions.q: Listen. One person, or several?
questions.say: Ils vendent ici.
questions.why: A d arrived at the end of the verb. The pronoun ils is said exactly like il, so that d is the whole of the evidence.
opts: It is not a real form
Either, the sound does not say

questions.q: Listen. elle and elles are said the same. What told you it was one?
questions.say: Elle rend le livre.
questions.why: The verb stopped at the vowel. Nothing follows the d in the singular, so the d is at the end of the word and a French word does not say it there.
opts: No d at the end of the verb

questions.q: Tap the letters you do not say.
questions.why: Just the d, and only because it is at the end. Put anything after it, as -ons and -ez and -ent all do, and it comes back.

questions.q: Which of these could your ear NOT separate?
questions.why: Both are singular, both lose the d, and one of them writes an s the other does not. Three spellings and one sound is still true here.

questions.q: Listen. Which one is it?
questions.say: Nous vendons ici.
questions.why: Only one of these four ends on a nasal vowel after the d. The others are the bare form, a d on its own, and an -ay.

questions.q: Listen. How many people?
questions.say: Il descend ici.
questions.why: Nothing after the vowel, so the d is silent and the subject is singular. The plural of this verb would have put the d back.
opts: Several, and the verb says so
One, and the verb says so
Several, and the verb does not say so

rounds.say: Ending in -re is not enough. Two of these are about the ones that are not yours.
rounds.label: Where the family stops

questions.q: Which of these four verbs is in this lesson family?
questions.why: Only descendre. The other three end in -re and are built another way, and nothing in the naming form tells you that.

questions.q: prendre, mettre and battre all end in -re. Where are they taught?
questions.why: Lesson 9 in A2 takes all three and their compounds together. Until then, recognising that a verb is not in this family is the whole of what you need.
opts: Nowhere, they are learned one at a time

questions.q: Ils ___ le train. (entendre)
questions.why: Stem entend-, plural ending -ent. The -ent is silent and it still puts letters after the d, so the d is said.
accept: entendent
ils entendent
questions.answer: entendent

questions.q: Say it: he sells here.
questions.why: Stop at the vowel. If a d arrives at the end of the verb you have said several people, and this is the one place that mistake is audible.

questions.q: Fix this. The neighbours, at the next table: « Ils vend des fruits. »
questions.why: The written s of ils is silent, so the verb has to carry the number on its own. The bare stem is the singular cell and gives it away.
accept: Ils vendent des fruits
vendent
questions.answer: Ils vendent des fruits.

questions.q: Il ___ ici. (descendre)
questions.why: The longest naming form in the set and the shortest il form. descendre gives descend-, and the il cell writes nothing after it.
accept: descend
il descend
questions.answer: descend

sections.say: Four things, and then the pattern stops being regular.
sections.body: You can build the present tense of any regular -re verb, including ones nobody has shown you, and you can write the one cell in the three regular patterns where the page stops at the stem. Three groups, three endings on the il form, and one of them is nothing. That set is now finished: lesson 1 in A2 and lesson 3 in A2 gave you the other two and there is no fourth. What is left in this level are the verbs that had to be memorised outright, and the next unit begins them.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: The il form takes nothing, and that is the ending.
Cut the last two letters off the naming form, then put the person on what is left.
je and tu take an s, nous vous and ils take the endings you already had, and il takes nothing.
The d at the end of the stem is said whenever something follows it, and prendre, mettre, battre are not in this family at all.

errorTriggers.description: Writes the bare stem where je or tu is the subject, because the il form was the one that had to be learned.
Puts something after the stem on the il form: il vende, il vends, il vendt. The form looks unfinished and the reflex is to finish it.
Carries another group's third-person ending across: il vende with lesson 1's -e, or il vendit with lesson 3's -it.
Says the d where it is silent or drops it where it is said, so a singular arrives sounding plural or the other way round.
Runs the vendre model on prendre, mettre or battre, because the naming form looks identical.

grammarAssumed: The six subject pronouns and the nine they cover, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
The present tense of regular -er verbs as a stem plus six endings, introduced in a2.01
That -e, -es and -ent are silent and -ons and -ez are not, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -ir verbs, introduced in a2.10
nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one, introduced in a2.01
grammarIntroduced: The present tense of regular -re verbs, as a stem plus six endings
That the third-person singular of a regular -re verb carries no written ending at all
That the three regular groups differ in the third person by one letter, two letters and none
That the singular of a regular -re verb is three spellings and one sound
That a stem-final d is silent at the end of a word and said when letters follow it
That a verb ending in -re is not necessarily in this family

lessons.intro: Comparing two things in French is one sentence shape with one word in the middle of it, and that word is the whole choice. Get the shape once and it takes any describing word you will ever learn. Then the article arrives, and it brings an ending nobody can hear.

most.body: Put le, la or les in front of the same frame and you have gone from more than that one to more than all of them. Nothing else changes. The article is also what carries the agreement, so it is the word to pick first and the word that decides the ending.
most.title: The article does the work

examples.note: and it works for the worst as well

than.body: que is what the second thing hangs off, and nothing else does that job: you can never put it straight after the describing word. Il est plus grand. on its own is grammatical and unfinished, exactly the way taller is in English. Say it to somebody who does not already know what you are comparing to, and the first thing they ask is plus grand que qui.
than.title: que, and it is not optional

agree.body: Lesson 10 in A2 taught that a describing word matches what it describes. Nothing about the frame suspends that. le plus grand jardin, la plus grande maison, les plus grands jardins, les plus grandes maisons: four spellings, and two of them sound identical, so this is a thing you can only get right in writing.
agree.title: The ending still follows the noun

examples.note: and meilleure agrees the same way

frame.body: Something, then a middle word, then a describing word, then que, then the thing you are comparing it to. Those five slots stay where they are for every comparison you will ever make in French. You are never building a new sentence shape, only dropping different words into the same one.
frame.title: The part that never moves

better.body: English has one better and French splits it. meilleur goes with a noun and behaves like any describing word, with four endings. mieux goes with a verb and never changes. The corpus says mieux about six and a half times as often as meilleur, so if you can only keep one, keep that one.
better.title: Two words for one English one

examples.note: with chante, and the article in front: le mieux

middle.body: plus, moins or aussi. Three words, and picking one of them is the entire decision. Everything before it and everything after it stays exactly as it was, which is why you can do this at speed with a describing word you have only just learned.
middle.title: The one word that changes

examples.note: plus, in the corpus long before this lesson
aussi, and the describing word agrees

drills.coach: The frame is already right. Read the English and pick which of the three goes in the middle.
drills.title: Three words, one slot

drills.q: He meant he is taller than his brother. Which one says that?
drills.why: The first is correct French and means he is tall. The third makes him the tallest of a group. Only the second compares two people.
opts: Il est plus grand que son frère.
drills.coach: A comparison names both things. If you can only find one of them, the sentence is half said.
drills.title: And the second thing

drills.coach: Two piles. One thing, or several. The ending is the only thing that tells you, and only in writing.
drills.title: The last letter

drills.q: Ce gâteau est ... que l'autre. Which word?
drills.why: est, so it is describing the cake and it is meilleur. mieux would be describing an action, and there is no action here.
drills.coach: Look at the word in front of the gap. est, or something being done.
drills.title: Which better word

sheets.title: The whole frame, on one page

sections.body: The left column is the only thing that changes. Everything to the right of it is the frame, and the frame is the same for every describing word in the language. The bottom three rows are the two words that refuse the frame and the one that does not, which is the part worth screenshotting.
sections.title: How to read this

rowDetails.body: The s is silent in front of a describing word and comes back when nothing follows it. plü grand, and PLÜSS on its own.
rowDetails.title: plus, and what it means

rowDetails.body: English usually flips it and says shorter. French says less tall and is happy with it.
rowDetails.title: moins, and what it means

rowDetails.body: There is no superlative of aussi. Nothing can be the most equal, so the third column is empty on purpose.
rowDetails.title: aussi, and what it means

rowDetails.body: The plain form. Nothing is added, and this is the one every other cell is built from.
rowDetails.title: One masculine thing

rowDetails.body: grande and grandes are the only forms of the four where the d is pronounced. The e wakes it up; the s changes nothing.
rowDetails.title: One feminine thing, and you can hear it

rowDetails.body: An s on the article and an s on the describing word, and neither of them is said. It sounds exactly like the singular.
rowDetails.title: Several masculine things

rowDetails.body: les plus grandes sounds exactly like la plus grande. Nothing in speech separates them, which is why every scored question on this rule is typed.
rowDetails.title: Several feminine things, and it exists only on paper

rowDetails.body: Refuses plus. meilleur has all four endings: meilleur, meilleure, meilleurs, meilleures.
rowDetails.title: bon: good, better, best

rowDetails.body: Refuses plus. mieux never changes, for anybody. It is the one the corpus uses six and a half times as often as meilleur.
rowDetails.title: bien: well, better, best

rowDetails.body: Takes BOTH, and both are ordinary. So the rule is not that plus is forbidden; it is that exactly two words have their own form.
rowDetails.title: mauvais: bad, worse, worst

beats.text: Saturday morning at the cheese counter. Two wedges on the paper, one from each end of the case. The woman behind it has already cut a sliver off each and is waiting to hear which one goes in the bag.

beats.en: So, which one do you prefer?

beats.text: He has the words. He has had grand and bon and fort since his first month. He starts, and four words in he hears himself.

beats.en: The first one is more good...

cards.fr: plus
cards.body: The s hides in front of a consonant, comes back as a z in front of a vowel, and is said in full when nothing follows it.

cards.fr: moins
cards.body: You would say shorter; French says less tall. Both are ordinary. This one takes a fortnight to stop feeling translated.

cards.fr: aussi
cards.body: The same word that means also. Sitting between est and a describing word, it can only mean as much as.

cards.label: THE SAME

cards.fr: que
cards.body: The second thing hangs off que and off nothing else, so you can never put it straight after the describing word. Leave que out and the sentence is grammatical and unfinished, which is a worse place to be than wrong.
cards.head: and it is not optional

questions.q: The first one. Who is taller?
questions.why: plus puts him above you. The two words on either side of it are identical in all three of the first lines, so the middle one is the whole message.

questions.q: The second one. Who is taller?

questions.q: The third one. Who is taller?

questions.q: The fourth one. Which is longer?

sections.say: Pick the middle word and keep the frame.
sections.text: Nous avons visité deux appartements samedi. Le premier est plus grand que le second, mais il est aussi plus cher. Le second est moins lumineux, et la cuisine y est plus petite. En revanche, il est beaucoup plus proche de la gare, ce qui compte plus que tout le reste pour nous. Le premier a la plus belle vue du quartier, il faut le dire. Le second a le loyer le moins élevé des deux. Nous avons pris le second. C'est le meilleur choix pour cette année, même si ce n'est pas le plus agréable des deux appartements.

cards.fr: plus bon
cards.body: bon has its own comparison and will not take plus. There is no version of this that is merely informal or regional. It is the word from the market stall.
cards.head: French has no plus bon
cards.label: REFUSED

cards.fr: plus bien
cards.body: bien is the other one. Its comparison is mieux and plus bien is the same mistake in the other half of the pair.
cards.head: and no plus bien either

cards.fr: plus mauvais
cards.body: pire and plus mauvais are both ordinary French and both correct. So the rule is not never say plus. It is that two words have their own form.

cards.fr: le mieux de tous
cards.body: le meilleur for a noun, le mieux after a verb. Elle chante le mieux de toute la classe: chante is a verb, so it is mieux with le in front, and de follows it the same way.

rule.body: If the sentence has est, or any form of être, you are describing a thing and it is meilleur. If it has a verb doing something, you are describing the doing and it is mieux. One question, asked once, and it decides.

cards.fr: Elle chante mieux.

cards.fr: Cette tarte est meilleure.

cards.fr: Il travaille mieux.

cards.tip: The other way round: a verb has been given the describing word. mieux.

cards.ipa: /ɛl paʁl mjø kə mwa/
cards.tip: parle is a verb, and que moi finishes it properly.

errors.why: Reasonable, because plus works with every other describing word you own and there is no warning on this one. bon is one of exactly two words in the language that refuse it.
errors.right: Ce gâteau est meilleur que l'autre.
errors.wrong: Ce gâteau est plus bon que l'autre.

errors.why: Reasonable, and it is the same mistake as the one above wearing different clothes. bien is the other of the two, and its own form is mieux.
errors.right: Elle chante mieux que moi.
errors.wrong: Elle chante plus bien que moi.

errors.why: Reasonable, because English stops there too and nothing sounds broken. It is grammatical, and it is unfinished: plus grand than whom. If the brother has not already been mentioned, que son frère is the half that carries the message.
errors.right: Il est plus grand que son frère.
errors.wrong: Il est plus grand. (meaning: taller than his brother)

errors.why: Reasonable, because the ending on jeune does not change and it feels as though nothing has to. The article is carrying the agreement here, which is lesson 10 in A2 working in a position it never showed you.
errors.right: Elle est la plus jeune de la famille.
errors.wrong: Elle est le plus jeune de la famille.

errors.why: Reasonable, because English says in the city and dans is in. After a superlative French says of, every time, and de la contracts to du in front of a masculine one.
errors.right: C'est le plus grand bâtiment de la ville.
errors.wrong: C'est le plus grand bâtiment dans la ville.

questions.q: He is taller than me. Write the whole sentence, starting with Il.
questions.why: Five slots and you filled all five. plus goes in front of the describing word and que brings the other person in.
accept: Il est plus grand que moi
Il est plus grand que moi.

questions.q: He is less tall than me. Same sentence, one word different.
questions.why: Only the middle word moved. English would have reached for shorter and French does not have to.
accept: Il est moins grand que moi
Il est moins grand que moi.

questions.q: He is as tall as me. One word different again.
questions.why: aussi is the level one. The same aussi that means also, in a position where it can only mean this.

Il est plus grand que son frère

Cette rue est aussi longue que l'avenue
Cette rue est aussi longue que lavenue

Le train est plus rapide que le bus.

questions.why: que loses its e in front of a vowel and hier starts with a silent h, so qu'hier. The frame is otherwise untouched.

questions.why: que sits between the describing word and the second thing, never anywhere else and never missing.

questions.why: le in front of the same frame, and du because de la contracts in front of a masculine word.

C'est le plus grand jardin du quartier.
Cest le plus grand jardin du quartier

questions.q: It's the biggest house in the neighbourhood. maison is feminine.
questions.why: la and grande. This is the one of the four you can actually hear, because the e wakes up the d.

Cest la plus grande maison du quartier

Ce sont les plus grands jardins du quartier.

questions.why: The e and the s together, and it sounds identical to the singular feminine. This form exists only in writing, which is why you are typing it.

Ce sont les plus grandes maisons du quartier.

questions.why: jeune does not change shape at all, so the article is doing the whole job. That is where the agreement lives in this frame.

Elle est la plus jeune de la famille

questions.q: Il est ... que son collègue. Same sentence, different verb. Which word?

sections.title: The frame, one last time

sections.say: Pick the middle word and keep the frame.
sections.body: Pick the middle word and keep the frame. Three words go in the middle and everything else stays where it is, which is why a describing word you learn next month will already work in it. Put an article in front and you have the most or the least of a group. Two words refuse all of this and have their own forms, and that is the same shape lesson 8 in A2 taught you with savoir and connaître: English merges what French splits, and the split is the whole lesson. One warning for later: ne ... plus is a completely different plus and it means no longer, not more. Lesson 21 in A1 owns it and it is not this.
sections.title: One frame, one middle word
points: plus, moins, aussi. The frame never moves.
que and the other thing, or you have not compared anything.
The article arrives and it carries the ending.
meilleur after est, mieux after a verb. Lesson 12 in A2 left mieux here.

errorTriggers.description: Picks the wrong middle word, or puts it somewhere other than in front of the describing word.
Stops the sentence after the describing word, producing a grammatical sentence that never says what the comparison is with.
Leaves the superlative in its plain form, or agrees the describing word and not the article.
Builds plus bon or plus bien, or gives a verb meilleur and a noun mieux.

grammarIntroduced: The comparative as a single frame with one variable slot, so that a describing word never met before is comparable without further instruction
The three degrees plus, moins and aussi as one closed choice rather than as three constructions
That que and its object are obligatory, and that dropping them yields a well-formed sentence with a different meaning rather than an error
The superlative as the same frame with a definite article prefixed, and the article rather than the describing word as the carrier of agreement
That the four superlative forms are realised as two phonological forms, so the number contrast is undetectable by ear and testable only in writing
The suppletive comparatives meilleur and mieux, split by the category of what they modify, against a corpus in which mieux outnumbers meilleur six and a half to one
That mauvais admits both pire and plus mauvais, so the constraint is lexical to bon and bien rather than a general prohibition on plus
de, not dans, as the complement of a superlative

acts.title: Le rendez-vous manqué

opener.line: Tu donnes une date au comptoir, et l’employée ne note rien : ta phrase parlait d’une habitude. EN: You give a date at the counter and the clerk writes nothing: your sentence described a habit.

acts.milestone: Tu as vu une vraie réservation se perdre dans un présent, et tu sais maintenant ce que l’employée attendait. EN: You saw a real booking lost in a present tense and you know what the clerk was waiting for.

acts.title: Le futur des deux côtés

opener.line: Une phrase, deux moitiés, et le même moment devant toi : ici le futur se pose des deux côtés. EN: One sentence, two halves, one moment ahead: here the future goes on both sides.

acts.milestone: Tu mets le futur des deux côtés de quand, dans les deux ordres, sans y penser. EN: You put the future on both sides of quand, in either order, without thinking about it.

acts.title: La famille des charnières

opener.line: Six mots tiennent la même porte, et chacun l’ouvre un peu autrement : voici toute la famille de quand. EN: Six words hold the same door and each opens it a little differently: the whole family of quand.

acts.milestone: Tu choisis entre dès que, tant que, pendant que et une fois que par le sens, et le futur suit tout seul. EN: You choose between dès que, tant que, pendant que and une fois que by meaning, and the future follows.

acts.title: La même charnière, un autre moment

opener.line: Karim ouvre sa boulangerie chaque matin, et pas un seul verbe n’est au futur : ici tu apprends quand quand ne l’appelle pas. EN: Karim opens his bakery every morning with not one future verb: here you learn when quand does not call for it.

acts.milestone: Tu reconnais une habitude, une vérité et un souvenir, et tu ne leur mets plus de futur. EN: You recognise a habit, a general truth and a memory, and you stop putting a future on them.

acts.title: Si + présent, jamais le futur

opener.line: Une invitation, deux réponses qui manquent, et une règle que le français ne casse jamais : après si, pas de futur. EN: An invitation, two missing answers, and a rule French never breaks: no future after si.

acts.milestone: Tu poses une condition réelle sans jamais mettre le futur après si, dans les deux ordres. EN: You build a real condition and never put the future after si, in either order.

acts.title: Trois suites après si

opener.line: La même moitié en si peut promettre, expliquer ou ordonner : ici tu choisis laquelle des trois. EN: The same si half can promise, explain or order: here you choose which of the three.

acts.milestone: Tu construis les trois formes réelles après si : une promesse, une vérité et une consigne. EN: You build all three real shapes after si: a promise, a truth and an instruction.

acts.title: Quand ou si

opener.line: L’été arrivera de toute façon, la chaleur non : ici tu choisis le mot qui dit la vérité sur ton agenda. EN: Summer will come whatever happens, the heat may not: here you pick the word that tells the truth about your diary.

acts.milestone: Tu choisis entre quand et si par une seule question, et le temps du verbe suit tout seul. EN: You choose between quand and si with one question, and the tense follows by itself.

acts.title: À l’oral

opener.line: Personne n’écrit au café, et pourtant la moitié en quand ne change pas : ici tu apprends où aller a le droit d’entrer. EN: Nobody writes at a café, and still the quand half does not change: here you learn where aller may enter.

acts.milestone: Tu parles de tes projets avec aller et l’infinitif, sans jamais l’amener dans la charnière. EN: You talk about your plans with aller plus the infinitive, and never carry it into the hinge clause.

acts.title: Dans, en, d’ici

opener.line: Dans deux heures ou en deux heures : un mot, et ta réunion tombe ailleurs ou dure plus longtemps. EN: dans deux heures or en deux heures: one word, and your meeting either moves or lasts longer.

acts.milestone: Tu dis dans combien de temps, combien de temps ça prendra, et avant quelle limite. EN: You can say how long from now, how long it will take, and by when.

acts.title: Deux choses à venir, dans l’ordre

opener.line: Le billet avant l’hôtel, la réunion avant le déjeuner : ici tu ranges deux moments à venir et tu choisis le mot qui les tient. EN: The ticket before the hotel, the meeting before lunch: here you order two moments ahead and pick the word that holds them.

acts.milestone: Tu mets deux moments à venir dans l’ordre, avec une charnière ou avec des connecteurs. EN: You put two future moments in order, with a hinge word or with connectors.

acts.title: Écrire ton plan

opener.line: À toi : ta période, tes étapes dans l’ordre, ce qui n’est pas encore sûr, et une ligne pour fermer. EN: Your turn: your period, your steps in order, what is not yet certain, and one line to close.

acts.milestone: Tu as écrit ton propre plan et passé l’examen : quatre-vingt-huit questions, onze rounds. EN: You wrote your own plan and sat the exam: eighty-eight questions, eleven rounds.

recorded.desc: The two moving-house messages (act 1), one voice, Québec accent welcome, read at dictation pace. Every future ending must be audible: the whole act turns on hearing the extra r in aurai, appellerai, arrivera.

The corridor conversation (act 2), two voices, Belgian French welcome. Twelve futures in six lines: read them plainly, without stressing the endings, or the learner hears a grammar lesson instead of a conversation.
The rule deck of act 2. Read each pair of clauses as one breath, so the two futures sound like one sentence and not like two examples.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in authored order, at conversational speed. The learner separates plans from habits by ear alone, so any difference of performance between lines would give the answer away.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Read the six identically in pace; the wrong versions in promptSound are never spoken.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION (act 3): eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order. The hinge word opens each line and must be clean and unhurried, because it is the only thing the questions turn on.
The hinge deck of act 3. Four cards, four hinge words. Give each hinge word its own small beat before the rest of the clause, so dès que and une fois que do not blur into quand.

The bakery passage (act 4), one voice, France accent, natural reading pace. Even and unhurried through the present-tense paragraph; from « La semaine prochaine » the pace lifts slightly, because that is where the text turns to the future.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION (act 4): eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational speed. Three tenses are mixed on purpose and no line may be read more carefully than another.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence, three of which are in the present and one in the imparfait. Read all six as ordinary French, never as oddities.
The invitation exchange (act 5), two female voices, West African French welcome. After each si, the present must be clean and short: the learner is listening for the absence of the future r.
The si deck of act 5. Read the si clause level and unfinished, and let the second clause fall. The comma is where the future starts, and it should be audible.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION (act 6): eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order. Promises, truths and instructions in one take; do not act the imperatives, or the answer is given away.
The three-continuations deck of act 6. The first half is identical in tone on all four cards; only the second half changes character.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Six sentences, plain reading, same pace throughout: the trap is that the wrong versions sound perfectly natural to an English ear.

The Namur conversation (act 7), two voices. The quand lines and the si lines must be read with the same confidence: the difference is grammatical, not emotional, and a hesitant si would teach the wrong thing.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION (act 7): eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order. The pairs alternate quand and si with identical second halves, so the takes must be interchangeable in every respect except the words.

The café conversation (act 8), two voices, relaxed and fast, Lyon. This is the spoken register: contractions and elisions are welcome, and the futur proche should sound like ordinary speech rather than a form.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION (act 8): eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational speed. Every line carries aller plus an infinitive; the hinge clauses keep the futur simple and must not be softened.
The site update (act 9), one voice, a manager addressing a team, France accent. dans, en and d’ici carry the meaning, so each one must be clearly audible and never swallowed into the following word.
The delay deck of act 9. On the fourth card the two halves must sound identical except for the one word, because that is the whole point of the card.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Read the six at one pace: dans and en are short, unstressed words, and the learner has to catch them anyway.
The Saturday plan (act 10), one voice, read as somebody talking through a list. A small beat before each connector (d’abord, ensuite, puis, enfin) so the order is audible without being performed.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION (act 10): eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order. The questions are about which of two moments comes first, so no line may put extra weight on the hinge clause.

The model plan (act 11), one voice, calm, read as a message being spoken aloud. It is the shape the learner will imitate, so the four parts must be audible: the period, the ordered steps, the conditions, the closing line.

lessons.intro: You can build the futur simple and you know the irregular stems. This lesson is about where the future goes. A sentence with quand or dès que has two halves that meet at one moment, and French writes the future on both of them, where English keeps the present. A sentence with si is different: the condition stays in the present and never takes the future, whatever follows it.

oral.body: En parlant, la deuxième moitié prend souvent aller et l’infinitif. La charnière, elle, garde le futur simple : on ne dit pas « quand je vais arriver ». EN: In speech the second half often uses aller plus the infinitive; the hinge clause keeps the futur simple.
oral.title: Aller et l’infinitif, en parlant

delai.body: dans deux heures : on compte à partir de maintenant. en deux heures : c’est le temps qu’il faut pour finir. d’ici vendredi : avant cette limite. EN: dans counts from now, en is the time it takes, d'ici is a deadline.
delai.title: Dire dans combien de temps

seuil.body: dès que et aussitôt que donnent le seuil : la seconde exacte où la chose commence, pas une minute plus tard. quand est plus large. EN: dès que and aussitôt que give the exact instant something begins.
seuil.title: L’instant où ça commence

examples.note: aussitôt que : le même seuil, plus écrit

verite.body: Si les deux moitiés sont au présent, tu ne parles pas d’un projet : tu dis ce qui arrive à chaque fois. C’est une vérité, pas une promesse. EN: Two presents say what happens every time, not what you plan.
verite.title: Ce qui est vrai à chaque fois

examples.note: le café du soir, à chaque fois

consigne.body: Après si + présent, tu peux donner un ordre ou un conseil. C’est la forme des panneaux, des notices et des messages courts. EN: After si plus a present you can give an instruction: signs, notices and short messages.
consigne.title: Si, puis une instruction

deuxfois.body: En anglais, la moitié qui commence par when reste au présent. En français, non : si le moment est à venir, les deux verbes vont au futur. EN: English keeps the when clause in the present; French puts both verbs in the future.
deuxfois.title: Le futur des deux côtés

examples.note: aurai et appellerai, tous les deux au futur
ce que fait l’anglais, et pourquoi ça trompe

possible.body: Avec si, le moment est seulement proposé. Il peut ne jamais arriver, et c’est pour ça que le verbe reste au présent. EN: With si the moment is only proposed, and may never come at all.
possible.title: Ce n’est pas sûr

examples.note: assez chaud : on ne sait pas

certitude.body: Avec quand, le moment est dans l’agenda : tu ne sais peut-être pas le jour, mais tu sais qu’il arrivera. EN: With quand the moment is in the diary: the day may be open, the arrival is not.
certitude.title: Le moment viendra

charniere.body: quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, tant que, pendant que, une fois que : ce sont des charnières. Elles posent un moment, et les deux moitiés de la phrase tournent autour. EN: The hinge words that hold two halves of a sentence around one moment.
charniere.title: Le mot qui tient les deux moitiés

examples.note: quand : le moment le plus simple
une fois que : une étape franchie

condition.body: Une condition réelle commence par si et reste au présent, toujours. Le futur va dans l’autre moitié, jamais après si. EN: A real condition starts with si and stays in the present; the future goes in the other half.
condition.title: Après si, le présent

examples.note: viens au présent, préparerai au futur
ajoutes au présent, sera au futur

lessons.title: Le futur : quand, dès que, et les conditions réelles

drills.coach: Deux piles. Demande-toi : un moment précis, ou chaque fois ? EN: sort by one moment against every time.
drills.title: Projet ou habitude

drills.q: Quand nous ... prêts, nous partirons.
drills.why: Le départ est à venir, donc la charnière aussi. EN: the leaving is ahead.
drills.coach: Si la deuxième moitié est au futur, la charnière l’est aussi. EN: if the second half is future, so is the hinge.
drills.title: Le futur des deux côtés

drills.coach: Une pile pour « à la seconde où », une pile pour « pendant tout ce temps ». EN: sort by instant against stretch.
drills.title: L’instant ou la durée

drills.coach: Le mot quand ne décide de rien. Regarde le moment. EN: the word quand decides nothing; look at the moment.
drills.title: Chaque fois ou une fois

drills.q: Si tu ... demain, je préparerai un gâteau.
drills.why: Après si, jamais le futur. EN: never the future after si.
drills.coach: Le futur attend de l’autre côté de la virgule. EN: the future waits past the comma.
drills.title: Après si, le présent

drills.coach: Une pile pour ce qui est vrai chaque fois, une pile pour ce qu’on te dit de faire. EN: sort truths from instructions.
drills.title: Vérité ou consigne

drills.coach: Est-ce que ça arrivera de toute façon ? Trie sur cette question. EN: will it happen anyway? Sort on that.
drills.title: Sûr ou possible

drills.coach: Lis chaque phrase à voix haute et écoute où tombe aller. EN: read each aloud and hear where aller falls.
drills.title: Chacun à sa place

drills.q: Elle a préparé le dossier ... trois jours.
drills.why: C’est le temps que le travail a pris. EN: the time the work took.
drills.coach: dans compte à partir de maintenant ; en donne la durée. EN: dans counts from now, en gives the length.
drills.title: Dans ou en

drills.coach: Pour chaque phrase, dis à voix haute ce qui arrive en premier. EN: for each sentence say aloud what comes first.
drills.title: Dans l’ordre

drills.q: Ton plan s’arrête sur « je m’inscrirai à un cours du soir ». Que manque-t-il ?
drills.why: Une dernière ligne dit ce que tu feras au bout. EN: a last line closes it.
opts: une ligne qui ferme le plan
drills.coach: Une période, des étapes, une condition, une fin. Vérifie les quatre. EN: period, steps, condition, ending: check all four.
drills.title: Un plan complet

sections.body: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si. Les sept charnières se comportent toutes de la même façon : si le moment est à venir, le verbe qui les suit va au futur, et l’autre moitié aussi. Ce qui change d’un mot à l’autre, ce n’est pas le temps, c’est ce que le mot dit du moment. L’ordre des deux moitiés est libre. EN: all seven hinge words behave alike; what changes is what each one says about the moment, not the tense.
sections.title: Sept mots, une seule règle

rows: Quand tu arriveras, je serai déjà là.
Lorsque nous serons à Genève, nous visiterons le lac.
Dès que tu seras prêt, on partira.
Aussitôt que la réunion finira, je t’appellerai.
Tant que j’habiterai ici, je prendrai le bus.
Pendant qu’il conduira, je lirai la carte.
Une fois que tu connaîtras le code, tu pourras entrer.
sections.title: Les sept charnières

rows: Quand je serai à la retraite, je voyagerai.
Quand je rentre du travail, je prends une douche.
Lorsque le soleil se couche, la place se vide.
Quand j’étais étudiant, je travaillais le samedi.
Quand le film a commencé, la salle est devenue silencieuse.
sections.title: La même charnière, trois moments

sections.body: Dans une condition réelle, le verbe qui suit si reste au présent, quelle que soit la distance du moment. Le futur, lui, vit dans l’autre moitié. L’ordre des deux moitiés est libre : « Je passerai te voir si j’ai le temps » est la même phrase. EN: in a real condition the verb after si stays present however far ahead the moment is; the future lives in the other half.
sections.title: Le présent, toujours

rows: une promesse : Si tu viens demain, je préparerai un gâteau.
une conséquence : Si tu ajoutes trop de sel, le plat sera trop salé.
une vérité : Si on chauffe l’eau à cent degrés, elle bout.
une information : Si on paie en ligne, la livraison est gratuite.
une consigne : Si tu as froid, ferme la fenêtre.
une sécurité : Si l’alarme sonne, sortez par la porte de gauche.
sections.title: Les trois suites réelles

sections.body: Il existe une autre forme, « si tu m’aidais, nous finirions plus vite », qui ne dit pas « c’est possible » mais « ce n’est pas le cas ». Elle appartient à la leçon 10 du B1 et le conditionnel lui-même à la leçon 8 du B1. Si tu la rencontres avant, reconnais-la et laisse-la de côté. EN: a second shape exists which means it is not the case; it belongs to a later lesson.
sections.title: Ce que cette leçon ne traite pas

sections.body: Pose-toi : est-ce que ça arrivera de toute façon ? Oui, alors quand, et le futur des deux côtés. Non, alors si, et le présent juste après. Avec quand, le doute porte sur la date seulement ; avec si, il porte sur la chose elle-même. EN: ask whether it will happen anyway: yes gives quand plus the future, no gives si plus the present.
sections.title: Une seule question

rows: Quand je partirai à la retraite, je déménagerai.
Si je pars à la retraite plus tôt, je déménagerai.
S’il rentre à temps, nous mangerons ensemble.
Quand tu auras ton diplôme, tu chercheras du travail.
Si tu as ton diplôme, tu chercheras du travail.
Quand l’été arrivera, nous ouvrirons la terrasse.
S’il fait assez chaud, nous ouvrirons la terrasse.
Quand le bébé naîtra, nous changerons d’appartement.
Si le bébé arrive plus tôt, nous changerons nos plans.
Quand je te verrai, je t’expliquerai.
Si je te vois ce soir, je t’expliquerai.
sections.title: Six paires

sections.body: dans deux heures se compte à partir de l’instant où tu parles. en deux heures est le temps que la chose prend, du début à la fin, et ne dit pas quand elle commence. d’ici vendredi donne une limite : avant vendredi, sans promettre le jour. Lesson 14 in A2 a posé les prépositions ; ici elles servent à situer un projet. EN: dans counts from now, en is how long it takes, d'ici is a deadline.
sections.title: D’où on compte

rows: Le train partira dans dix minutes.
Je finirai ce rapport en deux heures.
D’ici là, ne dis rien à personne.
Il va pleuvoir tout à l’heure.
On se verra la semaine prochaine.
sections.title: Les expressions

sections.body: Un plan tient avec quatre morceaux : une phrase qui annonce la période, des étapes dans l’ordre, au moins une chose qui n’est pas sûre, et une ligne qui ferme. Range tes moments avant de choisir tes mots, mets le premier des deux dans la charnière, et relis-toi en soulignant chaque charnière. EN: a plan needs a period, ordered steps, one uncertainty and a closing line.
sections.title: Quatre morceaux

rows: Ensuite, nous prendrons le train de dix-huit heures.
Je passerai à la banque, puis j’irai au marché.
Après, on se retrouvera devant la gare.
Avant de partir, je vérifierai les billets.
Enfin, nous rentrerons par le dernier bus.
sections.title: Les connecteurs

rows: Souligne-les : quand, dès que, tant que, une fois que
Cherche si, et vérifie que le verbe suivant est au présent
dans, en ou d’ici, une fois au moins
Le premier des deux moments est dans la charnière
Une phrase qui dit ce que tu feras au bout

overview.subFr: Le futur : quand, dès que, et les conditions réelles
overview.introFr: Tu sais former le futur et tu connais les radicaux irréguliers. Cette leçon t’apprend où le poser. Une phrase avec quand ou dès que a deux moitiés qui se rejoignent à un même moment, et le français écrit le futur sur les deux, là où l’anglais garde le présent. Avec si, c’est l’inverse : la condition reste au présent et ne prend jamais le futur.

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.

beats.text: Tu déménages le mois prochain. Au comptoir, une employée ouvre un calendrier et attend une date pour réserver le camion.

beats.en: Tell me when you will have the keys, and I will hold the truck.

beats.en: Whenever I have the keys, I call you.

beats.en: So you call every time. What do I write in the calendar.

beats.text: En anglais, « when I get the keys » suffit : le présent dit déjà l’avenir. En français, le présent dit l’habitude, et l’habitude n’a pas de date.

beats.body: Après quand, le présent parle de ce qui se répète. Pour un moment à venir, le français met le futur des deux côtés. EN: after quand a present means whenever; ahead of you, the future goes on both sides.
beats.coach: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si. EN: The future is said on both sides of quand, and never after si.

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.
sections.text: Salut Nadia. Je déménage le quinze mars. Le notaire m'a dit que la signature était prévue le douze. Quand j'aurai les clés, je vous appellerai tout de suite, et le camion arrivera à huit heures le lendemain. Dès que le propriétaire signera, tout ira vite. Nous commencerons par la cuisine, parce que c'est la pièce la plus longue. Il faudra tout emballer avant vendredi, donc j'ai déjà acheté les cartons. Si tout va bien, je déménagerai samedi. Quand je serai installé, je t'inviterai. On se verra la semaine prochaine pour les derniers détails. Je ne sais pas encore la date exacte de la remise des clés, mais je te préviendrai dès que je la connaîtrai.

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.
sections.text: Karim travaille dans une boulangerie à Liège. Quand il arrive à cinq heures, la rue est encore noire et le four est déjà chaud. Dès que la première fournée sort, il ouvre la porte et les clients entrent. Pendant qu'il sert au comptoir, sa collègue prépare les sandwichs. Tant que le pain se vend bien, la journée passe vite. Une fois que le dernier client est parti, Karim nettoie tout et compte la caisse. Quand il était étudiant, il détestait se lever tôt ; dès que le réveil sonnait, il éteignait et se rendormait. Aujourd'hui, il aime ce moment où la ville dort encore. La semaine prochaine, il changera d'horaire. Quand il commencera à midi, il ne verra plus le lever du soleil, et ça lui manquera.
sections.frSub: Compte les futurs, il y en a quatre

errors.why: Normal : les deux moitiés parlent bien de demain, et l’acte 2 vient d’apprendre à doubler le futur. Après si, on ne le double pas. EN: both halves do point at tomorrow; si is the one place you do not double the future.

errors.wrong: Si tu viendras demain, je préparerai un gâteau.

errors.why: Le verbe avoir au futur sonne juste ailleurs. Ici il ferme la porte que si laisse ouverte. EN: correct elsewhere, wrong after si.
errors.right: Si j’ai le temps, je passerai te voir.
errors.wrong: Si j’aurai le temps, je passerai te voir.

errors.why: Deux futurs se répondent bien dans une phrase avec quand. Avec si, seul le second reste. EN: two futures work after quand, not after si.
errors.right: Si le train est à l’heure, nous serons là à midi.
errors.wrong: Si le train sera à l’heure, nous serons là à midi.

errors.why: Cette forme existe et elle est la leçon 10 du B1. Elle dit « ce n’est pas le cas », pas « c’est possible ». EN: that form exists and means it is not the case.

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.
sections.text: Bonjour à tous. Voici où nous en sommes. Les plans arriveront dans une semaine, et le bureau les validera en deux jours. D'ici vendredi, tout sera prêt pour la commande. Le chantier commencera dans un mois, une fois que la mairie signera l'autorisation. Les ouvriers monteront la structure en trois semaines, ce qui est rapide pour un bâtiment de cette taille. Je serai de retour dans deux heures, donc écrivez-moi si quelque chose bloque. D'ici la fin du mois, je vous donnerai une réponse sur le budget. Dans quelques jours, vous recevrez le planning complet par courriel. Si le temps reste sec, nous finirons avant l'hiver ; s'il pleut beaucoup, nous perdrons deux semaines.

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.
sections.text: Samedi, j'ai une longue journée. D'abord je finirai le rapport, ensuite je partirai. Je passerai à la banque, puis j'irai au marché. Quand j'aurai le billet, je réserverai l'hôtel : dans l'autre sens, ça ne marche pas, parce que l'hôtel dépend de la date du train. Dès que la réunion finira, nous irons déjeuner. Ensuite, nous prendrons le train de dix-huit heures. Une fois que tout sera réglé, je te téléphonerai. Après, on se retrouvera devant la gare. Avant de partir, je vérifierai les billets, parce que je les oublie une fois sur deux. Enfin, nous rentrerons par le dernier bus. Tant que nous n'aurons pas de réponse pour dimanche, nous attendrons.

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.
sections.text: Voici ce que je ferai le mois prochain. Je pars à Sherbrooke pour un stage de six semaines. D'abord, je réglerai le logement : dès que l'agence me donnera une réponse, je signerai et j'enverrai le dépôt. Quand j'aurai l'adresse, je commanderai une carte de transport. Si le stage commence le lundi, je prendrai le train du dimanche soir ; si tout va bien, je serai installé avant le premier jour. Une fois que je connaîtrai mes horaires, je m'inscrirai à un cours du soir. Tant que je serai là-bas, j'écrirai chaque semaine à ma famille. D'ici la fin du stage, je saurai si je veux rester. Je vous raconterai tout à mon retour.

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.
steps: 1. Écris tes moments dans l’ordre, en trois mots chacun. EN: list your moments in order, three words each.
2. Ouvre par une phrase qui annonce la période. EN: open with one sentence naming the period.
3. Relie deux moments avec une charnière, et mets le futur des deux côtés. EN: join two moments with a hinge and put the future on both sides.
4. Ajoute une vraie condition avec si + présent, suivie d’un futur. EN: add one real condition with si plus a present.
5. Ferme par une ligne qui dit ce que tu feras au bout. EN: close with one line saying what you will do at the end.
