sections.setting: Tu prépares un stage à Sherbrooke. L’agente du logement veut des dates et ne veut pas d’à-peu-près.

sections.brief: Tu prépares quelque chose : un voyage, un déménagement, une formation ou un projet au travail. Ton amie Salma, à Casablanca, te demande comment tu vas t’organiser. Écris-lui un message. Annonce la période, mets tes étapes dans l’ordre, et dis ce qui n’est pas encore sûr.
sections.title: Écris ton plan

criteria.label: Le futur des deux côtés
descriptors: 4 : Trois charnières différentes au moins, et chacune porte le futur des deux côtés. Aucun présent ne traîne dans une moitié qui parle de l’avenir.
3 : Trois charnières, et une ou deux moitiés seulement restent au présent par distraction. Le plan se lit sans hésitation.
2 : Une ou deux charnières, ou plusieurs moitiés au présent. Le lecteur ne sait plus si tu racontes une habitude ou un projet.
1 : Les charnières manquent, ou toutes leurs moitiés sont au présent. On lit une routine, pas un plan.

criteria.label: Une vraie condition
descriptors: 3 : Au moins une condition avec si, le présent juste après si, et un futur, un présent ou un impératif de l’autre côté.
2 : Une condition est là, mais le temps après si hésite une fois, ou la suite manque de clarté.
1 : Pas de condition, ou un futur après si.

criteria.label: Un plan qui se suit
descriptors: 3 : Les étapes sont dans l’ordre, guidées par d’abord, ensuite, puis, enfin, et une expression de délai situe le tout.
2 : L’ordre est lisible mais les liens sont pauvres, ou le délai manque.
1 : Des phrases isolées. Le lecteur ne voit pas ce qui vient avant quoi.

criteria.label: La mission complète
descriptors: 2 : Un vrai projet, entre 90 et 130 mots, et une ligne finale qui ferme le plan.
1 : Il manque un élément : pas de fin, moins de 90 mots, ou le texte ne parle pas de l’avenir.

sections.briefEn: You are getting something ready: a trip, a move, a course or a project at work. Your friend Salma in Casablanca asks how you will organise it. Write her a message: name the period, put your steps in order, and say what is not yet certain.
sections.produce: Écris un plan de 90 à 130 mots au futur, avec au moins trois charnières différentes (quand, dès que, lorsque, tant que, pendant que, une fois que), au moins une vraie condition avec si, une expression de délai (dans, en ou d’ici), et une ligne qui ferme le plan.

watchFor.pattern: A present tense in the charnière clause of a plan (quand j’arrive, dès que je finis, une fois que tout est réglé), carried over from English.
watchFor.feedback: Cette moitié parle de l’avenir, elle aussi. Mets le futur des deux côtés : quand j’arriverai, dès que je finirai.

watchFor.pattern: One future only, in the second half, with the charnière clause left in the present.
watchFor.feedback: Compte tes futurs : il en faut un de chaque côté de la charnière.

watchFor.pattern: A future after si (si j’aurai le temps, si le train sera à l’heure, si je viendrai).
watchFor.feedback: Après si, jamais le futur. Le verbe reste au présent : si j’ai le temps, si le train est à l’heure.

watchFor.pattern: A conditionnel after si (si tu m’aiderais, si je pouvais), which belongs to the present-unreal lesson.
watchFor.feedback: Cette forme dit « ce n’est pas le cas », et elle appartient à la leçon 10 du B1. Ici, si plus le présent suffit.

watchFor.pattern: si used where the event will happen anyway (si l’été arrive, si je pars à la retraite), or quand used for something genuinely uncertain.
watchFor.feedback: Pose-toi la question : est-ce que ça arrivera de toute façon ? Oui, alors quand et le futur. Non, alors si et le présent.

watchFor.pattern: Fewer than three charnières, or the same one repeated (quand, quand, quand).
watchFor.feedback: Varie : dès que dit l’instant, tant que dit la durée, une fois que dit l’étape franchie.

watchFor.pattern: dans and en swapped (je finirai le rapport dans deux heures for a length of work, je serai de retour en deux heures for a point in time).
watchFor.feedback: dans deux heures compte à partir de maintenant ; en deux heures, c’est le temps que ça prend.

watchFor.pattern: The two moments in the wrong order across a charnière (quand je réserverai l’hôtel, j’aurai le billet).
watchFor.feedback: Le premier des deux moments va dans la charnière. Range-les avant d’écrire.

watchFor.pattern: A futur proche inside the charnière clause (quand je vais arriver, dès qu’il va être là).
watchFor.feedback: Aller et l’infinitif restent après la virgule. Dans la charnière, le futur simple : quand j’arriverai.

watchFor.pattern: Future-stem errors carried over from the formation lessons (je finirai written je finerai, je viendrai written je venirai, il faudra written il falera).
watchFor.feedback: Revois la forme du futur : « Le radical change, la fin ne change jamais. »

watchFor.pattern: A list of sentences with no connectors and no delay expression, or a plan that stops without an ending.
watchFor.feedback: Guide ta lectrice : d’abord, ensuite, puis, enfin. Et ferme le plan par une dernière ligne.

watchFor.pattern: Under 90 words, no real project, or a text written about the past rather than what is ahead.
watchFor.feedback: Relis la mission : un vrai projet, au futur, de 90 à 130 mots, avec une fin.

graderNotes: Count a charnière only when it is one of quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, tant que, pendant que, une fois que. Avant de and après are ordering words, not charnières, and do not count towards the three.
THREE DIFFERENT charnières means three different words, not three occurrences. Two uses of quand plus one dès que is two, not three.

A present tense inside a charnière clause is an error ONLY when the passage is about the future. If the learner writes a habit on purpose (« quand je rentre, je cuisine »), leave it alone and say nothing.
Word count EXCLUDES the greeting and the sign-off (Paul, 2026-09-22). Count the body only, with 10% tolerance (81-143) before criterion « tache » loses its point.
The futur proche is fully acceptable in the second half, including in a written message. Mark it only inside a charnière clause.
Do NOT mark a futur antérieur (« quand j’aurai fini ») as an error. It is correct French and belongs to a later unit; it simply earns no extra credit here.
Do NOT mark si + imparfait + conditionnel as a grammar failure in isolation; name it, say it belongs to a later lesson, and score criterion « condition » on whether a REAL condition is also present.
Accept regional vocabulary (un stage / une formation, un courriel / un mail, une carte de transport / un abonnement).
Feedback language: simple French (B1), addressed as « tu », with one short English gloss allowed per comment.
sections.modelAnswer: Salut Salma ! Voici ce que je ferai le mois prochain. Je pars à Sherbrooke pour un stage de six semaines. D’abord, je réglerai le logement : dès que l’agence me donnera une réponse, je signerai et j’enverrai le dépôt. Quand j’aurai l’adresse, je commanderai une carte de transport. Si le stage commence le lundi, je prendrai le train du dimanche soir. Une fois que je connaîtrai mes horaires, je m’inscrirai à un cours du soir. Tant que je serai là-bas, j’écrirai chaque semaine. D’ici la fin du stage, je saurai si je veux rester. Je te raconterai tout à mon retour. Bises !
sections.modelAnswerEn: Hi Salma! Here is what I will do next month. I am going to Sherbrooke for a six-week placement. First I will sort out the accommodation: as soon as the agency answers me, I will sign and send the deposit. When I have the address, I will order a travel card. If the placement starts on the Monday, I will take the Sunday evening train. Once I know my hours, I will sign up for an evening class. As long as I am over there, I will write every week. By the end of the placement I will know whether I want to stay. I will tell you all about it when I get back. Love!

sections.title: Toute la leçon sur un écran

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.
sections.body: Tu mets le futur des deux côtés de quand, tu choisis entre dès que, tant que et une fois que, et tu ne mets plus jamais le futur après si. Le piège qui reste est le réflexe inverse : un futur posé sur une habitude parce que la phrase commence par quand. Avant l’examen, relis ta mission. Souligne chaque charnière, puis demande-toi pour chacune si ce moment est déjà passé, s’il revient chaque fois, ou s’il est encore devant toi. Si les trois réponses collent aux trois temps que tu as écrits, la leçon a marché. EN: Underline every hinge word in your task and ask, for each one, whether the moment is past, repeated or still ahead.

sections.title: Une dernière fois

sections.say: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si.
sections.body: Le futur se dit des deux côtés de quand, et jamais après si. Tu poses un moment avec une charnière, tu ouvres une possibilité avec si, et tu sais lequel des deux ton agenda demande. La prochaine leçon garde ces deux moitiés et change le ton : le conditionnel, pour demander poliment et pour dire ce que tu ferais. EN: Next lesson keeps these two halves and changes the tone: the conditional.
sections.title: Le plan, en résumé
points: Après quand, dès que, tant que : le futur des deux côtés.
Après si, jamais le futur. Le présent, toujours.
quand, c’est sûr. si, c’est seulement possible.
dans compte de maintenant ; en, c’est le temps qu’il faut.

errorTriggers.description: Leaves the quand clause in the present when the sentence is about a future moment, so a plan reads as a habit.
Writes one future instead of two, usually keeping it in the main clause and dropping it from the hinge clause.
Picks a hinge word by habit rather than by meaning, so dès que, tant que and pendant que become interchangeable.
Puts a future after quand even for a habit, a general truth or a memory, because the word now triggers the tense.
Puts a future or a conditional straight after si in a real condition.
Treats si + présent as always leading to a future, so general truths and instructions come out as promises.
Chooses between quand and si by feel rather than by whether the event will happen anyway.
Carries aller plus the infinitive into the hinge clause, producing quand je vais arriver.
Swaps dans and en, so a starting point becomes a duration or the other way round.
Puts the second of two future moments in the hinge clause, so the plan reads back to front.
Produces a plan with no hinge word, no real condition or no ending, whatever the tenses are.

grammarIntroduced: The futur simple required in the subordinate clause after quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, tant que, pendant que and une fois que when the main clause is future, against English, which keeps the present there
The same seven conjunctions with a present main clause (habit or general truth) and with a past main clause (imparfait habit, passé composé single event), where no future appears at all

The semantic contribution of each conjunction: the bare moment (quand, lorsque), the exact instant (dès que, aussitôt que), the shared stretch (tant que, pendant que) and the completed step (une fois que)
Either clause order, with the conjunction clause first or second, without change of tense
The real condition si + présent followed by a futur simple, and the absolute prohibition on a future or a conditional directly after si
Si + présent followed by a present for a general truth, and si + présent followed by an imperative for an instruction
The choice between quand and si as certainty against possibility, tested by whether the event will happen anyway
The futur proche in the main clause of these patterns in speech, and its exclusion from the conjunction clause
Future time expressions: dans plus a duration counted from now, en plus a duration as the time taken, and d’ici plus a point as a deadline
Sequencing two future events, with the earlier one placed in the conjunction clause or the order carried by d’abord, ensuite, puis and enfin

acts.title: Le mur du présent

opener.line: Tu demandes quelque chose et ça sort comme un ordre : ici tu apprends à reculer d'un pas. EN: You ask for something and it comes out as an order: here you learn to step back one pace.

acts.milestone: Tu reconnais les quatre métiers du conditionnel dans un texte ordinaire. EN: You can spot the four jobs the conditional does in an everyday text.

acts.title: La recette

opener.line: Tu as déjà payé les deux morceaux : il ne reste qu'à les coller. EN: You have already paid for both pieces: all that is left is gluing them together.

acts.milestone: Tu construis le conditionnel de n'importe quel verbe régulier, aux six personnes. EN: You can build the conditional of any regular verb, in all six persons.

acts.title: Les radicaux rendus

opener.line: Quinze radicaux irréguliers t'attendent, et tu les as tous déjà payés au futur. EN: Fifteen irregular stems are waiting, and you paid for every one of them in the future tense.

acts.milestone: Tu écris le conditionnel de être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, vouloir et devoir sans réfléchir. EN: You can write the conditional of the seven commonest irregular verbs without stopping to think.

acts.title: Ai ou ais

opener.line: Une lettre muette sépare une promesse d'une idée : ici tu apprends à la placer. EN: One silent letter separates a promise from an idea: here you learn where to put it.

acts.milestone: Tu choisis entre -ai et -ais par le contexte, pas par l'oreille. EN: You choose between -ai and -ais by context, not by ear.

acts.title: Le souhait

opener.line: Tu sais déjà ce que tu veux : ici tu apprends à le dire sans fermer la porte. EN: You already know what you want: here you learn to say it without closing the door.

acts.milestone: Tu ouvres une envie avec voudrais, aimerais ou préférerais, et tu choisis la bonne des trois. EN: You can open a wish with voudrais, aimerais or préférerais, and pick the right one of the three.

acts.title: Demander sans imposer

opener.line: Tu demandes la même chose, mais tu laisses une porte ouverte : ici tu apprends à la placer. EN: You ask for the same thing, but you leave a door open: here you learn where to put it.

acts.milestone: Tu choisis ta demande selon la gêne que tu causes, du tu pourrais au ça vous dérangerait de. EN: You can pick your request to match the trouble you are causing.

acts.title: Le conseil

opener.line: Ton conseil est bon et il passe mal : ici tu apprends à le poser sans ordonner. EN: Your advice is good and it lands badly: here you learn to give it without ordering.

acts.milestone: Tu conseilles avec tu devrais, il faudrait ou à ta place, et tu sais lequel vise qui. EN: You can advise with tu devrais, il faudrait or à ta place, and you know which one aims where.

acts.title: Pouvoir, vouloir, devoir

opener.line: Trois verbes portent la moitié de ta journée : ici tu les prends au conditionnel. EN: Three verbs carry half your day: here you take them in the conditional.

acts.milestone: Tu proposes, tu offres, tu conseilles et tu estimes avec pouvoir, vouloir et devoir. EN: You can propose, offer, advise and estimate with pouvoir, vouloir and devoir.

acts.title: Si c'était vrai

opener.line: Tu décris une vie que tu n'as pas encore : ici tu apprends à la dire au bon temps. EN: You describe a life you do not have yet: here you learn to say it in the right tense.

acts.milestone: Tu écris le résultat d'une situation imaginée sans avoir besoin du mot si. EN: You can write the result of an imagined situation without needing the word si.

acts.title: Selon la police

opener.line: Tu ouvres la radio et tout est au conditionnel : ici tu apprends pourquoi. EN: You turn on the radio and everything is in the conditional: here you learn why.

acts.milestone: Tu lis un bulletin et tu sais qui garantit quoi, phrase par phrase. EN: You can read a news bulletin and tell who is vouching for what, sentence by sentence.

acts.title: Un pas en arrière, par écrit

opener.line: À toi d'écrire : ton souhait, ta demande, ta proposition, et ce que tu ne garantis pas. EN: Your turn to write: your wish, your request, your proposal, and what you are not vouching for.

acts.milestone: Tu as écrit ton propre courriel et passé l'examen : quatre-vingt-huit questions, onze rounds. EN: You wrote your own email and sat the exam: eighty-eight questions, eleven rounds.

recorded.desc: The listing and the two emails (act 1), one female Belgian voice, one take, read at dictation pace. The quoted listing is read a shade flatter than the narration so the learner hears a document being read out. Every final -rait is a clean [ɛ] with no audible t.

Karim and the coach (act 2), two voices, one take. The coach is unhurried and slightly amused: the whole point of the exchange is that nothing new is being sold. The four deck cards are read by the same coach voice.
The six endings deck. Read -ais, -ait and -aient identically, with no helpful extra stress, because the card's claim is that they ARE identical. Let the -ions and -iez cards breathe the i.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in authored order, at conversational speed. The nous and vous forms must not be over-articulated; the learner is meant to hear an ordinary sentence and find the i in it.
The four irregular-stem cards (act 3). One coach voice. Say the stem and the full form as one breath, not as two separate items: the card claims they are the same thing.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Read the six plainly and identically in pace; the imparfait versions in promptSound are NEVER spoken. The r must be audible in every one of the six.
Karim and the coach (act 4), two voices, one take. Karim reads his own draft sentence flat, as someone rereading their screen. The coach is matter of fact, never triumphant.

The four pair cards (act 4). The je pair MUST be read naturally, with no exaggerated separation of [e] and [ɛ]: the card says most speakers barely separate them, so a helpful reading would contradict the lesson. The nous and vous pairs are read normally, where the i does the work.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace. The je forms carry no extra help; the learner answers from the time words and the conditions, which is the whole point of the act.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Six lines, same pace, same voice. Do not lean on the final syllable.
The two travellers at the ticket counter (act 5). ONE TAKE, and the clerk must be read identically both times: the mission only works if nothing changes except the traveller sentence.

The three wish openers (act 5). One voice. Je voudrais is brisk and businesslike, j’aimerais is warmer and slower, je préférerais lands on the second option. The difference in delivery IS the teaching.

The hotel reception exchange (act 6), two voices, one take. The receptionist answers the first request with a flat confirmation and the second with a genuine question, and the gap between those two deliveries is what the act is about.
The four request openers (act 6). One voice, rising politely on each question, with no sarcasm anywhere: these are ordinary forms, not performances of deference.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order. Line two uses tu and line seven uses vous; the register difference must be carried by the words alone, not by a change of voice.

Awa and Karim in a café (act 7), two voices, one take, and the deck cards read by the coach voice. Karim’s first line lands as an instruction and his third as an opinion; Awa’s reaction in between must not be annoyed, only unhelped.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Six lines, one voice. The future versions in promptSound are never spoken.

The group message thread (act 8), read as three separate voices: Karim, Awa and Malik. One take each is fine, but the three voices must be clearly distinct, because the reading questions turn on who proposes and who advises.
The pouvoir, vouloir, devoir deck (act 8). One voice. The fourth card is devoir ESTIMATING rather than advising, so it is read as a calculation, not as a suggestion.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, conversational pace.
Karim and Awa on the pavement after the viewing (act 9), two voices, one take. Everything is imagined, so the delivery stays light and quick; nothing here should sound like a decision.
The four hypothesis cards (act 9). One voice. The fourth card quotes a full si sentence: read it as an ordinary sentence, with no pause at si, because the act deliberately does not dwell on it.

The one o clock news bulletin (act 10), ONE news-reader voice, France or Belgium, at real bulletin pace. Every conditional is read completely flat: a newsreader does not signal doubt with the voice, only with the verb. The one present-tense sentence is read at the same pace as the rest.
The four reported-speech cards (act 10). Same flat news delivery as the bulletin. The fourth card holds a contrast pair; read both halves identically so only the verb separates them.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, authored order, bulletin pace. No pause before or after selon and d’après, or the learner hears the source instead of the verb.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT sentence. Six lines, one voice, flat. Three of the six are in the present because the speaker witnessed them, and they are read exactly like the other three.

The model email (act 11), one voice, read as someone reading a message aloud rather than performing it. The four parts must be audible through the pauses: why I write, my wish, my request, my proposal.

lessons.intro: You can already build the future stem and the imparfait endings. The present conditional is those two things glued together, which makes it the cheapest form you will ever buy. What it costs instead is judgement: one form does six different jobs, from asking for a coffee to reporting what the police have not confirmed, and the spelling difference between je parlerai and je parlerais is almost inaudible.

piege.body: Je parlerai est un projet. Je parlerais est une idée. À l'oreille, c'est presque pareil. C'est le contexte qui décide : un moment précis annonce le futur, une condition annonce le conditionnel. EN: The context decides, because the ear cannot.
piege.title: Une lettre, deux mondes

examples.note: demain : un moment, donc le futur
à ta place : une condition, donc le conditionnel
la forme nous sépare les deux clairement

recul.body: Le conditionnel recule d'un pas par rapport au réel. Tu ne dis plus ce qui est, tu dis ce qui serait. C'est pour ça qu'il sert à souhaiter, à demander, à conseiller et à rapporter. EN: The conditional steps back from what is, to what would be.
recul.title: Un pas en arrière

examples.note: le même souhait, un pas en arrière

rumeur.body: Dans la presse, le conditionnel signale une information qu'on rapporte sans la garantir. Selon la police, d'après le journal : la source parle, le journaliste ne signe pas. EN: Reported, not vouched for.
rumeur.title: Dit, mais pas vérifié

conseil.body: Tu dois devient tu devrais. Il faut devient il faudrait. Et à ta place, je ferais met le conseil dans ta bouche à toi. Personne ne reçoit d'ordre. EN: Advice given as advice, not as an order.
conseil.title: Conseiller, pas ordonner

radical.body: Les radicaux irréguliers sont les mêmes qu'au futur : ser-, aur-, ir-, fer-, pourr-, voudr-, devr-, saur-, viendr-, verr-, faudr-. Tu les connais déjà, tu ne les rachètes pas. EN: The irregular stems are the future ones; you already own them.
radical.title: Le radical finit toujours par r

examples.note: falloir donne faudr-, toujours avec il

recette.body: Prends le radical du futur, celui qui finit toujours par r. Colle dessus les terminaisons de l'imparfait : -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Tu n'apprends rien de neuf. EN: Take the future stem, add the imparfait endings; nothing here is new.
recette.title: Deux morceaux déjà payés

examples.note: vendre perd son e avant le r

souhait.body: Je voudrais, j'aimerais, je préférerais : trois ouvertures pour dire une envie sans la poser comme un fait. Je veux annonce une décision, je voudrais annonce une envie. EN: Wishes, said as wishes rather than as decisions.
souhait.title: Ce que tu aimerais

examples.note: préférer met deux options sur la table

hypothese.body: Le conditionnel dit le résultat d'une situation imaginée. La condition peut être un mot, un groupe ou rien du tout. La phrase complète avec si arrive à la leçon 10. EN: The result of an imagined situation; the full si pattern comes later.

sheets.title: La recette et les six fins

sections.body: Le futur dit ce qui sera. Le conditionnel dit ce qui serait. Le radical est celui du futur et finit toujours par r. Les terminaisons sont celles de l'imparfait : -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Quatre des six cases se prononcent pareil, alors c'est le pronom qui porte la personne. EN: The future says what will be. The conditional says what would be. The stem is the future one and always ends in r; the endings are the imparfait ones, and four of the six sound identical.
sections.title: Deux morceaux, zéro nouveauté

sections.body: Les radicaux irréguliers du conditionnel sont EXACTEMENT ceux du futur, appris à la leçon 6 du B1. « Le radical change, la fin ne change jamais. » Si tu sais dire « je serai », tu sais déjà dire « je serais ». EN: the irregular stems are the future ones; if you can say je serai, you can say je serais.

sections.body: Le futur dit ce qui sera. Le conditionnel dit ce qui serait. La forme ne change pas d'un emploi à l'autre : c'est la situation qui dit lequel des six tu es en train de faire. Quand tu hésites, demande-toi de quoi tu recules : d'une décision, d'un ordre, d'un fait, ou d'une garantie. EN: The future says what will be. The conditional says what would be. One form, six jobs; ask what you are stepping back from.

overview.introFr: Tu sais déjà former le radical du futur et les terminaisons de l'imparfait. Le conditionnel présent, c'est les deux collés : c'est la forme la moins chère de ton année. Ce qu'elle coûte, c'est du jugement. Une seule forme fait six métiers, du café qu'on commande à l'information que la police n'a pas confirmée, et l'écart entre je parlerai et je parlerais s'entend à peine.

sections.text: Bruxelles, rue Haute. L'annonce disait : « Bel appartement de deux chambres, deuxième étage, avec balcon. Le loyer serait négociable pour un bail de trois ans. » Karim a lu la ligne deux fois. Selon l'agence, le chauffage serait collectif et les charges seraient comprises, mais rien n'était écrit noir sur blanc. Il a écrit à l'agente : « Bonjour Madame Lemoine, je voudrais visiter l'appartement cette semaine. Pourriez-vous me confirmer l'adresse exacte ? Nous serions disponibles samedi à partir de dix heures. » La réponse est arrivée le soir même. « Ce serait possible samedi matin. Vous devriez apporter vos trois dernières fiches de paie. Il faudrait aussi prévoir un état des lieux avant la signature. » Karim a relu le message et il a souri. Personne ne lui donnait d'ordre, personne ne lui promettait rien, et pourtant tout était clair. Avec un balcon et un loyer correct, ce serait parfait pour eux.

sections.title: Quatre façons de trancher
points: Change de personne dans ta tête : nous partirons ou nous partirions. Le i tranche. EN: switch to nous; the i settles it.
Cherche un mot de temps : demain, lundi, dès que. Un moment réel annonce le futur. EN: a real moment points to the future.
Cherche une condition : à ta place, avec un balcon, dans ce cas. EN: a condition points to the conditional.
Demande-toi si tu t'engages. Si oui, pas de s. EN: if you are committing, drop the s.

rule.body: Un moment réel dans la phrase, et c'est le futur, sans s. Une condition, une envie ou un conseil, et c'est le conditionnel, avec son s. L'oreille ne tranchera jamais. EN: context decides, because the ear never will.
rule.title: Le contexte écrit la lettre

sections.text: Karim a écrit au groupe jeudi soir. « Bonjour à tous. Nous pourrions visiter l'appartement samedi matin, vers dix heures. Awa, tu voudrais venir avec nous ou tu préférerais qu'on te raconte après ? Il faudrait aussi quelqu'un pour mesurer la chambre du fond. » Awa a répondu vingt minutes plus tard. « Je pourrais passer vers midi, pas avant : je travaille jusqu'à onze heures. Vous devriez commencer sans moi. » Le troisième message est arrivé de Malik, qui n'avait rien demandé. « Moi, à votre place, je demanderais à voir la cave. Les agences ne la montrent jamais, et elle devrait faire vingt mètres carrés d'après le plan. » Personne n'a donné d'ordre, personne n'a promis d'être là, et pourtant le rendez-vous s'est organisé tout seul.

sections.text: Trois informations ce midi. Selon la police, le suspect serait en fuite depuis mardi soir. Il habiterait dans le quartier et travaillerait dans une usine de la zone nord. Aucune arrestation n'a été annoncée. Deuxième information : d'après le journal du matin, cette même usine fermerait en juin. La direction n'a pas voulu répondre. Le maire, lui, aurait une autre solution, mais il ne l'a pas encore présentée au conseil communal. Enfin, la circulation. Les travaux de la rue Haute commenceraient au printemps et dureraient huit mois. Selon l'agence régionale, le tram serait dévié pendant toute la durée du chantier. Rien n'est signé. Une seule phrase de ce bulletin est au présent, et c'est celle qui dit qu'aucune arrestation n'a été annoncée.

sections.text:
Bonjour Madame Lemoine,

Je vous écris au sujet de l'appartement de la rue Haute. J'aimerais savoir si la visite de samedi est confirmée. Nous serions disponibles à partir de dix heures, et mon frère viendrait avec nous.

Pourriez-vous me confirmer l'adresse exacte ? Je voudrais également poser une question sur les charges : selon l'annonce, le chauffage serait collectif, mais le montant n'est pas indiqué. Il faudrait aussi prévoir un état des lieux avant la signature. Ce serait plus simple pour tout le monde.

Une dernière chose : à votre place, je proposerais deux créneaux, parce que la rue est difficile d'accès le samedi matin. Dans les deux cas, je vous préviendrais rapidement.

Je vous remercie d'avance de votre réponse et je reste joignable tout le week-end.

Bien à vous,
Karim Benali

steps: Dis pourquoi tu écris, au présent, en une phrase. EN: say why you are writing, in the present, in one sentence.
Ouvre ton souhait avec j'aimerais ou je voudrais, une seule fois. EN: open your wish once, with j’aimerais or je voudrais.
Pose ta demande avec pourriez-vous ou auriez-vous. EN: put your request with pourriez-vous or auriez-vous.
Ajoute ce que tu proposes avec il faudrait ou ce serait. EN: add what you are proposing with il faudrait or ce serait.
Relis chaque verbe en -rai et demande-toi s'il manque un s. EN: reread every -rai and ask whether an s is missing.

sections.brief: Tu as vu une annonce : un appartement, un studio ou une chambre, dans une ville que tu connais. Quelque chose n'est pas clair dans l'annonce. Écris un courriel à l'agence ou au propriétaire pour organiser une visite et poser ta question.
sections.title: Écris à l’agence

criteria.label: Des formes justes
descriptors: 4 : Chaque conditionnel est bien construit : radical du futur, terminaison de l'imparfait. Les radicaux irréguliers sont corrects.
3 : Presque tous les conditionnels sont justes. Une seule forme boite, et on comprend quand même.
2 : Plusieurs formes mélangent le radical du présent ou de l'imparfait avec la bonne terminaison.
1 : Les formes sont devinées. Le radical du futur n'apparaît pas de façon fiable.

criteria.label: Le bon métier au bon moment
descriptors: 4 : Le souhait, la demande, la proposition et l'information rapportée sont là, chacun à sa place et avec son ouverture.
3 : Les quatre sont là, mais l'un d'eux est ouvert avec la mauvaise formule.
2 : Deux des quatre manquent, ou deux d'entre eux se répètent avec la même ouverture.
1 : Une seule formule sert à tout, ou le courriel ne demande rien de précis.

criteria.label: Aucun ordre resté au présent
descriptors: 2 : Rien ne sonne comme une instruction. Vous devez, il faut et je veux ont tous reculé.
1 : Il reste au moins une phrase qui donne un ordre au lecteur.

criteria.label: La mission complète
descriptors: 2 : Le courriel fait 110 à 150 mots, il ouvre, il demande et il se termine poliment.
1 : Il manque l'ouverture, la question ou la formule de fin, ou la longueur est hors des bornes.

sections.briefEn: You have seen a listing for a flat, a studio or a room. Something in it is unclear. Write an email to arrange a viewing and ask your question.
sections.produce: Écris un courriel de 110 à 150 mots avec : une phrase au présent qui dit pourquoi tu écris, un souhait ouvert par j'aimerais ou je voudrais, une demande avec pourriez-vous ou auriez-vous, une proposition avec il faudrait ou ce serait, et une information de l'annonce que tu rapportes sans la garantir.
scaffold: Je vous écris au sujet de

watchFor.pattern: An order left in the present: « Vous devez me rappeler », « Il faut me répondre avant vendredi », « Je veux visiter ».
watchFor.feedback: Ton message donne un ordre. Recule d'un pas : « Pourriez-vous me rappeler », « Il faudrait une réponse avant vendredi », « Je voudrais visiter ».

watchFor.pattern: The imparfait endings attached to the present or imparfait stem: « je parlais » for « je parlerais », « je faisais » for « je ferais », « je voulais » for « je voudrais ».
watchFor.feedback: Il manque le r du radical. Le conditionnel part du radical du FUTUR : parler-, fer-, voudr-. Relis l'acte 3.

watchFor.pattern: A missing s on the je form where the sentence is not a dated plan: « Demain je signerai » is right, « Dans ce cas je signerai » is not.
watchFor.feedback: Regarde ce que la phrase fait. Si elle imagine, si elle propose ou si elle conseille, le s est obligatoire.

watchFor.pattern: An added s on a genuine dated plan: « Je vous enverrais le dossier demain matin » where the writer is actually committing.
watchFor.feedback: Ici tu t'engages vraiment, avec une date. Enlève le s : « je vous enverrai ».

watchFor.pattern: A conditional after « si »: « si je serais », « si vous pourriez ».
watchFor.feedback: Après si, on n'écrit jamais je serais. Utilise « à votre place » ou « dans ce cas », qui font le même travail.

watchFor.pattern: « de » inserted after pouvoir or vouloir: « Pourriez-vous de m'envoyer », « Je voudrais de visiter ».
watchFor.feedback: Après pouvoir, vouloir et aimer, l'infinitif arrive nu. Le de appartient à « ce serait possible de ».

watchFor.pattern: The wish, the request, the proposal or the reported information missing from the email.
watchFor.feedback: Relis le plan en cinq étapes. Il te manque un des quatre morceaux : le souhait, la demande, la proposition ou l'information de l'annonce.

watchFor.pattern: One opener doing every job: three or four sentences all starting « je voudrais ».
watchFor.feedback: Varie : j'aimerais pour le souhait, pourriez-vous pour la demande, il faudrait pour la proposition.

watchFor.pattern: Information taken from the listing and stated as fact: « le chauffage est collectif » where the writer has only read it.
watchFor.feedback: Tu n'as pas vérifié : écris « selon l'annonce, le chauffage serait collectif ». Sinon, c'est toi qui signes.

watchFor.pattern: « vouloir que » plus an indicative: « Je voudrais que vous m'envoyez le contrat ».
watchFor.feedback: Vouloir que appelle un temps que tu verras plus tard. Ici, une question avec pourriez-vous fait le même travail.

watchFor.pattern: An email with no reason for writing, or with no closing thanks.
watchFor.feedback: Ouvre par une phrase au présent qui dit pourquoi tu écris, et ferme par un remerciement, au présent aussi.

watchFor.pattern: A body outside 110 to 150 words, counted without the greeting and the sign-off.
watchFor.feedback: Compte tes mots sans le bonjour et sans la signature. En dessous de cent dix, il manque un des quatre morceaux.

graderNotes: Word count EXCLUDES the greeting and the sign-off (Paul, 2026-09-22). Count the body only, with 10% tolerance (99-165) before criterion « tache » loses its point.

DO NOT SCORE si CLAUSES. « si + imparfait + conditionnel » is the ground of lesson 10 in B1 and has not been taught. A learner who writes one correctly is not rewarded and one who writes it wrongly is not penalised, EXCEPT for a conditional placed directly after si, which this lesson does name as an error.
Do not score the subjunctive. « il faudrait que » and « je voudrais que » are outside this lesson; a wrong verb after them is ignored.
The conditionnel passé (« j’aurais voulu », « il aurait fallu ») is outside this lesson. Accept it if correct, do not penalise it if wrong.
Judge « le bon métier » by what the sentence DOES in the email, not by the opener alone. « Ce serait plus simple » can be a proposal or a hypothesis and both count.
Writer gender is unknown: judge adjective agreement for internal consistency only.
Accept regional vocabulary and currency (euros, francs suisses, dollars canadiens, francs CFA) and regional address forms (Madame, Monsieur, Chère Madame).
Accept a rented room or a shared flat in place of a studio: the situation is the learner’s to choose.
Feedback language: simple French (B1), addressed as « tu », with one short English gloss allowed per comment.
sections.modelAnswer:
Bonjour Madame,

Je vous écris au sujet du studio de la rue des Tanneurs, annoncé à six cent vingt euros. J'aimerais savoir si une visite serait possible cette semaine, de préférence en fin de journée. Je travaille jusqu'à dix-sept heures, mais je serais libre à partir de dix-huit heures du lundi au jeudi.

Pourriez-vous me confirmer l'étage et la surface exacte ? Selon l'annonce, le studio ferait trente mètres carrés, mais le plan en montre vingt-cinq. Il faudrait aussi savoir si les charges sont comprises dans le loyer.

Enfin, à votre place, je proposerais deux créneaux, parce que la rue est fermée le mercredi. Ce serait plus simple pour tout le monde.

Je vous remercie d'avance de votre réponse.

Bien à vous,
Samira Cheriet
sections.modelAnswerEn: Hello Madame, I am writing about the studio on rue des Tanneurs, listed at six hundred and twenty euros. I would like to know whether a viewing would be possible this week, preferably late in the day. I work until five, but I would be free from six o clock, Monday to Thursday. Could you confirm the floor and the exact size for me? According to the listing, the studio is said to be thirty square metres, but the plan shows twenty-five. It would also be necessary to know whether the charges are included in the rent. Finally, in your place, I would offer two slots, because the street is closed on Wednesdays. That would be simpler for everyone. Thank you in advance for your reply. Best wishes, Samira Cheriet

sections.body: Tu construis le conditionnel de n'importe quel verbe, tu souhaites, tu demandes, tu conseilles, tu imagines et tu rapportes. Le piège qui reste est le s de la case je : l'oreille ne te le donnera jamais. Avant l'examen, reprends ton courriel et souligne chaque verbe en -rai ou -rais. Pour chacun, écris à côté ce qu'il fait : un projet, un souhait, une demande, un conseil, un résultat imaginé ou une information rapportée. Si tu n'arrives pas à nommer le métier d'un verbe, c'est celui-là qu'il faut réécrire. EN: Underline every -rai and -rais in your email and name the job each one does; the one you cannot name is the one to rewrite.

sections.title: Une dernière fois

sections.say: Le futur dit ce qui sera. Le conditionnel dit ce qui serait.
sections.body: Le futur dit ce qui sera. Le conditionnel dit ce qui serait. Tu as payé cette forme deux fois déjà, au futur et à l'imparfait, et elle te sert maintenant à souhaiter, à demander, à conseiller, à imaginer et à rapporter. La prochaine leçon prend la demande toute seule et en fait un métier complet, du service au bureau. EN: Next lesson takes the request on its own and builds the whole repertoire.
sections.title: Un pas en arrière, en résumé
points: La recette : radical du futur, terminaisons de l'imparfait.
Le radical finit toujours par r, et les irréguliers sont ceux du futur.
Une seule forme fait six métiers : la situation dit lequel.
Le s de la case je ne s'entend pas : c'est le contexte qui l'écrit.

errorTriggers.description: Asks, advises and speculates in the present, so every sentence arrives as a decision already taken and the reader has nothing left to answer.
Builds the conditional with the future endings, or attaches the imparfait endings to the present stem, so the r of the future stem goes missing.
Writes the imparfait of an irregular verb in place of its conditional: je faisais for je ferais, je voulais for je voudrais.
Chooses between -ai and -ais by ear, so a dated plan gains an s and an imagined result loses one.
States a wish in the present, or opens every wish with the same formula whatever the situation, so the choice between voudrais, aimerais and préférerais is never made.
Asks for a service in the present, or reaches straight for the heaviest polite form whatever the trouble caused.
Gives advice with the present or the future of devoir and falloir, so an opinion is delivered as an instruction.
Keeps pouvoir, vouloir and devoir in the present where the sentence is proposing, offering or estimating rather than stating a fact.
Uses the future for the result of a situation that does not exist, or the conditional for something that is already true.
Repeats an unverified claim in the present, taking on a guarantee the speaker cannot give, or hedges a fact they witnessed themselves.
Writes a whole message with the right forms but the wrong jobs: no wish, no request, or an order left standing in the middle.

grammarIntroduced: Formation of the present conditional: the future stem plus the imparfait endings -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient
The irregular conditional stems, identical to the irregular future stems and reused rather than retaught
The je parlerai / je parlerais contrast: [e] against [ɛ], settled by context rather than by ear, and the persons where the contrast is audible
The conditional of wish and desire: je voudrais, j’aimerais, je préférerais
The conditional as request softener: pourriez-vous, auriez-vous, ça vous dérangerait de, est-ce que ce serait possible de
The conditional of advice: tu devrais, vous devriez, il faudrait, il vaudrait mieux, à ta place je ferais
pouvoir, vouloir and devoir in the conditional as the three verbs that carry most everyday softening
The result half of a hypothetical, with the condition carried by a prepositional phrase rather than a si clause
The journalistic conditional: reported information the speaker does not vouch for, introduced by selon or d’après

recorded.desc: The same sentence twice, eight times over. ONE TAKE PER CARD, both halves inside it, and NO extra stress on the small word. Stressing it would teach that the difference is audible, and the whole point is that what settles it is the noun rather than the sound.

REQUIRED LAYOUT 3, AND THE ONE CONSTRAINT IN THIS LESSON THAT CANNOT BE RECOVERED LATER. « Regarde ce livre. » and « Regarde cet homme. » are ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, RECORDED ADJACENTLY, in that order, with « Regarde cet hôtel. » and « Regarde cette robe. » in the same take. Recorded apart, the learner compares two performances instead of two sounds and hears the reader rather than the language. The t of cet runs onto the front of homme and hotel: seh-TOM, seh-toh-TEL, never a t released on its own.

The audio step plays each card's fr, which is the CORRECT form every time. The bare version lives in promptSound and must be read at the same pace and with the same intonation as the correct one, then stopped dead where the speaker ran out of sentence. A bare form read as though it were obviously wrong teaches nothing, because the learner producing it does not hear it as wrong.

lessons.intro: French has one small word for pointing at a thing and a second one for pointing at it without saying what it is. They share a root, they share a gender, and the only question is whether the noun comes next. Then one of them grows a consonant, for a reason you have already met twice.

tail.body: celui, celle, ceux and celles always have something after them: -ci, -là, de plus an owner, or qui plus what it does. English lets that one finish the sentence and French does not, so the half-second where you would stop is exactly the half-second where you add two letters.
tail.title: Four of them cannot end a sentence

examples.note: qui, and what it is doing

point.body: ce, cet, cette and ces all sit in front of a noun and none of them can stand without one. They say this one here rather than any old one, which is the whole of what they do. Which of the four you use is decided by the noun, never by you.
point.title: When the thing is named

sound.body: Both are said SEHT and your ear will never separate them. The difference is only on the page: cet goes with a masculine noun starting with a vowel, cette goes with any feminine noun. So this is a thing you get right by knowing the noun, and there is no version of it you can get right by listening.
sound.title: cet and cette are the same noise

examples.note: the same SEHT, one more time

vowel.body: ce becomes cet in front of a word that starts with a vowel sound, and that is the only reason it exists. It is not a different meaning and it is not a different gender: ce homme would put two vowels together and French will not have it. A silent h counts as a vowel, because the rule listens rather than reads.
vowel.title: The one that only exists for the sound

examples.note: a silent h, and still cet

gender.body: Lesson 5 in A1 taught you to store a noun with its gender and this is where you spend it. Nothing in this lesson tells you whether a bag is masculine; it tells you what to do once you know. If the gender is not in your head the eight forms are eight guesses, and that is the one thing worth going back for.
gender.title: You are spending lesson 5 in A1 here

examples.note: chaussures is feminine and plural, and ces does not care which

replace.body: celui, celle, ceux and celles stand where the noun would have been. You still had to know its gender to pick one, so nothing about the choice is easier. The saving is that you do not say the word twice, which is exactly what English does with the one.
replace.title: When the thing is not named

sections.body: The top four take a noun and cannot be said without one, and you pick between them the same way lesson 6 in A1 taught you to pick le, la and les. The bottom four take anything except a noun and cannot be said without something. Read down the middle column and you are reading the gender; read across a row and you are reading the choice this lesson is about.
sections.title: How to read this

rowDetails.body: The default masculine. It becomes cet the moment the next word starts with a vowel sound, including a silent h, and it never changes for anything else.
rowDetails.title: ce, and when it is not enough

rowDetails.body: Masculine, vowel only. It is the same masculine word with a consonant added so two vowels do not meet, and it is said exactly like cette.
rowDetails.title: cet, and why it exists

rowDetails.body: Feminine, in front of anything at all. There is no second feminine form, because the e already puts a consonant in front of whatever follows.
rowDetails.title: cette, and the one thing it is not

rowDetails.body: Plural, both genders, no exceptions. This is the one place in the whole system where the gender does not have to be known.
rowDetails.title: ces, and what it stops asking

rowDetails.body: Masculine singular, standing in for a noun. Never on its own: -ci, -là, de plus an owner, or qui plus what it is doing.
rowDetails.title: celui, and what has to follow it

rowDetails.body: Feminine singular. celle and celles are one sound, so the s exists only on the page and only writing can get it wrong.
rowDetails.title: celle, and the silent plural

rowDetails.body: Masculine plural. ces covered both genders going in and this is one of the two words that separate them coming out.
rowDetails.title: ceux, and where the plural splits again

rowDetails.body: Feminine plural, and it sounds identical to the singular. Between them ceux and celles do the job ces did on its own.
rowDetails.title: celles, and the fourth cell

sections.text: Elle a posé deux sacs sur le comptoir. Ce sac est en cuir et celui-là est en toile. Le premier coûte cent vingt euros, le second quarante. À côté des deux sacs, il y a une valise qui n'est pas à vendre. Cet homme regarde les deux sacs depuis dix minutes sans rien dire. Il touche celui de gauche, puis celle de sa femme. Il ne dit rien à la vendeuse, qui attend. Elle voit trois clients comme ça par jour. Il finit par montrer celui en toile et il dit deux mots. Elle enveloppe le sac en toile.
sections.title: Two bags, one counter

glossary.note: The flat surface you pay at, and the only place in the shop where both bags are.
en plus a material is how French says what a thing is made of.
The same en, a cheaper material, and the whole of why the two bags differ.
From vendre. A thing on a counter is not automatically for sale, which is the joke in this sentence.
The woman doing the selling. From the same vendre.
Feminine, and the only feminine thing in the shop, which is why one word later has to change.
From envelopper. What she does once he has finally said which one.

questions.a: la valise, introduced two sentences earlier and the only feminine thing in the shop. That is why the word had to change from celui to celle: it agrees with what it replaces, not with the person who owns it.

rule.body: If you have said celui, celle, ceux or celles and the sentence is about to stop, it is not going to. Add -ci or -là and you are finished. That is two letters, and it is the difference between a sentence and a pause.

errors.why: Reasonable, because English stops there. That one is a complete answer in English and the French word it looks like cannot end a sentence at all. Two letters finish it.
errors.right: Je prends celui-ci.
errors.wrong: Je prends celui.

errors.why: Reasonable, and it is what the rule you just learned produces if you only apply the gender half of it. homme is masculine, so ce is right about the gender and wrong about the sound.
errors.right: Regarde cet homme.
errors.wrong: Regarde ce homme.

errors.why: Reasonable, because both words mean roughly this one and nothing in English separates them. The noun is there, so it is the other four you want.
errors.right: Je prends ce livre.
errors.wrong: Je prends celui livre.

errors.why: Reasonable, and it is the first error in a mirror. This one cannot stand without a noun any more than the other one can stand without a tail, so a bare ce is a sentence with a hole in it.
errors.right: Je prends celui-ci.
errors.wrong: Je prends ce.

errors.why: Reasonable, because ces covered both genders on the way in and it feels as though nothing has to be decided on the way out. Coming out they split, and gants is masculine.

errors.wrong: Ces gants sont noirs, mais celles-là sont blancs.

sections.body: You can point at a thing by name in all four forms and stand in for it in all four more, including for a noun this lesson never listed. The thing to check is the one you cannot hear. cet and cette are one sound, so you will never catch that pair by listening and nobody will ever tell you out loud that you got it wrong. Go back to the four cards in act 2 and write all eight forms out, from the English, without looking. If the small word is right eight times, the lesson has landed.

questions.why: The noun is there, so the word in front of it points. ce, because livre is masculine and starts with a consonant.
accept: Je prends ce livre
Je prends ce livre.
questions.answer: Je prends ce livre

questions.q: I'll take this one, and the one is the book. Same sentence, no book in it.
questions.why: No noun, so the word stands where the noun would have been. You still needed to know livre was masculine to get here.
accept: Je prends celui-ci
Je prends celui-ci.
Je prends celui ci
questions.answer: Je prends celui-ci

questions.q: Which of these names the thing it is pointing at?
questions.why: livre is in the sentence, so ce points at it. The other two have no noun anywhere and stand in for one instead.

questions.q: ce livre and celui-ci. What is actually different?
questions.why: That is the only difference. Both are masculine, both mean this one, and one of them says the word book while the other does not.

questions.q: robe is feminine. I'll take this dress. Start with Je prends.
questions.why: A noun follows, and it is feminine, so cette. There is only one feminine form and it never changes for what comes next.
accept: Je prends cette robe
Je prends cette robe.
questions.answer: Je prends cette robe

questions.q: I'll take this one, and the one is the dress.
questions.why: The feminine of the four that replace, and the two letters on the end are what make it a sentence rather than a pause.
accept: Je prends celle-ci
Je prends celle-ci.
Je prends celle ci
questions.answer: Je prends celle-ci

questions.q: Which of these can never have a noun after it?
questions.why: ceux stands where the noun would have been, so putting one after it leaves the sentence with two things doing one job. The other two require a noun.

questions.q: One word is doing the wrong job. Write the sentence out.
questions.why: livre is right there, so the word in front of it has to be one of the four that point. celui was standing in for a noun that had not gone anywhere.
accept: Je prends ce livre.
Je prends ce livre
questions.answer: Je prends ce livre.
questions.prompt: Je prends celui livre.

questions.q: homme is masculine and starts with a vowel. Look at this man. Start with Regarde.
questions.why: Masculine rules out cette and the vowel rules out ce, so there is exactly one form left. The t runs onto the front of homme.
accept: Regarde cet homme
Regarde cet homme.
questions.answer: Regarde cet homme

questions.q: Look at this dress. Same sentence, and robe is feminine.
questions.why: cette, and it sounds exactly like the one before it. The only thing that told you which to write was the gender of the noun.
accept: Regarde cette robe
Regarde cette robe.
questions.answer: Regarde cette robe

questions.q: Look at this book. livre is masculine and starts with a consonant.
questions.why: A consonant follows, so no extra letter is needed and the plain form does the job.
accept: Regarde ce livre
Regarde ce livre.
questions.answer: Regarde ce livre

questions.q: Look at these gloves. gants is plural.
questions.why: ces, and it is the one of the four that does not ask about gender at all. Masculine or feminine, plural is plural.
accept: Regarde ces gants
Regarde ces gants.
questions.answer: Regarde ces gants

questions.q: un aéroport is masculine, and this lesson has never shown it to you. This airport is
questions.why: Masculine rules out the feminine one, and the vowel it starts with rules out the plain one. You had never seen this word and the rule handled it anyway.

questions.q: hôtel is masculine and its h is silent. Look at this hotel.
questions.why: The h is not said, so what the word actually starts with is a vowel. The rule listens rather than reads, and this is the proof of it.
accept: Regarde cet hôtel
Regarde cet hôtel.
Regarde cet hotel
questions.answer: Regarde cet hôtel

questions.q: Listen. Is he looking at one thing or more than one?

questions.why: SUH, which is the singular. This is the one contrast in the lesson your ear can actually settle.

questions.q: Listen again. One thing or more than one?
questions.say: Regarde ces gants.
questions.why: SAY this time, and it is a completely different vowel. ce against ces is audible where cet against cette is not.

questions.q: He meant: I want that one. Write what he should have said.
questions.why: What he wrote is not a French sentence. Two letters finish it, and this is the line from the shop at the start of the lesson.
accept: Je veux celui-là.
Je veux celui-là
Je veux celui-la
Je veux celui la

questions.q: She meant: I'll take this one, and the one is the dress. Write it out.
questions.why: The feminine has exactly the same problem and exactly the same fix. Nothing about the gender changes whether the tail is needed.
accept: Je prends celle-ci.
Je prends celle-ci
Je prends celle ci
questions.answer: Je prends celle-ci.
questions.prompt: Je prends celle.

questions.q: I want that one, the further one. Start with Je veux.
questions.why: The far one. In real speech people use this form for both near and far and nobody minds, so it is the one worth keeping.
accept: Je veux celui-là
Je veux celui-là.
Je veux celui-la
Je veux celui la
questions.answer: Je veux celui-là

questions.q: Which one of these is French?
questions.why: The third stops before the sentence is finished and the first puts an article in front of a word that already has one built in. Only the middle one is a sentence.

questions.q: I want Marie's one. Start with Je veux.
questions.why: de plus the owner, and the owner goes last. That finishes the sentence exactly as well as two letters would.
accept: Je veux celui de Marie
Je veux celui de Marie.
questions.answer: Je veux celui de Marie

questions.q: Which of these is spelled correctly?
questions.why: The accent goes on the a, and it is the same là that means over there. This has to be a picked question, because a typed one cannot see an accent at all.

questions.q: He meant: take these ones here. Write what he should have said.
questions.why: Plural masculine, and the rule has not changed. Four words in this lesson cannot end a sentence and this is the third of them.
accept: Prends ceux-ci.
Prends ceux-ci
Prends ceux ci
questions.answer: Prends ceux-ci.
questions.prompt: Prends ceux.

questions.q: sac is masculine. This bag is small, but that one is big. Start with Ce sac.
questions.why: Named on the way in, replaced on the way out, and both words took their shape from the same masculine noun.
accept: Ce sac est petit, mais celui-là est grand
Ce sac est petit, mais celui-là est grand.
Ce sac est petit mais celui-la est grand
questions.answer: Ce sac est petit, mais celui-là est grand

questions.q: robe is feminine. This dress is blue, but that one is black. Start with Cette robe.
questions.why: The same shape one gender along. cette going in and celle coming out, and the describing words agreed as well.
accept: Cette robe est bleue, mais celle-là est noire
Cette robe est bleue, mais celle-là est noire.
Cette robe est bleue mais celle-la est noire
questions.answer: Cette robe est bleue, mais celle-là est noire

questions.q: chaussures is feminine and plural. These shoes are new, but those are old.
questions.why: ces going in, because the plural stops asking about gender, and celles coming out, because it starts again.
opts: Ces chaussures sont neuves, mais celles-là sont vieilles.
Ces chaussures sont neuves, mais ceux-là sont vieilles.
Celles chaussures sont neuves, mais celles-là sont vieilles.

questions.q: gants is masculine. One word has the wrong gender. Write it out.
questions.why: ces was right and told you nothing, because it covers both genders. The word that replaces the noun does not, and gants is masculine.
accept: Ces gants sont noirs, mais ceux-là sont blancs.
Ces gants sont noirs, mais ceux-là sont blancs
Ces gants sont noirs mais ceux-la sont blancs
questions.answer: Ces gants sont noirs, mais ceux-là sont blancs.
questions.prompt: Ces gants sont noirs, mais celles-là sont blancs.

questions.q: Ce sac est joli, mais celui de Marie est plus grand. Why celui the second time?
questions.why: sac is said once and never again. Whose it is comes from de Marie, and whether it is near or far does not come into this sentence at all.
opts: because it belongs to somebody else
because the noun is not said again

questions.q: gants is masculine. These gloves are black, but those are white. Start with Ces gants.
questions.why: The masculine plural, written out. ceux is the form people forget exists, because ces did the job for both genders on the way in.
accept: Ces gants sont noirs, mais ceux-là sont blancs
Ces gants sont noirs, mais ceux-là sont blancs.
Ces gants sont noirs mais ceux-la sont blancs
questions.answer: Ces gants sont noirs, mais ceux-là sont blancs

questions.q: One word is a pointing form doing a replacing job. Write it out.
questions.why: There is no noun after the second one, so it cannot be cette. The two letters on the end do not rescue it; the whole word has to change.
accept: Cette robe est bleue, mais celle-là est noire.
Cette robe est bleue, mais celle-là est noire
Cette robe est bleue mais celle-la est noire
questions.answer: Cette robe est bleue, mais celle-là est noire.

sections.title: The eight, one last time

sections.say: A noun after it means it points. No noun means it replaces.
sections.body: A noun after it means it points. No noun means it replaces. Four forms name the thing and four stand in for it, and the four that stand in for it always carry something on the end. Lesson 21 in A2, lesson 22 in A2 and lesson 23 in A2 all put a small word in front of the verb. This one is not that word and it does not go there. One thing to leave alone for now: You have said c'est since your first week, and ce sont is its plural. That ce is a third job, it never takes a noun, and this lesson is not about it. And one thing coming next: lesson 34 in A2 does the same trick for whose a thing is, and the shape will already be familiar.
sections.title: One root, and the noun decides
points: ce, cet, cette, ces. A noun follows every one of them.
celui, celle, ceux, celles. Something follows every one of them too, and it is never a noun.
cet is there for the sound, which is lesson 11 in A2 and lesson 8 in Sounds for the third time.
The gender is still lesson 5 in A1's and you spend it eight times a lesson.

errorTriggers.description: Uses a form that points where the noun is absent, or one that replaces where the noun is present.
Picks the wrong one of the four that point, usually by applying the gender and not the sound.
Ends a sentence on celui, celle, ceux or celles with nothing after it.
Carries ces across into the plural that replaces, and loses the gender the second word needs.

grammarIntroduced: The demonstrative adjectives ce, cet, cette and ces as a four-cell paradigm selected by the gender and number of the following noun
The pre-vocalic masculine cet as a phonologically conditioned allomorph of ce, triggered by a following vowel sound including one written with a silent h
That cet and cette are homophonous, so the contrast is orthographic only and cannot be assessed by ear
The demonstrative pronouns celui, celle, ceux and celles as the same four cells with the noun suppressed
That a demonstrative pronoun is obligatorily complemented, by -ci, -là, a de phrase or a relative clause, and is ungrammatical bare
That the plural neutralises gender in the adjective series and restores it in the pronoun series, which is the single asymmetry in the system
That celle and celles are homophonous, so the number contrast in the feminine pronoun is orthographic only
That the ce of c'est and ce sont is a distinct impersonal subject and not a member of either series

recorded.desc: THE TWO JOBS, IN ONE TAKE, AND THE FIRST FOUR WORDS MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE: « Je viens de Paris. » then « Je viens de manger. », then « Il vient de Nantes. » then « Il vient de partir. » This is the single most important instruction in this lesson. The whole screen is that nothing before the last word tells you which sentence you are in, so the reader must NOT lean on the de, must not pause after it, and must not colour the opening differently for the two meanings. A reader who knows the sentence is about a city will naturally soften the run-up to it; that instinct has to be suppressed completely. If a listener can tell from the first four words alone which of the two is coming, the recording has taught the opposite of what the screen teaches. Conversational pace, no teaching pause anywhere, and the two halves of each pair back to back.

THE SIX tôt LINES, IN THREE PAIRS, SINGULAR THEN PLURAL, EACH PAIR IN ONE TAKE: Il finit tôt / Ils finissent tôt, Il part tôt / Ils partent tôt, Il vient tôt / Ils viennent tôt. Here the difference MUST be audible, which is the opposite instruction from the two-jobs clip and is why they are separate recordings. Pair one inserts a syllable (fee-nee against fee-NEES), pair two lands a consonant at the very end (par against part), pair three lands a consonant AND opens the vowel (vyaⁿ against vyenn). The third pair is the one that matters: the singular vowel is fully nasal with no n released at all, and the plural is an oral vowel with a clear n. Do not nasalise the plural even slightly. In every pair the PRONOUN must sound identical on both sides, because it is: il and ils are one sound. Any difference in the pronoun destroys the pair, because the learner will use it instead of the verb. The first two pairs are a2.10.l1's and a2.10.l2's own sentences and should be read at the same pace those lessons use.

THE RECENT PAST, SIX SENTENCES, ONE TAKE, FLAT. Je viens de manger / Tu viens de rentrer / Il vient de partir / On vient de finir / Nous venons de vendre la maison / Ils viennent d'arriver. The instruction is restraint: this construction is completely ordinary in French and a reader who performs it as news will teach the learner to save it for dramatic moments, which is exactly wrong. It is what somebody says when they are asked whether they want lunch. Even pace, no emphasis on de, and no lift at the end of any of them. The scene break card plays from this clip and needs « Non merci, je viens de manger. » in the same flat register, because the whole point of the scene is that the correct sentence is unremarkable.
clipIds: Nous venons de vendre la maison.
Non merci, je viens de manger.

recorded.desc: ALL THREE PARADIGMS, IN THE USUAL PRONOUN ORDER (je, tu, il, nous, vous, ils), one voice, one speed, aller then venir then tenir, then the fifteen dictée sentences in the same take. Within each verb the FIRST THREE MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM EACH OTHER where the spelling says they are: vas and va are one sound, viens/viens/vient are one sound, tiens/tiens/tient are one sound. Do not help by touching the final letter of any of them. vais is genuinely different from vas and va and should be left different. The dictée sentences are the ones a learner replays four times while typing, so they need to be even in pace and completely flat in emphasis: any lean on an ending is a hint the screen is not supposed to give.

The six forms of aller alone, read as two groups with a short gap between them: vais, vas, va, vont, then allons, allez. The grouping IS the teaching and the gap is what carries it: four of the six begin with a v sound and two with a vowel, and no rule joins the two halves. Keep tu vas and il va identical; they are one sound and the s is written for tu and said by nobody. Do not slow down for the two all- forms, which a reader will want to do because they are longer.

The six naming forms, read as a flat list at conversational pace, one voice: aller, venir, tenir, revenir, devenir, obtenir. The last five all end in the same -NEER and that sameness is the teaching, so do not vary the intonation to keep the list interesting. Keep roughly a second between them so a learner can repeat into the gap. aller is the odd one out and should not be given any extra weight for it.

The opening scene, French bubbles only. A woman in her sixties in her own kitchen, entirely at ease, already serving before the question is answered. She is not pressing and she is not offended: the whole scene turns on nobody minding and nobody checking, so any hint of insistence or of hurt in « Voilà. Ce n'est pas beaucoup, mangez. » would destroy it. She heard an answer she understood and acted on it, and she is right to have done so.
clipIds: Vous arrivez juste à temps. Asseyez-vous.
Voilà. Ce n'est pas beaucoup, mangez.

lessons.intro: Three verbs that will not come apart, and the reason they are worth it: by the end of this one you can say what you did twenty minutes ago, which is a past tense nobody was going to give you for a while yet.

noStem.body: The three patterns you have are all one move: take the last two letters off the naming form and put the person on what is left. aller does not work like that. vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont. Four of the six do not contain a single letter of the naming form, and no rule joins them. This is the first verb in the level you have to hold in your head rather than build, and knowing that is the whole of what makes it easy: you stop looking for the reason.
noStem.title: Nothing to cut off

examples.note: And here it is, in two cells out of six.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, which on this verb means on vient and never on venons. So the commonest spoken way of saying we have just done something is On vient de, and it uses the singular form of an irregular verb, which is the one cell of the six you are most likely to need in a hurry.
nousOn.title: The we you will actually hear

examples.note: The spoken we, taking the il form.
And the written one, with its own ending.

justDid.body: Say you are coming from an action and French hears that you have just finished it. Je viens de manger is I have just eaten. It is not a special tense and there is nothing new to build: it is venir, which you now have, plus de, plus the naming form of whatever you did. It is also the only way you can talk about the past for a long time yet, and it covers most of what anybody actually asks you in a day.
justDid.title: venir de, and what it buys you

examples.note: Coming from eating, so the eating is over.
And the sentence you will use most: he has gone, a minute ago.

notYours.body: aller with a place after it is where you are going, and that is what this lesson uses it for. Put something else after it and it does another job entirely, which is lesson 15's lesson and not this one. Which small word goes in front of the place is a question of its own and it is lesson 13. Here there is one place and one small word, used six times without variation, so that the only thing on the screen is the verb.
notYours.title: One job of aller is not in this lesson

examples.note: A place after it. That is this lesson.

sameShape.body: tenir is venir with a t on the front, cell for cell. viens and tiens, vient and tient, venons and tenons, viennent and tiennent. Six cells, one difference, and it is the first letter every time. That is the only reason the second verb is in this lesson: learning it costs you nothing you have not already paid for, and it turns one irregular verb into a family.
sameShape.title: venir and tenir, cell for cell

examples.note: And the one you get for nothing.

theFamily.body: revenir is venir with re- on the front, and it takes exactly the same forms. So do devenir and obtenir. Il revient is Il vient with two letters added and nothing else changed. That is worth knowing here because it is why the two verbs above are worth the trouble at all, and where it stops being a handy coincidence and starts being a rule is lesson 9 in A2.
theFamily.title: revenir, devenir, obtenir

examples.note: Il vient tôt, with re- on it.
And Il tient la clé, with ob- on it.

vowelBack.body: In the singular the vowel is in the nose and no n is said at all: vyaⁿ. In the plural an n arrives at the end of the verb and the vowel comes out of the nose: vyenn. That is the one place in this lesson your ear does the work for you, and it is the same move lesson 3 showed you on il part against ils partent, with the vowel changing as well. Three lessons have now put a singular and a plural on the word tôt, and this is the third.
vowelBack.title: vient against viennent

examples.note: One person, and the word stops in the nose.
Several, and an n lands at the end.

whatFollows.body: Same three words twice, and two completely different sentences. Nothing in venir de tells you which one you are in: a place after de is where you are from, an action after de is what you have just finished, and there is no third option. So you do not read venir de and then work out the rest. You wait for the next word, and the next word settles it. This will happen to you again with other words later on, and it always works the same way.
whatFollows.title: Je viens de Paris. Je viens de manger.

examples.note: A place. Where you are from.
An action. When you did it.

theNamingForm.body: The naming form, always, and it does not move for anybody. Je viens de manger, tu viens de manger, ils viennent de manger: the front changes for the person and manger stays exactly as it is. That is the part learners drop, because in English the second verb changes too. Nothing after de ever changes for the person, and nothing after de ever agrees with anything.
theNamingForm.title: What goes after de

examples.note: arriver, untouched, with only the de shortened in front of the vowel.

sheets.title: Three verbs that have to be held
contains: All three, every person, in one table
The two jobs of venir de

sections.title: venir de, and its two jobs

sections.body: Every reference sheet before this one in the level lists ENDINGS, because every pattern before this one had them: lesson 1 holds the -er set in full and lesson 3 holds the -ir set, and lesson 4 in A2 puts all three regular sets in one table. That is the whole of the method and it is now finished. These three verbs have no endings to list. There is no stem to put an ending on, so what is written above is the forms themselves, and the only way in is to hold them. Read the third row of the first table and nothing else if you are in a hurry: va, vient, tient. Those are the three you will need in a hurry more than any of the others, because on takes the same form as il, so they cover the spoken we as well. The second and third tables are the part that is actually new. tenir is venir with a t on the front, cell for cell.
sections.title: Why this sheet lists forms and not endings

sections.body: Two things leave this lesson and neither of them is a table. The first is Coming from an action is how French says you just did it. It works on every verb in the language and none of them changes shape to do it, so once you have the four words in front you have the whole construction and there is nothing left to learn about it until lesson 16 in A2, 11 lessons from here, gives you a past for things that happened yesterday. The second is the shape rather than the phrase: what comes next decides. One set of words, two completely different jobs, and nothing but the next word to separate them. That happens three more times in this level and each time you will be pointed back here, to lesson 5 in A2. It is worth noticing now, because a learner who sees a pattern repeat stops believing the language is arbitrary, and this is the first place in the level where that is on offer.
sections.title: What carries forward

beats.fr: Ah, non, merci...

beats.heading: The plate

beats.text: Nobody corrected you and nothing was misheard. You ate a second lunch out of politeness, and the words that would have stopped it are four words long.

closing.text: Coming from an action is how French says you just did it. That is the sentence this lesson is for, and the three verbs around it are what make it work.

questions.q: Il finit tôt against Ils finissent tôt. What did the plural do?
questions.why: a whole syllable is pushed in, which is lesson 3's pattern and the one you met first.
opts: Added a whole syllable in the middle
Added one sound at the very end

questions.q: Now Il part tôt against Ils partent tôt.
questions.why: a consonant comes back. The singular drops the last consonant of the stem and the plural puts it back, and no syllable is added.
opts: One consonant came back at the end

questions.q: And Il vient tôt against Ils viennent tôt. This one does two things.
questions.why: a consonant comes back and the vowel leaves the nose. vyaⁿ has the vowel in the nose and no n said at all; vyenn lands the n and brings the vowel back out.

questions.q: So which of the three verbs behaves most like the one you are learning now?
questions.why: partir. The consonant coming back at the end is the same move; venir adds the vowel change on top of it. finir is the one that is not like this at all.

errors.why: Without the de it is not about the past at all. It says you are coming to eat, which in the kitchen this lesson opens in is the opposite of what you meant.

errors.wrong: Saying « Je viens manger ».

errors.why: English puts the past on the second verb and French puts it on nothing. What follows de is the naming form, always, and it does not move for the person or for the time.
errors.right: Saying « Il vient de partir ».
errors.wrong: Changing the second verb: « Il vient de parti ».

errors.why: The two plural stems are the other way round from what the singular suggests. nous and vous use the short one, and only ils doubles the n and brings the vowel out of the nose.
errors.right: Saying « Nous venons » and « Ils viennent ».

sections.title: The Whole Thing, One Deck

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have met three verbs that do not come apart, and you have found that two of them are the same verb wearing different first letters. More usefully, you can now put something in the past. Coming from an action is how French says you just did it. It works on every verb in the language and none of them changes shape to do it. You also know the one thing that can go wrong with it, which is not a matter of form at all: the same three words do a completely different job when a place follows instead of an action. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
