sections.say: Four things, and one of them was not supposed to arrive for a while yet.
sections.body: You can build three verbs that do not come apart, and you have found that two of the three are the same verb with a different first letter, which is why revenir, devenir, obtenir came free with them. A past tense, 11 lessons before anybody teaches you one. Coming from an action is how French says you just did it. It runs on every verb in the language and none of them changes shape to do it, so there is nothing more to memorise. And you know the one way it goes wrong, which is not a form at all: the same three words say where somebody is from when a place follows instead of an action.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Coming from an action is how French says you just did it.
A place after de is where you are from, an action after de is when you did it, because what comes next decides.
The naming form goes after de and never changes for anybody.
tenir is venir with a t on the front, cell for cell.

errorTriggers.description: Builds aller off a stem that is not there: je alle, ils allent, nous vons. Four lessons of derivation make the reflex very strong.
Drops the de, or conjugates what follows it: je viens manger, il vient de parti. The first stops it being a past and the second is English leaking through.
Reads or writes the wrong job of venir de, usually the origin one, because the corpus has taught it 52 times and the other one never.
Carries the singular stem into the plural or the reverse: nous viennons, ils venent. The two stems are the other way round from what the singular suggests.
Treats a compound as a separate verb to be learned, or runs venir's pattern onto aller because both are irregular.

grammarAssumed: The six subject pronouns and the nine they cover, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -er verbs as a stem plus six endings, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -ir verbs, and that some -ir verbs take no -iss-, introduced in a2.10
The present tense of regular -re verbs, introduced in a2.11
That de elides to d' in front of a vowel, introduced in sons.07
grammarIntroduced: The present tense of aller, venir and tenir, as forms that cannot be derived from a stem
That the third-person singular of venir and tenir is nasal and the third-person plural is not
venir de plus an infinitive as the recent past
That the infinitive after venir de is invariable for every person
That venir de plus a place and venir de plus an infinitive are one form doing two jobs, separated only by what follows
That the compounds of venir and tenir take their base verb's forms

recorded.desc: The same thing said twice, four times over. ONE TAKE PER CARD, both halves inside it, and NO extra stress on the article. Stressing it would teach that the article is the point; the point is that the article and the ending move together.

The four cells. ONE TAKE PER CARD. le mien and la mienne must be read with the difference that is actually there and no more: mien ends on a vowel made through the nose and stops, mienne puts a real n after it. Do not lengthen either, and do not stress the ending, because the learner has to hear a sound rather than a performance.

REQUIRED FOR THE ONLY EAR MISSION IN THE LESSON, AND THE CONSTRAINT CANNOT BE RECOVERED LATER. All four lines are ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, RECORDED ADJACENTLY, in the order they are authored. Recorded apart, the learner compares four performances instead of four sounds. The plural s on miens and miennes is NOT said, in either line, and a reader who lets one through makes the third question measure something that is not in the language.

The card that says le sien is his and hers must be read IDENTICALLY on both halves of Paul a le sien et Marie a le sien: same pace, same pitch, no lengthening on the second. The whole card says the French does not change, and a reader who separates them teaches the opposite of what it says.

The audio step plays each card's fr, which is the CORRECT form every time. The wrong version lives in promptSound and must be read at the same pace and with the same intonation as the correct one. leur and leurs are ONE SOUND and must be read as one: no audible s anywhere, on any card, because the entire trap is that the difference is not there to hear.

The register pair. C'est le mien and C'est à moi are one take each, both read as ordinary speech rather than one careful and one casual: the difference between them is which one people choose, not how they sound. The liaison in c'est à is obligatory and the t starts the next syllable, seh tah, never seh ah and never a t released on its own.

lessons.intro: English says mine for a man, a woman, a bag and a suitcase. French has eighteen ways of saying it and picks between them by looking at the thing rather than at you. You already know how to make that decision. What is new is that it now takes two words, and the first of them is the little word you were taught to leave out.

owned.body: A bag is masculine, so a man and a woman both say le mien about it. A suitcase is feminine, so both say la mienne. Nothing in the sentence changes for who is speaking, which is the opposite of what English does with his and hers. Lesson 20 in A1 gave you this rule and this lesson spends it on two words instead of one.
owned.title: It was never about you

third.body: le sien is his and it is also hers. There is no third-person form that says which, and everything up to now has taught you that French cares about gender more as you go rather than less. It is a real loss of information and it is also one less thing to get wrong. Lesson 22 in A2 met the same collapse with lui.

The accent is the only thing on the page that separates them, and it is not a sound: your ear will never catch it and neither will anything you type, because the app strips accents before it marks you. So this is the one thing in the lesson you can only ever be shown rather than tested on.

spoken.body: You will hear C'est à moi long before you hear C'est le mien, and both are correct. The à version does not change for what the thing is, which is why it is easier and why people reach for it. The two-word version is what you write and what you need when the thing has already been named. Learn both and know which is which.

twoWords.body: mon sac is one word and a noun. le mien is two words and no noun at all. The article is the part that surprises people, because lesson 20 in A1 spent a whole lesson teaching that a possessive goes where le goes. It still does. It just brings le back with it when the noun leaves.

Lesson 20 in A1 handed you the test and it still sorts the first two: a possessive has a thing behind it. This one has nothing behind it at all, which is the new case.

sections.body: Read across a row and you are reading one owner. Read down a column and you are reading one kind of thing. The owner picks the row and you knew that before this lesson started; the thing picks the column, and that is the part lesson 20 in A1 taught you and this lesson spends on two words instead of one. The bottom three rows stop after three cells, because their plural covers both kinds of thing at once. And every form on this page has an article in front of it, which is the single thing that separates the whole table from lesson 20 in A1.

sections.text: Il y a quatre valises sur l'étagère et deux sont noires. La valise noire de gauche est la mienne et la valise noire de droite est la sienne. Nous avons acheté les deux le même jour, dans le même magasin. À côté des valises il y a un sac gris, et ce sac est le nôtre : nous le partageons depuis des années. L'employé demande un ticket pour chaque bagage. Je donne le mien tout de suite. Ma sœur cherche le sien pendant deux minutes et le trouve dans sa poche. Les deux tickets sont bleus et les numéros sont différents. L'employé regarde les numéros et descend les valises dans le bon ordre.

sections.body: You can say mine, yours and theirs about a thing you have not named, in all four cells, including for a word this lesson never showed you. The thing to check is the one nobody will correct out loud. Getting the gender wrong here does not stop you being understood, so it can sit in your French for years. Go back to act two and write all four out, from the English, without looking. If the article and the ending agree four times, the lesson has landed.

sections.body: Two words, and the thing owned picks them both. Lesson 32 in A2, lesson 33 in A2 and this lesson all put a small word where a noun used to be, and this is the last of the three. One thing to leave alone: a possessive pronoun does not sit in front of the verb, which is where lesson 22 in A2 and lesson 23 in A2 put theirs. And lesson 10 in A2's idea is under all of it: a French word takes its shape from a noun, and here the noun is not even in the sentence.
sections.title: The thing decided, every time
points: Lesson 20 in A1's question, still the only one: what kind of word is the thing, and how many.
Six families. Three of them have four forms and three have three.
le sien is his and hers, and les leurs is masculine and feminine.
Lesson 1 in A2 set the register axis, and C'est à moi sits on it beside on.

errorTriggers.description: Agrees the possessive with the person who owns the thing rather than with the thing itself.
Drops the article and produces the possessive bare, the way English does with mine.
Carries the invariable leur of lesson 22 in A2 into the possessive, where the plural puts an -s on both words.
Writes notre or votre where the pronoun needs the accent, or puts the accent on the one that has a noun behind it.

grammarIntroduced: The possessive pronouns le mien, le tien and le sien as four-cell paradigms selected by the gender and number of the possessum rather than of the possessor
That a possessive pronoun is obligatorily preceded by a definite article, which is the reverse of the possessive determiner taught in a1.17
That le nôtre, le vôtre and le leur have three cells rather than four, because their plural neutralises gender
That the third-person singular sien is unmarked for the gender of the possessor, so le sien is both his and hers
That the plural -s is orthographic on every one of the eighteen forms, so number is carried audibly by the article alone
The orthographic distinction between the determiners notre and votre and the pronouns nôtre and vôtre, which is inaudible and cannot be assessed by any typed surface
That leur has three distinct grammatical roles across a1.17, a2.24 and this unit, and takes an -s in two of the three
The prepositional possessive à plus a stressed pronoun as the spoken register alternative to the possessive pronoun

desk.body: The person behind the counter speaks in fixed formulas with no je in them, delivered fast because they say them forty times a day. They are not hard French. They are hard because they arrive whole and you were listening for words.
desk.title: The half of the conversation you never hear

examples.note: A formula, and the numbers are the only part that changes.
The refusal, and it is short.

move.body: Asking for a thing, reporting a fault, or getting somebody else involved. Each one can be made at any of the three rungs, and choosing the rung is a separate decision from choosing the move.
move.title: What you are actually doing

rung.body: Three of them, and they go in order. Ask once, softly. Say it again, without the person. Ask for the person who can fix it. Most people have only the bottom one and the top one, and the whole of this lesson is the middle.
rung.title: One step on the ladder

examples.note: Rung 1, and it costs you nothing.
Rung 2, which is the one nobody taught you.

brake.body: Rung 3 works once. Ask for the manager on your first sentence and you have spent the only move you had, in front of somebody who would have fixed it anyway. Start low, and keep the top rung for when the bottom two have failed.
brake.title: Why you do not start at the top

examples.note: What you say instead, when you have only asked once.
And this is what you keep in reserve.

quebec.body: In France it is lunch. In Quebec it is breakfast, and the evening meal is le souper. The sign on the dining room door is the same word either side of the Atlantic and it does not mean the same sitting.
quebec.title: The word that moves one meal along

examples.note: A Quebec morning, with the maple syrup to prove it.

softener.body: Short pieces you learn whole and never take apart, the way you learned bonjour. They go at the front of a request and they buy you room. You get five of them here and you are not expected to build any of them yourself.
softener.title: The words you put in front

examples.note: The one this course had never published.
This one you have already met, well before now.

impersonal.body: French complaints put the fault where it happened rather than on the person in front of you. La douche ne marche pas is a fact about a shower. Vous devez réparer la douche is an instruction to a stranger, and it lands like one.
impersonal.title: The room is the subject, not the human

examples.note: The problem has a place, and no owner.
Still no owner, one rung further up.

repairMove.body: Lesson 24 in A2 authored six, ordered by what each one costs you. Rung 1 gives away nothing; the last one concedes that speaking has failed and asks for it in writing. Reach for the lowest one that will actually fix the problem.
repairMove.title: Lesson 24's six ways to say you did not catch it

examples.note: The cheapest thing you can say.
The first one that names what went wrong.

drills.q: Listen and pick the room number.
drills.why: Quatre-vingt-cinq. The difference is at the front of the word, which is the half that arrives first.
drills.title: Which number was it?

drills.title: Front or end?

drills.why: Ten minutes is not a broken promise yet. The brake accepts it, sets a time, and keeps rung 3 for when you need it.

overview.introFr: La plupart des gens ont deux modes à la réception : s'excuser, ou se fâcher. Le français a une marche au milieu, et c'est celle-ci.

sections.say: You have said this in English a hundred times. In French there is a step between apologising and shouting, and nobody teaches it.

beats.text: Eleven at night. You have been travelling since six in the morning, the room is yours, and there is no hot water.
You went down to the desk an hour ago and asked. Somebody said they would look into it. Nobody came.

beats.en: Yes? Can I help you?
beats.fr: Oui ? Je peux vous aider ?
beats.respell: [wee zhuh puh voo zay-DAY]
beats.speaker: La réception

beats.prompt: You have one sentence. Which one do you say?

options.en: You have to fix the shower.
options.fr: Vous devez réparer la douche.
options.respell: [voo day-VAY ray-pah-RAY lah DOOSH]

options.en: Excuse me, there is a problem with the shower.
options.fr: Excusez-moi, il y a un problème avec la douche.
options.respell: [ex-kü-ZAY mwah eel ee ah uhⁿ proh-BLEM ah-vek lah DOOSH]

beats.body: The first is built out of devoir, which lesson 7 in A2 taught you, and it is a perfectly formed sentence. It also hands a stranger an instruction at eleven at night. The second says the same about the same shower and mentions nobody.
beats.coach: Neither of these is a grammar mistake. That is what makes this hard to notice and worth a whole lesson.

right.en: Excuse me, there is a problem with the shower.
right.fr: Excusez-moi, il y a un problème avec la douche.
right.ipa: /ɛks.ky.ze.mwa il i.a œ̃ pʁɔ.blɛm a.vɛk la duʃ/
right.respell: [ex-kü-ZAY mwah eel ee ah uhⁿ proh-BLEM ah-vek lah DOOSH]

wrong.en: You have to fix the shower.
wrong.fr: Vous devez réparer la douche.

beats.heading: Both of those are correct French

beats.text: One of those gets the shower looked at tonight. The other gets you a form to fill in.

sections.title: No hot water, and one sentence to fix it

closing.text: You are about to learn the sentence in the middle, and the two either side of it.

setting.place: The front desk of a small hotel

goals.s: Understand the four things the desk always says, and answer them.
goals.t: Check in without rehearsing it first

goals.t: Ask for something and get it

goals.s: Say it again, without the person.

sections.title: By the end of this one

sections.say: Nothing here is difficult French. It is fast, and it arrives whole.

lines.en: Good evening, do you have a booking?
lines.fr: Bonsoir, vous avez une réservation ?

lines.en: Under what name, please?
lines.fr: C'est à quel nom, s'il vous plaît ?

lines.en: Your room is on the third floor.
lines.fr: Votre chambre est au troisième étage.

lines.en: Breakfast is served from seven to ten.
lines.fr: Le petit déjeuner est servi de sept heures à dix heures.

sections.title: The desk, at the speed the desk talks

questions.q: Which floor is the room on?
questions.why: Troisième. And in a French building the ground floor is le rez-de-chaussée and is not counted, so the third floor is four flights up.

questions.q: What is the last hour you can still get breakfast?
questions.why: De sept heures à dix heures. The de … à pair carries both ends, and the second number is the one that costs you a meal.

questions.q: What is the desk asking for in the second line?
questions.why: À quel nom means under what name. It is asked at every desk in France and it is four words long, so it goes past easily.
opts: The name the booking is under

questions.q: What does the first line want from you?
questions.why: Vous avez une réservation ? is a yes-or-no question said as a plain statement with the voice going up at the end. Nothing is added to the front and nothing is swapped round.

sections.say: Three rungs across the top, and three things you might be trying to do down the side. Nine sentences and then we stop.
cols: Say it again, without the person.
Ask for the person who can fix it.

rows.say: Est-ce que je peux avoir une serviette, s'il vous plaît ?
cells: Est-ce que je peux avoir une serviette, s'il vous plaît ?
Je vous ai demandé une serviette il y a une heure.
Je voudrais parler au responsable, s'il vous plaît.

detail.say: Est-ce que je peux avoir une serviette, s'il vous plaît ?
detail.body: The same towel, three rungs apart. Rung 1 asks. Rung 2 says when you asked before, and says nothing about whose fault that is. Rung 3 stops asking the person in front of you.
detail.title: Asking for a thing

rows.say: Excusez-moi, il y a un problème avec la douche.
cells: Il y a un problème avec la douche.
L'eau chaude ne fonctionne toujours pas.
Est-ce que quelqu'un peut venir voir ?

detail.say: L'eau chaude ne fonctionne toujours pas.
detail.body: The shower is the subject of all three. Nobody is accused at any rung, and that is what lets you climb without the conversation turning.
detail.title: Reporting a fault

rows.say: Est-ce que ce serait possible d'avoir une autre chambre ?
cells: Est-ce que ce serait possible d'avoir une autre chambre ?
Est-ce que je peux parler à quelqu'un d'autre ?

detail.say: Ça ne marche toujours pas.
detail.body: Toujours pas is the whole of rung 2 in two words. It says this has happened before without saying who let it happen.
detail.title: When it is still not fixed

sections.title: Three rungs, three moves

sections.say: Take the person out of the sentence.
sections.title: Rung 1: ask once, softly

items.en: Could I have a towel, please?
items.fr: Est-ce que je peux avoir une serviette, s'il vous plaît ?
items.note: lesson 7's asking-permission pouvoir, and it is the plain everyday form you already use.

items.en: Could you bring me a towel, please?
items.fr: Pourriez-vous m'apporter une serviette, s'il vous plaît ?
items.note: One piece, learned whole. Do not take it apart.

items.en: Could I have one more pillow?
items.fr: Est-ce que je peux avoir un oreiller de plus ?
items.note: De plus, at the end, is how you ask for one more of something.

items.en: Excuse me, there is a problem with the shower.
items.fr: Excusez-moi, il y a un problème avec la douche.
items.note: The shower has the problem. Nobody caused it.

items.en: Excuse me, there is a lot of noise in the corridor.
items.fr: Excusez-moi, il y a beaucoup de bruit dans le couloir.
items.note: The corridor is noisy. Not the people in it, and not the person you are telling.

check.q: Your room is freezing. You have not mentioned it before. Which one is rung 1?
check.why: The room is cold. That is a fact about a room, and it is the first time you have said it. The second puts a stranger under an instruction; the third is rung 2 and you have not earned it yet.
opts: Il fait très froid dans la chambre.
Ça fait deux fois que je le dis.

sections.say: Take the person out of the sentence.
sections.title: Rung 2: say it again, without the person

items.en: I asked you for a towel an hour ago.
items.fr: Je vous ai demandé une serviette il y a une heure.
items.note: A fact about the last hour, and then a full stop.

items.en: That is twice I have asked.
items.fr: Ça fait deux fois que je demande.
items.note: Counting is not complaining. Say the number and stop talking.

items.en: I called the front desk last night, and nobody came.
items.fr: J'ai appelé la réception hier soir, et personne n'est venu.
items.note: Personne n'est venu. Nobody came, and no one is named.

groups.label: The same towel, an hour later

items.en: The hot water still is not working.
items.fr: L'eau chaude ne fonctionne toujours pas.
items.note: Toujours pas is the whole rung, in two words.

items.en: It still does not work.
items.fr: Ça ne marche toujours pas.
items.note: Once the thing has been named, ça is enough.

items.en: It is still the same problem.
items.fr: C'est toujours le même problème.
items.note: Le même problème. The problem is the same one; nobody has become the problem.

check.q: You reported the broken lift this morning. It is evening and it is still broken. What is rung 2?
check.why: Toujours pas carries the whole day without accusing anybody of anything. The first makes the desk the subject of a failure. The third is rung 3, and you have only said this once.
opts: Vous ne faites rien pour cet ascenseur.

sections.title: Rung 3: ask for the person who can fix it

items.en: I would like to speak to the manager, please.
items.fr: Je voudrais parler au responsable, s'il vous plaît.
items.note: Je voudrais is already yours. What is new is when you spend it.

items.en: Could somebody come and look?
items.fr: Est-ce que quelqu'un peut venir voir ?
items.note: Quelqu'un asks for a person without asking for the boss.

items.en: Who can I see about this problem?
items.fr: Qui est-ce que je peux voir pour ce problème ?
items.note: Still about the problem. The question is who, and the answer is somebody, not you.

items.en: I will come back in an hour, then.
items.fr: Je repasse dans une heure, alors.
items.note: This is what rung 2 sounds like when it ends well, and it costs you nothing.

items.en: Is the manager here this evening?
items.fr: Le responsable est là ce soir ?
items.note: A question, not a demand. It finds out whether rung 3 is even available before you spend it.

groups.label: The brake: what you say instead

check.q: It is your first sentence of the evening. The shower is cold. What happens if you open with Je voudrais parler au responsable ?
check.why: It is perfectly correct French and it is the wrong first move. The person at the desk can almost always fix a cold shower, and once you have gone over their head there is nowhere left to go.
opts: It is the strongest opening, so the problem gets fixed fastest.
You have spent your last move on somebody who would have fixed it anyway.
It is grammatically wrong at the start of a conversation.

sections.say: You met the middle two in lesson 7 in A2. The outside two are new, and neither of them is a rule you have to build.
sections.title: The same want, four distances

examples.en: Give me a towel.
examples.fr: Donnez-moi une serviette.
examples.note: Correct, and it is what you say to a machine. Nobody at a desk hears it as neutral.

examples.en: I would like a towel, please.
examples.fr: Je voudrais une serviette, s'il vous plaît.
examples.note: Yours already, from lesson 7 in A2. This is the floor, and it is fine everywhere.

examples.en: Could I have a towel?
examples.fr: Est-ce que je peux avoir une serviette ?
examples.note: Also lesson 7's, and it is the same everyday pouvoir you have been using since then.

examples.en: Could you bring me a towel?
examples.fr: Pourriez-vous m'apporter une serviette ?
examples.note: A piece you learn whole. It is the softest of the four and it costs one extra word.

examples.en: Would it be possible to have a different room?
examples.fr: Est-ce que ce serait possible d'avoir une autre chambre ?
examples.note: Notice there is no you and no I doing anything. The room is what is being discussed.

sections.hint: Swipe. None of these come apart.

cards.fr: je voudrais · est-ce que je peux
cards.body: Lesson 7 in A2 gave you these two and told you to learn them the way you learned bonjour. That was right, and they are still the two you will use most. Nothing below replaces them.
cards.head: The two you have
cards.label: Lesson 7 in A2, and already yours

cards.fr: J'aimerais changer de chambre, si c'est possible.
cards.sub: I would like to change rooms, if possible.
cards.body: Interchangeable with je voudrais almost everywhere, and it sounds a shade warmer. Si c'est possible on the end is what turns a want into a question.
cards.head: j'aimerais
cards.label: New, and one piece

cards.fr: Pourriez-vous m'apporter une serviette ?
cards.sub: Could you bring me a towel?
cards.body: You have met this already without being told: it is in the alphabet lessons, asking you to spell a street name. It puts the asking on the other person instead of on your own wanting, and that is why it lands softly.
cards.head: pourriez-vous
cards.label: New, and one piece

cards.fr: Est-ce que ce serait possible d'avoir une autre chambre ?
cards.sub: Would it be possible to have a different room?
cards.body: The longest of the five and the one with nobody in it. No I wanting, no you doing. Keep it for the ask you think might be refused.
cards.head: ce serait possible de
cards.label: New, and the rarest

cards.fr: Un bloc, pas une règle.
cards.body: These are five fixed pieces. You will meet where they come from much later and it has a name you do not need tonight. Until then they go on the front of a sentence exactly as written.
cards.head: Do not take them apart
cards.label: The rule for all five

sections.title: Five ways in, learned whole

sections.say: Take the person out of the sentence.
sections.title: Take the person out

items.en: The room has not been made up.
items.fr: La chambre n'a pas été faite.
items.note: The room was not made up. Whoever did not make it stays out of the sentence.

items.en: There are no towels in the bathroom.
items.fr: Il n'y a pas de serviettes dans la salle de bain.
items.note: The towels are absent. Who forgot them is not the news and saying so gets them no faster.

items.en: There is a blanket missing in the room.
items.fr: Il manque une couverture dans la chambre.
items.note: Il manque. Something is missing. Nobody lost it.

items.en: The window does not close.
items.fr: La fenêtre ne ferme pas.
items.note: The window is doing the failing.

items.en: The key does not work.
items.fr: La clé ne marche pas.
items.note: The key is doing the failing, not whoever handed it across the desk.

items.en: The lift is not working.
items.fr: L'ascenseur ne fonctionne pas.
items.note: Ne fonctionne pas and ne marche pas are the same news. Use either.

items.en: The people next door make noise all night.
items.fr: Les voisins font du bruit toute la nuit.
items.note: The one place a person is allowed in: they are not the person you are talking to.

items.en: It is very cold in the room.
items.fr: Il fait très froid dans la chambre.
items.note: Il fait, with no real subject at all. The most impersonal sentence in the lesson.

items.en: The heating is too high.
items.fr: Le chauffage est trop fort.
items.note: Trop fort, not too hot. The heating is the thing that is too much.

groups.label: Loud, cold, and still nobody's fault

check.q: You want to say: you gave me a dirty room. Which version gets it fixed?
check.why: Both of the others are true and both put the person in front of you at the end of an accusation. The middle one describes the same room and asks for the same repair, and it leaves them somewhere to stand.
opts: Vous m'avez donné une chambre sale.
La chambre n'a pas été faite.
C'est votre faute, la chambre est sale.

sections.hint: Swipe. Three cards.

cards.fr: Excusez-moi de vous déranger.
cards.body: It goes first, before you have said what you want. English usually buries the apology halfway in: sorry, but the shower is broken. French puts it on the front, finishes it, and then starts the real sentence.
cards.head: Excusez-moi de vous déranger.
cards.label: The opener

cards.fr: Désolé de vous déranger, il y a un problème avec la douche.
cards.sub: Sorry to bother you, there is a problem with the shower.
cards.body: Same job, slightly less formal, and it joins straight onto the complaint with a comma. Say it as one breath and the whole sentence lands as one polite thing rather than two.
cards.head: désolé de vous déranger
cards.label: Warmer, and just as fixed

cards.fr: Une serviette, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: Not everything polite goes at the front. S'il vous plaît goes at the END, and putting it first is one of the few word-order mistakes that sounds odd rather than merely foreign.
cards.head: s'il vous plaît
cards.label: Where it does not go

sections.title: Sorry to bother you, and where it goes

sections.hint: Swipe. Lesson 24 in A2 taught these.

cards.fr: Pardon ?
cards.body: Lesson 24 in A2 authored six of these, ordered by what each one costs you. This is the cheapest thing you can say and it gives away nothing at all.
cards.head: Pardon ?
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 1

cards.fr: Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: The first of the six that names what actually went wrong. Asking for a repeat gets you the same sentence at the same speed; asking for slower gets you a different one.
cards.head: Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 3

cards.fr: Vous pouvez me l'écrire, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.sub: [voo poo-VAY muh lay-KREER seel voo PLEH]
cards.body: The last one. It concedes that speaking has failed and changes medium, which at a hotel desk is often exactly right: a room number and a breakfast time are easier read than heard.
cards.head: Vous pouvez me l'écrire ?
cards.label: Lesson 24 in A2, rung 6

cards.fr: Vous avez bien noté ? Chambre quatre-vingt-cinq.
cards.body: You will climb the whole ladder correctly and then lose the answer, because the reply comes back at the speed the desk always talks. Reach for the lowest of lesson 24's six that will actually fix it.
cards.head: The desk answers fast
cards.label: Why it belongs here

sections.title: When you did not catch the answer

sections.hint: One card. Nothing here is tested.

cards.fr: Le petit déjeuner est servi de sept heures à dix heures.
cards.sub: In Quebec that sign would say le déjeuner.
cards.body: In France le déjeuner is lunch and breakfast is le petit déjeuner. In Quebec le déjeuner is breakfast, le dîner is lunch and le souper is the evening meal. Everything scored in this lesson uses the French of France; this is the one place the two split in a way that changes which door you walk through in the morning.
cards.head: le déjeuner
cards.label: Quebec

rule.body: English says you need to fix this and means please fix this. French hears vous devez as an instruction from a stranger, because it is one. Every trap below is a perfect sentence from lesson 7 in A2, and each costs you the room.
rule.title: A correct sentence can still be the wrong move

cards.fr: Excusez-moi, il y a un problème avec la douche.
cards.ipa: /ɛks.ky.ze.mwa il i.a œ̃ pʁɔ.blɛm a.vɛk la duʃ/
cards.tip: Take the person out. The shower has the problem.

cards.fr: Est-ce que ce serait possible d'avoir une autre chambre ?
cards.ipa: /ɛs.kə sə sə.ʁɛ pɔ.sibl da.vwaʁ yn otʁ ʃɑ̃bʁ/
cards.tip: Ask whether it is possible. Do not tell them it is required.

cards.fr: Il n'y a pas de serviettes dans la salle de bain.

cards.ipa: /la ʃɑ̃bʁ na pa e.te fɛt/
cards.tip: The room was not made up. Say that, and it gets made up.
cards.promptLabel: You gave me a dirty room

steps.label: The rule
steps.title: Correct, and still the wrong move

sections.title: The politeness trap

errors.why: Devoir is not wrong and this is not a grammar mistake. It is an instruction handed to a stranger, and the reply you get back will be shaped by that rather than by the shower.
errors.right: Excusez-moi, il y a un problème avec la douche.
errors.wrong: Vous devez réparer la douche.

errors.why: S'il vous plaît goes at the end. Excusez-moi goes at the front. There is no single rule that covers both, which is why the polite word going first is a habit worth unlearning one word at a time.
errors.right: Une serviette, s'il vous plaît.
errors.wrong: S'il vous plaît, une serviette.

errors.why: Only wrong as an opening. Rung 3 works once, and spending it on your first sentence leaves you nothing when the first two rungs have genuinely failed.
errors.right: Excusez-moi, il y a un problème avec la douche.
errors.wrong: Je voudrais parler au responsable.

sections.body: You arrived with apologetic and furious and nothing in between, which is why the argument at the desk always went one of two ways. Take the person out of the sentence. That is the middle setting, and it is the one that gets the shower fixed.

recorded.desc: THE TWELVE CELLS, TWO TAKES, ONE PER VERB, EACH VERB'S SIX IN ONE BREATH GROUP. Within the first three of EACH verb the verb itself must be acoustically identical: « Je sais nager. » « Tu sais nager. » « Il sait nager. » and then « Je connais Paris. » « Tu connais Paris. » « Il connaît Paris. » A reader who knows the third one is spelled differently will put a fraction of a t on it or brighten the vowel, and every one of those instincts destroys the screen that asks the learner to fail to hear a difference. If a listener with their eyes shut can say which of the three they just heard, the take is unusable. In the plural the opposite is required: the double s of connaissons, connaissez and connaissent must be clean and audible, because it is the only thing separating the plural from the singular by ear, and the v at the end of savent must not be swallowed. AND nager MUST SOUND IDENTICAL IN ALL SIX savoir LINES, and Paris in all six connaître lines. They are the control: the learner is being shown that only the middle of the sentence moves.

THE FOUR CARDS OF THE OWNS DECK AND THE FIVE SITUATION ROWS. « Je sais nager. » « Je connais Paris. » « Je sais que c'est loin. » « Je connais ce quartier. » then « Tu connais Marie ? » « Je sais où elle habite. » « Je peux nager. » THE READING MUST NOT MARK THE JOIN. There is a strong temptation to leave a teaching pause after the verb, because the word after the verb is the whole point of the screen, and that pause is exactly what must not be there. The learner has to hear these as ordinary sentences said at ordinary speed, because that is the speed at which they will have to make the choice. Conversational throughout, no emphasis on any verb, and no lift before the complement.

THE FOUR PLACE LINES, IN THIS ORDER, AS ONE TAKE: « Je connais ce quartier. » « Je sais où elle habite. » « Il connaît bien la ville. » « Vous savez où est la gare ? » This is the mission the lesson exists for and the recording carries half its weight. All four are about places and two take each verb, so the reader must give NO clue which is which. Same warmth, same pace, same weight on the verb in all four. If the two savoir lines are read as though they were the interesting ones, the learner hears which answer is being pointed at instead of working it out. The fourth line rises at the end because it is a question; the third does not.
clipIds: Vous savez où est la gare ?

recorded.desc: THE THREE-WAY TRAP, AS TWO PAIRS. « Je sais nager. » then « Je peux nager. » then « On peut nager ici. » then « Je sais nager, mais je ne peux pas aujourd'hui. » The first pair is a minimal pair and must be read as one: same speed, same pitch, same length, with ONLY the verb different. The learner is being shown that nothing else in the sentence moved, and any difference in delivery is the recording contradicting the screen. The fourth line is one sentence and not two; the mais is unstressed and there is no dramatic pause before it. It should sound like the ordinary, slightly regretful thing it is.
clipIds: Je sais nager, mais je ne peux pas aujourd'hui.

recorded.desc: THE SIX SINGULAR CELLS FOR THE LISTENING SCREEN, savoir's three then connaître's three, WITH AUDIO BEFORE TEXT. Same instruction as the grid take and it is worth repeating because it is counter-intuitive: within each group of three the verb must be indistinguishable, and the PRONOUN must be clear, unhurried and slightly forward, because it is the only information in the line. Between the two groups the difference should be obvious without being performed: one syllable against two, and completely different consonants.

THE SKILL SET. « nager », « cuisiner », « conduire » as single words, conversational and unstressed, then « Je sais nager. » « Tu sais cuisiner ? » « Elle sait conduire. » The three single words come from three different lessons and the learner should hear no family resemblance and no grouping: they are a bag of ordinary verbs, which is the point. The second of the three sentences is a question and rises; the other two do not.

THE FOUR KINDS OF THING: « Tu connais Marie ? » « Je connais Paris. » « Nous connaissons ce restaurant. » « Vous connaissez cette chanson ? » One take. The first and last rise, the middle two do not. The double s in the third and fourth must be audible, and Marie and Paris must be said the way somebody says a name they know, not the way somebody reads one off a card.

WRONG THEN RIGHT, AND THE WRONG ONE IS THE DIFFICULT INSTRUCTION. « Je connais où il habite. » is not French and has to be read as though it were: at ordinary speed, with no hesitation, no apology and no strangeness in the voice. It is what an English speaker actually produces, fluently and confidently, and if the reader signals that something is wrong the learner will conclude they would never say it. They would. Then « Je sais où il habite. » in exactly the same voice at exactly the same speed, so that the only audible difference is the verb.

THE FOUR PUBLISHED ROWS, READ AS WHAT THEY ARE: sentences written for other lessons that happen to prove this one. « Tout le monde connaît le nom du champion. » « Il connaît la vraie raison de son retard ce matin. » « Je ne sais pas si c'est l'heure. » « je ne sais pas. » Ordinary pace, no teaching emphasis anywhere, and in particular no weight on the verb. The whole value of the screen is that nobody was thinking about savoir and connaître when these were written.
clipIds: Tout le monde connaît le nom du champion.
Il connaît la vraie raison de son retard ce matin.
Je ne sais pas si c'est l'heure.

recorded.desc: TWO CLIPS. « reconnaître » alone, then « Je reconnais cette chanson. » Unremarkable and quick. This is a recognition card and nothing else, and a reader who gives it weight will make the learner think it is being taught.

THE STAIRWELL. The neighbour is friendly, slightly out of breath, holding shopping, and completely uninterested in teaching anybody French. « Tu connais la nouvelle voisine ? » is casual and quick, the way you ask somebody something on a landing. « Ah, parfait. Tu lui diras pour les poubelles, alors ? » is warm and already turning to go, and it must not sound like a trap closing: he is pleased, and he has misunderstood, and neither of those is audible. Nothing in this scene is unkind and nothing is slowed down. The whole cost of the exchange is invisible to both people in it.
clipIds: Ah, parfait. Tu lui diras pour les poubelles, alors ?

lessons.intro: English has one word for both of these and gives you no instinct at all, so a learner who guesses is wrong about half the time. The forms take a few minutes. The question that picks between them is the rest of the lesson, and you will run it in every sentence from here on.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say.
nousOn.title: The we people actually say

examples.note: on takes the il form, so what follows it here is peut and nothing longer.

theChoice.body: English has one verb here and French has two, so nothing you already own tells you which to reach for. connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. Ask one question before you pick: does my sentence stop here, or does it keep going? That is the whole lesson, and it is worth more than both sets of forms put together: those take a few minutes and the choice is the thing you will be making in every sentence for the rest of your life in French. A learner who guesses is wrong about half the time, and wrong in a way the other person hears immediately, because the two verbs do not mean nearly the same thing.
theChoice.title: One English verb, two French ones

theChrome.body: The heading at the top of this screen is « Ce que vous savez faire », and it has been at the top of the last screen of every lesson you have finished. It is savoir followed by a verb: what you know how to do. Nobody explained it at the time because there was nothing yet to explain it with. Now there is, and you can read it. That is a small thing and it is the kind of small thing that turns a language from a subject into something you are inside of.

theFamily.body: reconnaître [ruh-koh-NEHTR] means to recognise, and it takes every ending connaître takes: je reconnais, nous reconnaissons, ils reconnaissent. That is all you need from it here, and it is recognition rather than something to produce. What it can take AFTER it is a different question and a more interesting one, and it belongs to lesson 9 in A2, which is the very next lesson. Do not assume it takes the same things after it, because it does not.
theFamily.title: The same endings, three letters longer

examples.note: Same endings. Do not read anything else into it yet.

thePlural.body: The three plural forms of connaître all take a double s: connaissons, connaissez, connaissent. It arrives with nous and it never leaves. savoir does the opposite and gets shorter: savons, savez, savent, and the last of those is four letters. The endings themselves are the ones you have had since lesson 1 in A2 and none of them is new. What is new is which stem they land on.
thePlural.title: Where connaître grows

examples.note: The double s, and the ordinary -ons.
The -ent is silent, so what you hear is the double s.

savoirReach.body: savoir takes a verb, or a whole sentence. Je sais nager is a verb; je sais où elle habite is a whole sentence hanging off the first one. Both keep going, and that is what they have in common. The thing savoir does NOT take is a plain name on its own: if the only thing left to say is a name, you have reached for the wrong verb. English hides all of this because it says know for every one of them.
savoirReach.title: A verb, or a whole sentence

examples.note: A whole sentence, and it is about a place.
Another whole sentence, this time a fact.

theSingular.body: Je sais, tu sais, il sait. Two of those are spelled identically and the third differs by one silent letter, and all three are one sound in the mouth. connais, connais, connaît does exactly the same thing. Lesson 7 in A2 spent a whole screen proving it on vouloir, pouvoir and devoir, so this lesson is not going to prove it again: it is simply true of these two as well. In writing you must pick the right one; in speech there is nothing to pick, and the word in front is carrying all of it.
theSingular.term: why je, tu and il sound the same
theSingular.title: 3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound. Lesson 7 in A2 found the same thing on three other verbs.

examples.note: sait, and not one sound different.

whatFollows.body: what comes next decides. Lesson 5 in A2 named that, on one verb doing two jobs. This lesson is the same shape turned round: two verbs doing one job, and again it is the next word that picks. French does this often enough that it is worth learning the habit rather than the instance. The instinct to decide what a sentence means before it has finished is a hard one to switch off, and it is exactly the instinct that produces the wrong verb here.
whatFollows.title: You met this shape at lesson 5

examples.note: Keeps going into a whole sentence. savoir.

theThirdVerb.body: Je sais nager and je peux nager are both I can swim in English, and they are not the same claim. sais is about having learned: at some point somebody taught you and now you can do it. peux is about nothing standing in the way: the pool is open, the water is warm, nobody has stopped you. Lesson 7 in A2 built pouvoir in full and this lesson does not build it again; what it does is put the two side by side, because a learner who has these three straight has something most English speakers never fully sort out.
theThirdVerb.title: Lesson 7 in A2 gave you a verb that also becomes can

examples.note: Nothing is stopping me. It says nothing about lessons.
Both at once, and they disagree.

theTwoFrames.body: Lesson 7 in A2 put eighteen sentences on one verb so that nothing at the back would move. Here the back of the sentence is the whole point, so the two sides cannot share one. Every sentence on the savoir side of the grid ends in nager and every sentence on the connaître side ends in Paris, and those two words are doing the teaching as much as the verbs are. Read across a line and the only differences are the verb and what kind of word is behind it. That is the shape you are being asked to notice, and it is the shape you will run in your head every time you build one of these.
theTwoFrames.term: why the two sides look different
theTwoFrames.title: One verb behind, one name behind

theCircumflex.body: Only connaît carries it, and it appears on no other form of either verb. It changes nothing at all about how the word is said. Spelling reform allows the version without it and this course has never used one: every one of the 82 places an -aître word appears in this app spells it with the hat, so that is what you will read and that is what you should write. It is the kind of thing worth deciding once and never thinking about again.
theCircumflex.title: One form, one accent, no sound

examples.note: One person earlier, and it is gone.

theImpossible.body: « Je connais où il habite. » is what an English speaker builds by translating word for word, and it is the single commonest thing to get wrong here. connaître has to land on a thing. « où il habite » is a whole sentence, so it cannot. The right one is « Je sais où il habite. », and notice that nothing about the meaning changed: it was never a choice between two ways of saying it. Picking the right verb from a list is easy and producing this shape under pressure is not, which is why the exam makes you write it out rather than choose it.
theImpossible.title: connaître and a whole sentence

examples.note: The sentence keeps going, so savoir carries it.
The same shape in the form you will actually need.
The same shape again, with que run into the word after it.

connaitreReach.body: connaître takes a thing: a person, a place, a song, a street, and then the sentence is over. It never takes a whole sentence. That is not a tendency or a preference; there is no such sentence in French, and « Je connais où il habite. » is not a clumsy way of saying something, it is not a sentence at all. What connaître means underneath all of this is having been there or having met them: you have stood in the place, you have shaken the hand, you have heard the song.
connaitreReach.title: A thing, and then it stops

sections.title: What may come next, and what it means

sections.body: The obvious version of this table would put people and places on one side and facts and skills on the other, and it is what the most-quoted rule about these two verbs says. It is also what one sentence already published in this app says, in French. It breaks in a week, and the sentence that breaks it is « Je sais où elle habite. ». That is a place, and it takes savoir, and a learner running the meaning rule reaches for the wrong verb on one of the most useful sentences in the language. The version in the first table above cannot break that way, because it does not ask you what the sentence is about. connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. Ask one question before you pick: does my sentence stop here, or does it keep going? One caution: a sentence can put its thing in front of the verb rather than behind it, and later lessons will show you how. When that happens the thing is still there, which is the part that matters.
sections.title: Why this sheet does not sort them by meaning

sections.body: Three things leave this lesson. The first is the question: connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. It is a syntax rule rather than a meaning rule, and that is why it holds. The second is that English gives you one word, can, for two completely different claims, having been taught and having nothing in your way, and French keeps them apart with savoir and lesson 7's verb. Learners who never sort that out say the wrong one for years and are understood every time, which is why nobody corrects it. The third is small and it will come back: what comes next decides. You met that shape at lesson 5 in A2 on one verb doing two jobs, and this lesson is the same shape turned round. Lesson 9 in A2 is next and it takes up the family reconnaître belongs to, which is worth waiting for: verbs in a family share their endings, and they do not always share anything else.
sections.title: What carries forward

errors.why: connaître has to land on a thing. « où il habite » is a whole sentence, so it cannot. Word for word out of English it looks right, and there is no version of French in which it works. Not building it under pressure is the skill.
errors.right: Saying « Je sais où il habite. ».
errors.wrong: Saying « Je connais où il habite. ».

errors.why: Nothing is ungrammatical about the first one, which is exactly why it costs you something. You will be understood to have said you have heard of her, and nobody will correct you.

errors.why: The double s arrives with nous and stays for all three plural forms. It is audible, so if you can say it you can hear which one you meant to write.
errors.right: Writing « connaissons » and « connaissez ».

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have two verbs where English gave you one word, and every ending on both of them is one you already write. That was the short half. The long half is the question you now run before you open your mouth: connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. You have used it on a place that takes savoir and on a place that takes connaître, which is the pair no semantic rule survives. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.

sections.say: Four things, and then read the two words at the top of this screen again.
sections.body: You have two verbs where English gave you one, and one question that picks between them: connaître stops at a thing. savoir keeps going. You used it on a place that takes savoir and a place that takes connaître, which is the pair that no rule about meaning survives. You know that the third verb from lesson 7 in A2 turns into the same English word and means something else again, and that « Je connais où il habite. » is not clumsy French but no French at all. And the heading at the top of this screen, « Ce que vous savez faire », has been there at the end of every lesson you have finished. It is savoir with a verb behind it: what you know how to do. Nobody explained it before because there was nothing to explain it with. Lesson 9 in A2 is next, and it takes the family this lesson only pointed at.

3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound. Lesson 7 in A2 found the same thing on three other verbs.

errorTriggers.description: Picks by what the sentence is about rather than by what follows the verb: connaître for anything involving a person or a place, savoir for anything involving a fact. It works most of the time and fails on exactly the sentences a learner needs.

Builds « Je connais où il habite. » by translating word for word out of English. It is not a clumsy sentence, it is not a sentence, and no amount of choosing the right verb from a list stops a learner producing it under pressure.
Writes connaisons, connaisez or connaisent with one s. The double s arrives with nous and stays for all three plural forms, and it is audible, so the mistake is written rather than spoken.
Uses the lesson 7 in A2 verb where the sentence is about having been taught. English gives can for both, so the reflex is strong and the resulting sentence is grammatical and says something else.
Drops or slurs the pronoun on the singular forms, where three persons are one sound and the pronoun is carrying all of the information. Nothing in the verb recovers it.
Answers a connaître question with savoir or the reverse. Both sentences are correct, neither is corrected, and the conversation continues on a false footing until somebody acts on what they heard.

recorded.desc: THE KETTLE ON A MONDAY, AND THE SAME COLLEAGUE AS lesson 16 in A2 AND lesson 17 in A2. She has asked a friendly question and is expecting a short answer. THE LEARNER'S OWN LINE IS THE TAKE THAT HAS TO BE RIGHT. « Hier soir, j'ai... je suis... j'ai... » is somebody deciding out loud, twice, and settling on the wrong one. THE TWO FALSE STARTS MUST NOT BE RUSHED TOGETHER. There is a real pause after each, and the second « j'ai » should sound like a decision rather than like a stumble: he has chosen, and he has chosen wrongly. HER LINE « Tu as sorti quoi ? » IS THE EXPENSIVE ONE AND IT IS NOT A CORRECTION. She heard a complete, well-formed sentence about carrying something out of the house and she is asking what the something was. Read it as a genuine question with real interest in the answer. Any note of patience, puzzlement at a foreigner, or gentle correction turns the scene into somebody being helped, and the whole point is that nothing went wrong that she could hear.
clipIds: Tu es allée où hier soir ?
Hier soir, j'ai... je suis... j'ai...
Je suis sortie avec des amis.
Ah, avec des amis. Je comprends.

recorded.desc: THE AUDIO STEP OF THE FIRST-WORD TRAP, AND IT IS A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. Four lines, one take, in this order: « Elle a allé au marché. » then « Elle est allée au marché. », then « Elle a mangé au restaurant. » then « Elle a passé un examen. » READ THE FIRST LINE PLAINLY AND AT ORDINARY PACE rather than comically or hesitantly. It is a perfectly pronounceable French shape and it is exactly what a careful learner produces; a reading that signals the error teaches that the error is audible. LINES TWO AND THREE MUST NOT HAVE THEIR SECOND WORDS COLOURED DIFFERENTLY. « allée » and « mangé » are both ordinary middles of ordinary sentences and the learner is being asked to attend to the FIRST word, not the second. DO NOT SEPARATE THE FIRST TWO LINES WITH A LONG PAUSE. The pair is the teaching and it works when the two lines sit against each other.

THE FOUR SPELLINGS, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TAKE IN THE LESSON. Four lines in this order: « Il est allé. » « Elle est allée. » « Ils sont allés. » « Elles sont allées. » THE SECOND WORD MUST BE IDENTICAL IN ALL FOUR. Not similar: identical. The whole lesson rests on the learner hearing that there is nothing to hear, and any difference at all in length, weight or vowel colour teaches that the ending is audible when it is not. THE THIRD AND FOURTH LINES ARE COMPLETELY IDENTICAL OUT LOUD except for il against elle, and they must be read that way: « sont » is the same word twice and « allés » and « allées » are the same three sounds. RECORD THEM AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE. Four separate recordings are four performances and the learner will hear the performances.

THE ONE PAIR IN THIS LESSON THAT IS NOT IDENTICAL, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, FOUR LINES: « Il est mort en mars. » « Elle est morte en mars. » « Ils sont morts en mars. » « Elles sont mortes en mars. » THIS TAKE IS THE OPPOSITE INSTRUCTION TO rec-a2-21-cells AND THE TWO MUST NOT BE RECORDED IN THE SAME FRAME OF MIND. THE T AT THE END OF « morte » AND « mortes » MUST BE CLEARLY AUDIBLE. It is the only ending in the lesson a learner can hear and the whole mission is built on hearing it. AND THE PLURAL MUST STILL BE INAUDIBLE. « mort » and « morts » are the same, « morte » and « mortes » are the same. Lines one and three are one sound and so are lines two and four; the learner is being taught that gender arrives here and number never does. THE SUBJECT IS A DEATH IN A FAMILY. Read it plainly and without weight. It is a fact in a sentence, not an occasion.

THE SECOND TRAP, ONE TAKE, FOUR LINES: « Il est allé. » « Elle est née ici. » « Elle est restée à la maison. » « Le verre est tombé. » NOT A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. All four are correct French and none is an error being demonstrated. EVERY ONE OF THESE IS A REPORT OF SOMETHING THAT HAPPENED and the reading has to carry that. A learner meeting « il est allé » on paper hears an English shape, "he is gone", and reads it as a description. The take should sound like somebody telling you what happened, at the pace of ordinary speech, with the second word given no more weight than the rest of the sentence. DO NOT STRESS « est ». It is the word carrying the tense and the learner has to get used to catching it unstressed, because that is the only way it will ever arrive.
clipIds: Elle est restée à la maison.

recorded.desc: THE DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to rec-a2-21-cells: there the learner is comparing and here they are spelling, and a paired reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. FOUR OF THE SIX LINES ARE THE SAME VERB AND THEY WILL SOUND ALMOST THE SAME. That is correct and must not be corrected for. The learner works out which cell is meant from the words in front of the verb, and the take must not help by leaning on the ending. THE FIRST TWO WORDS ARE WHERE THE INFORMATION IS. « Il est », « Elle est », « Ils sont », « Elles sont »: these must be clearly and evenly said, because they are the only thing distinguishing four of the six lines. SAY IT THE WAY SOMEBODY WOULD SAY IT, at the pace of somebody dictating an address to a friend.

THE CONVERSATION, HER LINES ONLY, ONE TAKE, AS ONE CONTINUOUS EXCHANGE RATHER THAN AS FIVE SEPARATE PROMPTS. She is the same colleague, later in the week, and this time the exchange works. EVERY QUESTION IS ASKED WITHOUT INVERSION and should sound completely ordinary: « Tu es rentrée à quelle heure ? » is a statement with a question mark on it, which is what people say. NEITHER « es » NOR « est » NOR « êtes » MAY BE STRESSED anywhere in the take. They are the words carrying the tense and the learner has to get used to catching them unstressed. AND HER OWN ENDINGS ARE AGREED THROUGHOUT. « Tu es rentrée » and « elle est venue » both carry one and neither is audible; nothing in the reading should mark them.
clipIds: Tu es allée où hier soir ?
Tu es rentrée à quelle heure ?

lessons.intro: Almost every verb in French builds its past with a form of avoir. Fifteen of them use être instead, and once you have done that, something happens that has never happened to a verb before: the second word changes for who the sentence is about, exactly the way a describing word does. A man who left and a woman who left are spelled differently and sound identical. Nobody can hear this and everybody who reads it can see it, which makes writing the only place it can be checked and the dictée the longest part of the lesson.

Lesson 1 in A2 said « Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person. » in the first lesson of this level, and this is the same thing seventeen lessons later.

firstWord.body: One verb, two words, and the small ones go in between. That is lesson 16's line and the shape has not moved. What moves is the first word: for fifteen verbs it is a form of être rather than a form of avoir, and there is no way to hear which one a sentence needs until you know the verb.

sections.say: mort and morte are the one pair in this lesson you can hear apart. Listen to all four and then answer. This is the only place in the lesson where listening tells you anything.

sections.title: The One You Can Hear

questions.q: Il est mort en mars against Elle est morte en mars. What did you hear?
questions.why: mort ends on the r and morte ends on a t. The e wakes the t up, which is what an e does everywhere else in French and does not do to any of the other fourteen verbs here.
opts: A t at the end of the second word

questions.q: Ils sont morts en mars against Elles sont mortes en mars. And here?
questions.why: The number is still silent: morts is the first sound and mortes the second. The plural adds a letter and no sound, exactly as it does on the other fourteen.

questions.q: Why does this one verb behave differently from the other fourteen?
questions.why: The other fourteen end in a vowel sound, and an e after a vowel adds nothing. mort ends on a consonant, so the e gives it something to say.
opts: Its past form ends in a consonant, so an e after it can be heard

questions.q: What can you check by ear in the rest of this lesson?
questions.why: Être and avoir are completely different words, so the first word is audible everywhere. You cannot check this by listening. For fourteen of the fifteen, all four spellings are one sound.

sections.say: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. That is lesson 9's line, and here it settles the first word as well as the second. Three verbs this lesson has not listed, and one of them is not in the crutch either.

check.q: Devenir. He became a teacher. Il ___ professeur.
check.why: Cover the de and venir is underneath. venir takes être, so devenir takes être, and the form is venu with de in front. Il is masculine and singular, so nothing goes on the end.

cards.say: Il est allé.
cards.back: être. Twelve of the fifteen move, and the other three change what is true rather than where you are.
cards.front: Which first word do these fifteen take?

cards.say: Elle est allée.
cards.back: After être, the second word ends like a describing word. Add nothing for a man on his own, e for a woman, s for more than one, and es for more than one woman.
cards.front: And what happens to the second word?

cards.say: Elles sont allées.
cards.back: You cannot check this by listening. For fourteen of the fifteen, all four spellings are one sound.

cards.say: Elle est morte en mars.

cards.say: Nous sommes passés devant chez toi.

sections.say: Six rounds of six. Most of it is typed, because writing the ending is the thing this lesson claims you can do.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Six on avoir against être.
rounds.label: Which first word

questions.q: Elle ___ allée au marché. Which first word?
questions.why: aller is one of the fifteen and elle is one person, so est. The first option is what a learner who has only met lesson 16 in A2 reaches for.

questions.q: Elle ___ mangé au marché. And here?
questions.why: manger is an ordinary verb, so avoir, and nothing goes on the end of mangé either.

questions.q: rester. Does it take être?
questions.why: rester is the one that breaks it. Nothing moves and nothing changes, and it is the one people forget, which is the reason the mnemonic exists at all.

questions.q: Fix this. You mean that she went to the market.
questions.why: avoir on a verb that takes être, which is the error the whole lesson exists to prevent. It comes from having used avoir for one lesson and nothing else.
accept: Elle est allée au marché.
Elle est allee au marche
questions.answer: Elle est allée au marché.
questions.prompt: Elle a allé au marché.

questions.q: tomber. Which first word does it take?
questions.why: Falling is going down, which is one of the four kinds. It is also a letter of the crutch, so both ways of checking give the same answer.

questions.q: Nous ___ arrivés à huit heures.
questions.why: arriver takes être and nous takes sommes. The s on arrivés is already there because there is more than one of you.
accept: sommes
questions.answer: sommes

rounds.say: Six on the last two letters, and the subject is fixed in every one.
rounds.label: Write the ending

questions.q: A woman speaking. Je suis ___ au marché. (aller)
questions.why: She is one woman, so the e and nothing else. It sounds exactly like allé and it is not spelled like it.
accept: allée
questions.answer: allée

questions.q: Two men. Ils sont ___ tôt. (partir)
questions.why: More than one, and not all women, so the s alone. Two men, or a man and a woman, take the same ending.
accept: partis
questions.answer: partis

questions.q: Three women. Elles sont ___ à midi. (descendre)
questions.why: The past form of descendre is descendu, then the e for the women and the s for the number. Both, in that order.
accept: descendues
questions.answer: descendues

questions.q: One woman. Elle est ___ à la maison. (rester)
questions.why: rester takes être even though nothing moves, and the ending goes on exactly as it does on the twelve that do.
accept: restée
questions.answer: restée

questions.q: Which one is written about a group of women?
questions.why: The e is the women and the s is the number, so both. All four of these are one sound, which is why this is a reading question and not a listening one.

questions.q: Le verre est ___. (tomber)
questions.why: The subject is a thing rather than a person and the rule is the same: le verre is masculine and singular, so nothing goes on.
accept: tombé
questions.answer: tombé

rounds.say: Six on where the ending does not go, which is everywhere avoir is.
rounds.label: Not after avoir

questions.q: Fix this. You mean that she ate at the market.
questions.why: The rule applied where it does not run. After avoir the second word never changes, in any person. Lesson 16 in A2 taught that and this lesson does not touch it.
accept: Elle a mangé au marché.
Elle a mange au marche
questions.answer: Elle a mangé au marché.
questions.prompt: Elle a mangée au marché.

questions.q: Elle a ___ un examen. (passer)
questions.why: avoir, because there is an exam after the verb, and after avoir nothing goes on the end however many women there are.
accept: passé
questions.answer: passé

questions.why: After avoir the second word never changes, in any person. Lesson 16 in A2 taught that and this lesson does not touch it. Three women and an ordinary verb, so avoir and a bare second word.

questions.q: Fix this. You mean that they went to the market.
questions.why: The plural forgotten. More than one person and the s goes on, exactly as it would on a describing word.
accept: Ils sont allés au marché.
Ils sont alles au marche
questions.answer: Ils sont allés au marché.
questions.prompt: Ils sont allé au marché.

questions.q: Elle est ___ au restaurant. (aller)
questions.why: être this time, so the e goes on. The same woman and the same restaurant as the avoir sentence, and one word decides it.
accept: allée
questions.answer: allée

questions.q: What tells you whether to put an ending on at all?
questions.why: être puts it on and avoir never does. The subject then tells you WHICH ending, but only once être has already decided that there is one.

rounds.say: Six where more than one of the letters is needed.
rounds.label: Both endings

questions.q: Two women. Elles sont ___ ensemble. (arriver)
questions.why: The e and the s, in that order. Forgetting the s is the commonest of the two, because the e is the one people are told about.
accept: arrivées
questions.answer: arrivées

questions.q: A man and a woman. Ils sont ___ tôt. (partir)
questions.why: One woman in a group does not make the group feminine. Anything other than all women takes the s alone.
accept: partis
questions.answer: partis

questions.q: Which of these is a group of women?
questions.why: Both letters. The second option is one woman and the first is a mixed group, and all four are one sound.

questions.q: Vous êtes ___ tôt, said to several women. (partir)
questions.why: Vous is plural here, so both letters. Said to one person it would be parti or partie, and vous alone never tells you which.
accept: parties
questions.answer: parties

questions.q: Elles sont ___ en mars. (mourir)
questions.why: The past form of mourir is mort, then both letters. The number is still silent: morts is the first sound and mortes the second.
accept: mortes
questions.answer: mortes

questions.q: How many of these four endings can you hear on aller?
questions.why: None. allé, allée, allés and allées are one sound, and that is true of fourteen of the fifteen verbs in this lesson.

rounds.say: Six on verbs this lesson never listed, and two of them are not in the crutch.
rounds.label: Verbs nobody listed

questions.q: Devenir, about a woman. Elle est ___ professeur.

accept: devenue
questions.answer: devenue

questions.q: Repartir. Which first word?
questions.why: partir is underneath and partir takes être, so this does too. DR MRS VANDERTRAMP has no letter for it, which is what the pattern is for.

questions.q: Repasser, "to go past again", about two women. Elles sont ___ devant la gare.

questions.answer: repassées

questions.q: Which of these tells you about a verb the crutch does not list?
questions.why: passer is not one of its letters, and it takes être twenty-six times in this app.
opts: Whether it is about moving or about starting or stopping

questions.q: Rentrer, about a woman. Elle est ___ vers minuit.

accept: rentrée
questions.answer: rentrée

questions.q: Redescendre, about a man. Il est ___.
questions.why: Cover the re and descendre is underneath, which gives descendu and takes être. One man, so nothing on the end.
accept: redescendu
questions.answer: redescendu

rounds.say: Six on what these sentences are actually saying.
rounds.label: What it means

questions.q: Je suis allé à Paris. What does it mean?
questions.why: A form of être plus a second word is a past tense, not a description. The first option is what the words look like one at a time and it is not what the sentence says.

questions.q: Elle est fatiguée. Is this the same shape?
questions.why: The shape is identical and the second word decides. fatiguée describes her and partie reports something she did.
opts: It is the same shape and it describes her now
Yes, and it is a past tense too

questions.say: morte

sections.body: After être, the second word ends like a describing word. Lesson 16 in A2 gave you the whole shape two lessons ago and lesson 17 in A2 gave you the forms that could not be built. Both of those stay exactly as they were. What is new is which first word you reach for, and what happens to the second one afterwards.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Twelve of the fifteen move, and the other three change what is true rather than where you are. rester is the one that breaks it. Nothing moves and nothing changes, and it is the one people forget, which is the reason the mnemonic exists at all.
Add nothing for a man on his own, e for a woman, s for more than one, and es for more than one woman.
After avoir the second word never changes, in any person. Lesson 16 in A2 taught that and this lesson does not touch it.
You cannot check this by listening. For fourteen of the fifteen, all four spellings are one sound.
mort and morte are the one pair in this lesson you can hear apart. The number is still silent: morts is the first sound and mortes the second.
Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. And with it comes the first word, so devenir, revenir and repartir all arrive free.
Sixteen letters for sixteen verbs, and it is an accident of English spelling rather than anything about French. passer is not one of its letters, and it takes être twenty-six times in this app.

A few of them take avoir instead when something is being moved rather than moving. You will meet it; you are not being asked to produce it. A whole family of verbs carries a little word in front of it and they take être as well. That is lesson 19 in A2 and then lesson 20 in A2, and the rule on this screen is the one they will use.

errorTriggers.description: Uses avoir on a verb that takes être: « elle a allé ». THE ERROR THIS LESSON EXISTS TO PREVENT, and it comes from lesson 16 in A2 having taught avoir and nothing else, so it is produced by a learner doing exactly what they were told.

Picks être correctly and writes nothing on the end: « elle est allé ». It survives longer than any other error in the lesson, because nobody hears it and the learner never gets a signal that anything is wrong.

Learns the ending and then puts it everywhere: « elle a mangée ». It is the rule being applied where it does not run, and it appears the moment the lesson has worked, which is what makes it worth a round of its own.

Remembers the e and forgets the s: « elles sont allée ». The e is the ending people are told about and the s is the one that gets lost, and both are needed in the cell a learner writes most often about a group.

Has DR MRS VANDERTRAMP and nothing else, so a verb outside it produces a guess. It is the predictable cost of teaching a list of initials as though it were a rule, and it is why the pattern is taught beside it.

Reads « je suis allé » as a description of how somebody is rather than as a report of what they did, because the shape is identical to « je suis fatigué ». English says "I am gone" and means something else by it, which makes the misreading feel right.

grammarAssumed: The passé composé with avoir, in six persons, introduced in a2.05
That the participle is invariable after avoir, introduced in a2.05
That ne … pas encloses the auxiliary and not the participle, introduced in a2.19 and extended in a2.05
The irregular past participles, including venu, né and mort, introduced in a2.20
Adjective agreement as four inflectional classes, introduced in a2.03
That -e, -es and -ent are silent, and that silent agreement is a systematic property of French orthography, introduced in a2.01
The present of aller and venir, introduced in a2.02
The present of partir and sortir, introduced in a2.10
The present of descendre, introduced in a2.11
The compound-verb principle, that a prefixed verb inflects like its base, introduced in a2.15
grammarIntroduced: être as the auxiliary of the passé composé for a closed class of fifteen intransitive verbs of motion and change of state
Participle agreement with the subject under être, in gender and number, using the same four exponents as adjectival agreement in a2.03
That the agreement is orthographic only for fourteen of the fifteen, and phonologically realised for mourir alone, where the feminine exponent licenses the final /t/
That number is not phonologically realised for any of the fifteen, which is the converse of the adjectival system a2.03 introduced
The semantic generalisation behind the class: movement, and change of state, with rester as the sole member that is neither
The DR MRS VANDERTRAMP mnemonic, taught explicitly as a memory aid rather than as a generalisation, with passer named as a member it does not cover
That the compound-verb principle of a2.15 selects the auxiliary as well as the participle, so devenir, revenir and repartir are derivable without instruction
The transitive uses of sortir, monter, descendre, passer, rentrer and retourner, which take avoir and do not agree, for RECEPTION ONLY and produced nowhere
That a form of être plus a participle is a compound past rather than a copula plus a predicative adjective, an ambiguity English reproduces in "I am gone"
Reflexive verbs also take être and their agreement is named and reserved for a2.22 and a2.23
