acts.title: Your slot, and the register in it
acts.milestone: You can answer each of his questions with the amount of French it actually wants.

acts.title: When the script breaks
acts.milestone: You have six ways to say you missed it, and you know which one to reach for.

acts.title: The whole encounter
acts.milestone: You have read a real board and run the whole evening end to end.

acts.title: Measure
acts.milestone: Thirty questions, and the repair move is the part you keep.

lessons.intro: Twenty-three lessons have taught you how to order. This one is about everything he says back.

rung.body: Six ways of saying you did not catch that, ordered from the cheapest to the most explicit. Rung 1 costs you nothing. Rung 6 admits the spoken word has failed and asks for it in writing.
rung.title: A rung of the repair ladder

examples.note: Rung 4, and it says so outright.

chunk.body: Some phrases are worth recognising without taking them apart. « Il n'y en a plus » is one of them: you meet it as a single sound that means there is none left, and the pieces inside it are somebody else's lesson.
chunk.title: A whole phrase, learned whole

stage.body: A restaurant meal runs in a fixed order and each step has its own question. There are eight of them, from the greeting to the bill, and they arrive in the same order almost every time.
stage.title: A stage of the encounter

binary.body: Plate ou gazeuse ? En terrasse ou à l'intérieur ? Two options and no frame around them. They are the easiest questions to answer and the easiest to miss, because there is no verb to hold on to.
binary.title: A two-way question

examples.note: Four, and still no verb you need.

hisHalf.body: Everything the waiter says. You have been taught how to order for twenty-three units; almost nothing has been said about what gets said to you.
hisHalf.title: The half you did not learn

examples.note: You are being asked, not asking.

faceCost.body: How much you give away by saying it. Pardon gives away nothing. Je n'ai pas bien compris says plainly that you did not follow. Neither is rude; one is just more expensive than the other.
faceCost.title: What a rung costs you

gradient.body: Five ways of saying what you want, from the softest to the flattest. All five are ordinary French. Only one of them, je veux, is the wrong one at a table.
gradient.title: The ordering gradient

handBack.body: When you cannot choose, make him choose. It keeps the turn moving and it is what a French speaker does too.
handBack.title: Handing the choice back

examples.note: The whole move, in one sentence.

someOfIt.body: Lesson 8 in A1 settled this: un is one of them, du is some of it. This lesson only asks you to run it at the moment of ordering, where the two are a syllable apart and mean different things.
someOfIt.title: Du, de la, de l'

deviation.body: The moment the encounter stops following the order you rehearsed. Something is off the menu, something is wrong, and the sentence you prepared no longer fits.
deviation.title: When the script breaks

secondPart.body: A question and its answer come as a pair. When somebody asks « Et comme boisson ? » a French speaker does not say a sentence; they say a drink. Knowing the pair is faster than building a reply.
secondPart.title: The answer that fits

lessons.title: At the Restaurant

drills.coach: Read the English. Say the French, out loud, and never reach for je veux at a table.
pairs: I'll have the dish of the day
Je prends le plat du jour.
I'm going to have the fish
For me, it'll be the steak
drills.title: The one rung to drop

drills.coach: Read what he says. Say which part of the evening you are in.
drills.title: Which stage is he on

drills.coach: He asked two words. Give one of them back and stop talking.
pairs: How would you like it cooked? (medium)
drills.title: Answer it short

drills.coach: Cheapest first. Say each one out loud and notice how little the first two give away.
pairs: Can you say that again, please?
Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
Could you write it down for me, please?
Vous pouvez me l'écrire, s'il vous plaît ?
drills.title: The six rungs

lessons.reframe: You never start. He asks, you answer.

overview.introFr: Vous ne commencez jamais.

say.text: You have practised ordering for twenty-three lessons. Nobody has practised him.

beats.text: A bistro in Lyon, a Thursday evening. You have been practising one sentence since the tram, and it is a good sentence.
He arrives with the pad already open. You get your sentence out cleanly, all of it, no hesitation.

beats.prompt: You have rehearsed it. Which one did you rehearse?

options.en: the one that says what you want
options.fr: Je veux le poulet.

options.en: the one that says what you would like
options.fr: Je voudrais le poulet.

followUp.works: Yes. One syllable longer, and it is the one a French speaker actually says at a table.
followUp.breaks: Every word is correct and he understood you perfectly. Watch what happens next anyway.

beats.en: (I want the chicken.)
beats.fr: Je veux le poulet.

beats.en: How would you like it cooked?
beats.fr: Quelle cuisson ?
beats.stage: Two words. He is already writing. The pad does not stop moving.
beats.speaker: The waiter

beats.body: You got your order out and he answered with a question you had not planned for. It is not the chicken and it is not your accent. You prepared what you would say, and everything he says back is a thing nobody taught you.
beats.coach: You rehearsed your half. He has a half too, and it is the half that decides how the evening goes.

right.en: what a French speaker says at a table
right.fr: Je voudrais le poulet.

wrong.en: understood perfectly, and one rung too blunt
wrong.fr: Je veux le poulet.

beats.heading: You rehearsed the easy half

beats.en: And to drink?
beats.fr: Et comme boisson ?
beats.stage: He has not finished. There are six more of these coming.
beats.speaker: The waiter

beats.text: He asked four questions before the food arrived. You answered one of them.

sections.title: The Half You Did Not Rehearse

closing.text: You never start. He asks, you answer.

setting.place: A bistro with eleven tables and no menu in English
setting.ambience: room-tone-lobby

sections.say: Four goals, and every one of them is about catching something rather than saying it.

goals.s: Catch which stage of the meal you are in, from one short question and nothing else.
goals.t: Place any line he says

goals.s: Plate ou gazeuse ? Et ensuite ? Four of his questions have no verb you can anchor on.
goals.t: Catch the verbless ones

goals.s: When the dish is off and your sentence no longer fits, say something rather than freeze.
goals.t: Survive the deviation

goals.s: Six ways of saying you missed it, and what each one costs you to say.
goals.t: Ask him to say it again

sections.title: What You Will Be Able To Do

sections.say: You never start. He asks, you answer. Eight stages, arriving in this order almost every time.

rows.say: Bonsoir, vous avez réservé ?

detail.say: Vous êtes combien ?
detail.body: The greeting and the seating. He asks whether you booked, how many you are, and where you want to sit. Three questions before you have taken your coat off.
detail.title: Stages 1 and 2

rows.say: Et comme boisson ?

detail.say: Plate ou gazeuse ?
detail.body: Drinks come before food and they come fast. Plate ou gazeuse ? is two words with no verb in it, and it is the question learners miss most.
detail.title: Stage 3

rows.say: Vous avez choisi ?

detail.say: Et ensuite ?
detail.body: The pivot of the whole meal, and it arrives in the passé composé. Et ensuite ? means what is your main course, and nothing in those two words says so.
detail.title: Stage 4

rows.say: Tout se passe bien ?

detail.say: Ça a été ?
detail.body: Asked mid-meal with your mouth full. It wants oui or a problem, nothing else. Ça a été ? is the same move said while clearing your plate.
detail.title: Stage 5

rows.say: Ce sera tout ?

detail.say: Un café pour finir ?
detail.body: The upsell. Dessert, coffee, a digestif. Un café pour finir ? has no verb either, and saying nothing gets you the dessert menu anyway.
detail.title: Stage 6

rows.say: Vous réglez comment ?

detail.say: Ensemble ou séparément ?
detail.body: Service and the bill. Ensemble ou séparément ? decides how the table pays, and it is asked once, quickly, while he is holding the card machine.
detail.title: Stages 7 and 8

sections.title: The Eight Stages, In Order

sections.say: Five things he says before the food is even discussed.

cards.fr: Bonsoir, vous avez réservé ?
cards.body: The first thing said to you, and it is a yes or no question in the passé composé. Non, on n'a pas réservé is the whole answer.
cards.head: Stage 1
cards.label: he asks · you answer

cards.fr: Vous êtes combien ?
cards.body: How many of you. He may also say C'est pour combien de personnes ?, which is the same question with more words in it. Answer with a number and nothing else.
cards.head: Stage 1
cards.label: a number is a whole answer

cards.fr: En terrasse ou à l'intérieur ?
cards.body: A two-way question with no verb you need. Pick one of the two words he gave you and hand it straight back.
cards.head: Stage 2
cards.label: two-way

cards.fr: Et comme boisson ?
cards.body: Comme here means by way of, a use you have not met. Et comme entrée ? at stage 4 is the same frame with a different noun.
cards.head: Stage 3
cards.label: the comme frame

cards.fr: Une carafe d'eau, ça ira ?
cards.body: This is a check, not an offer. Ça ira means will that do, and answering it wrongly is how you end up paying for a bottle.
cards.head: Stage 3
cards.label: a check, not an offer

sections.title: Arriving, Sitting, Drinking

sections.say: The pivot of the meal, and he has four ways of getting to it.

cards.fr: Vous avez choisi ?
cards.body: The question you have been waiting for, and it arrives in the passé composé rather than the present. Have you chosen, not are you choosing.
cards.head: Stage 4
cards.label: the pivot

cards.fr: Vous avez fait votre choix ?
cards.body: The same move in different words. A script is not a fixed string, and this is the proof: two forms, one question.
cards.head: Stage 4
cards.label: same move, other words

cards.fr: Et ensuite ?
cards.body: Two words that mean what is your main course. Nothing in them says so. He says it the moment you finish naming your starter.
cards.head: Stage 4
cards.label: two words, one meaning

cards.fr: Quelle cuisson ?
cards.body: Only ever asked about meat, and there are three answers: saignant, à point, bien cuit. He will not offer them to you.
cards.head: Stage 4
cards.label: three answers, none offered

sections.title: Taking The Order

sections.say: Mid-meal, and then the part where he wants you to order more.

cards.fr: Tout se passe bien ?
cards.body: Asked mid-meal, mouth full. It wants oui merci or a problem, and it does not want a sentence.
cards.head: Stage 5
cards.label: oui, or a problem

cards.fr: Ça a été ?
cards.body: Three syllables, said while clearing your plate. A passé composé with no subject you recognise, and it is the hardest short question of the evening.
cards.head: Stage 5
cards.label: the hardest three syllables

cards.fr: Je vous débarrasse ?
cards.body: Shall I clear these away. A question shaped exactly like a statement, marked only by his voice going up at the end.
cards.head: Stage 5
cards.label: a question by intonation alone

cards.fr: Ce sera tout ?
cards.body: Will that be all. The answer that fits is his own words handed back: Ce sera tout, merci.
cards.head: Stage 6
cards.label: hand his words back

cards.fr: Un café pour finir ?
cards.body: No verb at all. Most of the upsell is said this way, and Vous prendrez un dessert ? is the same move with a verb put back in.
cards.head: Stage 6
cards.label: no verb

sections.title: Checking, And Selling

sections.say: The last two stages, and one card that is not about France.

cards.fr: Je vous apporte ça tout de suite.
cards.sub: [zhuh voo-z a-port sa too duh SÜEET]
cards.body: Nothing is being asked. He is closing the ordering stage, and the only thing required of you is merci.
cards.head: Stage 7
cards.label: nothing is asked

cards.fr: Vous réglez comment ?
cards.body: How are you paying. Par carte or en espèces, and he is already holding the machine. What the total actually is belongs to another lesson.
cards.head: Stage 8
cards.label: how, not how much

cards.fr: Ensemble ou séparément ?
cards.body: Together or separately, asked once and quickly. If you miss it he will ask again as Je vous fais une seule addition ?
cards.head: Stage 8
cards.label: asked once

cards.fr: Le service est compris.
cards.body: Service is included, and it is a statement of fact rather than a hint. Le pourboire on top is yours to decide and nobody is waiting for it.
cards.head: Stage 8
cards.label: a fact, not a hint

cards.fr: l'addition · la facture
cards.body: In Quebec the bill is often la facture, the evening meal is le souper rather than le dîner, and the tip is not included the way it is in France. Colour only: everything this lesson drills and quizzes is France-standard French.
cards.head: Au Québec
cards.label: colour, never scored

sections.title: Serving, And The Bill

sections.say: Six lines at the speed he actually says them. The question is never what the words were.

lines.en: Good evening, do you have a reservation?
lines.fr: Bonsoir, vous avez réservé ?

lines.en: Still or sparkling?
lines.fr: Plate ou gazeuse ?

lines.en: And then?
lines.fr: Et ensuite ?

lines.en: Was everything OK?
lines.fr: Ça a été ?

lines.en: A coffee to finish?
lines.fr: Un café pour finir ?

lines.en: Together or separately?
lines.fr: Ensemble ou séparément ?

sections.title: Which Stage Was That

questions.q: Line 1. Where in the evening are you?
questions.why: Stage 1. It is the first thing said to you, before you have sat down or seen a menu.
opts: You are halfway through the main course

questions.q: Line 2. What is he asking about?
questions.why: Stage 3, drinks. Plate is still and gazeuse is sparkling, and there is no noun in the question to tell you it is about water.

questions.q: Line 3. What does he want to know?
questions.why: Stage 4. Two words meaning what is next, said the moment you finish naming a starter.

questions.q: Line 4. When is this said?
questions.why: Stage 5, and it is a passé composé of être. It is asked after eating, never before.

questions.q: Line 5. Which stage?
questions.why: Stage 6, the upsell. Pour finir is what places it: it only makes sense once the food is done.
opts: The drinks order at the start

questions.q: Line 6. What is being decided?
questions.why: Stage 8. It decides whether one bill comes or several, and it is asked once, quickly.

cards.fr: Plate.
cards.sub: one word, and it is enough
cards.body: He gave you both words. Give one of them back. Adding s'il vous plaît is plenty of politeness for a two-word question.

cards.sub: or: Je vais prendre le plat du jour.
cards.body: This is the one slot where you produce a full sentence, and it is the sentence you have been rehearsing since lesson 8 in A1.

cards.label: your one full sentence

cards.body: Three words exist and he will offer none of them. À point is the middle one and the safe one.

cards.body: Or Non, je voudrais aussi un café. Either way you are reusing his words rather than building your own.

sections.title: The Answer That Fits

sections.say: Five rungs. Four of them are fine. One of them is the reason the waiter paused.

rows.say: Je voudrais le poulet.

detail.say: Je voudrais le poulet.
detail.body: The default, and the one to reach for if you only keep one. It is soft, it is short, and no French speaker has ever been surprised by it.
detail.title: « je voudrais »

rows.say: Je prendrais plutôt le poisson.

detail.say: Je prendrais plutôt le poisson.
detail.body: Softer still, and useful when you are changing your mind out loud. Learn it as one fixed phrase; the family it comes from is another lesson.
detail.title: « je prendrais »

rows.say: Je prends le plat du jour.

detail.say: Je prends le plat du jour.
detail.body: Present tense, brisk, completely normal. This is what people at the next table are saying.
detail.title: « je prends »

rows.say: Je vais prendre le plat du jour.

detail.say: Je vais prendre le plat du jour.
detail.body: The futur proche, which lesson 15 in A2 already gave you. It sounds like a decision just made, which at a table is exactly what it is.
detail.title: « je vais prendre »

rows.say: Ce sera le menu du jour.

detail.say: Pour moi, ce sera l'entrecôte.
detail.body: The flattest of the five and still perfectly polite. Pour moi, ce sera l'entrecôte is how it is said at a table of four.
detail.title: « ce sera »

rows.say: Je voudrais le poulet.

detail.say: Je voudrais le poulet.
detail.body: Grammatical, understood, and wrong here. It is what a child says about a toy. Nobody will correct you, and that is exactly why nobody has told you.
detail.title: « je veux » is the one to drop

rule.body: English answers a question at a table with a sentence. French answers it with the thing. When he says two words, two words back is not rude, it is the register.

sections.title: None Of The Eight

questions.q: Line 1. What does he want from you?
questions.why: He is looking for a booking. Your surname is the whole answer, and it is the word learners are least ready to say aloud.

questions.q: Line 2. What should you do?
questions.why: It is a courtesy said while already reaching past you. Nothing is really being asked, and the only wrong answer is a long one.
opts: Move your arm and say je vous en prie

questions.q: Line 3. Is he asking you anything?
questions.why: A warning, not a question. A learner running the script hears a question in it and answers oui, which is how you burn your hand.
opts: Yes, about the temperature you want

questions.q: Line 4. Which stage does this belong to?
questions.why: It looks like the upsell and is not: this is about bread or water while you eat, not about buying another course.

questions.q: Line 5. What does it mean for you?
questions.why: A statement that is really an instruction. Nothing in it is a question and everything in it is urgent.
opts: Order now or not at all

questions.q: Line 6. You did not catch it at all. Which rung?
questions.why: Rung 1, and it costs nothing. He is walking away mid-turn, so a cheap rung now beats an expensive one later.
opts: Vous pouvez me l'écrire, s'il vous plaît ?

sections.say: Six rungs, cheapest first. Every one of them is ordinary French and none of them is an apology.

cards.fr: Pardon ?
cards.body: One word, and it gives away nothing about why you missed it. It is also the one a French speaker uses without thinking, which is why it is first.
cards.head: Rung 1
cards.label: costs you nothing

cards.fr: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.body: Asks for the whole thing again and still says nothing about what went wrong. If rung 1 got you a repeat at the same speed, this is the next one.
cards.head: Rung 2
cards.label: the whole thing again

cards.fr: Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
cards.body: The first rung that names the problem: it was the speed. Use it when you caught the shape of the sentence but none of the words.
cards.head: Rung 3
cards.label: names the problem

cards.fr: Je n'ai pas bien compris.
cards.body: Says outright that you did not follow. Bien is what softens it: without bien you are saying you understood nothing at all.
cards.head: Rung 4
cards.label: says it outright

cards.fr: Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ?
cards.body: Narrows it to one word rather than the whole turn. Point at the thing on the menu and this question does the rest.
cards.head: Rung 5
cards.label: one word, not the turn

cards.fr: Vous pouvez me l'écrire, s'il vous plaît ?
cards.sub: [voo poo-VAY muh lay-KREER seel voo PLEH]
cards.body: The most expensive rung, and the one that always works. It concedes that listening has failed and asks to change medium.
cards.head: Rung 6
cards.label: always works

sections.say: A real board, written the way they are written. The questions are about how it is laid out, not what the words mean.
sections.text:
CHEZ MARTHE · ARDOISE DU JOUR

FORMULE MIDI · 22 €
entrée + plat  ou  plat + dessert
Servie du mardi au vendredi, jusqu'à 14h.

ENTRÉES
Soupe à l'oignon gratinée · 9 €
Salade de chèvre chaud · 11 €
Terrine maison, cornichons · 10 €

PLATS
Entrecôte, sauce au poivre, frites · 24 €
Saumon à l'oseille, riz · 21 €
Risotto aux champignons · 18 €   sans viande

DESSERTS
Tarte Tatin · 8 €
Mousse au chocolat · 7 €

Boissons non comprises. Service compris.
Les plats sont susceptibles de contenir des fruits à coque.
sections.title: Reading The Board

glossary.note: The slate the day's dishes are chalked on. If it is on the ardoise it is today only.
Two courses for one price, usually at lunch and usually on weekdays only.
Finished under the grill with cheese. It describes how, not what.
Served cold in a slice, with cornichons. It is meat.
A sharp green leaf cooked down into a sauce, almost always with fish.
The board's own marking. Only one dish carries it.
What the price does NOT cover. Read it next to service compris, which is the opposite.
The formal term used on allergy notices. Not the same as les noix, which is walnuts.

questions.a: Two, not three. The line under the price reads entrée + plat OU plat + dessert, so you take two of the three and choose which two.
questions.q: It is Thursday at one o'clock and you take the formule at 22 €. How many courses do you get, and why?

questions.a: Yes. The risotto is a plat and the tarte is a dessert, which is one of the two pairings offered. Nothing on the board excludes either dish.
questions.q: You want the risotto and then a tarte Tatin, on the formule. Does the board allow it?

questions.a: It is not available. Servie du mardi au vendredi puts Saturday outside it, and the jusqu'à 14h limit is a second condition on top of that rather than instead of it.
questions.q: You come back on Saturday and want the same deal. What does the board say?

questions.a: It warns that any dish might contain them: les plats sont susceptibles de contenir des fruits à coque. It does not tell you which ones, which is exactly why you still have to ask.
questions.q: You are allergic to nuts. What does the board tell you, and what does it not?

questions.a: The service is in it and the drinks are not. Boissons non comprises. Service compris. The two lines sit together and say opposite things.
questions.q: You order the entrecôte and a glass of wine. What is in the price and what is not?

questions.a: The risotto is marked sans viande. The terrine is meat despite reading like a vegetable dish, and the soupe à l'oignon is not marked either way, so it is not a safe read.
questions.q: You do not eat meat. Which dish is safe on this board, and which one looks safe and is not?

sections.title: Everything He Said

sections.say: Twenty-three missions. Here is what changed.
sections.body: You came in able to order and left able to be spoken to. The eight stages are the same eight almost everywhere in France, so the next bistro is not a new problem. And when a sentence goes past you, you no longer have to smile and hope: there are six things to say and you know what each one costs.

sections.say: Six rounds of five. Most of it is catching what he said.

rounds.label: Which stage

questions.q: He says « Ça a été ? ». Where are you?
questions.why: A past tense, so the eating is over. Tout se passe bien ? is the present-tense version asked mid-meal.

questions.q: He says « Et ensuite ? ». What does he want?
questions.why: Stage 4. Ensuite means next, and next at this point is the main course.

questions.q: « Une carafe d'eau, ça ira ? » is
questions.why: Ça ira means will that do. He is confirming rather than offering, and silence counts as yes.
opts: A check on a decision he has made

questions.q: « Vous réglez comment ? » asks about
questions.why: Comment is how. Combien would be how much, and that is a different question at a different moment.

questions.q: Which of these comes FIRST in the evening?
questions.why: Stage 1. The other three are stages 4, 6 and 8, in that order.

rounds.say: Five you have to hear rather than read.
rounds.label: What he said

questions.q: Listen. What is he asking about?
questions.say: Plate ou gazeuse ?
questions.why: There is no noun in the question at all. It is a drinks question and the two words are the two kinds of bottled water.

questions.q: Listen. What is being decided?
questions.say: Ensemble ou séparément ?
questions.why: Stage 8. It is asked once, quickly, while he is holding the card machine.
opts: Whether one bill comes or several

questions.q: Listen. Is this a question?
questions.say: Je vous débarrasse ?
questions.why: It is shaped exactly like a statement and marked only by his voice going up at the end.
opts: No, it is a statement about the bill
Yes, and it asks to clear your plate
Yes, and it asks what you want

questions.q: Listen. What does comme mean here?
questions.say: Et comme boisson ?
questions.why: Comme frames a category: by way of a drink. Et comme entrée ? at stage 4 is the same frame with a different noun.

questions.q: Listen. What has happened?
questions.say: Je suis désolé, il n'y en a plus.
questions.why: Take it whole: it is one sound meaning there is none left. Taking it apart at the table costs you the seconds you needed.

rounds.say: Five on saying the right amount, which is usually less than you think.
rounds.label: The answer that fits

questions.q: He says « Plate ou gazeuse ? ». Best answer?
questions.why: He gave you two words. Hand one back. It is not curt; it is the register.
opts: Je voudrais de l'eau qui n'est pas gazeuse.

questions.q: He says « Ce sera tout ? » and you want nothing else.
questions.why: Reusing his frame is faster and more natural than building a new sentence.

questions.q: He asked « Vous réglez comment ? ». Fix the answer.
questions.why: Comment asks the method, not the amount. Answering with a price question means he has to ask again.
accept: Par carte.
par carte
Par carte, s'il vous plaît.
En espèces.
en espèces
questions.answer: Par carte, s'il vous plaît.
questions.prompt: Ça fait combien ?

questions.q: He says « Quelle cuisson ? ». Which is an actual answer?
questions.why: Three words exist and he will offer none of them: saignant, à point, bien cuit.

questions.q: He says « Vous êtes combien ? ». Best answer?
questions.why: A number is a whole answer to a number question. Nothing else needs to be built around it.

rounds.say: Five on the one rung that is wrong at a table.
rounds.label: How you ask

questions.q: You are at a table ordering. Fix this.
questions.why: Je veux is grammatical and understood, and it is one rung too blunt at a table. Nobody corrects it, which is why nobody learns it.
accept: Je voudrais le poulet.
je voudrais le poulet
Je prends le poulet.
Je vais prendre le poulet.
questions.answer: Je voudrais le poulet.
questions.prompt: Je veux le poulet.

questions.q: Write the softest of the five ways to order, using vouloir. Three words, then the dish: « ... le poulet. »
questions.why: Voudrais against veux is one syllable and the whole difference in register. Both survive folding, so this is a real contrast rather than a spelling test.
accept: Je voudrais le poulet.
je voudrais le poulet
Je voudrais le poulet
questions.answer: Je voudrais le poulet.

questions.q: Which of these would you NOT say at a restaurant table?
questions.why: The other three sit at different points on the gradient and all four are grammatical. Only the first one lands wrong.

questions.q: « Pour moi, ce sera l'entrecôte. » Where does this sit?
questions.why: Ce sera is the flattest of the five rungs and it carries no rudeness at all. It is how it is said at a table of four.
opts: Flat and confident, and perfectly polite

questions.q: You are telling him what you do not eat. Fix this.
questions.why: After a negative it is de, never du. Lesson 8 in A1 taught this one; the table is where you have to run it fast.
accept: Je ne mange pas de viande.
je ne mange pas de viande
de viande
questions.answer: Je ne mange pas de viande.
questions.prompt: Je ne mange pas du viande.

rounds.say: Five on the six rungs, and this is the part the rest of the course quotes.
rounds.label: When you miss it

questions.q: The cheapest thing you can say when you catch nothing. One word.
questions.why: Rung 1. It gives away nothing about why you missed it, and it is what a French speaker says without thinking.
accept: Pardon
Pardon ?
pardon
questions.answer: Pardon ?

questions.q: Say that you did not QUITE catch it. Five words: « Je n'ai pas ... compris. »
questions.why: Bien is what softens it. Without bien you are saying you understood nothing at all, and the two do not fold together, so the word is genuinely being tested.
accept: Je n'ai pas bien compris.
je n'ai pas bien compris
bien
questions.answer: Je n'ai pas bien compris.

questions.q: He repeated it once at exactly the same speed. Which rung now?
questions.why: Rungs 1 and 2 both just ask for a repeat. Only rung 3 tells him what to change, and he cannot fix a problem you have not named.
opts: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

questions.q: You caught the whole sentence except one word on the board.
questions.why: Repeating it will not help, because you heard it. Rung 5 narrows the problem to the one word actually stopping you.
opts: Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?

questions.q: He says the dish is off. What keeps the turn?
questions.why: You cannot choose, so make him choose. Freezing costs you the turn and he starts suggesting things at full speed.
opts: Saying nothing while you rebuild the sentence
Alors qu'est-ce que vous me conseillez ?

rounds.say: Five that need more than one part of the lesson.
rounds.label: The whole evening

questions.q: The formule is 22 € for entrée + plat or plat + dessert. You want all three courses.
questions.why: The board says OU: two of the three, and you pick which two. A third course is off the deal.
opts: The formule does not cover it

questions.q: « Le service est compris. » What does this mean for you?
questions.why: It is a statement of fact, not a hint. Anything on top is yours to decide and nobody is waiting for it.
opts: The service charge is already in the price

questions.q: Say it out loud. The dish you wanted is off and the queue behind you is waiting.
questions.why: Alors buys you the half-second and the rest is one fixed question. Said whole, it sounds like a decision rather than a stall.
questions.target: Alors qu'est-ce que vous me conseillez ?

questions.q: Say rung 4 out loud, to a waiter who has just said something fast.
questions.why: Four rhythmic beats and no pause in the middle. Said as one block it sounds ordinary; said word by word it sounds like an apology.

questions.q: Across the whole evening, how many questions does he ask before the food arrives?
questions.why: Reservation, how many, where, drink, still or sparkling, chosen, and the cooking. You start none of them, which is the whole reframe.

sections.say: Three things, and the third one works everywhere, not just at a table.
sections.body: You never start. He asks, you answer, and there are eight stages that arrive in the same order almost every time. Answer short: when he gives you two words, one of them back is the whole answer. And when a sentence goes past you, there are six rungs from Pardon ? to Vous pouvez me l'écrire ?, and you now know what each one costs. That last one is not about restaurants. It is the thing you will use in a pharmacy, at a station, and on the phone.
sections.title: What You Take With You
points: You never start. He asks, you answer.
Eight stages, in the same order almost every time.
A short question wants a short answer. Two words back is not curt, it is the register.
Je veux is the one rung too far down. Je voudrais costs you one syllable.
Six rungs from Pardon ? to Vous pouvez me l'écrire ?, and the ladder works anywhere.

errorTriggers.description: Orders with je veux, which is grammatical, understood, and one rung too blunt for a table. Nobody corrects it, so nobody learns it.
Reaches for the wrong point on the ordering gradient for the situation, usually by building a long sentence where a short one is expected.
Cannot say which part of the meal a line belongs to, so answers the wrong question or answers nothing.
Hears the words but not the stage, most often on Ça a été ? and Et ensuite ?, which carry no noun to anchor on.
Answers a two-word question with a full sentence, which is understood and marks the speaker as translating rather than talking.
Answers oui to a two-way question such as Plate ou gazeuse ?, which selects nothing and forces him to ask again.
Fails on the four questions with no verb to anchor on: Plate ou gazeuse ?, Et ensuite ?, Un café pour finir ?, Ensemble ou séparément ?
Says nothing when the script deviates, rebuilding the sentence internally while the turn is lost.
Reaches too high or too low on the repair ladder: asking for a repeat when the speed was the problem, or asking for it in writing when Pardon would have done.

grammarAssumed: The partitive du, de la, de l' and its reduction to de under negation, delivered whole by a1.29 at seq 8
The futur proche as a way of stating a decision just made, from a2.19 at seq 15
The passé composé with avoir, from a2.05, which the server uses in Vous avez choisi ? and Ça a été ?
The third-person direct object pronoun before the verb, from a2.06 at seq 21, met here only as exposure in Je vous le remplace
Yes/no question formation and est-ce que, from a1.19
grammarIntroduced: The eight-stage structure of a French restaurant encounter, received in the server's voice rather than produced in the learner's
Recognition of the server's eight canonical questions, including the four that contain no verb the learner can anchor on
The adjacency-pair principle: that a short question takes a short answer, and that reusing the server's own frame is the native response
A five-rung ordering gradient inside the restaurant frame, from je prendrais to ce sera, with je veux identified as the one register error
The repair move as a six-rung ladder ordered by face cost, owned here for the whole A2 situations band and cited by unit id elsewhere
Recovery from a script deviation by handing the choice back rather than rebuilding the sentence
Reading a French menu board for its layout: what a formule includes, what its conditions are, and what is excluded
The partitive at the point of ordering as RECALL of a1.29, with no new claim made about it
That l'addition, le service and le pourboire are stages of the script; the amount, the change and the coins are reserved for a2.26
That il n'y en a plus is recognised as unanalysed lexis, with y and en reserved entirely for a2.25

acts.title: The word that would not come out
acts.milestone: You know what stopped the sentence, and it was not a word you had never learned.

acts.title: Five shapes, not four
acts.milestone: You can see all five shapes of all three words at once, and you already owned four of them.

acts.title: The short one, and where it comes from
acts.milestone: You can build the short form of any of the three without having learned it, because it was never a new word.

acts.title: The two traps
acts.milestone: You will not put the woman form in front of a masculine thing, and you will not put an s where an x goes.

acts.title: Out loud
acts.milestone: You held the conversation the scene lost, and every answer in it wanted a shape rather than a phrase.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: You got the two written rounds right, which is the half of this no listening test could ever have found.

recorded.desc: THE THREE CONTRAST PAIRS, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TAKE IN THE LESSON. Each pair is ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, the two lines recorded back to back with the smallest gap the recording allows and no change of pitch, pace or weight between them: « C'est un beau sac. » then « C'est un bel arbre. »; « C'est un nouveau sac. » then « C'est un nouvel ami. »; « C'est un vieux sac. » then « C'est un vieil homme. » RECORDED APART, THE LEARNER COMPARES TWO PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF TWO SOUNDS AND THE ENTIRE TEACHING IS LOST. The third pair matters most and is the hardest: the h of homme is silent, so the reader must NOT pause before it or aspirate it, and the l of vieil runs straight into the vowel exactly as it does in vieil ami. If the reader gives homme even a breath of a consonant, the take proves the opposite of the screen. What must be audible in every pair is the describing word and nothing else; the two nouns differ and that is not the point.

THE FIFTEEN CELLS, THREE TAKES, ONE PER WORD, EACH WORD'S FIVE IN ONE BREATH GROUP. Within each take the FIRST AND FOURTH lines must be acoustically identical, and so must the SECOND, THIRD AND FIFTH: « Il est beau. » and « Ils sont beaux. » differ on the page and not in the mouth, and a reader who knows the fourth is spelled with an x will lengthen something or put a fraction of a z on it, and that instinct destroys the screen. If a listener with their eyes shut can tell the first from the fourth, or the second from the third, the take is unusable. FIVE WRITTEN SHAPES MUST REACH THE EAR AS TWO. That is the whole claim of the lesson and this take is where it is either proved or lost.

THE FOUR LINES FOR THE LISTENING SCREEN, WITH AUDIO BEFORE TEXT, IN THIS ORDER: Il est beau, Ils sont beaux, Elle est belle, Elles sont belles. The first pair and the second pair are each ONE take and must be indistinguishable within the pair; the learner is being asked to fail to hear a difference and to notice that they failed. Between the pairs the difference is real and should be left exactly as large as the language makes it, with no help. Do not put anything on the end of beaux.

THE THREE FEMININE-AGAINST-SHORT PAIRS, WHICH ARE THE SAME SOUND TWICE. « belle » then « bel »; « nouvelle » then « nouvel »; « vieille » then « vieil ». Each pair is one take and the two members MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. This is the only take in the lesson whose value is that nothing happens in it, and it is the one a reader will be most tempted to help with, because the two words look different on the page and a reader who can see the page will differentiate them without meaning to. If it is possible to record this take without the reader seeing the spelling of the second member, do that.

THE SIXTEEN DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to every other take in the lesson: here the learner is spelling rather than comparing, and any pair-reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. The x on beaux and nouveaux and the s on belles and vieilles must be neither helped nor hidden; say the sentence the way somebody would say it, which is the whole difficulty the exercise exists to create.

THE BREAK CARD, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE IN THIS LESSON A WRONG FORM IS SPOKEN. « un beau immeuble » then « un bel immeuble », one take, back to back. The first is NOT to be read as a mistake, with a wince or a rising edge or a pause: it must be read as somebody genuinely trying to say it, which means the two vowels grinding into each other and the phrase almost stopping. That difficulty IS the teaching, and a clean, confident reading of it would teach that the wrong form is perfectly sayable. The second should then arrive easily and at ordinary pace, and the contrast between the effort in the first and the ease of the second is the whole card.

OUTSIDE THE OFFICE IN NANTES. He is friendly, in a hurry, and asking to be polite rather than because he needs to know. « C'est un grand appartement ? » is quick and light. The learner's own line, « Oui, et c'est un beau... un beau... euh... », is the take that has to be right: two false starts and a stall, and the stall must sound like somebody whose mouth has stopped rather than like somebody who has forgotten a word. There is a difference and it is audible. His last line is cheerful and completely unbothered; nothing in the delivery should suggest he noticed anything, because he did not, and that is what makes it expensive.
clipIds: Oui, et c'est un bel immeuble.

lessons.intro: Three describing words in French have a fifth shape that nothing else has, and you use it in front of anything that starts with a vowel sound. It is not a new word to learn: it is the form you already use about a woman, with the last two letters taken off, and it sounds exactly the same. This lesson is about when to reach for it, why it is there at all, and the one mistake it causes that nobody can hear.

fiveForms.body: 5 ways to write each of these three, and 2 ways to say them. Lesson 10 in A2 gave you four of the five and this is the one it could not. Five ways to write it and two ways to say it. Three of the five are one sound and the other two are the other. The extra shape is the one you use in front of a word that starts with a vowel sound, and it is only ever used about a man or about a masculine thing. Everything else on the grid you already know how to build, because lesson 10 in A2 taught you the system these three sit inside.
fiveForms.title: Three words that have one more shape than the rest

examples.note: The extra one, and the reason the other four are not enough.
And the one the extra one borrows its sound from.

theXPlural.body: beaux and nouveaux take an x. vieux already ends in one, so it takes nothing at all, and lesson 17 in A1 and lesson 10 in A2 both told you so. None of the three is audible: an x on the end of a describing word has never been pronounced in French, any more than an s has, so the plural of all three sounds exactly like the singular. That is the half of this you can only get by having seen it written.
theXPlural.title: Two of them take an x and one takes nothing

examples.note: An x. Not an s, and not for any reason you could work out.
And the third, which is the same four letters as the singular. Lesson 17 in A1 told you about this word by name.

onlyForAMan.body: Nobody hears this mistake, including the person making it. The two forms are one sound, so only the page shows it. The short form exists to run into the word after it, so it only turns up in front of a thing. The woman form already ends in a consonant sound, so there is no collision for a short form to prevent and French never made one. Writing « une belle amie » is right and writing « une belle appartement » is not, and the two sound exactly the same, which is the whole difficulty. The only way to catch it is to know which word you are describing.
onlyForAMan.title: There is no woman version of the short one

examples.note: A masculine thing, so the short form.
And the full woman form, which is what goes in front of anything feminine, vowel or no vowel.
A masculine thing again. If this were feminine the word would be four letters longer and sound identical.

theShortOne.body: The form before a vowel is not a new word. It is the woman form two letters shorter, and it sounds the same. belle without the le is bel, nouvelle without the le is nouvel, vieille without the le is vieil. Three words, one operation. That is why it is worth knowing rather than memorising: you are not learning three new words, you are shortening three you already have. Say the woman form out loud, stop two letters early, and you have said the right thing. Before a vowel, say the feminine and drop its last two letters.
theShortOne.title: It is the woman form with two letters taken off

examples.note: Now say it two letters shorter. Same sound, and it is a different word on the page.
Third word, and the same two letters have come off again.

whereItGoes.body: Where these three go is lesson 18 in A1 and it has not changed: they are three of the small set that stand in front of the thing. That is the one thing about placement worth saying here, and it is worth saying because it is the CAUSE: a describing word that comes after the thing never meets the sound that starts it, so it never needs a short form. These three come first, so they do. Lesson 12 in A2 is next and it is built on the woman form, which you have now used more than any other shape of these three. Nothing here expires when you get there.
whereItGoes.title: Not this lesson, and it is why this lesson exists

examples.note: In front of the thing, which is where all three of these live.
In front of the thing, and now the sound of the thing has changed the word.
After the verb, where nothing follows it and nothing has to happen.

aVowelIsComing.body: Lesson 8 in Sounds put it this way: Two vowels collide, the little word gives way. It said that about the little words in front of a noun. This is the same pressure on the word after them. Lesson 20 in A1 taught you « mon amie » rather than « ma amie ». Same trade, other direction: a form borrowed from the other side so a consonant lands in front of the vowel. 3 of your lessons have made you do it already. What decides it is the SOUND at the front of the next word rather than the letter, which is why a silent h counts as a vowel and why you have to listen to the word rather than look at it. Nothing about the thing being described matters here: not what it means, not how long it is, only what noise it starts with.
aVowelIsComing.title: What sets the whole thing off

examples.note: A vowel at the front of the next word, so the short form.
A consonant at the front of the next word, so the plain form and nothing to do.
An h on the page and a vowel in the mouth. French listens to the mouth.

whatYouCanHear.body: You can hear the plain one against the one before a vowel, and that is the only difference here your ear will ever get. Five ways to write it and two ways to say it. Three of the five are one sound and the other two are the other. So the ear tells you one thing and one thing only: whether the speaker used the plain form or the short one. It will not tell you whether they meant one thing or several, and it will not tell you whether the short form or the woman form came out, because those two are the same noise. Everything else on this grid is a decision you make with your eyes and your grammar rather than your ears.
whatYouCanHear.title: Five shapes reaching your ear as two

examples.note: And the other one. This is the whole of what is audible in this lesson.
Back to the first sound. The x makes no more noise than nothing would.

beats.text: A Tuesday evening in Nantes. A colleague you like but do not know well has asked where you have moved to, and you have been waiting all week for somebody to ask.

beats.en: Is it a big flat?
beats.fr: C'est un grand appartement ?
beats.speaker: Le collègue

beats.en: Yes, and it is a lovely... a lovely... er...
beats.fr: Oui, et c'est un beau... un beau... euh...
beats.stage: You know the word. You have said « beau » a thousand times. It went into your mouth, it hit the front of the next word, and it would not come out.

beats.prompt: You have stopped twice now and he is still waiting. What comes out?

options.en: the word you own, two letters shorter
options.fr: Oui, et c'est un bel immeuble
options.respell: [wee ay seh-tuhⁿ beh-lee-MUHBL]

options.en: and you have given up on the sentence you wanted
options.fr: It is very nice.

followUp.works: He asks which street, in French, and you spend the rest of the walk to the tram talking about the neighbourhood.
followUp.breaks: He says "oh, nice" and asks somebody else about their weekend. Nothing went wrong and you told him nothing.

beats.en: Ah, cool. Right, see you tomorrow!
beats.fr: Ah, cool. Bon, à demain !
beats.stage: Nobody corrected anything, because there was nothing to correct. You stopped before the wrong word arrived and the sentence stopped with it.
beats.speaker: Le collègue

beats.body: You did not stall on a word you had not learned. You stalled because the word you had ran straight into the front of the next one and your mouth stopped before your grammar did.
beats.coach: Listen to the front of the next word.

wrong.en: what would not come out

sections.text: Nous avons déménagé le mois dernier. C'est un bel immeuble, assez vieux, dans une rue calme. Notre appartement est petit mais il est très beau : les fenêtres sont belles et il y a un vieil arbre devant la porte. Le voisin du troisième est un vieil homme très gentil ; il connaît tout le monde ici. Il y a aussi un nouvel habitant au deuxième, et deux nouveaux commerces au coin de la rue. Les rues sont vieilles et les magasins sont nouveaux, et c'est ce que nous voulions.
sections.title: The Flat, Described

questions.why: The same four letters as the singular. Lesson 17 in A1 and lesson 10 in A2 both told you so and it is a fact about the letter x rather than about this word.
accept: vieux
Ils sont vieux.
questions.answer: vieux

questions.q: Which of these four is spelled correctly?
questions.why: An x on the end. The first is the s a learner reaches for, the second is the woman form and the third has no plural on it at all.

questions.q: Fix this.
questions.why: There is no room after an x for another letter, so nothing goes on the end and the word is finished already.
accept: Ils sont vieux.
vieux
Ils sont vieux
questions.answer: Ils sont vieux.
questions.prompt: Ils sont vieuxs.

questions.q: Elles sont ___ .   (vieux)
questions.why: And here an ordinary s does turn up, because the woman form gave it somewhere to go.
accept: vieilles
Elles sont vieilles.
questions.answer: vieilles

rounds.say: Six, and each one wants a different one of the five shapes.
rounds.label: All of it at once

questions.q: C'est un ___ immeuble.   (vieux)
questions.why: A vowel at the front of the next word, and a masculine thing, so the short form.
accept: vieil
un vieil immeuble
questions.answer: vieil

questions.q: Elle est ___ .   (vieux)
questions.why: Nothing follows it, so nothing can collide with it, and the woman form is what stands here.
accept: vieille
Elle est vieille.
questions.answer: vieille

questions.q: C'est un ___ habitant.   (nouveau)
questions.why: A silent h, so a vowel sound, so the short form. The reading passage had this exact phrase in it.
accept: nouvel
un nouvel habitant
questions.answer: nouvel

questions.q: Fix this.
questions.why: The short form exists to run into the word after it, so it only turns up in front of a thing.
accept: Il est vieux.
vieux
Il est vieux
questions.answer: Il est vieux.
questions.prompt: Il est vieil.

questions.q: Listen. Did the describing word change?
questions.say: C'est un vieux sac.
questions.why: VYUH against VYEY, and this was the first one.

questions.q: You are about to say a describing word and you have half a second. What do you check?
questions.why: Before a vowel, say the feminine and drop its last two letters. Where these three go is lesson 18 in A1 and it has not changed: they are three of the small set that stand in front of the thing.
opts: Whether the thing is one or several
Whether the word goes in front of the thing or after it
What sound the next word starts with
Whether you have said this word before

sections.body: Before a vowel, say the feminine and drop its last two letters. Listen to the front of the next word, not to its spelling. If a vowel is coming, take the woman form and drop its last two letters.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: 5 ways to write each of these three, and 2 ways to say them. Lesson 10 in A2 gave you four of the five and this is the one it could not.

The form before a vowel is not a new word. It is the woman form two letters shorter, and it sounds the same. belle without the le is bel, nouvelle without the le is nouvel, vieille without the le is vieil. Three words, one operation.
Lesson 8 in Sounds said it about the little words in front of a noun: Two vowels collide, the little word gives way. It was the same rule then and it is the same rule now.

Lesson 20 in A1 taught you « mon amie » rather than « ma amie ». Same trade, other direction: a form borrowed from the other side so a consonant lands in front of the vowel. 3 of your lessons have made you do it already.
beaux and nouveaux take an x. vieux already ends in one, so it takes nothing at all, and lesson 17 in A1 and lesson 10 in A2 both told you so.
You can hear the plain one against the one before a vowel, and that is the only difference here your ear will ever get. That is why two of the five exam rounds are written.
Lesson 12 in A2 is next and it is built on the woman form, which you have now used more than any other shape of these three. Nothing here expires when you get there.
Lesson 18 in A1 owns where the word goes and lesson 10 in A2 owns the four shapes underneath these five. Neither of them is this.

errorTriggers.description: Uses the plain form in front of a vowel, which is the error the scene opens on. It is not a slip: the learner owns the plain form completely and has never been given a reason to reach past it.

Builds the short form off the plain form rather than off the feminine, producing something with the right letters and the wrong sound. The learner who does this has understood that a form is needed and not what it is made of.

Writes the woman form in front of a masculine noun starting with a vowel. It is the commonest error in this subject and it is INAUDIBLE: the two forms are one sound, so the learner hears themselves say the right thing.
Writes beaus or nouveaus. The learner is applying the plural rule they have and it is the right rule for almost every other describing word in the language.

Puts the short form where nothing follows it, as in « Il est bel. » Comes from learning the form as a property of the word rather than of the position, which is exactly what lesson 18 in A1 warned it would.

grammarAssumed: That a describing word changes shape to match what it describes, introduced in a1.13 through colour
The feminine -e and the plural -s on a describing word, and that the -s is never pronounced, introduced in a1.13
The irregular feminines belle and vieille by suppletion, introduced in a1.14
That a word already ending in -s or -x does not change in the masculine plural, introduced in a1.14 for vieux and mauvais and generalised to the class in a2.03
The pre-nominal position of this closed set, introduced in a1.16, including bel, vieil and nouvel as position-bound
Adjective agreement as a system of inflectional classes, introduced in a2.03
Elision and the distinction between h muet and h aspiré, introduced in sons.07
The pre-vocalic mon, ton and son in front of a feminine noun, introduced in a1.17
être in the present, introduced in a1.06, which is the frame twelve of the fifteen cells use
grammarIntroduced: The pre-vocalic masculine as a fifth inflectional cell rather than as a positional variant, completing the account a1.16 began
That the pre-vocalic masculine is phonologically identical to the feminine singular and derivable from it by deletion of the final -le, uniformly across beau, nouveau and vieux
Anti-hiatus as a single productive principle across the language, with elision, the pre-vocalic possessive and the pre-vocalic adjective as three of its realisations
That h muet is transparent to the pre-vocalic rule, extending sons.07 h-aspire-vs-h-muet distinction from proclitics to the adjective
The -eaux masculine plural on beau and nouveau, claimed by no unit at any level before this one
That the pre-vocalic form has no feminine counterpart, because the feminine is already consonant-final and licenses no hiatus
That the pre-vocalic form is licensed only pre-nominally and is ungrammatical in predicate position
That five written forms are realised as two phonological forms, so the pre-vocalic against feminine contrast is undetectable by ear and testable only in writing

lessons.intro: One round for each of the thirty-four A2 units, five questions each, in the order you walked them. Nothing new is taught. A round that goes badly names the unit to sit again, and drills it before the next round starts.
lessons.title: Bilan A2 : leçon par leçon

drills.coach: Three regular families and the verbs that stand outside them. The plural is where they separate: one adds nothing, one adds a syllable, one wakes a consonant up.
drills.title: One cell from each family

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: ils finissent. The regular -ir family puts -iss- in front of every plural ending.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Two different jobs. The e and the cedilla protect a soft consonant in front of a back vowel. The doubled l and the turned accent hold a vowel open in front of a silent ending.
drills.title: The spelling moves so the sound can stay

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: nous mangeons. Without the e the g would harden in front of the o.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: One frame, six meanings. The second verb never takes a person and never changes, whichever verb is in front of it.
pairs: I am not going to leave
drills.title: Only the first verb moves

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: Elle veut partir. Conjugating the second verb as well is the reflex this frame exists to stop.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: After avoir nothing agrees. After être everything does. The little word in front is the reliable signal: wherever it appears, the first word is être.
drills.title: Which first word, and what it does to the second

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: Elle est allée. Two things move together: the first word becomes être and the second one then agrees.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The family ending does not predict these. An -re verb can give -is, an -ir verb can give -ert, and eu is said with none of the sounds its three letters suggest.
drills.title: The ones you reach for

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: J’ai pris. Cover the prefix and apprendre gives appris the same way.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The wrap goes round the verb that changed, and takes any little words in front of it with it. The verb carrying the meaning stays outside.
pairs: I am not going to leave
I do not get up early
Je ne me lève pas tôt
Je ne me suis pas levé
drills.title: What the two halves go round

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: Je ne vais pas sortir. The half that moved is aller, so that is the half that gets wrapped.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The plain form gives you the other three, and the feminine is usually audible where the plural never is. Two colours named after things never move at all.
drills.title: What moves, and what you can hear

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: sportive. The -if class swaps its consonant rather than adding to it.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: In front of the verb, always. A person behind à takes lui or leur; anything else takes le, la or les. The past form agrees with the second kind and never with the first.
pairs: Je lui ai donné le livre
drills.title: Which one, and where it goes

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: Je le vois. English word order survives the vocabulary, which is why this comes out wrong in the mouth.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Each of these two swallows a preposition as well as its noun, so saying à or de again after it doubles it. And English lets you stop at I do, where French will not.
drills.title: The preposition is already inside

drills.q: Answer « Vous avez du pain ? » Which?
drills.why: Oui, j’en ai. The pronoun is required rather than optional.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Neither series looks at the owner. Both look at the thing, and the pointing word also looks at whether a vowel is coming after it.
drills.title: The thing owned picks the word

drills.q: Whose car? Which?
drills.why: C’est la mienne, because voiture is feminine, and the article in front is compulsory.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The place words differ by what they do to the article: à folds it in, en throws it out, chez leaves it alone. The time words differ by whether the span is still open.
drills.title: Places, and lengths of time

drills.q: Which is right?
drills.why: Je vais au marché. À le is never written; it is always au.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: These are scripts and the other person usually starts. Your half is short, it reuses their frame, and the rung you pick costs you something or nothing.
drills.title: The rung, and whose turn it is

drills.q: You are ordering. Which?
drills.why: Je voudrais. Je veux reads as an instruction rather than a request.
drills.title: One more time
