lessons.intro: Three verbs that will not come apart, and one of them turns up in 30 everyday expressions: the shopping, the cooking, the queue, the weather. The forms take ten minutes. The reach is the rest of the lesson.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Both are correct and both mean we. on takes the same form as il, which on this verb means on fait and never on faisons. So the spoken we uses the same three letters as the weather does, and the only thing telling them apart is the word that comes next.
nousOn.title: The we you will actually hear

examples.note: The written we, with its own ending.

theOnt.body: 4 verbs end ils on -ont, and you already had 3 of them. être at lesson 10 in A1, avoir at lesson 11 in A1, aller at lesson 5 in A2, and now faire. That is the whole list: no other verb in the language ends its ils form that way, so once you have these four you never have to wonder again. It is a closed set and this is the lesson that closes it.
theOnt.title: sont, ont, vont, font

examples.note: And the singular it belongs to, which sounds nothing like it.

theTes.body: 3 verbs in the language end vous on -tes. Every other verb you will ever meet ends it on -ez. You have had one of them since lesson 10 in A1: vous êtes. These are the other two, and they are the single most-corrected forms at this level, because every regular pattern you own says the vous form ends in -ez and these two do not. Say faisez to a French person and you will be understood and you will also be heard.
theTes.title: vous faites, vous dites

examples.note: Not disez, for the same reason.

theReach.body: French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. Do the shopping, make the bed, go swimming, take a trip, be sunny, cook, queue, pretend. Eight English verbs there and one French one, and the work that English gives to the verb is done in French by the noun after it. That is not a list of odd phrases: it is how the language divides up doing, and once you have seen it the thirty stop being thirty separate things to learn.
theReach.title: One verb, a dozen English ones

examples.note: And English has a whole verb here, cook.

theControl.body: lire keeps the endings you already have, and that is the whole reason it is here. vous lisez ends in -ez like every verb you have built since lesson 1 in A2, and ils lisent ends in -ent like every plural you have ever written. Put it beside faites and font and you can see what those two are doing wrong. Without it, irregular reads as a warning about the whole language; with it, it is a short list you can finish.
theControl.title: lire, beside the other two

examples.note: The ordinary ending, in the cell where the other two break.

notTheNouns.body: The word after faire belongs to somebody else's lesson. What you are learning is the verb in front. The weather words belong to lesson 14 in A1, and the shopping words to lesson 25 in A2, and you do not need either of them to use what is here: take each expression as one piece, the way you take a single word, and the noun inside it will make sense later when somebody teaches it to you properly.
notTheNouns.title: Which half is this lesson

examples.note: One piece. You are not learning the word for dishes.

whatFollows.body: Two words, twice, and two sentences that have nothing to do with each other. Nothing in il fait tells you which one you are in: a word for how it is outside means the weather, a word for a thing means somebody is doing it, and there is no third option. So you do not read il fait and then work it out. You wait for the next word. You met this shape at lesson 5 in A2 on a different pair of words, and it works the same way here.
whatFollows.title: Il fait beau. Il fait le lit.

examples.note: How it is outside. Nobody is doing it.

saySomething.body: dire takes a thing: bonjour, the truth, no. Il dit bonjour. Elle dit non. That is all it does in this lesson, and it is most of what it does in a day. There is a second way of using it, for reporting what somebody else said, and it needs machinery you do not have yet; you will not be shown it here and you will not need it. Compare lesson 7 in A2, which is the next lesson and is about three other verbs that will not come apart.
saySomething.title: dire, and one thing at a time

examples.note: A thing, straight after the verb.
And the plural, which is ordinary in shape.

nobodyDoingIt.body: Lesson 14 in A1 gave you this and gave it to you whole, as a phrase with nothing inside it. It is this verb. il fait is the same form as in Il fait le lit, and the difference is that here the il stands for no person at all: nobody is doing the weather. French needs a subject in every sentence, so it puts one there that means nothing. You now know the verb, which means you can hear what that sentence is made of.
nobodyDoingIt.title: il fait beau

examples.note: And the same two words with a person behind them.

sections.body: Every reference sheet before this one in the level lists ENDINGS, because every pattern before this one had them: lesson 1 in A2 holds the -er set in full, lesson 3 in A2 the -ir set, lesson 4 in A2 all three regular sets in one table, and lesson 5 in A2 lists forms because its three verbs have none. This lesson's forms take ten minutes and they are in the second table above. The first table is the part you will actually come back for. French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. That is a fact about vocabulary rather than about grammar, and there is no rule anywhere that will produce those thirty phrases for you: they are learned as pieces, the way single words are. Read the left-hand column if you are in a hurry. Once you have noticed that English is the language changing verb, the French stops looking like a list of exceptions and starts looking like one habit.
sections.title: Why this sheet lists expressions and not endings

sections.body: Three things leave this lesson. The first is French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. Every time you catch yourself hunting for a French verb, try faire and a noun first; you will be right more often than not. The second is that two lists closed here, and the third table above holds both: no other verb in the language ends vous on -tes, and no other verb ends ils on -ont, so those are two questions you never have to ask again. The third is smaller and it will come back: what comes next decides. Il fait beau and Il fait le lit are the same two words doing completely different jobs, and only the word after them settles it. You met that shape at lesson 5 in A2 on a different pair, and you will meet it again. Lesson 7 in A2 is next and it is three more verbs that will not come apart, so the ten minutes you spent on the forms here are about to pay for themselves.
sections.title: What carries forward

sections.say: The first one is the commonest mistake in the lesson and it is two letters long.

errors.why: Every pattern you own says the vous form ends in -ez, so the reflex is very strong and this is the form it breaks on. 3 verbs in the language end vous on -tes. Every other verb you will ever meet ends it on -ez.
errors.right: Saying « Vous faites le lit. ».
errors.wrong: Saying « Vous faisez le lit ».

errors.why: The plural is not built off the singular and it is not built off the nous form either. 4 verbs end ils on -ont, and you already had 3 of them. That is the whole list and nothing else in the language joins it.
errors.right: Saying « Ils font le lit. ».
errors.wrong: Saying « Ils faisent » or « Ils fontent ».

errors.why: French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. There is no verb waiting for either of those, and the half-second you spend looking for one is the half-second the sentence dies in.
errors.right: Saying « faire la cuisine » and « faire la queue ».
errors.wrong: Looking for a French verb meaning to cook, or to queue.

sections.say: One screen before the exam, so you know what you are walking into.
sections.body: You have three more verbs that will not come apart, and only three cells across all of them are actually strange. That was the short half. The long half is that one of those three verbs turns up everywhere: French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. You have also finished two lists that were open before you started, because the verbs that end vous on -tes and the ones that end ils on -ont are both closed sets and this lesson supplied the last of each. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. The drill is the teaching, not the punishment.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Four things, and the biggest of them is not a form at all.
sections.body: You can build three more verbs that will not come apart, and you found that only three cells across the eighteen are actually strange. Two lists closed while you did it: the verbs that end vous on -tes and the ones that end ils on -ont are both finished, and you will never have to wonder about either again. One verb, and 30 everyday things you could not say before. French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time. And you know what the lesson 14 in A1 weather phrases were made of all along, which is this verb with nobody behind it.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: French keeps faire where English reaches for a different verb every time.
3 verbs in the language end vous on -tes. Every other verb you will ever meet ends it on -ez.
4 verbs end ils on -ont, and you already had 3 of them.
lire keeps the endings you already have, and that is the whole reason it is here.

errorTriggers.description: Puts -ez on the two verbs that refuse it: faisez, disez. Every regular pattern the learner owns says vous ends in -ez, so the reflex is strong and this is where it breaks.
Goes looking for a French verb that does not exist, because English has one: a verb for cook, for queue, for pack. The sentence stops before the noun arrives.
Picks the wrong expression for the situation by translating the English noun rather than knowing the phrase: faire le ménage where the shopping was meant.
Runs the strangeness of faire and dire onto lire, or onto every verb in sight: lisez becomes lites, and irregular turns into a warning about the whole language.
Builds the ils form off some other form of the verb: faisent, fontent. The plural of faire shares no letters at all with its own singular.

recorded.desc: A LANGUAGE EXCHANGE, WEEK THREE, AND THE OTHER PERSON IS PLEASED TO BE ASKING. HER LINE « Raconte-moi ta matinée. » IS A GENUINE INVITATION and should sound like somebody settling in to listen. She is not testing him. THE LEARNER'S TWO LINES ARE THE TAKES THAT HAVE TO BE RIGHT. « Je lève à sept heures. » IS SAID FLUENTLY AND WITH CONFIDENCE. This is the single most important instruction in the take: it is a complete, well-formed French sentence and he believes he has said what he meant. Any hesitation on it teaches that the error is audible, and the whole point of the scene is that it is not. THE SECOND LINE « Et après, je... je douche... » IS WHERE IT BREAKS. The two false starts are real pauses, and the take ends unresolved rather than tailing off gently: he has run out of sentence and stopped. NOBODY CORRECTS HIM AND NOBODY REACTS. There is no third voice and no sound of patience. The scene works because nothing happened that anyone could point at.
clipIds: Je me lève à sept heures.

recorded.desc: THREE LINES, ONE TAKE, ORDINARY PACE: « Je m'appelle Sophie. » « s'appeler » « se dépêcher » then « Tu te dépêches. » THE FIRST LINE MUST SOUND COMPLETELY UNREMARKABLE. It is the sentence the learner has said a hundred times and the point of the card is that nothing about it ever sounded special. DO NOT LEAN ON THE m'. A reading that marks it teaches that the learner should have noticed it, and the card's claim is that there was nothing to notice.

THE SIX CELLS, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TAKE IN THE LESSON. Six lines in this order: « Je me lave. » « Tu te laves. » « Il se lave. » « Nous nous lavons. » « Vous vous lavez. » « Ils se lavent. » THE VERB MUST BE IDENTICAL IN FOUR OF THE SIX. Lines one, two, three and six all end on the same single syllable, and line three and line six are identical from start to finish. Not similar: identical. The learner is being taught that the little word is the only thing carrying the person, and any difference in the verb teaches the opposite. THE DOUBLED WORDS IN LINES FOUR AND FIVE MUST NOT BE RUN TOGETHER. « Nous nous » is two words with a real boundary between them, said at ordinary pace and without emphasis on either. A reading that elides them into one sound makes the doubling inaudible, which is the thing learners already do not believe. RECORD ALL SIX AS ONE CONTINUOUS TAKE. Six separate recordings are six performances.

THREE LINES, ONE TAKE: « Nous nous lavons. » « Vous vous lavez. » « Nous nous levons tard le dimanche. » THE DOUBLED WORD IS THE WHOLE POINT AND IT MUST BE CLEARLY TWO WORDS. There is a real, unhurried boundary between them in all three lines. NEITHER OF THE TWO MAY BE STRESSED. They are the same word twice and stressing one to distinguish them teaches a difference that does not exist in speech.
clipIds: Nous nous levons tard le dimanche.

recorded.desc: THE ONE CONTRAST IN THIS LESSON THE EAR CAN SETTLE, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, FOUR LINES: « Je lave la voiture. » « Je me lave. » « Il se lave. » « Ils se lavent. » THE FIRST TWO ARE THE PAIR AND THEY DIFFER BY A WHOLE SYLLABLE. Read them at the same pace so the extra syllable is the only difference; slowing the second one hands the learner the answer for the wrong reason. LINES THREE AND FOUR ARE THE OPPOSITE INSTRUCTION AND THEY ARE IN THE SAME TAKE DELIBERATELY. They must be completely identical: same speed, same weight, same everything. The mission asks the learner to hear a difference in the first pair and no difference at all in the second, and it only works if one voice does both in one sitting.

FOUR LINES, ONE TAKE, PLAINLY: « Je m'appelle Sophie. » « Tu te dépêches. » « Nous nous dépêchons. » « se souvenir » NONE OF THESE IS AN ERROR AND NONE IS A CONTRAST. They are four ordinary sentences and the reading should carry no teaching intent at all. THE LITTLE WORD MUST NOT BE MARKED IN ANY OF THEM. The card's claim is that it is there and means nothing, and a reading that points at it argues the opposite.

THREE LINES, ONE TAKE: « Je m'habille vite. » « Ils s'habillent vite. » « Je me douche avant de m'habiller. » THE ELISION IS NOT A PAUSE. « m'habille » is one smooth run and the apostrophe is silent; a reading that breaks at it teaches a boundary that is not there. THE h IS SILENT IN ALL THREE. Nothing is aspirated and nothing is caught in the throat. LINES ONE AND TWO ARE A PAIR and the only difference is the first word and the vowel of the little word. Read them at the same pace.
clipIds: Je me douche avant de m'habiller.

recorded.desc: THE STEM CHANGE, ONE TAKE, FOUR LINES: « Je me lève à sept heures. » « Je me lève tôt. » « Nous nous levons tôt. » « Je me lave. » LINES TWO AND THREE ARE THE CONTRAST AND THE VOWEL IS THE ONLY THING BEING COMPARED. The è in « lève » is open and the e in « levons » is the quiet one; both must be clearly said and neither exaggerated. THE LITTLE WORD MUST SOUND THE SAME IN ALL FOUR. That is the card's claim: the vowel moved and the little word did not notice. Any variation in « me » undoes the mission. LINE FOUR IS THERE TO SHOW A VERB WHERE NOTHING MOVES and should sound entirely ordinary.
clipIds: Je me lève à sept heures.

recorded.desc: THE NEGATIVE, ONE TAKE, FOUR LINES: « Je me lave. » « Je ne me lave pas. » « Il ne se lave pas. » « Tu ne te laves pas. » NOT A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. All four are correct French. THE ne MUST BE AUDIBLE AND UNSTRESSED IN ALL THREE NEGATIVES. It is the word whose POSITION the whole mission is about, so it cannot be swallowed the way ordinary speech swallows it; and it cannot be leaned on either, because the learner would then hear it as the important word rather than as a word in a particular place. THERE IS NO PAUSE BETWEEN ne AND THE LITTLE WORD. « ne me » is one run. A break there is exactly the reading that makes the error sound plausible.

THE AUDIO STEP OF THE TRAP, AND IT IS A WRONG-THEN-RIGHT TAKE. Four lines, one take, in this order: « Je me ne lave pas. » then « Je ne me lave pas. », then « Il ne se lave pas. » then « Je lave la voiture. » READ THE FIRST LINE PLAINLY AND AT ORDINARY PACE rather than comically or hesitantly. It is perfectly pronounceable and it is exactly what a careful learner produces from the rule they were given; a reading that signals the error teaches that the error is audible when it is not. DO NOT SEPARATE THE FIRST TWO LINES WITH A LONG PAUSE. The pair is the teaching and it works when the two sit against each other. THE FOURTH LINE HAS NO LITTLE WORD AT ALL and is there to show the wrap doing its ordinary job. Nothing about it should sound like a comparison.

THE DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to rec-a2-22-persons: there the learner is comparing and here they are spelling, and a paired reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. SIX OF THE TWELVE ARE THE SAME VERB AND FOUR OF THOSE END ON THE SAME SYLLABLE. That is correct and must not be corrected for. The learner works out which cell is meant from the two words in front of the verb. THE FIRST TWO WORDS ARE WHERE THE INFORMATION IS. « Je me », « Tu te », « Il se », « Nous nous », « Vous vous », « Ils se »: these must be clearly and evenly said, because they are the only thing distinguishing four of the six lines. THE DOUBLED PAIRS ARE TWO WORDS. « Nous nous » and « Vous vous » each need a real boundary, at ordinary pace, or the learner writes one word. SAY IT THE WAY SOMEBODY WOULD SAY IT, at the pace of somebody dictating an address to a friend.

THE CONVERSATION, HER LINES ONLY, ONE TAKE, AS ONE CONTINUOUS EXCHANGE RATHER THAN AS FIVE SEPARATE PROMPTS. She is the same binôme from the opening scene, a week later, and this time the exchange works. EVERY QUESTION IS ASKED WITHOUT INVERSION and should sound completely ordinary: « Tu te couches tard, toi ? » is a statement with a question mark on it, which is what people say. HER OWN LINES CARRY THE LITTLE WORD THREE TIMES and none of them may be marked or slowed. She is using the structure, not demonstrating it. THERE IS NO PAUSE INSIDE « te réveilles » OR « se lève ». The little word and the verb are one run.
clipIds: Raconte-moi ta matinée. Tu te réveilles à quelle heure ?
Ta famille se lève en même temps que toi ?
Et tes collègues, ils ont le temps le matin ?

lessons.intro: About half the verbs in a French day arrive with a small word in front of them, and lesson 28 in A1 asked you to store it with the verb. That was the right thing to do while you only needed three of them. It is not a fixed piece of the verb: it is the person you have just named, said again, and it changes every time they do. This is all six of them, the one place saying no goes wrong, and the three verbs that carry it and mean nothing by it.

doubled.body: Four of the six little words are different from the person in front of them and two are identical. Nous nous levons has the same word twice doing two different jobs, and lesson 28 in A1 already put that exact sentence on a screen. It looks like a mistake in a way the others do not, and it is the form learners quietly drop.
doubled.title: nous nous, and vous vous, are not typos

theWrap.body: Lesson 21 in A1 gave you two words either side of the verb and lesson 15 in A2 said which verb: « Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. » lesson 16 in A2 and lesson 18 in A2 both quote that line and it has not changed. Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. So the first half goes in front of the little word, not behind it.
theWrap.title: Both little words go inside it

eachOther.body: Ils se parlent can mean they talk to each other rather than to themselves, and nothing in the spelling tells you which. It is worth recognising so it does not read as an error, and it is not part of what you are asked to produce. Lesson 20 in A2 and lesson 22 in A2 are where it gets its own treatment.
eachOther.title: A third thing the same word can mean

extraWord.body: About half the verbs in a day carry a second little word between the person and the verb: je ME lave, tu TE laves, il SE lave. Lesson 28 in A1 asked you to store it with the verb, which was the right thing to do while you only needed three of them. It is not a fixed piece of the verb. It is the person you already named, said a second time, and that is why it changes every time they do.
extraWord.title: It is the subject again, in a different shape

secondJob.body: These same little words do a second job later, standing in for a thing rather than pointing back at the subject. Two lessons cover that and this one does not touch it. Lesson 21 in A2 and lesson 22 in A2 are where that happens. Everything on these screens points back at the person doing it, and that is the only use you need today.
secondJob.title: The same words come back doing something else

samePerson.body: The first one says who is doing it and the second says who it is being done to, and in these sentences those are the same person. That is the whole idea. Je lave la voiture washes something else and names it; je me lave has nothing to name, because the answer is already at the front of the sentence.
samePerson.title: Two words, one person, one job each

vowelMoves.body: The spelling changes so the sound does not. The vowel moves for the reason lesson 2 in A2 gave, in the four cells where the ending goes silent. That is a different rule running at the same time as this one, and it is not part of carrying a pronoun. Se lever is doing both at once: the little word changes for the person, and the vowel in the middle opens in the four people where the ending makes no sound. Se laver does neither, which is why the table uses it.
vowelMoves.title: A second rule, running at the same time

presentOnly.body: In the present nothing on the end of the verb knows who the subject is. Only the extra word changes. Every one of these has a past, and it does something no other verb does. That is the next lesson.
presentOnly.title: Nothing on the end knows who you are

notAboutSelf.body: S'appeler, se souvenir and se dépêcher carry the little word and mean nothing reflexive by it. Nobody hurries themselves. The word is simply part of how the verb is built, and it still changes for the person, which is the only thing you have to get right. Lesson 1 in Sounds taught « Je m'appelle » in the first lesson in the app, so you have been saying one of these all along.
notAboutSelf.title: Some of them point at nothing at all

drills.coach: Say the person out loud before you reach for the middle word, and the middle word is that person in another shape. Se is not a default: it belongs to il, elle and ils.

drills.q: Vous ___ lavez. Which one?
drills.why: Vous, identical to the person in front of it. It is one of the two that look like typos and it is not one.

drills.coach: Each pair is one verb, twice. The one with the little word has nothing after the verb because there is nothing left to name; the one without it names something. Dropping it leaves a verb that means doing the thing to something else, and a listener will wait for you to say what.
drills.title: With it and without it

drills.q: You meant to say you get up at seven. Which is it?
drills.why: The second one is correct French about lifting something, which is why nobody corrects it and why the sentence stalls instead.

drills.title: One more

drills.coach: Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. Two words changed for the person here rather than one, so both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. Ne in front of the little word, pas straight after the verb.
drills.title: Both of them inside

drills.q: Make « Il se lave. » negative.
drills.why: Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap.
drills.title: One more

sections.body: The pronoun changes with the subject, because it is the subject. It is the person you have already named, said again in the shape French uses when they are on the receiving end. Four of the six are a different word from the person and two are identical, which is why nous nous and vous vous look like mistakes and are not.
sections.title: The rule, in one line

sections.body: Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. Je me lave becomes Je ne me lave pas. Ne in front of the little word, pas straight after the verb, and never between the two of them.
sections.title: Saying no

sections.body: The spelling changes so the sound does not. The vowel in je me lève opens for a reason lesson 2 in A2 gave you, in the four people where the ending makes no sound, and it has nothing to do with the little word. And the little word loses its e in front of a vowel, which is the elision rule you already have: je m'habille, ils s'habillent.
sections.title: Two things that are not this rule

sections.body: In the present nothing on the end of the verb knows who the subject is. Only the extra word changes. Every one of these has a past, and it does something no other verb does. That is the next lesson. And the same five words do a second job standing in for a thing rather than pointing back at the person, which is lesson 21 in A2 and lesson 22 in A2.

sections.say: Three cards, none of which you have to do anything with today. They are here so that meeting one does not look like an error.

cards.body: In the present nothing on the end of the verb knows who the subject is. Only the extra word changes. Every one of these has a past, and it does something no other verb does. That is the next lesson.

cards.fr: me · te · se · nous · vous

rule.body: Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. Here two words changed for the person, not one: the verb and the little word in front of it. Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap.
rule.title: Both of them changed, so both of them are inside

cards.fr: Je me ne lave pas.
cards.ipa: /ʒə mə nə lav pa/
cards.tip: Ne straight in front of the verb that changed, which is exactly what the rule says if lave is the verb. This is the error, and it is a careful learner's error rather than a careless one.
cards.promptLabel: reading the rule too literally gives
cards.promptSound: Je me ne lave pas.

cards.fr: Je ne me lave pas.
cards.ipa: /ʒə nə mə lav pa/
cards.tip: Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. Ne goes in front of the whole cluster.
cards.promptLabel: and the little word is part of the verb now
cards.promptSound: Je ne me lave pas.

cards.fr: Il ne se lave pas.
cards.ipa: /il nə sə lav pa/
cards.tip: Se is inside the wrap for the same reason me was. Nothing about the position depends on which person you are in.
cards.promptSound: Il ne se lave pas.

cards.fr: Je lave la voiture.
cards.ipa: /ʒə lav la vwa.tyʁ/
cards.tip: When there is nothing between the person and the verb, the wrap has one word to go round and it goes round it. Je ne lave pas la voiture. Nothing new happens.
cards.promptLabel: and with no little word at all
cards.promptSound: Je lave la voiture.

sections.title: What Goes Wrong

errors.why: Dropping it leaves a verb that means doing the thing to something else, and a listener will wait for you to say what. It survives because it is correct French about something else.
errors.right: Je me lève à sept heures.
errors.wrong: Je lève à sept heures.

errors.why: The wrap went round the verb and left the little word outside it. Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. This is what the inherited rule produces when it is read at its word.
errors.right: Je ne me lave pas.
errors.wrong: Je me ne lave pas.

errors.why: The doubled word looked like a mistake, so it was corrected out. It is the form learners drop most, and the sentence that is left means getting something else up.
errors.right: Nous nous levons tôt.
errors.wrong: Nous levons tôt.

errors.why: Se is not the default and it is not a particle. It belongs to il, elle and ils. The pronoun changes with the subject, because it is the subject.
errors.right: Vous vous lavez.
errors.wrong: Vous se lavez.

sections.setting: The same language exchange, a week later, and this time the question does not stop the sentence. Every answer is about a morning and every one of them carries the little word.

cards.say: Je me lave. Je lave la voiture.
cards.back: Je lave la voiture washes something and names it. Je me lave has nothing left to name, because the answer is already the first word of the sentence.
cards.front: Why is there a little word in je me lave and not in je lave la voiture?

cards.say: Il se lave.
cards.back: The pronoun changes with the subject, because it is the subject.
cards.front: How do you pick which little word?

cards.say: Nous nous levons tôt.
cards.back: No. The first says who and the second says who it is happening to, and they are the same people. Lesson 28 in A1 already put that sentence on a screen.
cards.front: Nous nous levons. Is that a typo?

cards.say: Je ne me lave pas.
cards.back: Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. Ne in front of the little word, pas straight after the verb.

cards.say: Je m'appelle Sophie.
cards.back: It is the same little word, elided because a vowel follows. This verb has no reflexive meaning at all and carries it anyway.
cards.front: Je m'appelle. What is the m doing?

cards.say: Je me lève tôt.
cards.back: The spelling changes so the sound does not. That is lesson 2's rule about the vowel and it has nothing to do with the little word.
cards.front: Je me lève. Why is there an accent that se laver does not have?

cards.say: Il se lave. Ils se lavent.
cards.back: Nothing. They are the same sounds in the same order. Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person.
cards.front: Il se lave against ils se lavent. What can you hear?

sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Six rounds of five. Most of it is typed, because the little word is something you produce rather than something you recognise.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Five on picking it off the person.
rounds.label: Which little word

questions.q: Je ___ lave. Type the missing word.
questions.why: Je takes me. Say the person out loud first and the little word is that person in another shape.
accept: me

questions.q: Tu ___ laves. Type the missing word.
questions.why: Tu takes te. It is the same person in the shape French uses when they are on the receiving end.
accept: te

questions.q: Nous ___ lavons. Type the missing word.
questions.why: Nous, written twice. It looks like a mistake and it is the form learners drop most.
accept: nous

questions.q: Vous ___ levez tôt. Which one?
questions.why: Vous, and it is identical to the person in front of it, which is the other of the two that look like typos.

questions.q: Ils ___ lavent. Which one?
questions.why: Se belongs to il, elle, ils and elles. It is not a default that the others replace.

rounds.say: Five on what the little word is doing.
rounds.label: Why it is there

questions.q: Je lave la voiture and Je me lave. What is the difference?
questions.why: The little word is where the object would have been. There is nothing left to name because the answer is already the first word of the sentence.
opts: The first names what is being washed and the second does not need to
The second is in the past

questions.q: One word is missing. Type the sentence correctly: « Je lève à sept heures. »
questions.why: Dropping it leaves a verb that means doing the thing to something else, and a listener will wait for you to say what. The sentence as written is correct French about lifting something.
accept: Je me lève à sept heures.

questions.q: Type the French for: she goes to bed late. Use se coucher.
questions.why: Elle takes se, and the ending is the one every verb in this group takes. The verb was never in the table and nothing about it had to be learned separately.
accept: Elle se couche tard.

questions.q: Nobody hurries themselves. So why does se dépêcher carry the little word?
questions.why: Some of these point at nothing at all. The word is obligatory and it still changes for the person, which is the only part you have to get right.
opts: Because hurrying is done to yourself
It is optional on this verb
Because it is a polite form
It is simply part of how the verb is built

questions.q: Type the French for: you are hurrying. Speaking to one friend.
questions.why: Tu te dépêches. No reflexive meaning, and the little word moves for the person anyway.
accept: Tu te dépêches.

rounds.say: Five on where the first half goes.
rounds.label: Saying no

questions.q: Fix the word order: « Je me ne lave pas. »
questions.why: Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap. Ne goes in front of the whole cluster, not in front of the verb alone.
accept: Je ne me lave pas.

questions.q: Fix the word order: « Il se ne lave pas. »
questions.why: Se is inside the wrap for the same reason me was. Nothing about the position depends on the person.
accept: Il ne se lave pas.

questions.q: Make it negative: « Tu te laves. »
questions.why: Ne in front of te, pas straight after laves. Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap.
accept: Tu ne te laves pas.

questions.q: Which line quotes the rule these four lessons share?
questions.why: Lesson 15 in A2 said it, lesson 16 in A2 quoted it and lesson 18 in A2 quoted it again. This lesson adds one sentence to it rather than replacing it: Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap.
opts: Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning.
Put ne in front of the verb and pas after it.
The negative goes at the end of the sentence.
Ne and pas move together as one unit.

questions.q: Make it negative: « Nous nous lavons. »
questions.why: Both little words stay where they are and the wrap goes round the pair of them.
accept: Nous ne nous lavons pas.

rounds.say: Five on verbs the table never used.
rounds.label: Verbs you were not shown

questions.q: Type the French for: we rest in the evening. Use se reposer.
questions.why: The doubled shape on a verb you have not conjugated once. Any verb that arrives with se in front of it works this way.
accept: Nous nous reposons le soir.

questions.q: Type the French for: I get dressed quickly. Use s’habiller.
questions.why: Me, because the person is je, and then the e goes because a vowel follows. Two rules you already had.
accept: Je m'habille vite.

questions.q: Ils ___ habillent vite. Which one?
questions.why: Se, elided to s because a vowel follows. The apostrophe is joining two words that would otherwise collide and it does nothing else.

questions.q: Type the French for: you wake up late. Speaking to one friend, using se réveiller.
questions.why: Tu takes te, and the ending is the ordinary one. The verb was not in the table.
accept: Tu te réveilles tard.

questions.q: Vous ___ couchez tôt. Which one?
questions.why: Vous, doubled, on a verb the table never carried. The rule is the same one every time.

rounds.say: Five on the one audible difference, and on the four that are not.
rounds.label: What you can hear

questions.q: Which one did you hear?
questions.why: One is three syllables and the other is two. This is the only difference in the lesson you can hear, and it is the one that changes what the sentence is about.

questions.q: And this one?
questions.why: Two syllables rather than three. The little word is the syllable that is missing, and it is the only thing in this lesson the ear can settle.

questions.q: Il se lave and Ils se lavent. What can you hear?
questions.why: Il and ils are one sound, se is se, and lave and lavent are one sound. Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person.

questions.q: Tap the letters in lavent that make no sound.
questions.why: The whole -ent is silent, which is why this form and the il form are one sound. Four of the six forms sound the same, so the pronoun carries the person.

questions.q: You hear [eel suh LAHV] and the sentence is about several people. Write it.
questions.why: Nothing in the sound tells you it is plural. Only the writing does, and only on the first word and the ending.
accept: Ils se lavent.

rounds.say: Five last ones, mixed.
rounds.label: All of it

questions.q: Type the French for: we get up early. Use se lever.
questions.why: The little word is doubled and the vowel does NOT move here, because the ending is a syllable of its own. The spelling changes so the sound does not.
accept: Nous nous levons tôt.

questions.q: Je me lève has an accent and je me lave does not. Why?
questions.why: The vowel moves for the reason lesson 2 in A2 gave, in the four cells where the ending goes silent. That is a different rule running at the same time as this one, and it is not part of carrying a pronoun.
opts: Because lever is irregular in every person
Because it is a different little word
The vowel opens when the ending makes no sound, which is a rule about the verb

questions.q: One word is wrong. Fix it: « Vous se lavez. »
questions.why: Se is not a default. It belongs to il, elle and ils, and vous takes vous.
accept: Vous vous lavez.

questions.q: Type the French for: he does not wash.
questions.why: Ne in front of se, pas straight after lave. Both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap.
accept: Il ne se lave pas.

questions.q: Which of these carries the little word and means nothing reflexive by it?
questions.why: Se laver and se lever both point back at the person. S’appeler does not point at anything, and the little word is obligatory on it anyway.
opts: se laver, because washing is done to yourself
s'appeler, because nobody calls themselves anything
se lever, because getting up is done to yourself

sections.body: The pronoun changes with the subject, because it is the subject. Lesson 28 in A1 gave you these verbs and three of the six people to use them with, and said the rest was a whole band away. This is the rest. Nothing about the endings changes: lesson 1 in A2 still gives you every one of them.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Je lave la voiture washes something and names it. Je me lave has nothing left to name, because the answer is already the first word of the sentence.
Four of the six little words are different from the person in front of them and two are identical. nous nous and vous vous are not typos.
Wrap the verb that changed, not the one carrying the meaning. Here two words changed for the person rather than one, so both words changed for the subject, so both go inside the wrap.
Some of them mean nothing reflexive at all. Nobody hurries themselves, and nobody calls themselves anything, and the little word is obligatory on both.
The spelling changes so the sound does not. The vowel in se lève moves for a reason that has nothing to do with the little word, and lesson 2 in A2 already gave you it.

Any verb that arrives with se in front of it works this way, so the six the table never showed you cost nothing extra. In the present nothing on the end of the verb knows who the subject is. Only the extra word changes.

errorTriggers.description: Reaches for se whatever the person is, because se is the form the verb is listed under and it looks like the default. « Vous se lavez. »

Drops the little word altogether, which leaves a complete French sentence about doing the thing to something else. « Je lève à sept heures. » lesson 28 in A1 records the same error and this lesson opens on it.
Puts ne between the little word and the verb, which is what lesson 15 in A2's rule produces when it is read at its word. « Je me ne lave pas. »

grammarAssumed: The present of regular -er verbs, as a stem plus six endings, introduced in a2.01
That -e, -es and -ent are silent and that the subject pronoun carries the person, introduced in a2.01
The stem-vowel change in the four cells where the ending goes silent, introduced in a2.09
Reflexive verbs as whole lexical items in je, tu and il, introduced in a1.25
The daily-routine vocabulary and the parts of the day, introduced in a1.25
Standard negation with ne … pas around a finite verb, introduced in a1.18
That ne … pas encloses the verb that changed rather than the one carrying the meaning, introduced in a2.19 and extended in a2.05 and a2.21
The elision of a preverbal clitic before a vowel or mute h, introduced in sons.07
grammarIntroduced: The reflexive clitic paradigm in all six persons, as the subject pronoun in its object series rather than as a fixed particle
That the clitic is syntactically part of the verbal complex and is enclosed by ne … pas along with the finite verb, extending a1.18 and a2.19 to a preverbal clitic
That first and second person plural clitics are homophonous and homographic with their subject pronouns, which is orthographically indistinguishable from a dittography
Inherently pronominal verbs, where the clitic is lexically selected and carries no reflexive semantics: s'appeler, se souvenir, se dépêcher
The reflexive as a valency reduction, contrasted with the transitive use of the same verb: je lave la voiture against je me lave
Clitic elision before a vowel or mute h, extending sons.07 from determiners to the clitic series
That the clitic paradigm generalises without exception, so any verb listed with se is derivable from the six forms
That the present tense carries no participial agreement, stated explicitly as the clean background a2.23 changes
The reciprocal reading of the same forms, for RECEPTION ONLY and produced nowhere, and owned by no unit at any level
The direct and indirect object series proper, named and reserved for a2.06 and a2.24, and the compound past reserved for a2.23

recorded.desc: THE EIGHTEEN CELLS, THREE TAKES, ONE PER VERB, EACH VERB'S SIX IN ONE BREATH GROUP. Within the first three of EACH verb the verb must be acoustically identical: « Je prends la clé. » « Tu prends la clé. » « Il prend la clé. » A reader who knows the third is spelled differently will shorten the vowel or put a fraction of a d on it, and either instinct destroys the screen that asks the learner to fail to hear a difference. If a listener with their eyes shut can say which of the three they just heard, the take is unusable. In the plural the opposite is required and it is the whole lesson: the n at the end of « Ils prennent » must be clean, audible and unhurried, and it must be plainly a different sound from the nasal vowel that ends « Il prend ». Same for the t of « Ils mettent » and « Ils battent ». AND la clé MUST SOUND IDENTICAL IN ALL TWELVE prendre AND mettre LINES. It is the control: the learner is being shown that only the middle of the sentence moves.

THE PAIR THE LESSON TURNS ON, AS ONE TAKE, IN THIS ORDER: « Nous prenons la clé. » then « Ils prennent la clé. » then « Nous mettons la clé. » then « Ils mettent la clé. » The first two are a minimal pair in the strict sense and must be read as one: same speed, same pitch, same length, and the ONLY difference audible anywhere in the line is where the verb finishes. Read them as two separate sentences and the learner hears two performances instead of one contrast. The second pair is the control and must sound duller than the first: nothing surprising is happening in it and the reading should not pretend otherwise.

THE FAMILY, AS THREE ROWS OF THREE. « je prends · j'apprends · je comprends », then the nous row, then the ils row, and each row is ONE breath group with the smallest possible gap between the three verbs. This is the take that does the teaching on the identity screen: the learner has to hear that the end of all three words is the same sound, arriving three times. Any pause between them lets the ear treat them as three separate words rather than one word wearing three fronts. Do not stress the fronts. They are the part that does not matter.

THE mettre COMPOUNDS, AND ONE PAIR MATTERS MORE THAN THE REST. « Je mets la clé. » then « Je remets la clé. » must be one take, same speed, same everything, so that the two syllables of difference are the only thing in the line that moved. The learner is being shown that a compound is its base verb with something on the front, and this is the only place in the lesson where the two sentences are otherwise identical word for word.

THE SMALL ONE. « battre », « combattre », then « Je bats Paul. » « Il bat Paul. » « Nous battons Paul. » « Ils battent Paul. » Brisk and unremarkable, and that is a direction rather than an accident: battre gets two missions in this lesson because it earns two, and a reading that gives it the weight of the other two would be arguing with the design. The t at the end of « Ils battent » is the one thing that has to be clean, because it is the audible plural.

THE SIX LINES FOR THE LISTENING SCREEN, WITH AUDIO BEFORE TEXT, IN SINGULAR-PLURAL PAIRS: prendre, then mettre, then battre. Each pair is one take. The instruction is the opposite of the grid take and it is worth stating plainly: here the difference must be as clear as the language allows, because the learner is being asked to hear it. Land on the final consonant of each plural. Do not add one to the singular.

THE BOUNDARY. « il vend » then « il prend », then « vendre » then « prendre », then « Nous prenons la clé. » The first pair is the point: the two singular forms rhyme exactly, which is why the mistake is so easy to make, and the reading must let them rhyme rather than helping the learner tell them apart. The difference does not arrive until the plural, and the last clip is where it arrives.

THE THREE FAMILY LISTS, READ AS LISTS: « apprendre, comprendre, surprendre », « permettre, promettre, remettre », « combattre, débattre, abattre ». Even pace, even weight, no rising list intonation that would make the last item sound like a conclusion. Nine words in three groups, and the value of the take is that all nine sound like ordinary vocabulary rather than like a rule being announced.

THE FOUR PUBLISHED ROWS, READ AS WHAT THEY ARE: sentences written for other lessons that happen to prove this one. Ordinary pace, no teaching emphasis anywhere, and in particular no weight on the verb. The whole value of the screen is that nobody was thinking about prendre or mettre when these were written.
clipIds: J'apprends le français depuis le printemps.
Elle met sa veste et ferme la porte.
Tu mets du beurre sur tout, toujours.

recorded.desc: THE LAST MISSION BEFORE THE EXAM, AND IT IS TWO WORDS. « reprendre » and « admettre », each said once, plainly, with no example sentence and no conjugated form after them. That restraint is the mission: the learner is about to be asked to build four forms of these two and nothing in the audio may give one away. Do not read them slowly, do not separate the front from the rest, and do not follow either with a pause that invites the learner to expect more.

THE BREAK CARD. « je prends » then « j'apprends », as one take, back to back, with the smallest gap the recording allows. They must sound like the same word twice with something added at the front the second time, because that is what they are. Any pause, any change of pitch, any extra weight on the ap and the learner hears two words instead of one.

THE CLIMBING GYM. She is friendly, slightly out of breath, unhurried and completely uninterested in teaching anybody French. « Tu apprends le français ici ? » is casual and quick, the way you ask somebody something while pulling a shoe off. The English line afterwards is the important one and it must not sound like a defeat or a rebuke: she switches language without thinking about it, cheerfully, because it is the shortest route to a conversation. That is exactly what makes it expensive, and nothing in the delivery should point at it.

lessons.intro: Three verbs go in and a dozen come out. Each of these is the head of a family, and every verb in the family takes its endings exactly, without a single new form to learn. The last screen before the exam hands you a verb this lesson never shows you and asks for it anyway.

theEar.body: The singular ends on a nasal vowel and the plural ends on an n, and those are two completely different sounds. That makes this one of the few plurals in French you can hear without being told. Lesson 3 in A2 had the same gift on a different verb, where the plural grew a whole syllable in the middle. mettre and battre give you the same thing with a t: met has nothing at the end and mettent finishes on a hard consonant. Three verbs, three audible plurals, and it is the only place in this lesson the ear is on your side.
theEar.title: prend against prennent

examples.note: Ends on an n, and nothing else about the line moved.

theFrame.body: Every prendre sentence and every mettre sentence on these screens ends in la clé. That is deliberate and it is doing as much teaching as the verbs are: if the back of the sentence never moves, everything you notice is happening to the verb. Read down a column and the only thing changing is the middle. battre cannot join in, because you do not beat a key, and it takes Paul instead. That is the one place the pattern breaks and it breaks for a reason you can see.
theFrame.title: Why every sentence ends the same way

notVendre.body: Lesson 4 named these three and would not build them, because the model it taught you would have produced a form nobody says. This is the lesson it was waiting for. prendre ends in -re and it is not one of those verbs. Run the regular pattern on it and the plural comes out with a d in it, which is a sound no French speaker makes in this word. Look at prenons beside the regular plural and the difference is a whole letter that has left the building. This is the second time you have been shown a verb that looks like a group it is not in, and it will not be the last.
notVendre.title: What lesson 4 in A2 would not do

theFamily.body: Three verbs to learn, and 12 you can build. Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. A verb with something stuck on the front of it takes every ending the verb underneath it takes, without exception and without a single new form to learn. apprendre, comprendre, surprendre all run on prendre; permettre, promettre, remettre all run on mettre. That is the largest return on memorisation anywhere in this level, and it is the reason the last four lessons were worth the time.

theIdioms.body: prendre turns up in a great many set phrases where it has stopped meaning take at all, and English does not use take in any of them. Those belong to two later units and they are the whole opening of both: lesson 26 for the ones about getting somewhere and lesson 24 for the ones about ordering something. Nothing in this lesson teaches them, on purpose. What this lesson gives you is the six forms, which is what you will need on the day either of those arrives.
theIdioms.title: Where the fixed expressions are taught

examples.note: The plain meaning, which is the one being built here.

theControl.body: mettre and battre change once and stop. prendre changes twice. Both of them lose a t in the singular and get it back for the whole plural: mets, then mettons, mettez, mettent, and not one of those three is different from the others. That is worth noticing because it is what prendre does NOT do, and reading the two side by side is the fastest way to see what makes prendre the difficult one.
theControl.title: mettre and battre change once

examples.note: Two, and they stay for all three.
battre does the same thing on the same cell.

threeStems.body: prend- pren- prenn- for prendre. met- mett- for mettre and bat- batt- for battre. prendre keeps 3 stems where the other two keep 2. In the singular the d is written and never said, so prends, prends and prend are one sound. For nous and vous the d goes and an ordinary ending arrives. For ils a second n turns up. Three shapes in six cells is more than any verb you have met so far, and it is the only genuinely hard thing here.
threeStems.title: Where prendre keeps changing

examples.note: The d is there and you do not say it.
The d has gone and there is one n.

battreSmall.body: It is here because it finishes the set and because combattre is worth recognising, and it is not here in the same quantity as the other two. There is no sentence anywhere in this course that puts battre into one of its six forms, and there are two hundred and thirty-four holding a form of prendre. Learn its shape from mettre, which it copies exactly, keep combattre for recognition, and spend the time you saved on the first two. A course that gave all three equal weight would be teaching you that frequency does not matter.
battreSmall.title: battre is not the same size as the other two

examples.note: The naming form, and it did not exist until this lesson.
Two t in the plural, exactly like mettre.

theDoubling.body: One n for nous, two for ils. Lesson 2 doubled the l of appeler where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem must end in one. Lesson 2 in A2 said it first, about a different verb: The spelling changes so the sound does not. When the ending makes no sound, the stem is the last thing anybody hears, so there has to be something left in it to hear. prenons does not need a second n because the -ons is doing the sounding. prennent does, because the -ent is doing nothing at all. Two lessons, one reason, and it is the same reason both times.
theDoubling.title: Why prennent has two

examples.note: The ending sounds, so one n is enough.
The ending is silent, so the n has to carry the end of the word.

coverTheFront.body: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. A verb you have never seen? Take the front off it, and what is left is one you built ten minutes ago. It is a thing you do with your eye rather than a rule you recall, which is why it survives being needed halfway through a sentence. Somebody says remettre and you have never seen it: put a thumb over the re, read mettre, and every one of its six forms is already yours. Put the re back on the front and you are finished. Nothing else in this lesson is worth as much as that.
coverTheFront.title: What to do when a new one arrives

examples.note: And the same verb with a front on it.
The answer the scene wanted, built out of a verb you already had.

theParticiples.body: These three have past forms that nothing about the present tells you, and they are among the most useful in the language. They are not in this lesson and that is deliberate rather than an omission: lesson 17 is built around them and it comes after the two lessons that give you the tense they live in. What you have here is the present, in all six persons, for three families of verbs. That is enough to be going on with.
theParticiples.title: Lesson 17 takes that

examples.note: The present, which is what this lesson is.

theCompoundMeaning.body: re- usually means again or back, so remettre is to put back. com- and ap- and sur- do other things and none of it is predictable, so what a verb MEANS is a vocabulary question and you look it up. The endings are not a vocabulary question. They are settled the moment you can see which verb is underneath, and they are settled for every verb in the family that exists, including the ones nobody has taught you.
theCompoundMeaning.title: The front changes the meaning, not the endings

sections.body: Lesson 2 doubled the l of appeler where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem must end in one. That is not a rule about this verb, it is a rule about French, and lesson 2 in A2 stated it seven lessons ago in a lesson that had nothing to do with these three: The spelling changes so the sound does not. A silent ending leaves the stem holding the end of the word on its own, and a stem in that position has to end in something you can hear. prenons does not need it because the -ons is sounded. prennent does, because the -ent is not. Once you have seen it here you will recognise it everywhere, which is worth more than the cell itself.

sections.body: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. It is a syntax move rather than a memory one, and it holds for every compound of these three that exists, including the ones this course has not written a card for. Three verbs to learn, and 12 you can build. Two things are deliberately not in this lesson and both of them are worth waiting for. The past forms of these three do not follow from anything in the present and they are the centre of lesson 17. And prendre turns up in a great many fixed expressions where it stops meaning take entirely; those open lesson 24 and lesson 26, and what you have built here is exactly what both of them assume you arrive with.

say.text: Nobody in this scene is impatient and nobody is corrected. Watch what four seconds of hunting for a verb actually costs.

beats.text: A climbing gym in Grenoble on a Wednesday evening. You are sitting on a mat pulling your shoes off, and the person next to you starts talking.

beats.en: Are you learning French here?
beats.fr: Tu apprends le français ici ?
beats.speaker: La grimpeuse

beats.en: Yes... uh...
beats.fr: Oui... euh...
beats.stage: You have said « je prends » a hundred times this week. The word she used is that verb with two letters on the front of it, and you are searching for it as though you had never met it.

beats.prompt: Four seconds have gone. She is still waiting. What comes out?

options.en: the same verb she used, given back
options.fr: Oui, j'apprends le français ici.

options.en: and the conversation changes language
options.fr: Yes, I learn French here.

followUp.works: She nods and asks how long you have been at it, in French, and you are still in the conversation.
followUp.breaks: She switches to English without thinking about it and stays there. Everything after this is a chat about climbing shoes in your own language.

beats.en: Ah, you live here? How long have you been in Grenoble?
beats.fr: Ah, you live here? How long have you been in Grenoble?
beats.stage: Nobody was unkind and nobody corrected anything. She simply took the shortest route to being understood, and the shortest route was not French.
beats.speaker: La grimpeuse

beats.body: You did not need a new verb. You needed the one you already had, with two letters in front of it and nothing else changed at all.

sections.say: Five verbs. Cover the front of each one, decide which family it is in, then tap to hear it.

rows.say: apprendre

detail.say: apprendre
detail.body: apprendre [a-PRAHⁿDR] is to learn, and prendre is what is left when you cover the first two letters. Every one of its six forms is one you have already written. Ils apprennent le français.
detail.title: Take off the ap

rows.say: comprendre

detail.say: comprendre
detail.body: comprendre [kohⁿ-PRAHⁿDR] is to understand. Four letters in front and the same six endings behind. Ils comprennent la question.
detail.title: Take off the com

rows.say: promettre

detail.say: promettre
detail.body: promettre [proh-MEHTR] is to promise, and it has nothing to do with putting anything anywhere. The meaning of the front is a vocabulary question. The endings are not. Nous promettons une réponse.
detail.title: Take off the pro

rows.say: combattre

detail.say: combattre
detail.body: combattre [kohⁿ-BATR] is to fight. The same front as comprendre, on a different verb, and it does something different to the meaning. Ils combattent le feu.
detail.title: Take off the com

rows.say: vendre

detail.say: vendre
detail.body: vendre [VAHⁿDR] ends the same way and belongs to the regular group lesson 4 in A2 built. Cover its front and there is no verb underneath, because there is no front on it. That is how you tell.
detail.title: And this one is not in any of them

sections.title: Which Family

sections.say: The smallest of the three, and this is the whole of it. One compound to recognise and two more so you are not surprised by them.
sections.hint: Two cards, and then it is finished.

cards.fr: Ils combattent le feu.
cards.body: To fight, usually against something rather than somebody. Two t in the plural, exactly like the verb underneath it.
cards.head: combattre
cards.label: the one worth having

cards.fr: débattre · abattre
cards.body: To debate and to knock down. You will meet them in writing before you ever need to say one, and when you do they take the same six endings as the rest.
cards.head: Recognition only
cards.label: and two you will only ever read

sections.title: The Battre Family

sections.say: Four sentences nobody wrote for this lesson. Two of them use a compound and two use the verb underneath, and none of them was thinking about you.
sections.title: Already Everywhere

check.q: The first uses a compound and the second uses the verb underneath it. What is the same in both?
check.why: The form. One is apprends and the other is prend, and if you cover the two letters at the front of the first you are looking at the same word.

items.fr: J'apprends le français depuis le printemps.

items.fr: Maman prend toujours son temps.
items.note: [ma-MAHⁿ PRAHⁿ too-ZHOOR SOHⁿ TAHⁿ] · Mom always takes her time.

check.q: How many t are there in each of those two verbs?
check.why: One each, because both are singular. The second t arrives with nous and stays for the whole plural, which is exactly what you built two acts ago.

items.fr: Elle met sa veste et ferme la porte.
items.note: [EHL MEH SA VEHST AY FEHRM LA PORT] · She puts on her jacket and closes the door.

groups.label: and two from the mettre family

sections.say: Six lines. Listen before you read. Three of them are singular and three are plural, and for once you can hear which is which.

lines.en: They take the key.

sections.title: Prend Or Prennent

questions.q: Il prend la clé against Ils prennent la clé. What is the difference you can hear?
questions.why: The end of the verb. One finishes inside the nose and the other finishes on a consonant, and those are two completely different sounds.
opts: The first ends on a nasal vowel and the second on an n

questions.q: And Il met la clé against Ils mettent la clé?
questions.why: A t arrives. The one you have been writing since nous is the one you now hear, because the -ent behind it makes no sound to cover it.

questions.q: Lesson 3 in A2 gave you a plural you could hear as well. What is going on in all of these?
questions.why: A sound arrives at the end of the verb. Lesson 3 in A2 did it with a whole syllable in the middle and these three do it with one consonant, and both are rarer in French than you would like.
opts: The plural adds a sound the singular did not have
The pronoun is doing the work

questions.q: Which pairs in this lesson can the ear NOT separate?
questions.why: The three singular persons of every verb here are one sound. That is why the word in front is never optional, and it is the fourth lesson in a row to say so.
opts: je and tu and il, on any of the three

sections.say: Lesson 4 named these three and would not build them, because the model it taught you would have produced a form nobody says. This is the lesson it was waiting for.
sections.frSub: Ce n'est pas un verbe régulier
sections.title: It Is Not Vendre

examples.en: the regular one, and this one
examples.fr: il vend · prend
examples.note: Both end in -re in the naming form and both sound the same in this cell. So far nothing has gone wrong.

examples.en: where they part
examples.fr: vendre · pren-
examples.note: The regular verb keeps its d for every person. prendre drops it the moment the plural arrives, and that is the whole of the difference.

examples.en: We take the key.
examples.fr: Nous prenons la clé.
examples.note: One n, no d, and the regular pattern would have given you neither of those.

examples.en: They take the key.
examples.fr: Ils prennent la clé.
examples.note: And then a second n. Lesson 4 in A2 could not have shown you this without teaching the whole lesson, which is why it waited.

sections.say: Four cards and then six to prove it. Every one of them asks the same question: which of the three shapes does this person need?

rule.body: prend- pren- prenn- for prendre. met- mett- for mettre and bat- batt- for battre. The singular writes a d it never says, the middle two drop it, and the last one puts a second n in its place.
rule.title: Three shapes, six cells

sections.title: Three Stems, One Verb

sections.say: The first card is the form the regular pattern gives you, and it is the reason lesson 4 in A2 refused to show you any of this.
sections.title: Four Ways It Breaks

errors.why: The regular group keeps its d in every person and this verb does not have one past the singular. Lesson 4 in A2 named these three and would not build them for exactly this reason.
errors.right: Building « Ils prennent la clé ».
errors.wrong: Building ils prendent from the pattern lesson 4 in A2 taught.

errors.why: The -ent makes no sound, so the stem has to end in something. You can hear which one you meant: with one n the word would finish on a vowel, and it does not.
errors.right: Writing « prennent », with two.
errors.wrong: Writing prennent with one n.

errors.why: The other way round, and just as common. The -ons is doing the sounding here, so the stem has nothing to prove and stays short.
errors.right: Writing « prenons », with one.
errors.wrong: Writing prenons with two.

errors.why: mettre and battre change once and stop. prendre changes twice. Only one verb in this lesson has a third shape, and spreading its habit onto the other two costs you the thing that made them easy.
errors.right: Keeping mett- for all three plural persons.
errors.wrong: Giving mettons and mettent different stems, the way prendre does.

sections.say: Back at the wall, and this time you have all three. nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. Every answer needs a form you have built rather than a phrase you have memorised.
sections.title: The Gym, A Week On

check.why: Only ils. One n for nous, two for ils. Lesson 2 doubled the l of appeler where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem must end in one.

check.q: And here?
check.why: The same stem for both, and for vous as well. mettre and battre change once and stop. prendre changes twice.

sections.title: The Whole Thing

sections.say: One screen, and then one last thing to build before the exam.
sections.body: You have three verbs, all six persons of each, and one doubled letter in one cell. That was the short half. The long half is what you do with a verb nobody has taught you, and the next screen is going to hand you two of those and ask for the forms. It is the only screen in this lesson that matters, and if you can do it then everything in the three families is yours, including the parts of them nobody has written a card for yet. Each round of the exam is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: Where You Stand

sections.say: Two verbs. Neither of them appears anywhere else in this lesson and you are not going to be shown their forms. Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left.
sections.title: One You Have Not Met

check.q: reprendre means to take back, to start again. Which is the nous form?
check.why: Cover the re and you are looking at prendre, whose nous form loses the d and keeps one n. Two of the wrong answers give it a second n and the third leaves the d in.

groups.label: reprendre, and nothing else on this card

check.q: And the ils form of reprendre?
check.why: Two n, because the -ent is silent and the stem has to end in something. It is the same cell that moved on prendre and on both of its compounds.

check.q: admettre means to admit. Which is the ils form?
check.why: Two t and a silent -ent, which is what mettre does and what permettre and promettre do. Nothing about ad- changes any of it.

check.q: You have now built four forms of two verbs. How many of those forms were on a card in this lesson?
check.why: None. A verb you have never seen? Take the front off it, and what is left is one you built ten minutes ago. That is what three verbs are actually worth, and it is why the last five lessons were not a list.

sections.say: Six rounds. Miss too many in a round and you get a drill before the next one starts.
sections.title: The Exam

rounds.say: Six on the shapes themselves. Every question fixes the person for you.
rounds.label: The three of them

questions.q: Nous ___ la clé. (prendre)
questions.why: The d goes and one n is enough, because the -ons is doing the sounding.
accept: prenons
nous prenons
questions.answer: prenons

questions.q: Il ___ la clé. (mettre)
questions.why: One t in the singular. The second one arrives with nous and not before.
accept: met
il met
questions.answer: met

questions.q: Nous ___ Paul. (battre)
questions.why: Two t and the ordinary -ons, which is exactly what mettre does in this cell.
accept: battons
nous battons
questions.answer: battons

questions.q: Which of these four is spelled correctly?
questions.why: Two n and no d. The first is what the regular pattern gives you and it is the form lesson 4 in A2 refused to put in front of anybody.

questions.q: How many different stems does prendre use across its six forms?
questions.why: prend- pren- prenn- for prendre. met- mett- for mettre and bat- batt- for battre.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous mettons la clé. » in the ils form.
questions.why: Same stem, different ending. mettre settles into two t and stays there for the whole plural.
accept: Ils mettent la clé
mettent
questions.answer: Ils mettent la clé.

rounds.say: This is the round the lesson is really about. Lesson 2 in A2 taught the reason seven lessons ago.
rounds.label: One n or two

questions.q: Ils ___ la clé. (prendre)
questions.why: Lesson 2 doubled the l of appeler where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem must end in one.
accept: prennent
ils prennent
questions.answer: prennent

questions.q: Which one has the doubled letter?
questions.why: Only the last one, and only because its ending makes no sound. Every other cell has something audible after the stem.

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous prennons la clé. »
questions.why: One n. The -ons is sounded, so nothing has to be doubled to hold the end of the word up.
accept: Nous prenons la clé
prenons
questions.answer: Nous prenons la clé.

questions.q: Ils ___ le français. (apprendre)
questions.why: Two n, because the verb underneath has two n in this cell. The front of the word changes nothing at all.
accept: apprennent
ils apprennent
questions.answer: apprennent

questions.q: Why does prennent double its n and prenons not?
questions.why: Lesson 2 doubled the l of appeler where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem must end in one.
opts: It is an exception with no reason
One ending is silent and the other is not

questions.q: Nous ___ la question. (comprendre)
questions.why: One n, no d, and four letters at the front that have no say in any of it.
accept: comprenons
nous comprenons
questions.answer: comprenons

rounds.say: Cover the front of each one before you answer.
rounds.label: Which family

questions.q: Which of these follows mettre?
questions.why: promettre. Cover the pro and mettre is what is left. The second and fourth run on prendre and the third is a regular verb with no front on it at all.

questions.q: And which of these follows prendre?
questions.why: surprendre. The last one ends the same way and is a regular verb, which is the distinction this whole round turns on.

questions.q: Ils ___ le feu. (combattre)
questions.why: Two t and a silent -ent, because battre does that and combattre is battre with three letters on the front.
accept: combattent
ils combattent
questions.answer: combattent

questions.q: Je ___ la clé. (remettre)
questions.why: One t, because mettre has one t here. The re- means back and it does nothing to the ending.
accept: remets
je remets
questions.answer: remets

questions.q: A verb ends in -re. What tells you whether it is regular?
questions.why: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. vendre has no front on it, so there is nothing to cover and nothing underneath; that is how you tell it apart from the four verbs above it.
opts: The ending is enough on its own
Whether there is a familiar verb left when you cover the front

questions.q: Fix this. « Ils comprendent la question. »
questions.why: No d, two n. This is the regular pattern applied to a verb that is not in the regular group, one front along.
accept: Ils comprennent la question
comprennent
questions.answer: Ils comprennent la question.

rounds.say: Two verbs you have not been taught. You have everything you need for both of them.
rounds.label: One you have not met

questions.q: reprendre means to take back, to start again. Nous ___ la clé.
questions.why: Cover the re and prendre is what is left, and its nous form drops the d and keeps one n. You have never seen this word written down.
accept: reprenons
nous reprenons
questions.answer: reprenons

questions.q: And the plural. Ils ___ la clé. (reprendre)
questions.why: Two n, for the same reason ils prennent has two: the -ent makes no sound and something has to hold the end of the word up.
accept: reprennent
ils reprennent
questions.answer: reprennent

questions.q: admettre means to admit. Nous ___ notre erreur.
questions.why: Two t and the ordinary -ons. mettre is underneath it and mettre has settled into its plural stem by this cell.
accept: admettons
nous admettons
questions.answer: admettons

questions.q: And Ils ___ leur erreur. (admettre)
questions.why: Two t and a silent -ent. Four forms of two verbs, and not one of them was on a card anywhere in this lesson.
accept: admettent
ils admettent
questions.answer: admettent

questions.q: How did you build those four?
questions.why: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. It works on every verb in all three families, including the ones nobody has taught you and the ones nobody has written a card for.
opts: By covering the front and using the verb underneath

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous reprendons la clé. »
questions.why: The d does not survive into the plural on any verb in this family, and a front on the word does not bring it back.
accept: Nous reprenons la clé
reprenons
questions.answer: Nous reprenons la clé.

rounds.say: The plural is audible on all three of these, which is rarer in French than you would like.
rounds.label: Saying it

questions.q: Listen. Which one did you hear?
questions.say: Ils prennent la clé.
questions.why: The verb ends on an n, so it is the plural. The pronoun would not have told you: il and ils are one sound.

questions.q: And this one?
questions.say: Il met la clé.
questions.why: No t at the end, so it is the singular. The plural would have finished on a hard consonant you could not miss.

questions.q: Tap the letters you do NOT say.
questions.why: The d. It is written in all three singular persons and said in none of them, and it disappears from the spelling the moment the plural arrives.

questions.q: And here?
questions.why: The -ent, silent as it has been on every verb since lesson 1 in A2. What you do hear is the t in front of it.

questions.q: Say it: they take the key.
questions.why: Finish the verb on the n. If it comes out through the nose you have said the singular, and nothing else in the sentence will correct it.
questions.answer: Ils prennent la clé.

questions.q: Which three words in this lesson are said identically?
questions.why: Two spellings across three persons and one sound for all of them. mets, mets, met does the same thing, and so does bats, bats, bat.

rounds.say: The last round is the gym. Nothing here is a trick.
rounds.label: Out in the world

questions.q: Somebody asks « Tu apprends le français ici ? » What do you say?
questions.why: The verb she used, given back with the person changed. The second uses the wrong verb, the third drops the s, and the fourth is how the scene at the start went wrong.
opts: Oui, je prends le français ici.

questions.q: Vous ___ la clé à la fin ? (remettre)
questions.why: Two t and the ordinary -ez. It is mettez with two letters in front and nothing else moved.
accept: remettez
vous remettez
questions.answer: remettez

questions.q: Ils ___ la question. (comprendre)
questions.why: Two n. It is the cell that moves on prendre, and every compound of prendre moves in the same place.
accept: comprennent
ils comprennent
questions.answer: comprennent

questions.q: Which sentence would a French speaker actually say for we are taking the key?
questions.why: Both of the first two are correct and the second is what people say. nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say. on takes the il form, so it costs no new spelling at all.

questions.q: Fix this. « Vous mettes la clé ici. »
questions.why: The vous ending is -ez on every verb in this lesson and on every verb since lesson 1 in A2. Nothing about these three is irregular in that cell.
accept: Vous mettez la clé ici
mettez

questions.q: Which of these is NOT taught in this lesson?
