sections.body: Three verbs, eighteen cells, and one doubled letter in one of them. Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left. You used that on two verbs nobody showed you and it worked, which means it will work on every other verb in these three families, including the ones no lesson in this course has got to yet. Lesson 4 in A2 named these three and would not build them; that is finished now, and the irregular block is finished with it. Two things are deliberately not here. The past of all three belongs to lesson 17, and prendre in its fixed expressions belongs to lesson 24 and lesson 26, which open on them. What you have is the present, in six persons, for the 12 verbs this lesson names and for every other one in the three families.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: Cover the front of the verb. Build what is left.
Three verbs to learn, and 12 you can build.
One n for nous, two for ils. Lesson 2 doubled the l of appeler where the ending went silent. prennent doubles its n for the same reason: the -ent makes no sound, so the stem must end in one.
mettre and battre change once and stop. prendre changes twice.

errorTriggers.description: Runs the regular -re pattern on prendre and produces a plural with a d in it. It is the error lesson 4 in A2 predicted and refused to print, and it is what a learner reaches for when the naming form is the only thing they have looked at.

Writes ils prenent with one n, or nous prennons with two. The doubling belongs to exactly one cell and it is the cell whose ending makes no sound, which is lesson 2 in A2 principle arriving on a verb nobody expected it on.

Meets a compound and treats it as a verb they have never seen, stopping the sentence to look for a form they already own. It is the scene at the top of this lesson and it costs a conversation rather than a mark.

Covers the front of a compound, builds the verb underneath correctly, and then forgets to put the front back on: nous prenons where the sentence wanted nous reprenons. The half of the move that gets dropped is the half nobody drills.

Hears the plural and writes the singular, because il and ils are one sound and the only thing separating the two sentences is the end of the verb. It is the one place in this lesson where the ear can settle it, and a learner who is not listening for it will not hear it.
Spreads prendre habit of changing stem twice onto mettre and battre, which change once. It is the cost of teaching the hard one first, and it turns two easy verbs into two more hard ones.

recorded.desc: THE NINE SINGULAR CELLS, IN THREE GROUPS OF THREE, AND WITHIN EACH GROUP THE THREE MUST BE ACOUSTICALLY IDENTICAL ON THE VERB: « Je veux payer. » « Tu veux payer. » « Il veut payer. » then the same for peux/peux/peut and dois/dois/doit. This is the single most important instruction in this lesson and it is the opposite of what a reader will want to do. The whole screen is that these three cells CANNOT be told apart by ear, and the learner has to discover that by failing to hear a difference. A reader who knows the third one is spelled differently will put a fraction of a t on it, or brighten the vowel, or leave a hair more space before it. Every one of those instincts destroys the mission. If a listener with their eyes shut can say which of the three they just heard, the take is unusable. The PRONOUN must carry all the difference, and it must be clear and unhurried, because it is the only information in the line. Conversational pace, no teaching pause anywhere.

THE EIGHTEEN CELLS AS ONE FRAME, READ IN GRID ORDER, EACH VERB'S SIX IN ONE TAKE. Here the plural MUST be audible, which is the opposite instruction from the singular clip and is why they are separate recordings. veulent, peuvent and doivent each land a consonant at the very end of the verb, VUHL, PUHV, DWAHV, and that consonant is the only thing separating them from the singular, so it must be clean and unswallowed. The nous and vous rows add a syllable and go into the nose at nous; do not soften the nasal. AND payer MUST SOUND EXACTLY THE SAME IN ALL EIGHTEEN LINES. It is the control: the learner is being shown that the back of the sentence does not move, and any variation in stress, length or vowel on payer is the recording quietly contradicting the lesson. Read it as if it were one word you happened to say eighteen times.

THE FOUR REGISTER LINES, IN TWO PAIRS, BLUNT THEN POLITE: « Je veux payer. » / « Je voudrais payer. » then « Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît. » / « Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. » THE DIFFICULTY IS THAT THE DIFFERENCE MUST NOT BE PERFORMED. The blunt version is not rude, not aggressive and not clipped; it is exactly how a small child asks for something, and an adult saying it sounds like one. If the reader makes it sound hostile, the learner concludes it is a rudeness they would never commit, and the lesson fails. Read both halves of each pair in the same warm, ordinary voice at the same pace, and let the VERB do all the work. The please on the third line must be perfectly sincere and must not save it.
clipIds: Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît.
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.

recorded.desc: THE GENERALISATION MISSION. « arroser » alone, then « Je peux arroser le jardin. » then « Tu dois arroser le jardin. » The single word first, slowly and clearly, because this is the only time the learner will hear it before being asked to use it. Three syllables,, ah-roh-ZAY, stress on the last. Then the two sentences at completely ordinary pace, with NO emphasis on arroser at all. That is the point: it must sound like the least remarkable word in the sentence, because the claim is that an unknown verb behaves exactly like a known one. A reader who leans on it is telling the learner it is special, and it is precisely not.

THE THREE NAMING FORMS AND THE TEN BORROWED VERBS, each as a single word, conversational and unstressed. vouloir, pouvoir and devoir first: all three end in the same -oir and the reader must not differentiate them beyond what the spelling requires. Then payer, commander, attendre, choisir, boire, acheter, aider, chercher, conduire, arriver. These ten come from ten different lessons and the learner should hear no family resemblance and no grouping. They are a bag of ordinary verbs,, which is the whole reason they are in this lesson.

THE BAKERY. The boulangère is friendly, busy and completely uninterested in teaching anybody French, because she is closing in ten minutes. « Bonjour, je vous écoute. » is warm and quick. « Voilà. Et avec ceci ? » is already moving on to the next customer; the learner has to feel that the moment passed rather than that they were judged. Nothing in this scene is unkind and nothing is slowed down for them. The failure is entirely one of speed.

lessons.intro: Three verbs that will not come apart, and what they buy is every other verb in the language: put any one of them in front and the next verb never changes. The forms take ten minutes. What you can say afterwards is the rest of the lesson.

nousOn.body: nous parlons is what you write. on parle is what you say.
nousOn.title: The we people actually say

examples.note: on peut takes this form, never on pouvons.

theOwing.body: what comes next decides. Lesson 5 in A2 named that shape and this is another one of it. Put a verb after dois and it means have to. Put a thing after it and it means owe. Tu me dois de l'argent is not about obligation in general; it is about ten euros. You will not need to produce this for a while, and you should recognise it, because the two sentences look identical until the word after the verb.
theOwing.term: devoir with no verb after it
theOwing.title: The same word, owing money

theReach.body: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. That is the whole of it, and it is worth more than any list of verbs. Once you can say je veux, je peux and je dois, you can put ANY verb after them in the shape it has in the dictionary, including verbs nobody has taught you and verbs you met once on a sign. Six lessons have been building toward a point where changing the verb stops being necessary, and this is that point.
theReach.title: Three verbs, every other verb behind them

examples.note: One verb changed. payer did not.
And nobody taught you this second one.

theStems.body: Each of these verbs has a short stem for je, tu and il, a longer one for nous and vous, and a third for ils. The third is not a new thing to learn: take the short stem and add the last letter of the long one. veu + l = veul · peu + v = peuv · doi + v = doiv Three verbs, one recipe, no exceptions. If you can see that, you never have to memorise the ils row again.
theStems.title: Two stems, and the third one you can work out

examples.note: veu plus the l from voulons.
peu plus the v from pouvons.
doi plus the v from devons. Same recipe, third time.

thePolite.body: voudrais is not a present tense and it is not a version of veux you can build. It is one fixed form, and voudrions is the only other one worth carrying at this stage. Its proper name and its whole family come much later; for now, learn these two the way you learned bonjour. The reason to bother is not grammar: je veux un café is a demand and voudrais un café is a request, and the person behind the counter hears the difference immediately.
thePolite.title: A form to learn whole

examples.note: The same sentence, and now you will be served.

theSenses.body: English splits this across three words and French does not. may is asking whether you are allowed; might is saying a thing could happen; can is saying somebody is able. All three are pouvoir, and no French speaker feels a difference between them. This matters at the moment you want to ask for something: if you believe pouvoir means only being able, you will look for another verb to ask permission with, and there is not one.
theSenses.title: One French verb, three English ones

examples.note: may, asking whether you are allowed
might, saying a thing could happen

theUnseen.body: arroser means to water, and this lesson has not taught it, will not drill it, and does not expect you to keep it. It is here to prove something: you did not need the lesson. Put it after je peux or tu dois in the shape it has above, and the sentence is correct. That is true of every verb in the dictionary, which is roughly eleven thousand of them, and it is what these three verbs bought you.
theUnseen.title: The point of the whole lesson

examples.note: A verb you met thirty seconds ago.
And behind a different first verb, unchanged.

theRegister.body: Bonjour is the price of entry. That was lesson 1 in A1, and it also put voudrais in your mouth in the very first lesson without saying what it was. This is where that is paid off. The difference between the blunt form and the polite one is not correctness, because both are correct French. It is whether the interaction goes well, and in a shop, a station or a doorway that is the only thing being measured.
theRegister.title: Lesson 1 in A1 already gave you this

examples.note: Correct French, and it lands as a demand.
The sentence lesson 1 in A1 handed you before you could build it.

theSingular.body: Je veux, tu veux, il veut. Two of those are spelled identically and the third differs by one silent letter, and all three are one sound in the mouth. The same is true of peux, peux, peut and of dois, dois, doit. Nothing separates them when spoken except the word in front, which is why the pronoun is never optional here. In writing you must pick the right one; in speech there is nothing to pick.
theSingular.term: why je, tu and il sound the same
theSingular.title: 3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound.

examples.note: veut, and not one sound different.

whatFollows.body: what comes next decides You met that shape at lesson 5 in A2, and this lesson holds the cleanest example of it in the level. dois with a verb after it means having to. dois with a thing after it means owing money. Same verb, same person, nothing to tell them apart until the next word arrives. It is worth knowing that French does this at all, because you will meet it again and the instinct to decide what a word means before the sentence has finished is a hard one to switch off.
whatFollows.title: One form, two sentences

theNewLetter.body: 4 of the 6 endings are ones you already have. One letter here is new. That letter is the -x on veux and peux. It is silent, exactly as the -s has been silent on every verb since lesson 1 in A2, so it changes nothing you say and one thing you write. dois takes an ordinary -s instead, which is the singular you already met on the -RE verbs in lesson 4 in A2.
theNewLetter.title: veux and peux, and nothing else in the language you have met

theImpersonal.body: This one has no person at all. Il faut réserver does not say who has to book; it says booking is what is required. French reaches for it constantly, far more often than for any single form of the three verbs in this lesson, and you will hear it long before you need to produce it. Two words, one shape, no changes. Recognise it and move on: it is not part of what you are building here.
theImpersonal.title: Nobody is doing it

examples.note: Nobody named, and everybody knows who is meant.
The same two words, doing the same job.

theSecondVerb.body: payer, commander, attendre, choisir, boire, acheter, aider, chercher, conduire, arriver. Every one of those came from another lesson, and every one arrives here in exactly the shape the dictionary gives it. It does not matter whether it is an -ER verb, an -IR verb or an -RE verb; after one of these three, nothing happens to it at all. That is not a simplification for beginners. That is the rule, and it does not change later.
theSecondVerb.title: The second verb in every sentence here belongs to somebody else. What you are learning is the first one.

examples.note: attendre is an -RE verb from lesson 4 in A2, and it does not move.
choisir is an -IR verb from lesson 3 in A2, and it does not move either.

sections.body: Every reference sheet before this one in the level lists ENDINGS, because every pattern before it had them: lesson 1 in A2 holds the -er set in full, lesson 3 in A2 the -ir set, lesson 4 in A2 all three regular sets at once, and lesson 5 in A2 lists forms because its verbs have none. This lesson has eighteen forms, and only one of them is worth memorising as a shape, the plural, and even that one is produced by a rule. veu + l = veul · peu + v = peuv · doi + v = doiv Read the third table if you want to know why an ending looks familiar; read the second one if you have forgotten a plural. The first table is the one to photograph, because it is the only place in the course where three verbs sit on a single sentence and the difference between them is two letters wide. 3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound.
sections.title: Why this sheet gives you a recipe and not a list

sections.body: Three things leave this lesson. The first is the big one: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. Any verb at all goes behind these three in the shape a dictionary gives it, including verbs nobody has taught you, and nothing later in the course takes that back. The fourth table above is a starting set and it is not a limit. The second is that voudrais and voudrions are fixed forms worth carrying whole, and that the choice between them and veux is about how an exchange lands rather than about being correct, which is the same thing lesson 1 in A1 was telling you with Bonjour is the price of entry. The third is smaller and it will come back: what comes next decides. dois followed by a verb and dois followed by a thing are two unrelated sentences, and you met that shape at lesson 5 in A2 on a different pair. Lesson 8 is next and it brings pouvoir back to stand against a verb that also becomes can in English, so the eighteen cells you have just built are about to be worth more than they were.

questions.q: Je veux payer, Tu veux payer, Il veut payer. What is different in the verb?

questions.q: So what told you which one it was?
questions.why: The pronoun. This is why it is never optional in French: on these forms it is carrying the whole of the information.

questions.q: Now the other two verbs. Is Il peut payer distinguishable from Je peux payer by ear?

questions.q: Which of the six forms in this lesson can the ear actually separate?
questions.why: nous and vous both add a syllable, and the plural adds a consonant at the end. The three singular cells are where the ear stops being useful.

questions.q: Four sentences in the passage have two verbs in them. What happened to the second verb in each?

sections.title: Four Ways This Comes Apart

errors.why: Six lessons of building endings makes this reflex very strong, and this is the one place it must be switched off. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does.
errors.right: Saying « Je veux payer. » and « Nous pouvons payer. ».
errors.wrong: Saying « Je veux paye » or « Je peux payons ».

errors.why: Both are correct and only one of them is a request. Adding please to the first does not fix it, because the verb has already set the tone.
errors.right: Saying « Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. ».
errors.wrong: Saying « Je veux un café » to somebody you have never met.

errors.why: The plural stem is the short one plus a letter from the long one. veu + l = veul · peu + v = peuv · doi + v = doiv Building it off the nous form instead is the commonest written slip here.
errors.right: Writing « veulent » and « peuvent ».
errors.wrong: Writing « ils voulent » or « ils peuvent » with the wrong stem.

errors.why: English splits this across can, may and am able to. French does not split it at all, and the second you spend looking for the right one is the second the sentence dies in.
errors.right: Saying « Je peux commander ? ».
errors.wrong: Looking for another verb when you want to ask permission.

sections.body: You have three more verbs that will not come apart, and a recipe that builds the hardest row of all three of them. That was the short half. The long half is what they let you do: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. You proved it on a verb this course has never taught you, thirty seconds after meeting it. What is left is the part that says whether it stuck. Each round is tied to one of the mistakes this lesson exists to stop, and failing a round gets you its drill before the next one starts. questions.answer: attendre

questions.q: Ils peuvent ___. (choisir)
questions.why: Not choisissent. An -IR verb behaves here exactly as an -ER verb does, which is not at all.
accept: choisir
questions.answer: choisir

questions.q: Fix this. « Nous voulons payons. »
questions.why: The ending went on twice. Six lessons trained that reflex and this is the one place it is wrong.
accept: Nous voulons payer
payer
questions.answer: Nous voulons payer.

questions.q: You have never met the verb « ranger ». « Je dois ranger la cuisine. » What can you tell?
questions.why: A front, then a verb in its dictionary shape, like every sentence in this lesson. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. You will not know what ranger means and you will know what kind of sentence you are in.
opts: It is a form you have not learned
It is somebody having to do something, and ranger says what

questions.q: Which of these four is wrong?
questions.why: The third. Everything else on this screen leaves the second verb alone.

questions.q: Tu ___ arroser le jardin. (devoir)
questions.why: A plain -s on this verb rather than the new letter. And arroser did not move, because it never does.
accept: dois
tu dois
questions.answer: dois

questions.q: Vous ___ commander ? (vouloir)
questions.why: The ordinary -ez from lesson 1 in A2, on the long stem. Nothing about the vous form here is strange.
accept: voulez
vous voulez
questions.answer: voulez

rounds.say: The plural of all three is built the same way. If you can do one, you can do the other two.
rounds.label: The eighteen cells

questions.q: Ils ___ payer. (vouloir)
questions.why: veu plus the l from voul. Not voulent, which builds it off the wrong stem.
accept: veulent
ils veulent
questions.answer: veulent

questions.q: Ils ___ payer. (pouvoir)
questions.why: peu plus the v from pouv. Same recipe, second verb.
accept: peuvent
ils peuvent
questions.answer: peuvent

questions.q: Ils ___ payer. (devoir)
questions.why: doi plus the v from dev. Third verb, and it did not break.
accept: doivent
ils doivent
questions.answer: doivent

questions.q: Fix this. « Ils voulent payer. »
questions.why: The plural is built off the short stem, not the long one. voulent takes the nous stem and there is no such form.
accept: Ils veulent payer
veulent
questions.answer: Ils veulent payer.

questions.q: Nous ___ payer. (pouvoir)
questions.why: The long stem and the ordinary -ons. This is the row that supplies the letter the plural needs.
accept: pouvons
nous pouvons
questions.answer: pouvons

questions.q: Which pair shares a stem?
questions.why: nous and vous share the long stem. The plural is the odd one: it borrows from both.

questions.q: Il ___ payer. (devoir)
questions.why: A -t, and it sounds exactly like dois. In writing you have to pick; in speech there is nothing to pick.
accept: doit
il doit
questions.answer: doit

rounds.say: One letter in eighteen cells is new. This round is about which cells get it.
rounds.label: The one new letter

questions.q: Which two verbs take -x on je and tu?
questions.why: vouloir and pouvoir. devoir takes the ordinary -s you already write.

questions.q: Tu ___ payer. (pouvoir)
questions.why: Not peus. The letter is silent, so nothing about saying it changes, and everything about writing it does.
accept: peux
tu peux
questions.answer: peux

questions.q: Je ___ payer. (devoir)
questions.why: A plain -s. This is the singular you already met on the -RE verbs in lesson 4 in A2, arriving on a verb that is not one.
accept: dois
je dois
questions.answer: dois

questions.q: What does the -x sound like?
questions.why: Nothing, exactly as the -s has been silent since lesson 1 in A2.

questions.q: Fix this. « Je peus payer. »
questions.why: peus is not a form. Two of these three verbs take the new letter and this is one of them.
accept: Je peux payer
peux
questions.answer: Je peux payer.

questions.q: How many of the six endings in this lesson were already yours?
questions.why: 4 of the 6 endings are ones you already have. One letter here is new.

questions.q: Vous ___ payer. (devoir)
questions.why: The ordinary -ez. This is also the sentence a waiter says to you at the end of a meal.
accept: devez
vous devez
questions.answer: devez

rounds.say: Every question here has a situation in it, because politeness has no answer without one.
rounds.label: Asking, not demanding

questions.q: You are ordering from a waiter you have never met. Which one?
questions.why: The second is correct French and lands as a demand, and the please on the end does not rescue it. The verb has already set the tone.
opts: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît.

questions.q: Your close friend asks what you want to drink. Which one is fine?
questions.why: With a friend, veux is completely normal. The polite form is for people who are serving you or who you do not know, not for everybody all the time.
opts: Only the polite form is ever acceptable

questions.q: Je ___ payer, s'il vous plaît. (the polite form)
questions.why: A fixed form, learned whole. It is not built from veux and you cannot make it from anything in this lesson.
accept: voudrais
je voudrais
questions.answer: voudrais

questions.q: Can you build voudrais from the forms in this lesson?
questions.why: No. It belongs to a family this course has not reached, and two forms of it is all you are carrying for now.
opts: Yes, by adding -rais to the stem

questions.q: You want to ask whether you are allowed to sit down. Which verb?
questions.why: pouvoir. French does not have a separate verb for permission, and looking for one is the hesitation the sentence dies in.

questions.q: Fix this, said to a stranger behind a counter. « Je veux payer. »
questions.why: Nothing about the first is incorrect. One word changes it from a demand into a request, and everything after it holds still.
accept: Je voudrais payer
voudrais
questions.answer: Je voudrais payer.

questions.q: Nous ___ payer, s'il vous plaît. (the polite form, two of you)
questions.why: The only other one worth carrying. Two fixed forms now, and the family they come from waits until later.
accept: voudrions
nous voudrions
questions.answer: voudrions

questions.q: Lesson 1 in A1 already put one of these in your mouth. Which?
questions.why: Bonjour is the price of entry. The polite form arrived in the very first lesson as a whole phrase, with no way to explain it yet.
opts: Je veux un café, s'il vous plaît.
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.

rounds.say: English splits this three ways. Each question is one of the three.
rounds.label: One verb, three English words

questions.q: « Je peux commander ? » Which English word is pouvoir doing here?
questions.why: may, asking whether you are allowed. All three are the same French verb and no speaker feels a difference.

questions.q: « Il peut arriver demain. » Which English word is pouvoir doing here?
questions.why: might, saying a thing could happen. All three are the same French verb and no speaker feels a difference.

questions.q: « Elle peut conduire. » Which English word is pouvoir doing here?
questions.why: can, saying somebody is able. All three are the same French verb and no speaker feels a difference.

questions.q: Which of the three senses needs a different French verb?
questions.why: None. That is the point of the mission: one verb covers all three, and English is the language doing the splitting.

questions.q: Je ___ commander ? (pouvoir)
questions.why: Asking to be allowed, and the rising voice makes it a question exactly as it did in lesson 22 in A1.
accept: peux
je peux
questions.answer: peux

questions.q: Elle ___ conduire. (pouvoir)
questions.why: Being able, and it sounds identical to peux. Only the word in front separates them.
accept: peut
elle peut
questions.answer: peut

questions.q: You are told « Il peut arriver demain ». What does it mean?
questions.why: Nobody is able to do anything here. It says the thing could happen, and English reaches for might.
opts: He is able to arrive tomorrow

questions.q: Vous ___ m'aider ? (pouvoir)
questions.why: This is the form you will use most, because it is how you ask a stranger for anything at all.
accept: pouvez
vous pouvez
questions.answer: pouvez

rounds.say: Two things this lesson only asks you to recognise, and one it hands to the next one.
rounds.label: The edges

questions.q: « Tu me dois de l'argent. » What is this about?
questions.why: what comes next decides A verb after dois means having to; a thing after it means owing.

questions.q: Which of these is about obligation rather than money?
questions.why: The second. Same verb, same person, and only the word after it decides which sentence you are in.

questions.q: « Il faut réserver. » Who has to book?
questions.why: Nobody is named. It says booking is what is required, and it is the commonest way French says this.

questions.q: What happens to the verb after « il faut »?
questions.why: Nothing. It is the same shape as everything else in this lesson, on a front with no person in it.
opts: Nothing, as after the other three

questions.q: Ils ___ arroser le jardin. (devoir)
questions.why: The hardest cell of the three, on a verb nobody taught you. Both halves came from somewhere other than a list.
accept: doivent
ils doivent
questions.answer: doivent

questions.q: Fix this. « Vous devez attendez. »
questions.why: The ending is on twice. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does.
accept: Vous devez attendre
attendre
questions.answer: Vous devez attendre.

questions.q: Which of these does this lesson NOT teach you to do?
questions.why: That is a different verb and it is the whole payload of lesson 8, which is the next lesson on this trail.
opts: Say you have learned how to do something

sections.say: Four things, and the second one is bigger than the whole rest of the lesson.
sections.body: You can build three more verbs that will not come apart, and you found a recipe that produces the hardest row of all three of them from the two rows above it. 4 of the 6 endings are ones you already have. One letter here is new. That was the short half. One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does. You proved that on a verb this course has never taught you and never will, thirty seconds after meeting it, and it works the same way on every other verb in the language. You also know which sentence gets you served and which one gets you a baguette you did not ask for. Lesson 8 is next, and it brings one of these three back to stand against a verb you have not met.
sections.frSub: Ce que vous pouvez faire maintenant
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: One verb changes for the person, and the next one never does.
veu + l = veul · peu + v = peuv · doi + v = doiv
3 persons, 2 spellings, one sound.
voudrais rather than veux, and the difference is whether the exchange goes well.

errorTriggers.description: Puts an ending on the second verb: Nous voulons payons, Vous devez attendez. Six lessons of building endings have made this reflex automatic, and this lesson is the first place it is wrong.
Builds the plural off the long stem rather than the short one: voulent, pouvent, devent. The plural borrows from both stems and neither one alone produces it.
Writes veus and peus, or puts the new letter on devoir: doix. Two of the three take it and the third does not, and all of it is silent so the ear gives no help.
Uses veux with somebody serving them, and adds please to fix it. Both sentences are correct French and only one of them is a request; the please does not change what the verb already said.
Believes pouvoir means only being able, and goes looking for another verb to ask permission with. There is not one, and the hesitation is where the sentence dies.
Reads dois plus a thing as an obligation, or expects il faut to have a person in it. Both are recognition failures rather than production ones, and both are common in real reading.

grammarAssumed: The six subject pronouns and the nine they cover, introduced in a1.05
on takes third-person-singular agreement, introduced in a1.05
nous as the written first-person plural against on as the spoken one, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -er verbs as a stem plus six endings, introduced in a2.01
The present tense of regular -ir and -re verbs, introduced in a2.10 and a2.11
The bare singular in -s and -t on -re verbs, introduced in a2.11
The present tense of être and avoir, introduced in a1.06 and a1.07
The present tense of aller, venir and tenir as unanalysable forms, introduced in a2.02
Yes/no questions formed by intonation alone, introduced in a1.19
The definite and partitive articles inside the objects of these sentences, introduced in a1.04 and a1.29
Je voudrais as an unexplained fixed phrase, introduced in a1.01
grammarIntroduced: The present tense of vouloir, pouvoir and devoir, as three stems per verb rather than one
That the third-person-plural stem is derivable as the singular stem plus the final consonant of the nous stem, identically across all three verbs
The -x ending on the first and second person singular of vouloir and pouvoir, against the ordinary -s on devoir
The modal-plus-infinitive construction: a conjugated verb followed by a second verb in its infinitive, which does not agree
That the construction is productive over the entire verb lexicon, including verbs not taught anywhere in the course
je voudrais and nous voudrions as fixed polite forms, named as fixed and not analysed as conditional
The three senses of pouvoir (permission, epistemic possibility and ability) as one French verb against three English ones
devoir plus a noun phrase as the second sense to owe, distinguished from the modal only by what follows
il faut as an impersonal expression of obligation, for recognition only, owned by no unit in the curriculum

acts.title: The order that gave you away
acts.milestone: You know what stopped the sentence, and it was not a word you had never learned.

acts.title: Where it goes
acts.milestone: You can put the word for how in the one place French puts it, and you know why your first language kept offering the other one.

acts.title: Where it comes from
acts.milestone: You can build the word for how out of any describing word you own, including ones this lesson never showed you.

acts.title: The ones it does not reach
acts.milestone: You will not write bonnement, you will not put bon after a verb, and you know which two endings your ear cannot separate.

acts.title: Out loud
acts.milestone: You held the conversation the scene lost, and every answer in it wanted a word you built rather than a phrase you had.

acts.title: Prove it
acts.milestone: You built two words from describing words this lesson never listed, which is the half of this a list could never have taught you.

recorded.desc: THE THREE PAIRS FOR THE LISTENING SCREEN, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT TAKE IN THE LESSON. Each pair is ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, the two lines back to back with the smallest gap the recording allows and no change of pitch, pace or weight between them: « Il est lent. » then « Elle est lente. »; « Il est doux. » then « Elle est douce. »; « Il est sérieux. » then « Elle est sérieuse. » The learner is being asked to hear ONE CONSONANT ARRIVE and nothing else, so everything except that consonant must be identical across the pair. RECORDED APART, THE LEARNER COMPARES TWO PERFORMANCES INSTEAD OF TWO SOUNDS AND THE ENTIRE TEACHING IS LOST. The reader must NOT lean on the new consonant or lengthen it: it is an ordinary final consonant and the whole point is that it is simply there where it was simply not there before. If a listener with their eyes shut cannot say which member of the pair had the extra sound, the take has failed; if they can hear the reader pointing at it, it has failed the other way.

THE TWO SPELLINGS THAT ARE ONE SOUND, AND THE VALUE OF THIS TAKE IS THAT NOTHING HAPPENS IN IT. « évidemment » then « constamment », ONE TAKE, and the last two syllables of the two words MUST BE INDISTINGUISHABLE. One is spelled with an e and one with an a and the reader can see the page, which is exactly the problem: a reader who can see the spelling will differentiate them without meaning to, and the screen then teaches the opposite of what it says. If it is possible to record this take without the reader seeing the words written, do that. The FRONT of each word is a different matter and should be left exactly as distinct as the language makes it, because the stem is the only thing the learner's ear is allowed to use. Also in this take: « Il est évident. » and « Il est constant. », same instruction, and the two nasals on the ends of those two must match each other as closely as the two endings do.

THE FIVE PLACEMENT ROWS, ONE TAKE EACH, AT ORDINARY CONVERSATIONAL PACE AND WITH NO PAUSE BEFORE THE LAST WORD. The reader must not mark the word for how in any way: no lift, no comma, no breath in front of it. It is an ordinary part of the sentence and the whole claim of the screen is that it simply lives after the verb, so a delivery that sets it apart teaches that it is an addition rather than a position. Every one of these five was published by somebody else for another lesson and they should sound like it.

THE TWENTY-ONE DICTÉE LINES, ONE TAKE EACH, CLEAN AND UNHURRIED, WITH NO CONTRAST INTENT AT ALL. This is the opposite instruction to every other take in the lesson: here the learner is spelling rather than comparing, and any pair-reading would hand them the answer. Read each line as though it were the only line. TWO OF THE TWENTY-ONE ARE SINGLE WORDS , « évidemment » and « constamment » , and those two matter most: the learner is being asked for a letter the sound cannot give them, so the two endings must be read identically and neither may be helped. The final consonants on « lente » and « douce » must be neither helped nor hidden either; say them the way somebody would say them, which is the whole difficulty the exercise exists to create.

THE BREAK CARD, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE IN THIS LESSON THE ENGLISH WORD ORDER IS SPOKEN. « Je souvent mange ici. » then « Je mange souvent ici. », one take, back to back. The first is NOT to be read as a mistake, with a wince or a rising edge or a pause: it must be read as somebody genuinely trying to say it, at speed, the way a learner produces it before they hear themselves. A clean and confident reading of it would teach that the wrong order is perfectly good French. The second should arrive at the same pace and with the same weight, so the only difference between the two takes is the order of two words. Nothing else in the delivery may change.

THE AUDIO STEP OF THE GENERALISATION DRILL, FOUR LINES, ONE TAKE EACH: « lentement », « doucement », « parfaitement », « certainement ». The first two the learner has met and the last two they have not, and NOTHING in the delivery may distinguish those groups. The whole claim of the mission is that a word built by rule sounds like a word that was taught, so a reader who gives the last two any extra care, slowness or emphasis is teaching that they are harder. Read all four at the same ordinary pace, as though they were four items on a list. The consonant before the ending in each one is the thing to keep clean: the t in the first, the s in the second, the t in the third and the n in the fourth.

THE AUDIO STEP OF THE bon/bien DRILL, TWO PAIRS, EACH ONE TAKE: « C'est un bon jour. » then « Elle chante bien. »; « Il chante mal. » then the describing word « mauvais » on its own. The point of the pairing is that the two words in each pair are NOT alternatives for the same slot, so they must not be read as a contrast between two options: read each sentence as an ordinary statement somebody would make, at ordinary pace, with no lift on the word under test. A reader who leans on bon and bien turns the mission into a listening exercise, and there is nothing here to listen for: the learner has to know what the word is describing.

THE CANTEEN IN RENNES. She is friendly, unhurried, and asking to make conversation rather than because she needs to know; « Vous venez souvent ici ? » is light and comes out over a tray. The learner's own line , « Oui, je souvent... euh... je mange... souvent... » , is the take that has to be right: two false starts and a stall, and the stall must sound like somebody who has heard their own word order and stopped to fix it, NOT like somebody who has forgotten a word. There is a difference and it is audible: the first sounds like a correction beginning and the second sounds like a gap. Her last line is cheerful and completely unbothered, because she noticed nothing, and that is what makes it expensive.

lessons.intro: French has one word for how something is done and it is built out of a word you already have. Take the form you would use about a woman, say it out loud, and put an ending on it: that is the whole rule, and it works on every describing word you have met in this course including the ones nobody taught you here. This lesson is about that, about the one place the word goes, and about the three commonest ones in the language that are not built at all.

notYet.body: In a past tense the short ones move, and that rule arrives with the tense in lesson 16 in A2. If you meet « j'ai bien mangé » before then, nothing here is wrong: it is a rule you have not been given yet. And when you want to say somebody does it BETTER than somebody else, that is lesson 32 in A2 and it is a long way off. Everything on the other screens is about a sentence happening now, which is every sentence you can currently make. When lesson 16 in A2 gives you the past, the short words move and the long ones do not, and you will be told so then. Lesson 11 in A2 is the lesson you have just come from and its first two columns are the first two of this one.
notYet.title: What moves in a past tense, and where it goes

examples.note: Happening now, and the word sits after the verb.
The same, with one of the three that are not built.
And a long one, which does not move even when the tense does.

unseen.body: Two of these you have never seen in this lesson. If the rule is a rule, that does not matter. That is the whole point of learning a rule rather than a list. You have met dozens of describing words in this course and you can now build the matching word for how something is done out of every single one of them, including the ones nobody has taught you here. Find the word that describes a woman, say it, and put -ment on the end of it. If you cannot hear a consonant before the ending, you built it off the wrong form.
unseen.title: The rule works on words this lesson never showed you

examples.note: You met this one in the last lesson but one.
And this is the card you were given then.
Nobody had to teach you this. You built it.

alreadyE.body: Some of them already end in an e, so the woman form is the same word and there is nothing to change. The rule still ran. It just had nothing to do. rapide gives rapidement and facile gives facilement. This is not a second rule and it is worth being clear about that: the rule ran, it looked for the woman form, and the woman form was the word it started with. Treat it as an exception and you have two things to remember instead of one.
alreadyE.title: When step two changes nothing

examples.note: Rapide, and there was nothing to change.
Facile, same thing, same subject and same verb.
And this one, where there was.

theChain.body: The woman form is the plain one plus a consonant, and the word for how is the woman form plus a sound on the end. Nothing in the middle changes. lent becomes lente becomes lentement, doux becomes douce becomes doucement, sérieux becomes sérieuse becomes sérieusement. Say the feminine, then add -ment. A learner who goes straight from the plain form to the ending gets it right for the words that already end in an e and wrong for every other word in the language, and lesson 10 in A2 already gave them the step they are skipping.
theChain.title: Three steps, and the middle one is the one people skip

examples.note: Step one, and the t on the end of it makes no sound.
And step three, which keeps it.

notFromHer.body: And these two do not use the woman form at all. The ending on the adjective is taken off and replaced, so this is the one place in the lesson where the rule is not the answer. The ending on the describing word comes off and a different one goes on, so there is no point looking for the woman form here. It is the only place in this lesson where the rule you have just been given is not the answer, and it is worth knowing that it has a boundary.
notFromHer.title: The two that do not use the woman form

examples.note: And the word it gives. Nothing in between.
The same story with an a on the page.

theThreeOdd.body: Three of them are not built from anything. They are the three you will say most often, and they are the three the rule does not reach. bon gives bien, mauvais gives mal, vite comes from nothing at all. Bon goes with a thing and bien goes with what somebody does. English lets you say « he sings good » and be understood; French does not let you say it at all. There is no way to work any of these out and no reason to try. They are three words and you already know all three.
theThreeOdd.title: The three the rule does not reach

examples.note: Not bonnement. There is no such word.
This one has no describing word behind it at all.

afterTheVerb.body: The word for how goes after the verb. English puts it in front, and French never does. Out of 27,499 sentences in this course, 80 put it after the verb and 0 put it in front. There is no version of this you have to weigh up. The word goes after the verb, every time, and the only thing that makes it hard is that your first language will offer you the other order first. Lesson 21 in A1 wraps the verb in two words, and the word for how waits outside it: « Je ne mange pas souvent. »
afterTheVerb.title: Where it goes, and English disagrees

examples.note: Verb, then the word for how often.
Verb, then the same word. Somebody else wrote this sentence years ago.
And a long one, in exactly the same place.

twoSpellings.body: Two endings on the page and one sound in the mouth. One is spelled with an e and one with an a, and both of them come out as the same two syllables. évident ends -ent and gives évidemment, constant ends -ant and gives constamment. And these two do not use the woman form at all. The ending on the adjective is taken off and replaced, so this is the one place in the lesson where the rule is not the answer. So this is the one pair in the lesson where listening will not help you at all, and it is the reason two lines of the dictée are single words rather than sentences.
twoSpellings.title: One sound and two ways to write it

examples.note: Ends in -ant, and out loud that is the same ending.
And the word it gives, spelled with an e and said with an a.

youCanHearIt.body: That consonant is silent in the plain form and you say it in the long word. Build the long word off the wrong one and the mistake is a sound you can hear, not a spelling you cannot. lent has no t and lente does, doux has no s and douce does, sérieux has no z and sérieuse does. That is what makes this rule worth running rather than memorising: build the word off the wrong form and you have not made a spelling mistake, you have made a sound that is missing something, and you will hear it half a second after you say it. Your ear gets the front of the word. It does not get the ending, because every one of these ends the same way.
youCanHearIt.title: The consonant that comes back

examples.note: No s at the end of this one, whatever the page says.
And here it is. Say both out loud, one after the other.
The s is now in the middle of the word and it is the same s.

lessons.title: Les adverbes

drills.coach: Say each one out loud. The verb comes first and the word for how comes after it, every single time.
drills.title: Before or after

drills.q: Je ___ ici.
drills.why: The verb, then how.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The form for a woman is on the front. Say it out loud, listen to the consonant on the end, then say the long word.
drills.title: Say the middle one

drills.q: douce gives ___ .
drills.why: That consonant is silent in the plain form and you say it in the long word. Build the long word off the wrong one and the mistake is a sound you can hear, not a spelling you cannot.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Look for the ending. If the word does not have it, there was nothing to build it from.
drills.title: Built or not built

drills.q: Elle chante ___ .
drills.why: Three letters, and it is not built from anything.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: Ask what the word is describing. A day is a thing and singing is a doing, and French uses two different words for them.
drills.title: A thing or a doing

drills.q: Il travaille ___ .
drills.why: Bon goes with a thing and bien goes with what somebody does. English lets you say « he sings good » and be understood; French does not let you say it at all.
drills.title: One more time

drills.coach: The describing word is on the front. Its last three letters decide the spelling of the long word, and nothing you can hear does.
drills.title: e or a

drills.q: évident gives ___ .
drills.why: -ent gives -emment.
drills.title: One more time

sheets.title: Three steps, three exceptions, and one position

sections.title: The ones the rule does not reach

sections.body: The word for how goes after the verb. English puts it in front, and French never does. Out of 27,499 sentences in this course, 80 put it after the verb and 0 put it in front. Lesson 21 in A1 wraps the verb in two words, and the word for how waits outside it: « Je ne mange pas souvent. » In a past tense the short ones move, and that rule arrives with the tense in lesson 16 in A2. If you meet « j'ai bien mangé » before then, nothing here is wrong: it is a rule you have not been given yet.
sections.title: Where it goes

sections.body: Say the feminine, then add -ment. Find the word that describes a woman, say it, and put -ment on the end of it. If you cannot hear a consonant before the ending, you built it off the wrong form. That consonant is silent in the plain form and you say it in the long word. Build the long word off the wrong one and the mistake is a sound you can hear, not a spelling you cannot. lent has no t and lente does, doux has no s and douce does, sérieux has no z and sérieuse does. Two of these you have never seen in this lesson. If the rule is a rule, that does not matter. You can now do this to every describing word you have ever met in this course, and nobody has to give you the list.

questions.why: Not bonnement. There is no such word and there never has been.
accept: bien
Elle chante bien.
questions.answer: bien

questions.q: Il chante ___ .   (badly)
questions.why: Not mauvaisement. Three letters, and it is the opposite of the one above.
accept: mal
Il chante mal.
questions.answer: mal

questions.q: Fix this.
questions.why: The first one is built and the second one is not. There is no describing word behind the second, so there is nothing to build it from.
accept: Il parle rapidement et il court vite.
vite
questions.answer: Il parle rapidement et il court vite.
questions.prompt: Il parle rapidement et il court vitement.

questions.q: Which of these four is not a French word?
questions.why: Three of them are not built from anything. They are the three you will say most often, and they are the three the rule does not reach. bon gives bien, mauvais gives mal, vite comes from nothing at all.

questions.q: Listen. Which of these did you hear?
questions.say: Elle chante bien.
questions.why: Two of the three that are not built, in the same frame, and the difference is the whole word rather than an ending.

questions.q: Why are these three worth naming separately?
questions.why: Three of them are not built from anything. They are the three you will say most often, and they are the three the rule does not reach.
opts: Because they are the three you will say most often and the rule does not reach any of them
Because they only work with certain verbs

rounds.say: Six, and each one turns on whether the word is describing a thing or a doing.
rounds.label: A thing or a doing

questions.q: Fix this.
questions.why: Bon goes with a thing and bien goes with what somebody does. English lets you say « he sings good » and be understood; French does not let you say it at all. Singing is a doing.
accept: Elle chante bien.
bien
questions.answer: Elle chante bien.
questions.prompt: Elle chante bon.

questions.q: Fix this.
questions.why: Working is a doing too, and the same word goes with all of them.
accept: Il travaille bien.
bien
questions.answer: Il travaille bien.
questions.prompt: Il travaille bon.

questions.q: C'est un ___ jour.
questions.why: A day is a thing, so this one takes the describing word rather than the other one.
accept: bon
C'est un bon jour.
questions.answer: bon

questions.q: Which one goes with a doing?
questions.why: Bon goes with a thing and bien goes with what somebody does. English lets you say « he sings good » and be understood; French does not let you say it at all.

questions.q: Fix this.
questions.why: mauvais goes in front of a thing. For a doing it is the other word, and it is three letters long.
accept: Il chante mal.
mal
questions.answer: Il chante mal.
questions.prompt: Il chante mauvais.

questions.q: English lets you say « he sings good ». What does French do?
questions.why: Bon goes with a thing and bien goes with what somebody does. English lets you say « he sings good » and be understood; French does not let you say it at all.
opts: It does not allow it at all
It allows it after some verbs
It allows it in writing only

rounds.say: Six, and two of them ask for a letter your ear cannot give you.
rounds.label: All of it at once

questions.q: évident ends in -ent. Type the word for how.
questions.why: -ent gives -emment, and it is said as though it were spelled the other way. The woman form plays no part here.
accept: évidemment
questions.answer: évidemment

questions.q: constant ends in -ant. Type the word for how.
questions.why: -ant gives -amment. Same sound as the one above and a different letter on the page.
accept: constamment
questions.answer: constamment

questions.q: Which of these two is spelled correctly?
questions.why: The describing word ends -ent, so the ending is -emment. The last two options build it off the whole word, which is what the rule would tell you to do and it is wrong here.

questions.q: Il travaille ___ .   (sérieux)
questions.why: sérieuse plus the ending, and lesson 10 in A2 gave you the middle word.
accept: sérieusement
Il travaille sérieusement.
questions.answer: sérieusement

questions.q: Fix this.
questions.why: Built off the plain form, so the s never arrived. You would hear that it had not.
accept: Il parle doucement.
doucement
Elle parle doucement.
questions.answer: Elle parle doucement.
questions.prompt: Elle parle douxment.

questions.q: You are about to say how somebody does something and you have half a second. What do you say first, in your head?
questions.why: Say the feminine, then add -ment. Find the word that describes a woman, say it, and put -ment on the end of it. If you cannot hear a consonant before the ending, you built it off the wrong form.

sections.body: Say the feminine, then add -ment. Find the word that describes a woman, say it, and put -ment on the end of it. If you cannot hear a consonant before the ending, you built it off the wrong form.
sections.title: What You Can Do Now
points: The word for how goes after the verb. English puts it in front, and French never does. Out of 27,499 sentences in this course, 80 put it after the verb and 0 put it in front.

The woman form is the plain one plus a consonant, and the word for how is the woman form plus a sound on the end. Nothing in the middle changes. lent becomes lente becomes lentement, doux becomes douce becomes doucement, sérieux becomes sérieuse becomes sérieusement.

That consonant is silent in the plain form and you say it in the long word. Build the long word off the wrong one and the mistake is a sound you can hear, not a spelling you cannot. lent has no t and lente does, doux has no s and douce does, sérieux has no z and sérieuse does.
Lesson 10 in A2 said it first: The plain form tells you the other three. You have been building the middle step since then.

Three of them are not built from anything. They are the three you will say most often, and they are the three the rule does not reach. bon gives bien, mauvais gives mal, vite comes from nothing at all.

Two endings on the page and one sound in the mouth. One is spelled with an e and one with an a, and both of them come out as the same two syllables. évident ends -ent and gives évidemment, constant ends -ant and gives constamment. And these two do not use the woman form at all. The ending on the adjective is taken off and replaced, so this is the one place in the lesson where the rule is not the answer.
Some of them already end in an e, so the woman form is the same word and there is nothing to change. The rule still ran. It just had nothing to do.

In a past tense the short ones move, and that rule arrives with the tense in lesson 16 in A2. If you meet « j'ai bien mangé » before then, nothing here is wrong: it is a rule you have not been given yet. And when you want to say somebody does it BETTER than somebody else, that is lesson 32 in A2 and it is a long way off.
Lesson 21 in A1 owns the wrap and lesson 32 in A2 owns saying somebody does it better. Neither of them is this.

errorTriggers.description: Puts the word for how in front of the verb, which is where English puts it. It is not a slip: it is the learner's first language answering before they do, and it is the error the scene opens on.

Builds the word off the plain form rather than off the form for a woman, producing something with the right ending and a missing consonant. The learner who does this has the rule and has skipped its middle step.
Writes bonnement, mauvaisement or vitement. The learner is applying the rule they were just given, correctly, to three words it does not reach, and those three are the ones they will need most.
Puts the describing word after a verb, as in « elle chante bon ». English allows the equivalent in speech and French does not allow it at all, so the learner has no signal that anything went wrong.

Writes -amment where -emment belongs or the other way round. It is unhearable by construction: the two endings are one sound, so nothing in the learner's ear can settle it and only the describing word behind it can.

grammarAssumed: That a describing word changes shape to match what it describes, introduced in a1.13 through colour
The feminine -e on a describing word and the silent consonant it makes audible, introduced in a1.14
Adjective agreement as a system of inflectional classes, and the -eux class whose feminine is -euse, introduced in a2.03
The pre-vocalic masculine and the four-form grid it completes, introduced in a2.16
Standard negation with ne… pas around a finite verb, introduced in a1.18
The present of regular -er verbs and of the common irregulars, introduced in a2.01, a2.02 and a2.12
That a final consonant is silent unless a following -e makes it audible, introduced in sons.06
grammarIntroduced: The derivation of manner adverbs by suffixation of -ment to the feminine singular of the adjective, as a productive rule rather than as a list
That the derivation is PHONOLOGICALLY motivated as well as orthographic: the feminine consonant the masculine leaves unrealised is realised in the adverb, so the base is audible in the derivative
That an adjective whose masculine already ends in -e has a null feminine alternation, so the rule applies vacuously rather than being suspended
The suppletive adverbs bien and mal for bon and mauvais, and vite as an adverb with no adjectival base at all
The categorial distinction between an adjective modifying a noun and an adverb modifying a verb, which English neutralises in colloquial speech
The -ent/-ant class, whose adverbs are -emment and -amment by ending replacement rather than by suffixation to the feminine, and which are homophonous at /amɑ̃/
Post-verbal placement of the manner adverb in a simple tense, and its position outside the discontinuous negative morpheme
That placement in a compound tense is DEFERRED to a2.05, named on the learner surface rather than left silent

acts.title: Le camion de huit heures

opener.line: Une phrase correcte, et le camion arrive le mauvais jour : voilà ce que coûte un radical. EN: A correct sentence and the truck comes on the wrong day: that is what a stem costs.

acts.milestone: Tu sais reconnaître un radical qui refuse l'infinitif, et tu sais qu'il y en a une vingtaine. EN: You can spot a stem that refuses the infinitive, and you know there are about twenty.

acts.title: Les six grands

opener.line: Six verbes portent la moitié de tout ce que tu diras au futur : commence par eux. EN: Six verbs carry half of everything you will say in the future: start with them.

acts.milestone: Tu construis être, avoir, aller, faire, venir et vouloir au futur, aux six personnes. EN: You can build the six big verbs in the future, on all six persons.

acts.title: La famille en -rr-

opener.line: Tu écriras deux r et tu n'en entendras qu'un : ici, c'est la main qui apprend, pas l'oreille. EN: You will write two r and hear one: here it is the hand that learns.

acts.milestone: Tu écris pourrai, verrai, enverrai, courrai et mourrai avec leurs deux r. EN: You write the five double-r stems correctly.

acts.title: La famille en -dr-

opener.line: Cinq verbes font apparaître un d qui n'est dans aucun infinitif : apprends-les ensemble. EN: Five verbs grow a d that is in no infinitive: learn them together.

acts.milestone: Tu construis viendr-, tiendr-, vaudr-, faudr- et voudr- sans chercher le d. EN: You build the five -dr- stems without hunting for the d.

acts.title: Les verbes en -oir

opener.line: Quatre verbes perdent la moitié de leur nom au futur : enlève le -oi- et tu as le radical. EN: Four verbs lose half their name: take out the -oi- and you have the stem.

acts.milestone: Tu construis saur-, devr-, recevr- et pleuvr- en enlevant le -oi- sans hésiter. EN: You build the four -oir stems by taking the -oi- out.

acts.title: Les impersonnels

opener.line: Il pleuvra, il faudra, il y aura : six formes que tu ne conjugueras jamais, et qui servent tous les jours. EN: Six forms you will never conjugate, and that you will use every day.

acts.milestone: Tu annonces la météo, un besoin et une foule sans inventer de sujet. EN: You announce weather, a need and a crowd without inventing a subject.

acts.title: Les composés

opener.line: Un préfixe devant un verbe que tu connais, et tu gagnes cinq verbes sans rien apprendre. EN: A prefix on a verb you already know, and you gain five verbs for nothing.

acts.milestone: Tu conjugues revenir, devenir, obtenir, refaire et revoir, et tu connais l’exception. EN: You conjugate the five compounds and you know the exception.

acts.title: Les fins ne bougent pas

opener.line: Vingt radicaux appris, et pas une seule terminaison nouvelle : voilà ce que cette leçon t'a vraiment coûté. EN: Twenty stems learnt and not one new ending: that is the real price.

acts.milestone: Tu poses les six terminaisons sur n’importe quel radical, et tu vérifies le r avant la fin. EN: You put the six endings on any stem and check the r before them.

acts.title: Futur ou imparfait

opener.line: Tu viens de passer quatre leçons au passé : voilà comment ton oreille séparera les deux temps sans effort. EN: After four lessons in the past, here is how your ear will keep the two apart.

acts.milestone: Tu entends la différence entre je serai et j’étais dès la première syllabe. EN: You hear the difference at the first syllable.

acts.title: De vraies prédictions

opener.line: Un futur dans un message, ce n'est presque jamais une prédiction : c'est ta parole. EN: A future in a message is almost never a prediction: it is your word.

acts.milestone: Tu promets, tu annonces et tu refuses au futur, avec les bons radicaux. EN: You promise, announce and decline in the future, with the right stems.

acts.title: Tout ensemble

opener.line: Un modèle à imiter, tes propres cinq ans à écrire, puis l’examen des vingt radicaux. EN: A model to imitate, your own five years to write, then the exam on the twenty stems.

acts.milestone: Tu as écrit tes cinq prochaines années et passé les dix séries de l’examen. EN: You wrote your next five years and sat the ten rounds.

recorded.desc: Yannick's two lines, ONE TAKE, a Québécois voice, at a counter. Businesslike and slightly rushed: he is booking a slot, not making conversation. No stress on « aura ».

Sarah's message read as a voice note, ONE TAKE, one female voice, at dictation pace. Every future verb gets the same weight as the words around it: the learner has to find them, not be told where they are.
Léa and a colleague in a Geneva office, one take, two voices, ordinary Friday-afternoon pace. The six irregular stems are read flat, with no emphasis on any of them.
The seven cards of the big six, one take per card. « je serai » and « j’aurai » are short and unstressed.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in authored order, at conversational speed. The lines are hidden on screen, so nothing may be clarified for the microphone.
The audio step plays each card's fr, the CORRECT form. The promptSound lines are never spoken: they are words that do not exist and must not be given a pronunciation.
Two colleagues in a Brussels agency at the end of the day, one take, two voices. Slightly tired, friendly, never dramatic.
The six double-r cards, one take per card. CRITICAL: read the single r. « je pourrai » has one /ʁ/, and a reader who lengthens it teaches the opposite of the card.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in order. The whole point is that the doubled r is inaudible, so no line may be over-articulated.
A mechanic and a customer in a Lyon garage, one take, two voices. Matter-of-fact, no upselling tone: the estimate is just an estimate.
The six -dr- cards, one take per card. Here the d IS pronounced and must be audible, in deliberate contrast with the double r of the previous act.
Eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in order, natural pace.
The audio step plays each card's fr only. The promptSound forms do not exist and are never spoken.
The training letter read as a voice note, ONE TAKE, one voice, at dictation pace. The four -oir futures (recevrez, devrez, saurez, pourront) get no extra weight: the learner has to find them.
The five -oir cards, one take per card. « je saurai » is two syllables and must not be stretched into three.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in authored order, at conversational speed. The lines are hidden on screen.
Two neighbours in a Montreal kitchen, one take, two voices, relaxed Thursday-evening pace. The six impersonals are read as ordinary speech, never as a weather bulletin.
The six impersonal cards, one take per card. « il y aura » is three words run together, /i.lja.ʁa/, and must not be separated for clarity.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in order. Line 4 is negative and the ne is elided as in normal speech.
The audio step plays each card's fr only. « nous faudrons » and « nous pleuvrons » are not French and are never spoken.
A leaving party in a Nantes office, one take, two voices, a little noise behind. Warm, slightly loud, never sentimental.
The six compound cards, one take per card. The prefix is unstressed: « je reviendrai » has its stress on the last syllable, not on the re-.
Eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in order. Line 7 (prévoirons) and line 6 (reverra) must be read at the same pace: the contrast is in the vowels, not in the delivery.
The trip programme read as an announcement to a group, ONE TAKE, one voice, unhurried. Every person of the verb is given equal weight, because the mission is about the endings.
The five endings cards, one take per card. On the third card, the r of se-r-ons, pour-r-ons and dev-r-ons must be audible in all three.
The audio step plays each card's fr only. The promptSound forms (je seré, nous aurront, ils feronts) are misspellings and are never spoken.
Two colleagues on a Lausanne platform, one take, two voices, with a little station noise. The imparfait and future forms alternate and must be read flat: the contrast is lexical, not performed.
The six pair cards, one take per card. CRITICAL: read both halves of each pair with the SAME intonation. A reader who marks one as odd teaches the opposite of the card.
REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: eight lines, ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, in order, alternating tenses without any signal that they alternate.
The audio step plays each card's fr, the CORRECT sentence. The promptSound lines are grammatical French about the wrong day, so they are never spoken here.
The local-news piece read as a radio item, ONE TAKE, one voice, news pace. The quoted line from the committee president keeps the same voice, with a slight change of tone.
The five prediction cards, one take per card. The promise card is warm, the forecast card is neutral, the refusal card is apologetic but not grovelling.
Eight short messages, ONE TAKE, one voice, as if read aloud from a phone. Lines 1 and 5 are warm, lines 2 and 6 are flat.
The model text read as a voice note, ONE TAKE, one female voice, unhurried and a little hesitant where the text hesitates. The learner will imitate this, so the delivery is the model too.

lessons.intro: You can already build the future of almost any French verb: take the infinitive, add the ending. About twenty verbs refuse that, and they are the ones you use most. être becomes ser-, avoir becomes aur-, aller becomes ir-. This lesson gives you those stems in five small families rather than one long list, and it keeps saying the thing that makes them cheap: the six endings never change.

fin.body: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Ce sont les six terminaisons du futur, sur tous les verbes de la langue. Régulier ou irrégulier, tu ne changes jamais cette moitié du mot. Le radical change, la fin ne change jamais. EN: six endings, on every verb in the language, and you never change them.
fin.title: Les six mêmes terminaisons

examples.note: les six, sur une seule carte

compose.body: revenir, devenir, obtenir, retenir, refaire, revoir : un préfixe devant un verbe que tu connais déjà. Le radical ne change pas, tu colles seulement le préfixe devant. Un radical appris, cinq verbes gagnés. EN: a prefix on a verb you already have; the stem is unchanged.
compose.title: Le préfixe est gratuit

famille.body: Vingt radicaux appris un par un, c'est une liste. Groupés, ce sont cinq petites familles : les six grands, les -rr-, les -dr-, les -oir et les composés. Tu retiens la famille, puis les verbes dedans. EN: five small families instead of one long list.
famille.title: Par groupes, pas en liste

oreille.body: je serai et j'étais n'ont pas un son en commun ; j'aurai et j'avais non plus. Le futur et l'imparfait des mêmes verbes prennent des radicaux complètement différents, alors l'oreille tranche tout de suite. EN: the two tenses take different stems, so the ear decides at once.
oreille.title: Deux radicaux, zéro confusion

examples.note: les deux radicaux, côte à côte

radical.body: Le radical, c'est le début du mot, avant la terminaison. Pour la plupart des verbes, c'est l'infinitif entier. Pour une vingtaine de verbes très courants, c'est autre chose, et il faut le connaître. Chaque radical du futur finit par un r. EN: the stem is the front of the word; for about twenty common verbs it is not the infinitive.
radical.title: La partie qui bouge

examples.note: et ici, le radical EST l'infinitif

double-r.body: pourr-, verr-, enverr-, courr-, mourr- : deux r à l'écrit, un seul r à l'oreille. Personne n'entend la différence entre je pourrai et une forme à un seul r. C'est un point d'orthographe, et il se teste en écrivant. EN: two written r, one spoken r, so this is tested in writing.
double-r.title: Deux r, un seul son

promesse.body: Quand tu dis je serai là, je t'enverrai ça, je te tiendrai au courant, tu ne décris pas l'avenir : tu prends un engagement. C'est l'emploi le plus fréquent du futur dans un message. EN: in a message the future is usually a commitment, not a description.
promesse.title: Ce que tu engages

infinitif.body: Pour la plupart des verbes, le radical du futur EST l'infinitif : parler donne parlerai. Ton réflexe est donc de coller la terminaison derrière l'infinitif. Sur ces vingt verbes, ce réflexe donne une forme que personne ne dit. EN: the instinct is right most of the time and wrong on these twenty verbs.
infinitif.title: Le réflexe qu'il faut couper

prediction.body: Le colis arrivera jeudi, il pleuvra toute la semaine, les prix augmenteront : tu annonces quelque chose que tu ne contrôles pas. Ni promesse ni plan : une prévision. EN: an announcement about something you do not control.
prediction.title: Ce que tu annonces

impersonnel.body: il faudra, il y aura, il pleuvra, il vaudra mieux : ces verbes n'ont qu'une personne. Le il ne désigne personne, il tient juste la place du sujet. Tu ne diras jamais nous faudrons. EN: these verbs have one person only, and the il stands for nobody.
impersonnel.title: Un seul sujet, il

lessons.title: Le futur simple : les radicaux irréguliers

drills.coach: Une carte, un radical. Le radical change, la fin ne change jamais. EN: The stem changes; the ending never does.
drills.title: Les six grands

drills.q: Tu écris le futur de envoyer. EN: Write the future of envoyer.
drills.why: enverr-, avec deux r. EN: enverr-, two r.
drills.coach: Le son ne te dira rien. Regarde le radical. EN: the sound will not help; look at the stem.
drills.title: Un r ou deux

drills.coach: Deux tas : le d arrive, ou il n’arrive pas. EN: two piles: the d comes, or it does not.
drills.title: Le d qui apparaît

drills.q: Le futur de savoir, première personne. EN: The future of savoir, je.
drills.why: saur-. Le -oi- disparaît. EN: the -oi- vanishes.
drills.coach: savoir, devoir, recevoir, pleuvoir : enlève le -oi-. EN: take the -oi- out.
drills.title: Le -oi- qui part

drills.coach: Lis la carte et dis la phrase entière, avec son il. EN: say the whole line, with its il.
drills.title: Un seul sujet

drills.q: obtenir se conjugue comme : EN: obtenir behaves like:
drills.why: obtiendr-, exactement comme tiendr-. EN: exactly like tenir.
drills.coach: Trouve le verbe simple sous le composé. EN: find the simple verb underneath.
drills.title: Le préfixe est gratuit

drills.coach: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont. Le radical change, la fin ne change jamais. EN: The stem changes; the ending never does.
drills.title: Les six fins

drills.coach: Deux tas. Demain, ou hier. EN: two piles: tomorrow, or yesterday.
drills.title: Futur ou imparfait

drills.q: « Je te tiendrai au courant. » C’est : EN: This is:
drills.why: Tu t’engages. EN: you are committing.
drills.coach: Est-ce que tu t’engages, ou est-ce que tu annonces. EN: are you committing, or announcing.
drills.title: Promettre ou annoncer

drills.coach: Une carte, une famille. Chaque radical du futur finit par un r. EN: Every future stem ends in an r.
drills.title: Les vingt radicaux

sections.body: Le radical change, la fin ne change jamais. Pour chaque verbe, la colonne « radical » est la seule chose à apprendre : les terminaisons -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont se posent derrière sans jamais changer. Chaque radical du futur finit par un r. Si tu as construit une forme et qu'il n'y a pas de r avant la terminaison, la forme est fausse. Les composés de la dernière ligne viennent gratuitement avec leur verbe simple. EN: The stem changes; the ending never does. The stem column is the only thing to learn, and every stem ends in r.
sections.title: Comment lire cette page
Les six terminaisons, sur tous les verbes

sections.body: La famille en -rr- double un r que tu n'entendras jamais : pouvoir, voir, envoyer, courir, mourir. La famille en -dr- fait apparaître un d qui n'est dans aucun infinitif : venir, tenir, valoir, falloir, vouloir. La famille en -oir perd son -oi- : savoir, devoir, recevoir, pleuvoir. Deux verbes sont dans deux familles à la fois, parce qu'ils perdent leur -oir ET gagnent un d : vouloir et valoir. EN: three families, three moves, and two verbs belong to two of them.
sections.title: Trois familles, trois gestes

rows: être, avoir, aller, faire, venir, vouloir
sections.title: Ce que fait chaque famille

sections.body: il faudra, il y aura, il fera, il pleuvra, il neigera, il vaudra mieux : dans toutes ces phrases, le il ne remplace personne. Il tient la place du sujet, parce qu'une phrase française en veut un. Ces verbes n'ont donc qu'une seule forme au futur, et tu n'auras jamais à choisir la personne. « Ça ira » marche pareil avec ça. EN: the il stands for nobody and these verbs have one form only.
sections.title: Un sujet qui ne désigne personne

rows: Il y aura du monde au marché.
Il fera nuit avant six heures.
Il pleuvra sur toute la région.
sections.title: Les impersonnels les plus utiles

sections.body: Un composé est un préfixe collé devant un verbe que tu connais : re-venir, de-venir, ob-tenir, re-tenir, re-faire, re-voir. Le préfixe ne touche pas au radical. Si tu sais dire « je viendrai », tu sais déjà dire « je reviendrai » et « je deviendrai ». C'est le meilleur rapport entre ce que tu apprends et ce que tu peux dire. Une seule exception compte : prévoir garde son -oi- au futur, alors que revoir ne le garde pas. EN: the prefix never touches the stem, and prévoir is the one exception.
sections.title: Un radical appris, cinq verbes gagnés

sections.body: Le futur et l'imparfait des mêmes verbes ne se ressemblent pas du tout, parce qu'ils partent de deux radicaux différents. « Pars de nous, coupe -ons, ajoute la fin. » construit l'imparfait ; le futur, lui, prend le radical de cette leçon. Résultat : je serai et j'étais n'ont pas une lettre en commun, et l'oreille tranche dès la première syllabe. C'est l'un des rares endroits de la grammaire française où deux temps sont impossibles à confondre. EN: the two tenses take different stems, so the ear decides at the first syllable.

overview.introFr: Tu sais déjà construire le futur de presque tous les verbes. Une vingtaine refusent la recette, et ce sont ceux que tu utilises le plus. être donne ser-, avoir donne aur-, aller donne ir-. Cinq petites familles au lieu d'une longue liste, et une bonne nouvelle : les six terminaisons ne changent jamais.

sections.say: Lis d'abord. La règle vient après. Le radical change, la fin ne change jamais.
sections.text: Salut, voici le plan pour jeudi. Le camion arrivera à huit heures devant le 42. Je serai là avant, avec le café. J'aurai les clés de l'ancien et du nouveau, alors ne t'inquiète pas pour ça. Mon frère viendra vers neuf heures, il pourra porter les choses lourdes. Vers midi, il faudra sortir de l'ancien appartement, parce que les nouveaux locataires arrivent à treize heures. On ira manger un morceau au coin de la rue, ça ne prendra pas longtemps. L'après-midi, nous serons quatre, donc nous irons plus vite. Je t'enverrai l'adresse exacte ce soir. S'il pleut, on verra sur place : mon frère a une bâche. Tu sauras tout ce soir. Et je te préviens tout de suite : tu auras mal au dos vendredi. Mais samedi, tout sera rangé et on fera une vraie pause. Bises.

sections.say: Lis d'abord. La règle vient après. Le radical change, la fin ne change jamais.
sections.text: Bonjour, voici comment la formation se passera. Vous recevrez le programme complet lundi prochain, par courriel. Vous devrez choisir deux ateliers sur les six proposés, et vous saurez le jeudi si vos choix sont acceptés. Le nombre de places est limité, et il faudra répondre vite. Les cours du matin commencent à neuf heures. Ceux qui viennent de loin pourront suivre la première semaine en ligne : nous enverrons les liens la veille. À la fin du mois, vous recevrez une attestation. Elle ne vaudra pas un diplôme, mais elle prouvera que vous avez suivi les quarante heures. Une dernière chose : la sortie de terrain du douze aura lieu par tous les temps. Il pleuvra peut-être ce jour-là, alors prévoyez des bottes.
sections.title: La lettre de la formation

glossary.note: Un cours court, en petit groupe, sur un sujet précis.
Un papier qui prouve que tu étais là. Ce n’est pas un diplôme.
La veille du douze, c’est le onze.
Une journée de cours dehors, sur le lieu du travail.
Qu’il pleuve ou qu’il fasse beau, ça se fait.
Des chaussures hautes, pour la boue ou la neige.
